fields.title: Topic 3: Compile, Runtime, Link & Logic Errors
fields.content:
Topic 3

Compile, Runtime, Link & Logic Errors

In firmware development, bugs do not merely manifest as crash popups or error logs; they can cause frozen microcontrollers, scrambled motor drive PWM signals, silent memory corruption, or hardware damage. Understanding the lifecycle stage at which an error occurs—whether caught by the preprocessor/compiler, flagged during linking, triggered as a CPU fault at runtime, or hiding as a subtle logic race condition—is critical to diagnostic efficiency.

A skilled embedded engineer builds a mental model of the error taxonomy, transforming cryptic compiler warnings and catastrophic ARM Cortex-M HardFault exceptions into actionable root-cause investigations.

3.1 Taxonomy of Firmware Defects

Firmware defects are classified into four distinct operational categories based on where in the software engineering pipeline they are discovered.

Defect Class Detection Phase Typical Root Causes Detection Tool
Compile-Time Errors Translation / Compilation Syntax errors, missing semicolons, type mismatches, macro redefinitions, static assertion failures. gcc -Wall -Wextra -Werror
Link-Time Errors Object Linking Undefined symbol references (undefined reference to `foo`), multiple symbol definitions, memory region overflow (SRAM/Flash full). ld / Linker Map file
Runtime Faults Target Silicon Execution Null-pointer dereferences, stack overflows, unaligned memory access, division by zero, bus/memory faults. HardFault_Handler, GDB, SWD probe
Logic & Concurrency Errors Target Silicon Execution Off-by-one loop boundaries, interrupt race conditions, missing volatile on ISR flags, deadlocks. Unit tests, Logic Analyzers, ITM tracing

3.2 Linker Errors: Demystifying Common Linker Failures

Because C compilation operates strictly on individual translation units (.c files), the compiler only verifies that function declarations exist. The linker is responsible for knitting object files together and assigning physical addresses. The two most common linker traps are:

1. Undefined Reference (undefined reference to `foo`)

This occurs when a header file declares a function prototype extern void foo(void); and code calls it, but the object file containing the definition foo.o was omitted from the linker command line or Makefile.

2. Multiple Definition of Symbol (multiple definition of `bar`)

A catastrophic mistake in C is placing variable definitions inside a header file without the extern qualifier: 

/* IN config.h -- WRONG: Generates duplicate definitions in every .c file that includes it! */
uint32_t system_baud_rate = 115200;

/* IN config.h -- CORRECT: Declaration only */
extern uint32_t system_baud_rate;

/* IN config.c -- CORRECT: Single definition in exactly one compilation unit */
uint32_t system_baud_rate = 115200;
Program 3.1: Proper Header File Extern Declaration Pattern

3.3 Runtime Undefined Behavior (UB) & Hardware Faults

In C, Undefined Behavior (UB) refers to code executions where the ISO standard imposes no requirements. The compiler optimizer is legally permitted to assume that undefined behavior never occurs, leading to silent instruction elimination, infinite loops, or unpredictable processor traps.

Figure 3.1: Hardware Fault Escalation Hierarchy in ARM Cortex-M Processors
Key ARM Cortex-M Fault Registers:
  • CFSR (Configurable Fault Status Register): Combines MemManage, BusFault, and UsageFault flags. Pinpoints divide-by-zero or unaligned memory traps.
  • HFSR (HardFault Status Register): Indicates if a configurable fault escalated due to lack of handler or priority lockup.
  • BFAR (BusFault Address Register): Holds the exact 32-bit physical address that triggered an AHB/APB bus violation.
Real World Example: In 2010, Toyota experienced unintended acceleration investigations involving electronic throttle control firmware. Embedded safety audits highlighted the catastrophic danger of stack overflow into global memory and unhandled pointer errors. When the call stack collides with global variables in RAM, memory is silently overwritten, corrupting throttle angle setpoints without throwing an explicit compile error.

3.4 Hands-On Code Implementations

The following production C handler intercepts ARM Cortex-M HardFault exceptions, extracts the stacked CPU register frame, and logs the instruction address (Program Counter) that triggered the crash before invoking safe system reset. 

/**
 * Program 3.2: Cortex-M HardFault Diagnostic Frame Extractor
 * File: hardfault_handler.c
 * Target: ARM Cortex-M3 / M4 / M7
 */

#include <stdint.h>
#include <stdio.h>

/* Stacked exception frame layout pushed by ARM hardware onto MSP or PSP */
typedef struct {
    uint32_t r0;
    uint32_t r1;
    uint32_t r2;
    uint32_t r3;
    uint32_t r12;
    uint32_t lr;   /*!< Link Register (Return Address) */
    uint32_t pc;   /*!< Program Counter (Faulting Instruction!) */
    uint32_t psr;  /*!< Program Status Register */
} ExceptionStackFrame_t;

/* System Control Block Configurable Fault Status Register (CFSR) Address */
#define SCB_CFSR  (*(volatile uint32_t *)0xE000ED28UL)
#define SCB_HFSR  (*(volatile uint32_t *)0xE000ED2CUL)
#define SCB_BFAR  (*(volatile uint32_t *)0xE000ED38UL)

/**
 * @brief C-level HardFault decoder invoked from assembly stub.
 * @param[in] stack_frame Pointer to register context captured at time of fault.
 */
void HardFault_Decoder_C(const ExceptionStackFrame_t * const stack_frame) {
    /* Safe capture of fault diagnostic context */
    const uint32_t faulting_pc  = stack_frame->pc;
    const uint32_t faulting_lr  = stack_frame->lr;
    const uint32_t cfsr_val     = SCB_CFSR;
    const uint32_t hfsr_val     = SCB_HFSR;

    /* Print diagnostics to SWD ITM or non-volatile crash log buffer */
    printf("\n!!! HARDWARE HARDFAULT EXCEPTION DETECTED !!!\n");
    printf("Faulting PC  : 0x%08lX\n", (unsigned long)faulting_pc);
    printf("Return LR    : 0x%08lX\n", (unsigned long)faulting_lr);
    printf("SCB->CFSR    : 0x%08lX\n", (unsigned long)cfsr_val);
    printf("SCB->HFSR    : 0x%08lX\n", (unsigned long)hfsr_val);

    if (cfsr_val & (1UL << 25)) {
        printf("Cause: Divide-by-zero UsageFault attempted!\n");
    }
    if (cfsr_val & (1UL << 24)) {
        printf("Cause: Unaligned memory access attempted!\n");
    }
    if (cfsr_val & (1UL << 15)) {
        printf("BusFault Address: 0x%08lX\n", (unsigned long)SCB_BFAR);
    }

    /* In production: flush non-volatile flight log, disable actuators, and reset */
    while (1) {
        /* Hang in debugger or trigger Watchdog reset */
    }
}
Program 3.2: Cortex-M HardFault Diagnostic Frame Extractor in C

3.5 Buggy vs. Modern Safe Code Comparison

A subtle and prevalent logic error occurs when unsigned integer promotion interacts with loop termination conditions, producing an inadvertent infinite loop that never terminates.

View Buggy/Legacy Code

Because i is an unsigned 8-bit integer (uint8_t), the condition i >= 0 is always true! When i reaches 0, the next decrement wraps around to 255: 

/* BUGGY: Infinite loop due to unsigned integer underflow */
void transmit_buffer_reverse(const uint8_t *buf, uint8_t len) {
    uint8_t i;
    /* When i is 0, i-- wraps to 255. The loop condition (i >= 0) is NEVER false! */
    for (i = len - 1; i >= 0; i--) {
        uart_send_byte(buf[i]); /* Out of bounds access when i wraps! */
    }
}
Program 3.3-A: Infinite Loop Caused by Unsigned Type Underflow

Here is the safe modern implementation. By using a pre-decrement loop idiom or standard signed types, the loop terminates reliably at zero without relying on signed underflow: 

/* SAFE / PRODUCTION-GRADE: Pre-decrement loop idiom or size_t */
#include <stdint.h>
#include <stddef.h>

void transmit_buffer_reverse(const uint8_t * const buf, const size_t len) {
    if ((buf == NULL) || (len == 0U)) {
        return;
    }

    size_t i = len;
    while (i > 0U) {
        --i; /* Safely decrements from (len - 1) down to 0 */
        uart_send_byte(buf[i]);
    }
}
Program 3.3-B: Safe Reverse Buffer Traversal Idiom

Topic Quiz (10 Questions)

Test your ability to diagnose compile, link, runtime, and concurrency bugs.

1. What toolchain stage is responsible for reporting 'multiple definition of symbol' errors?
  • The Preprocessor (cpp)
  • The C Compiler (cc1)
  • The Linker (ld)
  • The Hardware Debugger (gdb)
The compiler checks symbols within a single file; only the linker resolves global symbols across multiple object files, catching duplicates.
2. Why does the compiler flag: 'warning: comparison is always true due to limited range of data type' on 'uint8_t i; if (i >= 0)'?
  • uint8_t cannot be compared to literals.
  • Unsigned integers can never be negative; any value from 0 to 255 is inherently >= 0.
  • The variable is in Flash memory.
  • i must be cast to a float first.
Unsigned types have a minimum value of 0. Checking if an unsigned integer is >= 0 is tautologically true, signaling a loop logic defect.
3. What is an 'undefined reference' linker error typically caused by?
  • A syntax error in a macro.
  • A function or variable is declared in a header, but the object file containing its definition was not provided to the linker.
  • A divide-by-zero in main().
  • A missing semicolon after a struct definition.
An undefined reference occurs when the linker searches all input object files and libraries but finds no address assigned to the requested symbol.
4. Which ARM Cortex-M hardware exception is triggered when code attempts an unaligned memory access with unaligned traps enabled?
  • SysTick Exception
  • UsageFault
  • NMI (Non-Maskable Interrupt)
  • PendSV Exception
UsageFault handles program errors such as executing undefined instructions, unaligned memory accesses, and division by zero.
5. What happens during a stack overflow in a bare-metal microcontroller without an MPU (Memory Protection Unit)?
  • The OS displays a blue screen.
  • The stack pointer grows downward past its allocated boundary, silently overwriting global variables or heap data in SRAM.
  • The CPU immediately halts clock cycles.
  • The linker refuses to flash the board.
Without hardware memory protection (MPU), stack growth beyond bounds silently corrupts neighboring global data (.data/.bss), causing unpredictable erratic behavior.
6. What is the danger of modifying a shared variable inside an Interrupt Service Routine (ISR) without the 'volatile' keyword?
  • The ISR will refuse to fire.
  • The main loop thread may cache the variable in a CPU register and never observe changes made by the ISR.
  • The variable will be stored in ROM.
  • The variable will overflow on every tick.
The compiler optimizes loops by caching variables in registers unless 'volatile' instructs it that external events (like ISRs) can alter memory asynchronously.
7. In C, what is the consequence of reading an uninitialized local variable?
  • The variable is guaranteed to be 0 by the standard.
  • It invokes Undefined Behavior; the variable contains whatever garbage was previously on the stack frame.
  • The compiler automatically triggers a hard fault.
  • The variable is allocated in the .bss section.
Local automatic stack variables are not zero-initialized by the C runtime. Reading them reads leftover stack garbage and constitutes undefined behavior.
8. What is a 'race condition' between a main superloop and a timer ISR?
  • A test to see which thread runs faster.
  • When an interrupt preempts the main loop in the middle of a non-atomic multi-byte read or write, leaving shared data in an inconsistent state.
  • When the CPU clock frequency exceeds the crystal oscillator rating.
  • When the linker script overlaps Flash and RAM.
Updating a 32-bit integer on an 8-bit MCU or updating multi-field structs non-atomically allows an ISR to interleave, reading half-updated corrupted data.
9. Which compiler flag instructs GCC to treat all warnings as fatal compilation errors?
  • -Wall
  • -Wextra
  • -Werror
  • -O3
-Werror turns all compiler warnings into build-halting errors, preventing developers from ignoring diagnostic warnings.
10. In an ARM Cortex-M stacked exception frame, which stacked register holds the exact instruction address where the fault occurred?
  • R0
  • LR (Link Register)
  • PC (Program Counter)
  • SP (Stack Pointer)
The hardware exception mechanism pushes PC (Program Counter) at offset +24 in the exception frame, recording the precise address of the faulting instruction.

Hands-On Assignments

Execute these 5 laboratory assignments to master defect identification and error recovery.

Assignment 1: Intentional Linker Error Reproduction

Task: Create a multi-file project with main.c, math.c, and math.h. Deliberately define a global variable int sensor_data = 10; in math.h without extern. Include math.h in both main.c and math.c. Build with GCC and document the exact linker error. Then fix it using extern.

Assignment 2: The Stack Smashing Canary Lab

Task: Write a function with a local buffer: uint8_t buffer[8];. Write a loop that writes 16 bytes into this buffer. Compile with GCC flag -fstack-protector-all. Run the program and observe the runtime abort triggered by the compiler's canary check mechanism.

Assignment 3: Unaligned Access Fault Trigger and Recovery

Task: Create a byte buffer in RAM. Cast an odd byte address (e.g. &buffer[1]) into a uint32_t * pointer and attempt a 32-bit write. On an ARM Cortex-M with the unaligned trap bit enabled in the CCR (Configuration and Control Register), verify that this generates a UsageFault and decode the stacked PC in GDB.

Assignment 4: Non-Atomic ISR Race Condition Simulation

Task: Write a program where a simulated 64-bit millisecond timestamp variable is incremented in an ISR. In the main loop, continuously read the timestamp and verify that the lower 32 bits never decrement relative to the upper 32 bits. Demonstrate how reading without a critical section produces temporary backward time jumps.

Assignment 5: Memory Section Overflow Detection

Task: Create an embedded project with a linker script allocating 16 KB of SRAM. Declare a static array consuming 18 KB of RAM. Run the linker and examine the error message. Inspect the generated linker map file (-Wl,-Map=output.map) to see how sections are arranged and where the boundary overflow occurred.

Official References, Research Papers & Standards

Deepen your engineering foundation with canonical publications and official standard specifications:

ARM Architecture Manual ARM Ltd.

ARMv7-M Architecture Reference Manual

Detailed architectural definitions of Cortex-M fault status registers, exception stacking frames, and bus fault handling.

View Official Resource →
Standard Guidelines SEI CERT

SEI CERT C Coding Standard

Rules for developing safe, reliable, and secure systems in the C programming language, focusing on undefined behavior avoidance.

View Official Resource →
Engineering Guide Joseph Yiu

The Definitive Guide to ARM Cortex-M3 and Cortex-M4

In-depth coverage of hardware fault analysis, register decoding, and HardFault exception handlers.

fields.title: Day 5: Timers, PWM & Real-Time Clocks
fields.content:
Session 1.4

Day 5: Timers, PWM & Real-Time Clocks

Problem Statement: Software delay loops burn 100% CPU time, drift with compiler optimizations, and break when interrupts fire. Hardware timers provide microsecond-accurate timekeeping, generate complex Pulse Width Modulation (PWM) waveforms, and measure incoming sensor pulses with zero CPU intervention. How do you master hardware timer peripherals, PWM, and Real-Time Clock calendars?
📋 Daily Plan & Learning Architecture
Session 1.4 Module 1: Embedded C Foundations Estimated: 3.5 hrs

🎯 Today's Mission & Relevance

  • Master general-purpose timer prescalers, auto-reload registers, and counter modes.
  • Generate precise hardware PWM waveforms for LED dimming, motor speed, and servos.
  • Implement Input Capture pulse measurement and battery-backed RTC calendars.

📐 Theoretical Milestones

  • Prescaler and Auto-Reload frequency equations ($f = \frac{f_{clk}}{(PSC+1)(ARR+1)}$).
  • Edge-aligned vs. Center-aligned PWM harmonics and duty cycle math.
  • Input Capture edge-latching and 32.768 kHz RTC quartz divider architectures.

💻 Hands-On Blueprint

  • Program 5.1: Periodic 1.0 Hz timer interrupt driver via TIM2.
  • Program 5.2: 1 kHz hardware PWM generator driving a breathing LED on PA6.
  • Program 5.3: 50 Hz RC servo motor angular positioning driver (1-2 ms pulse).
  • Program 5.4: Input Capture pulse-width and signal frequency measurement module.
  • Program 5.5: Real-Time Clock (RTC) BCD time extractor.

🛡️ Production Failure Modes

  • Setting PSC or ARR to target values instead of (target - 1), causing frequency error.
  • Neglecting counter rollover in Input Capture, resulting in negative delta values.
  • Modifying PWM duty cycles without preload buffering, causing electrical glitch spikes.
🏁 Daily Milestone Deliverables: 5 Interactive Register-Level Programs • 5 Architecture Diagrams • 10 Practice MCQs • 5 Hands-On Assignments

5.1 Hardware Timer Architecture: Prescalers, Counters, and Auto-Reload

Software delay loops are inherently inaccurate: their duration varies wildly with compiler optimization flags, CPU clock frequency, and interrupt preemption overhead. Modern microcontrollers offload all precise timekeeping to dedicated Hardware Timers. A general-purpose microcontroller timer is a programmable digital counter clocked independently from CPU instructions.

The core timer architecture consists of three fundamental register stages:

  • Prescaler (PSC): A 16-bit register that divides the input timer bus clock frequency ($f_{TIM}$) by $(PSC + 1)$.
  • Counter (CNT): A 16-bit or 32-bit register that increments (up-counting), decrements (down-counting), or counts up-and-down (center-aligned mode) on each prescaled tick.
  • Auto-Reload Register (ARR): Defines the counter overflow ceiling. When $CNT$ reaches $ARR$, the counter generates an Update Event (UIE), reloads its start value, and can trigger an interrupt or DMA transfer.
Real World Example: In an electric vehicle motor inverter, a center-aligned 3-phase timer operates at 20 kHz. The counter increments and decrements symmetrically, generating complementary Pulse Width Modulation (PWM) waveforms with microsecond hardware dead-time insertion to prevent shoot-through short circuits across the high-voltage IGBT bridge.
Figure 1.4-1: General-Purpose Hardware Timer Block Diagram
Figure Parameters Explained:
  • Prescaler (PSC): Divides input clock: f_CNT = f_CLK / (PSC + 1). Allows configuring tick resolutions from nanoseconds to milliseconds.
  • Auto-Reload (ARR): Determines timer period: Overflow Frequency f_OVF = f_CLK / ((PSC + 1) * (ARR + 1)).
  • CCR1 - CCR4 Registers: Store comparison thresholds for PWM duty cycles or capture timestamps of input pin transitions.
  • Update Event (UEV): Fires upon counter reaching ARR, reloading shadow registers and driving the TIMx_IRQHandler interrupt.

5.2 Pulse Width Modulation (PWM): Frequency, Duty Cycle, and Edge vs. Center Aligned

Pulse Width Modulation (PWM) generates an analog-equivalent average voltage from a purely digital pin by rapidly switching the output HIGH and LOW at high frequency. The ratio of the pulse HIGH duration ($T_{ON}$) to the total period ($T$) is defined as the Duty Cycle:

$$\text{Duty Cycle (\%)} = \frac{T_{ON}}{T} \times 100 = \frac{CCR}{ARR + 1} \times 100$$

In PWM Mode 1 (Edge-Aligned), the output pin stays HIGH while $CNT < CCRx$, and transitions to LOW when $CNT \ge CCRx$. By dynamically varying the value of $CCRx$ between $0$ and $ARR$, software commands exact duty cycles from 0% to 100% with zero CPU intervention.

Figure 1.4-2: PWM Waveform Generation via Counter and Compare Thresholds
Figure Parameters Explained:
  • ARR (Period Ceiling): Defines the PWM switching frequency. Higher ARR values provide finer duty cycle resolution at lower frequencies.
  • CCR (Duty Threshold): Controls pulse width: when CCR = ARR / 2, the output is a 50% duty square wave.
  • Edge-Aligned Mode: Counter ramps monotonically 0 to ARR; phase jitter occurs at the beginning/end of pulses.
  • Center-Aligned Mode: Counter counts up to ARR and down to 0; pulses are centered symmetrically, minimizing electromagnetic acoustic noise in motors.

5.3 Input Capture: Measuring Pulse Widths and Signal Frequency

While Output Compare generates signals, Input Capture Mode measures incoming external signals. When an electrical edge (rising or falling) occurs on a timer channel pin, the timer hardware latches the instantaneous value of the counter $CNT$ into the Capture/Compare Register ($CCRx$) in single-cycle silicon time and asserts an interrupt flag. By computing the difference between two successive capture values, software calculates frequency, period, and pulse widths with sub-microsecond precision.

Figure 1.4-3: Input Capture Mode Timing Waveform Analysis
Figure Parameters Explained:
  • Input Filter & Prescaler: Configures digital glitch rejection filters (eliminating sub-microsecond spikes) and prescales input pulses.
  • Direct Capture (IC1 -> CCR1): Hardware captures the counter value directly into the register upon detecting the programmed edge.
  • Counter Wrap-Around Handling: If the counter overflows between captures, software adds (ARR + 1) to the delta calculation: Delta = (t2 >= t1) ? (t2 - t1) : ((ARR - t1) + t2 + 1).

5.4 The Real-Time Clock (RTC) & Calendar Subsystem

Standard timers stop counting when the microcontroller enters low-power standby sleep modes. For calendar tracking (Year, Month, Day, Hour, Minute, Second) and battery-powered wakeups, microcontrollers incorporate an independent Real-Time Clock (RTC) peripheral. The RTC is clocked by a dedicated 32.768 kHz Low-Speed External (LSE) crystal oscillator powered through a dedicated battery backup pin ($V_{BAT}$) when main power is disconnected.

Figure 1.4-4: STM32 RTC Calendar Block Diagram and Clock Dividers
Figure Parameters Explained:
  • 32.768 kHz Crystal: Chosen because 32768 is exactly 2^15, allowing binary dividers to easily produce a precise 1 Hz (1 pulse per second) clock.
  • Binary Coded Decimal (BCD): RTC registers store time and date in BCD format (e.g. 0x25 represents decimal 25) for direct human-readable parsing.
  • Backup Domain (VBAT): Dedicated power domain containing the RTC, LSE oscillator, and backup registers powered by an external coin cell during main power outages.

5.5 Timer Cascading & Master/Slave Synchronization

When measuring very long time periods or generating complex synchronized multi-channel signals, microcontrollers support Timer Master/Slave Cascading. One timer (Master) outputs its internal trigger (TRGO) on update, reset, or compare events. Another timer (Slave) uses this trigger as its clock prescaler or gate, linking two 16-bit timers together to form a seamless 32-bit counter without software intervention.

Figure 1.4-5: Master-Slave Timer Cascading Architecture
Figure Parameters Explained:
  • Internal Trigger (ITR): Silicon interconnect routing trigger signals between timers without using external GPIO pins.
  • TRGO (Trigger Output): Configurable trigger output event (Reset, Enable, Update, Compare Pulse) broadcast to slave timers or ADC converters.
  • Gated Mode: Slave timer only counts when the master timer output signal is HIGH, enabling automated burst generation.

5.6 Hands-On Code Implementations


#include <stdint.h>
#include <stdbool.h>

#define RCC_APB1ENR     (*(volatile uint32_t *)0x40023840UL)
#define TIM2_BASE       0x40000000UL
#define TIM2_CR1        (*(volatile uint32_t *)(TIM2_BASE + 0x00UL))
#define TIM2_DIER       (*(volatile uint32_t *)(TIM2_BASE + 0x0CUL))
#define TIM2_SR         (*(volatile uint32_t *)(TIM2_BASE + 0x10UL))
#define TIM2_PSC        (*(volatile uint32_t *)(TIM2_BASE + 0x28UL))
#define TIM2_ARR        (*(volatile uint32_t *)(TIM2_BASE + 0x2CUL))

#define NVIC_ISER0      (*(volatile uint32_t *)0xE000E100UL)
#define TIM2_IRQn       28

static volatile uint32_t g_seconds_elapsed = 0;

void TIM2_IRQHandler(void) {
    if (TIM2_SR & (1UL << 0)) {
        TIM2_SR &= ~(1UL << 0); /* Clear Update Interrupt Flag (UIF) */
        g_seconds_elapsed++;
    }
}

/* Configure TIM2 for 1.0 Hz periodic interrupt assuming 16 MHz APB1 timer clock */
void tim2_init_1hz(void) {
    RCC_APB1ENR |= (1UL << 0); /* Enable TIM2 clock */

    /* Step 1: Prescaler divides 16,000,000 Hz down to 1,000 Hz */
    TIM2_PSC = 16000UL - 1UL;

    /* Step 2: Auto-Reload counts 1,000 ticks = exactly 1.000 second */
    TIM2_ARR = 1000UL - 1UL;

    /* Step 3: Enable Update Interrupt in DIER */
    TIM2_DIER |= (1UL << 0);

    /* Step 4: Enable TIM2 in NVIC */
    NVIC_ISER0 = (1UL << TIM2_IRQn);

    /* Step 5: Start counter */
    TIM2_CR1 |= (1UL << 0);
}
Program 1.5-1: Periodic 1-Second Timer Interrupt via Direct Register Configuration 

#include <stdint.h>

#define RCC_AHB1ENR     (*(volatile uint32_t *)0x40023830UL)
#define RCC_APB1ENR     (*(volatile uint32_t *)0x40023840UL)

#define GPIOA_MODER     (*(volatile uint32_t *)0x40020000UL)
#define GPIOA_AFRL      (*(volatile uint32_t *)0x40020020UL)

#define TIM3_BASE       0x40000400UL
#define TIM3_CR1        (*(volatile uint32_t *)(TIM3_BASE + 0x00UL))
#define TIM3_CCMR1      (*(volatile uint32_t *)(TIM3_BASE + 0x18UL))
#define TIM3_CCER       (*(volatile uint32_t *)(TIM3_BASE + 0x20UL))
#define TIM3_PSC        (*(volatile uint32_t *)(TIM3_BASE + 0x28UL))
#define TIM3_ARR        (*(volatile uint32_t *)(TIM3_BASE + 0x2CUL))
#define TIM3_CCR1       (*(volatile uint32_t *)(TIM3_BASE + 0x34UL))

/* Initialize 1 kHz PWM on PA6 (TIM3 CH1, Alternate Function AF2) */
void pwm_led_init_1khz(void) {
    RCC_AHB1ENR |= (1UL << 0); /* GPIOA clock */
    RCC_APB1ENR |= (1UL << 1); /* TIM3 clock */

    /* PA6 Alternate Function mode (MODER6 = 0b10) */
    GPIOA_MODER &= ~(3UL << (6 * 2));
    GPIOA_MODER |= (2UL << (6 * 2));

    /* Route PA6 to AF2 (TIM3_CH1): AFRL pin 6 is bits [27:24] = 0x02 */
    GPIOA_AFRL &= ~(0xFUL << 24);
    GPIOA_AFRL |= (0x2UL << 24);

    /* Timer clock = 16 MHz. Prescaler = 15 -> f_cnt = 1 MHz (1 tick = 1 us) */
    TIM3_PSC = 16 - 1;
    /* ARR = 999 -> Period = 1000 us = 1 ms (1 kHz PWM frequency) */
    TIM3_ARR = 1000 - 1;

    /* PWM Mode 1 on Channel 1: OC1M = 0b110, enable preload OC1PE = 1 */
    TIM3_CCMR1 |= (6UL << 4) | (1UL << 3);

    /* Enable output on Channel 1 (CC1E = 1) */
    TIM3_CCER |= (1UL << 0);

    /* Initial duty cycle = 0% */
    TIM3_CCR1 = 0;

    /* Enable auto-reload preload and start timer */
    TIM3_CR1 |= (1UL << 7) | (1UL << 0);
}

void pwm_set_duty(uint16_t duty_0_to_1000) {
    if (duty_0_to_1000 > 999) duty_0_to_1000 = 999;
    TIM3_CCR1 = duty_0_to_1000;
}
Program 1.5-2: Hardware PWM Generation: Breathing LED on TIM3 CH1 (PA6) 

#include <stdint.h>

#define TIM4_CCR1       (*(volatile uint32_t *)0x40000834UL)

/* Standard RC Servo requires 50 Hz PWM (20 ms period)
 * 1.0 ms pulse = 0 degrees
 * 1.5 ms pulse = 90 degrees (center)
 * 2.0 ms pulse = 180 degrees
 */
void servo_init_50hz(void) {
    /* Assuming TIM4 configured with 1 MHz tick (PSC = 15 at 16 MHz clock) */
    /* ARR = 20,000 - 1 = 19,999 (20 ms period -> 50 Hz) */
}

void servo_set_angle(uint8_t angle_degrees) {
    if (angle_degrees > 180) angle_degrees = 180;
    
    /* Map 0-180 degrees to 1000 - 2000 microsecond pulse width */
    uint32_t pulse_us = 1000 + ((uint32_t)angle_degrees * 1000) / 180;
    TIM4_CCR1 = pulse_us;
}
Program 1.5-3: Servo Motor Control: 50 Hz PWM with 1-2 ms Precision Pulse 

#include <stdint.h>
#include <stdbool.h>

#define TIM1_BASE       0x40010000UL
#define TIM1_SR         (*(volatile uint32_t *)(TIM1_BASE + 0x10UL))
#define TIM1_CCR1       (*(volatile uint32_t *)(TIM1_BASE + 0x34UL))

static volatile uint32_t t1 = 0, t2 = 0;
static volatile bool capture_ready = false;

void TIM1_CC_IRQHandler(void) {
    static bool first_edge = true;
    
    if (TIM1_SR & (1UL << 1)) { /* CC1IF Capture flag */
        if (first_edge) {
            t1 = TIM1_CCR1; /* First rising edge */
            first_edge = false;
        } else {
            t2 = TIM1_CCR1; /* Second rising edge */
            first_edge = true;
            capture_ready = true;
        }
    }
}

uint32_t calculate_measured_frequency(uint32_t timer_clk_hz) {
    if (!capture_ready) return 0;
    
    uint32_t delta = (t2 >= t1) ? (t2 - t1) : ((0xFFFFUL - t1) + t2 + 1);
    capture_ready = false;
    
    return timer_clk_hz / delta;
}
Program 1.5-4: Input Capture: Measuring Pulse Width and Frequency 

#include <stdint.h>

#define RTC_BASE        0x40002800UL
#define RTC_TR          (*(volatile uint32_t *)(RTC_BASE + 0x00UL))
#define RTC_DR          (*(volatile uint32_t *)(RTC_BASE + 0x04UL))
#define RTC_WPR         (*(volatile uint32_t *)(RTC_BASE + 0x24UL))

typedef struct {
    uint8_t hours;
    uint8_t minutes;
    uint8_t seconds;
} RTC_Time_t;

/* Convert BCD byte to standard binary decimal integer */
static inline uint8_t bcd_to_dec(uint8_t bcd) {
    return ((bcd >> 4) * 10) + (bcd & 0x0F);
}

void rtc_get_time(RTC_Time_t *time) {
    uint32_t tr = RTC_TR; /* Read Time Register */
    
    time->hours   = bcd_to_dec((tr >> 16) & 0x3F);
    time->minutes = bcd_to_dec((tr >> 8) & 0x7F);
    time->seconds = bcd_to_dec(tr & 0x7F);
}
Program 1.5-5: RTC BCD Calendar Initialization and Time Extraction

Hardware Timer Operating Modes Comparison

Timer ModePrimary Hardware ActionKey Control RegistersTarget Embedded Applications
Output CompareMatches CNT with CCRx to toggle or pulse an output pinTIMx_CCMRx, TIMx_CCER, TIMx_CCRxPrecise non-blocking time delays, camera shutter triggering
PWM GenerationContinuously drives pin HIGH/LOW based on CNT vs CCRx thresholdTIMx_ARR, TIMx_CCRx, TIMx_CCMRxDC motor speed control, LED brightness, audio tone synthesis
Input CaptureLatches CNT into CCRx on external pin edge transitionsTIMx_CCMRx, TIMx_CCER, TIMx_CCRxUltrasonic echo distance measurement, RPM tachometers
One-Pulse ModeGenerates a single pulse of exact duration after a trigger delayTIMx_CR1 (OPM bit), TIMx_ARR, TIMx_CCRxLaser pulse firing, solenoid stroke driving, ignition timing
Encoder InterfaceCounts quadrature phase A and B signals in hardwareTIMx_SMCR (SMS=001/010/011)Rotary dial knobs, CNC axis position feedback, wheel encoders

Topic Quiz (10 Questions)

Test your conceptual understanding of today's embedded systems architecture, registers, and runtime behaviors.

1. Given a 16 MHz timer clock, what Prescaler (PSC) and Auto-Reload (ARR) produce an exact 1.0 kHz PWM frequency with 1000 steps of resolution?
  • PSC = 16, ARR = 1000
  • PSC = 15, ARR = 999
  • PSC = 16000, ARR = 1
  • PSC = 0, ARR = 16000
f = f_clk / ((PSC + 1) * (ARR + 1)). With PSC = 15, timer ticks at 16 MHz / 16 = 1 MHz. With ARR = 999 (1000 steps), frequency = 1 MHz / 1000 = 1 kHz.
2. In PWM Mode 1, what happens to the output channel pin when the counter CNT equals or exceeds CCRx?
  • The output pin transitions from HIGH to LOW
  • The counter immediately resets to 0
  • The output pin transitions to High-Impedance (Hi-Z)
  • A HardFault exception is triggered
In PWM Mode 1, the channel is active (HIGH) as long as CNT < CCRx, and switches inactive (LOW) when CNT >= CCRx.
3. Why is 32.768 kHz universally chosen as the crystal frequency for Real-Time Clock (RTC) peripherals?
  • It is the resonant frequency of copper traces
  • 32768 is exactly 2^15, which can be divided down to exactly 1.000 Hz using a 15-bit binary ripple counter
  • It generates minimum electromagnetic interference at radio frequencies
  • It matches the human audible hearing threshold
2^15 = 32,768. A simple cascade of 15 flip-flops divides 32.768 kHz down to an exact 1 Hz tick with zero fractional rounding error.
4. What is the typical PWM frequency and pulse width range required to position a hobby RC servo motor across 0 to 180 degrees?
  • 1 kHz frequency, 50% to 100% duty cycle
  • 50 Hz frequency (20 ms period), with 1.0 ms to 2.0 ms pulse widths
  • 100 kHz frequency, 1 us to 2 us pulse widths
  • 10 Hz frequency, 10 ms to 90 ms pulse widths
Standard analog RC servos require a 50 Hz control frame (20 ms period) with pulse widths ranging between 1.0 ms (0 deg) and 2.0 ms (180 deg).
5. How does Input Capture mode handle measuring a pulse width if the timer counter overflows between the rising and falling edges?
  • The measurement is invalid and must be discarded
  • Software adds (ARR + 1) to the delta calculation upon detecting the timer overflow flag
  • The hardware automatically halts the timer
  • The input pin is reconfigured as an open-drain output
When an overflow occurs between edge captures, software accounts for the wrap-around by calculating: Delta = (ARR - t1) + t2 + 1.
6. What is the purpose of the Shadow Registers (Preload Registers) in ARM Cortex-M timer architectures?
  • To double the effective clock frequency
  • To prevent glitching by ensuring new ARR or CCR values only take effect synchronously on the next Update Event (counter rollover)
  • To mirror register values to external SPI Flash
  • To encrypt timer registers against hacking
Preload buffering ensures that if software writes a new CCR or ARR value mid-count, it is buffered and latched only at counter rollover, preventing truncated pulses.
7. Which timer mode allows two 90-degree out-of-phase encoder signals (Phase A and Phase B) to be decoded directly in hardware?
  • PWM Mode 2
  • Encoder Interface Mode
  • One-Pulse Mode
  • Forced Inactive Mode
Encoder Interface mode decodes quadrature signals automatically, incrementing or decrementing the counter based on phase relationship without CPU interrupts.
8. What format does the STM32 RTC peripheral use to store Hours, Minutes, and Seconds in the RTC_TR register?
  • Raw Unix Epoch 32-bit seconds
  • Binary Coded Decimal (BCD)
  • ASCII strings
  • IEEE-754 Floating Point
RTC registers store date and time components in BCD format, where each 4-bit nibble represents one decimal digit (0-9).
9. In center-aligned PWM mode, how does the counter operate?
  • It counts only on even clock edges
  • It counts up from 0 to ARR, then counts down from ARR to 0 symmetrically
  • It uses two separate hardware counters running in opposite directions
  • It stops when CNT reaches ARR/2
Center-aligned mode alternates up-counting and down-counting, centering output pulses around the midpoint to reduce acoustic and electrical harmonics.
10. What pin connects an external coin-cell battery to keep the RTC and backup domain alive when VDD power is lost?
  • NRST
  • BOOT0
  • VBAT
  • VREF+
The VBAT pin connects a 1.8V-3.6V coin-cell battery that powers the RTC and low-speed oscillator when main VDD drops below threshold.

Hands-On Assignments

Complete these 5 lab assignments to solidify your hands-on firmware engineering skills.

Assignment 1: Breathing LED Controller via Sine Look-Up Table

Task: Precompute a 64-element sine look-up table scaling duty cycles from 0% to 100%. Use a timer interrupt firing at 50 Hz to update TIM3_CCR1 sequentially, creating a visually smooth breathing illumination effect.

Assignment 2: Automatic 0-180 Degree Servo Sweeper

Task: Configure TIM4 in PWM mode at 50 Hz. Write an automated non-blocking state machine that smoothly sweeps an SG90 servo from 0 to 180 degrees over 2 seconds, pauses for 500 ms, and sweeps back continuously.

Assignment 3: Ultrasonic HC-SR04 Distance Sensor Driver

Task: Interface an HC-SR04 sensor: generate a 10 us trigger pulse using a GPIO, and use Input Capture on a timer channel to measure the return echo pulse width. Convert pulse duration into centimeters ($Distance = \frac{t_{us}}{58}$). Print distance over UART.

Assignment 4: Rotary Encoder Position & RPM Tachometer

Task: Configure a timer in Encoder Interface Mode. Connect an optical quadrature encoder; read counter position to track angular rotation, and compute rotational speed (RPM) every 100 ms.

Assignment 5: RTC Wakeup Alarm with Low-Power Standby

Task: Configure the internal RTC to trigger an Alarm Interrupt exactly 10 seconds into the future. Put the microcontroller into low-power sleep mode, observe current reduction on a meter, and verify scheduled wakeup.

Official References, Research Papers & Standards

Deepen your engineering foundations with seminal reference manuals, processor architecture standards, and industry specifications:

Hardware technical reference detailing counter modes, prescaler mechanics, PWM generation registers, and master-slave interconnect matrices.

Engineering guide explaining advanced timer features: dead-time generation, complementary outputs, input capture filtering, and motor control modes.

Covers timer peripheral clocking, prescaler mathematical derivations, and battery-backed RTC calendar design.

fields.title: Topic 4: Assertions, Logging & Debugging Methodology
fields.content:
Topic 4

Assertions, Logging & Debugging Methodology

When firmware fails in a laboratory setting or deployment field, developers rarely have access to rich terminal stack traces. Standard desktop C's assert() macro calls abort(), which on a bare-metal microcontroller typically jumps into an infinite loop or triggers a watchdog reset without preserving diagnostic clues.

Professional embedded firmware demands a tailored diagnostic framework: custom target-safe assertion handlers that capture the failed expression, filename, and line number in non-volatile battery-backed RAM; non-blocking ring-buffer logging that never stalls real-time interrupt service routines; and systematic hardware debugging techniques using ARM Cortex-M DWT (Data Watchpoint and Trace) cycle counters.

4.1 Assertions: Design-Time Contract Enforcement

An assertion is a statement verifying a condition that must strictly be true if the program is operating correctly. Unlike standard input validation (which handles expected real-world variations such as noisy sensor inputs or severed wires), assertions exist to detect programmer logic bugs and violated API contracts.

Golden Rule of Assertions: Never place side-effect operations inside an assertion! For example, ASSERT(read_fifo() != 0); will break completely in release builds when assertions are disabled via -DNDEBUG, because the FIFO read will be stripped from the binary!

4.2 Non-Blocking Telemetry & Ring Buffer Logging

Calling blocking serial functions like printf() over an 115,200-baud UART requires roughly 87 microseconds per character. Printing a 40-character diagnostic message takes approximately 3.5 milliseconds—an eternity in a 1 kHz motor control loop or inside an interrupt handler.

Figure 4.1: Decoupled Non-Blocking Circular Logging Architecture
Architectural Benefits:
  • Zero Timing Distortion: Pushing a log entry into a memory buffer takes under 2 microseconds, preventing probe effect / heisenbugs.
  • Safe in Interrupts: Single-producer single-consumer circular buffers require zero mutex locks or interrupt disabling if head and tail indices are updated atomically.

4.3 Retargeting printf in Newlib GCC

On ARM Cortex-M cross-compilers using the Newlib C runtime, standard I/O calls (printf, puts) route through low-level Unix system call stubs. By implementing the _write() syscall, developers retarget formatted output to a physical UART or ARM Serial Wire Output (SWO) instrumentation port.

4.4 Hands-On Code Implementations

The following complete module provides a production-grade custom assertion framework and an interrupt-safe non-volatile crash recorder: 

/**
 * Program 4.1: Target-Safe Embedded Assertion & Non-Volatile Crash Recorder
 * File: embed_assert.c
 * Target: ARM Cortex-M / Embedded Systems
 */

#include <stdint.h>
#include <stdbool.h>
#include <stdio.h>

/* Non-Volatile Crash Information Structure (Allocated in backup RAM or battery RAM) */
typedef struct {
    uint32_t magic_header;       /*!< 0xDEADBEEF indicates valid crash log */
    uint32_t timestamp_ms;       /*!< System uptime at crash */
    uint32_t line_number;        /*!< Source code line number */
    char     filename[32];       /*!< Base name of source file */
    char     expression[64];     /*!< String representation of failed condition */
    uint32_t checksum;           /*!< Simple additive parity checksum */
} CrashDiagnostic_t;

/* Located in a retained RAM section not zeroed out during reset */
static CrashDiagnostic_t g_crash_record __attribute__((section(".noinit")));

#define CRASH_MAGIC  (0xDEADBEEFUL)

/**
 * @brief Custom assertion failure handler.
 * @note Decorated with noreturn to enable compiler unreachable optimizations.
 */
void __attribute__((noreturn)) custom_assert_handler(const char *expr, const char *file, uint32_t line) {
    /* Disable all interrupts immediately to freeze system state */
    __asm volatile ("cpsid i" : : : "memory");

    /* Populate non-volatile diagnostic log */
    g_crash_record.magic_header = CRASH_MAGIC;
    g_crash_record.timestamp_ms = 45210UL; /* In real firmware: get_uptime_ms() */
    g_crash_record.line_number  = line;

    /* Safe bounded copy of filename and expression string */
    snprintf(g_crash_record.filename, sizeof(g_crash_record.filename), "%s", file);
    snprintf(g_crash_record.expression, sizeof(g_crash_record.expression), "%s", expr);

    /* Safe safe-state: Turn off motor drivers, heaters, high-voltage outputs */
    /* safe_hardware_shutdown(); */

#if defined(DEBUG_BUILD)
    /* If running under debugger, trigger hardware breakpoint instruction */
    __asm volatile ("bkpt #0");
#endif

    /* Trigger hardware reset via System Reset Request in NVIC AIRCR */
    volatile uint32_t * const aircr = (volatile uint32_t *)0xE000ED0CUL;
    *aircr = (0x5FAUL << 16) | (1UL << 2); /* SYSRESETREQ */

    while (1) {
        /* Wait for reset to complete */
    }
}

/* Custom assertion macro */
#if defined(ENABLE_ASSERTIONS)
    #define EMBED_ASSERT(expr) \
        do { \
            if (!(expr)) { \
                custom_assert_handler(#expr, __FILE__, (uint32_t)__LINE__); \
            } \
        } while (0)
#else
    #define EMBED_ASSERT(expr) ((void)0)
#endif
Program 4.1: Target-Safe Embedded Assertion & Non-Volatile Crash Recorder

4.5 Buggy vs. Modern Safe Code Comparison

Calling blocking serial I/O directly inside a high-speed Interrupt Service Routine is one of the most destructive bugs in real-time firmware, completely violating real-time deadlines.

View Buggy/Legacy Code

This ISR calls blocking printf() at 9600 baud. Transmitting 30 characters stalls the CPU inside the interrupt for 31 milliseconds, missing subsequent motor encoder pulses: 

/* BUGGY / DISASTROUS: Blocking I/O inside ISR */
void SysTick_Handler(void) {
    /* 9600 baud = ~1 ms per byte. 30 bytes = 30 ms blocking stall inside ISR! */
    printf("Tick event triggered: count=%d\n", tick_count++);
}
Program 4.2-A: Blocking Printf Inside Real-Time Interrupt Handler

The safe architecture pushes a compact, binary-formatted telemetry packet into an interrupt-safe circular ring buffer in microseconds, allowing the background superloop to stream the data asynchronously: 

/* SAFE / PRODUCTION-GRADE: Non-blocking binary telemetry logging */
#include <stdint.h>
#include <stdbool.h>

typedef struct {
    uint32_t timestamp;
    uint16_t event_id;
    int16_t  payload;
} LogEntry_t;

#define LOG_QUEUE_SIZE 64U
static LogEntry_t s_log_queue[LOG_QUEUE_SIZE];
static volatile uint8_t s_head = 0U;
static volatile uint8_t s_tail = 0U;

/* Lock-free push into circular ring buffer: takes only 8 CPU cycles */
bool log_event_isr(uint16_t event_id, int16_t payload) {
    uint8_t next_head = (s_head + 1U) & (LOG_QUEUE_SIZE - 1U);
    if (next_head == s_tail) {
        return false; /* Buffer full: drop gracefully without blocking */
    }
    s_log_queue[s_head].timestamp = 0; /* read HW timer */
    s_log_queue[s_head].event_id = event_id;
    s_log_queue[s_head].payload = payload;
    s_head = next_head;
    return true;
}

void SysTick_Handler(void) {
    /* Fast non-blocking push: finishes in < 1 microsecond! */
    log_event_isr(0x01, 100);
}
Program 4.2-B: Non-Blocking Lock-Free Telemetry Logger for Interrupts

Topic Quiz (10 Questions)

Test your knowledge of assertions, telemetry loggers, and embedded debugging workflows.

1. What is the fundamental distinction between an assertion and defensive runtime input validation?
  • Assertions run in SRAM; validation runs in Flash.
  • Assertions catch internal software logic bugs and contract violations; validation handles expected external data variations.
  • Assertions are written in assembly; validation is written in C.
  • Validation is disabled in release builds.
Assertions verify software design invariants that must never happen; input validation handles real-world corrupted data, packet timeouts, and noise.
2. What preprocessor macro disables standard C assert() statements when defined during compilation?
  • DISABLE_ASSERT
  • NDEBUG
  • RELEASE_BUILD
  • NO_CHECK
Defining NDEBUG causes <assert.h> to expand assert(expr) into ((void)0), stripping all assertion code from the binary.
3. Why is calling a standard blocking printf() over UART forbidden inside an Interrupt Service Routine (ISR)?
  • UART registers cannot be accessed inside interrupts.
  • Blocking serial transmission takes milliseconds, stalling the CPU, starving other interrupts, and violating real-time deadlines.
  • printf() modifies the link register.
  • The compiler emits a syntax error.
Transmitting serial characters at typical baud rates takes hundreds of microseconds to milliseconds, blocking all lower-priority interrupts and breaking real-time behavior.
4. Which low-level C runtime system call stub must be implemented in Newlib GCC to retarget printf() to a hardware UART?
  • _read()
  • _write()
  • _sbrk()
  • _exit()
In Newlib-based toolchains (like arm-none-eabi-gcc), printf() funnels output bytes through the _write(int file, char *ptr, int len) system call stub.
5. What is the ARM Cortex-M 'BKPT #0' instruction used for?
  • To restart the CPU clock.
  • To halt execution and trigger a hardware breakpoint for an attached JTAG/SWD debugger.
  • To clear the cache.
  • To enter sleep mode.
BKPT triggers a debug fault, causing the processor to halt and hand control to an attached hardware debugger like GDB via OpenOCD.
6. What is a 'Heisenbug' in firmware engineering?
  • A bug caused by radioactive decay in memory cells.
  • A timing defect that disappears or changes behavior as soon as debugging instrumentation (like printf) is introduced.
  • A bug that only occurs on German microcontrollers.
  • A linker script error.
Intrusive print statements alter system timing. When the print statement is added, a race condition may temporarily vanish, hiding the defect.
7. Which hardware component in ARM Cortex-M processors provides a non-intrusive 32-bit CPU cycle counter for microsecond profiling?
  • The SysTick Timer
  • The DWT (Data Watchpoint and Trace) CYCCNT register
  • The RTC (Real-Time Clock)
  • The Watchdog Timer
The DWT CYCCNT register increments once per CPU clock cycle, allowing cycle-accurate non-intrusive execution time benchmarking.
8. What is the advantage of using ARM Serial Wire Output (SWO) / ITM over standard UART for logging?
  • SWO uses 4 parallel data lines.
  • ITM hardware instrumentation transmits trace packets out a dedicated debug pin with minimal CPU cycle overhead.
  • ITM operates without a clock.
  • SWO eliminates the need for a C compiler.
The Instrumentation Trace Macrocell (ITM) outputs trace packets over the dedicated SWO pin without CPU busy-wait loops, minimizing probe effects.
9. Where should persistent crash diagnostic logs be stored so they survive a hardware reset?
  • On the CPU stack
  • In a local automatic variable
  • In an uninitialized RAM section (.noinit) or battery-backed backup registers
  • In the instruction cache
The .noinit RAM section is not modified during the C runtime startup code, allowing crash structures to survive a warm reset.
10. Why should an embedded assert handler be decorated with the [[noreturn]] or __attribute__((noreturn)) attribute?
  • To enable multi-threading.
  • To inform the compiler optimizer that the function never returns, allowing it to eliminate dead code and suppress false return warnings.
  • To store the function in EEPROM.
  • To disable compiler warnings on unused variables.
Marking the assertion handler noreturn informs the compiler that control flow ends there, generating cleaner machine code and eliminating spurious warnings.

Hands-On Assignments

Execute these 5 laboratory exercises to implement professional debugging and assertion workflows.

Assignment 1: Custom Assert with .noinit RAM Persistence

Task: Modify your project linker script to create a 256-byte .noinit section in SRAM. Implement a custom assertion macro that records the failed condition, file, and line into this section. Trigger an assertion, reset the board, and verify upon reboot that the startup code reads and prints the recorded crash details.

Assignment 2: Lock-Free Single-Producer Single-Consumer (SPSC) Ring Buffer

Task: Implement a circular ring buffer logger for 8-byte binary messages. Benchmark the push operation using the DWT cycle counter. Verify that pushing an entry from within a timer ISR finishes in under 20 CPU cycles without disabling global interrupts.

Assignment 3: Newlib _write() Syscall Retargeting

Task: In an ARM GCC project, provide a custom implementation of int _write(int file, char *ptr, int len) that routes stdout and stderr characters to a mock UART transmission function. Test by calling standard printf("Temperature: %d C\r\n", 25); and verify proper formatting.

Assignment 4: DWT Cycle Counter Micro-Benchmarking

Task: Enable the ARM Cortex-M DWT CYCCNT register (CoreDebug->DEMCR |= CoreDebug_DEMCR_TRCENA_Msk; DWT->CTRL |= DWT_CTRL_CYCCNTENA_Msk;). Measure the exact CPU cycle execution duration of an integer square root algorithm compared to floating-point sqrtf().

Assignment 5: Multi-Level Verbosity Logger Filter

Task: Design a preprocessor-driven logging module with 4 verbosity tiers: LOG_LEVEL_ERROR, LOG_LEVEL_WARN, LOG_LEVEL_INFO, and LOG_LEVEL_DEBUG. Show how setting the active build level to ERROR eliminates debug string literals completely from Flash memory.

fields.title: Day 6: ADC, DAC & Sensor Interfacing
fields.content:
Session 1.5

Day 6: ADC, DAC & Sensor Interfacing

Problem Statement: The physical world is analog, but microcontrollers process only discrete bits. Converting analog sensor voltages with microsecond accuracy requires mastering Successive Approximation (SAR) ADC architectures, quantization noise, impedance matching, and autonomous DMA streaming. How do you acquire clean sensor data and synthesize true analog outputs?
📋 Daily Plan & Learning Architecture
Session 1.5 Module 1: Embedded C Foundations Estimated: 3.5 hrs

🎯 Today's Mission & Relevance

  • Understand SAR ADC silicon architecture, quantization noise, and 1 LSB calculations.
  • Implement signal conditioning for NTC thermistors using the Steinhart-Hart equation.
  • Stream multi-channel sensor data autonomously using ADC Scan Mode and DMA.

📐 Theoretical Milestones

  • Nyquist-Shannon sampling theorem and analog anti-aliasing filter design.
  • Oversampling and decimation mathematics ($M = 4^k$ for $k$ extra bits).
  • True DAC resistor ladder synthesis vs. PWM low-pass filtering.

💻 Hands-On Blueprint

  • Program 6.1: Single-channel polled ADC reading on PA0 (ADC1_IN0).
  • Program 6.2: NTC thermistor temperature calculation via Steinhart-Hart equation.
  • Program 6.3: Multi-channel autonomous ADC + DMA streaming engine.
  • Program 6.4: DAC sine wave synthesis via timer TRGO and DMA transfers.
  • Program 6.5: Software 16x oversampling and decimation for 14-bit resolution.

🛡️ Production Failure Modes

  • Driving ADC with excessive source impedance (>10k ohm), corrupting sampling capacitor charge.
  • Omitting anti-aliasing filters, causing high-frequency noise to fold into sensor bands.
  • Allowing high thermistor bias currents to induce self-heating measurement error.
🏁 Daily Milestone Deliverables: 5 Interactive Register-Level Programs • 5 Architecture Diagrams • 10 Practice MCQs • 5 Hands-On Assignments

6.1 Bridging the Analog Real-World and Digital Computing

The physical physical universe is analog: temperatures shift smoothly, pressures fluctuate continuously, sound waves propagate as subtle voltage changes, and battery chemistry drains across gradual decay curves. Digital microcontrollers, however, compute strictly in discrete binary bits ($0$ and $1$). The Analog-to-Digital Converter (ADC) and Digital-to-Analog Converter (DAC) form the fundamental electronic sensory organs and physical vocal cords of embedded computing.

Real World Example: In an intensive care unit (ICU) patient pulse oximeter, an optical photodiode detects minute fluctuations in infrared light transmission through capillary blood vessels. A 12-bit SAR ADC samples this microvolt signal at 500 Hz, applying digital filtering to extract arterial blood oxygen saturation ($SpO_2$) and heart rate with medical-grade accuracy.
Figure 1.5-1: Successive Approximation Register (SAR) ADC Internal Silicon Architecture
Figure Parameters Explained:
  • Sample & Hold Stage: Samples input voltage onto internal holding capacitor during programmed sampling time, keeping voltage stable during conversion.
  • Comparator: Compares held analog voltage against the internal DAC output voltage.
  • Binary Search Logic: Tests bits from MSB to LSB. If V_in > V_dac, bit remains 1; otherwise, bit is cleared to 0.
  • Conversion Latency: Total time = Sampling Cycles + Conversion Cycles (typically 12 cycles for 12-bit resolution).

6.2 ADC Resolution, Reference Voltage, and Quantization Error

An ADC digitizes an analog voltage by mapping continuous voltages into $2^N$ discrete digital numbers, where $N$ is the converter's Bit Resolution. The voltage span represented by the Least Significant Bit ($1\text{ LSB}$) is defined by the Reference Voltage ($V_{REF}$):

$$1\text{ LSB} = \frac{V_{REF+}}{2^N - 1}$$

For a 12-bit ADC powered with $V_{REF+} = 3.30\text{ V}$, $1\text{ LSB} = \frac{3.30\text{ V}}{4095} \approx 0.8058\text{ mV}$. Any analog voltage between two discrete quantization steps incurs a rounding discrepancy known as Quantization Error (bounded theoretically by $\pm 0.5\text{ LSB}$).

Figure 1.5-2: ADC Quantization Staircase Transfer Function and Quantization Noise
Figure Parameters Explained:
  • Full-Scale Voltage (V_REF): The maximum measurable analog voltage corresponding to digital code 0xFFF (4095).
  • 1 LSB Step: The minimum voltage change detectable by the digital converter (0.806 mV at 3.3V / 12-bit).
  • Quantization Noise: Inherent statistical noise caused by discrete rounding; theoretical SNR = 6.02 * N + 1.76 dB (approx 74 dB for 12-bit ADC).
  • Integral Non-Linearity (INL): Maximum deviation of the actual transfer curve from the ideal line, measured in LSBs.

6.3 Sensor Signal Conditioning: Voltage Dividers & The Steinhart-Hart Equation

Most environmental sensors (such as thermistors, photoresistors, and strain gauges) do not output a clean, buffered voltage. A Negative Temperature Coefficient (NTC) Thermistor varies its electrical resistance non-linearly with temperature. To measure resistance using an ADC, engineers place the thermistor in a Voltage Divider circuit with a precision fixed resistor ($R_{fixed}$).

The resulting voltage is converted to accurate temperature using the empirical Steinhart-Hart Equation (or its simplified Beta formula):

$$\frac{1}{T} = \frac{1}{T_0} + \frac{1}{\beta} \ln\left(\frac{R_{NTC}}{R_0}\right)$$

Figure 1.5-3: NTC Thermistor Signal Conditioning Voltage Divider Circuit
Figure Parameters Explained:
  • Voltage Divider Formula: V_out = V_DD * (R_NTC / (R_fixed + R_NTC)). Solved in firmware to extract R_NTC dynamically.
  • Anti-Aliasing Filter: Low-pass RC filter removes high-frequency electromagnetic noise above the Nyquist frequency before sampling.
  • Input Impedance Match: STM32 SAR ADCs require source impedance R_in < 10k ohm to fully charge internal sampling capacitors within the programmed sampling window.
  • Self-Heating Effect: Current passing through the thermistor dissipates power (I^2 * R), artificially raising temperature if fixed resistor value is too small.

6.4 Multi-Channel Scanning and DMA Autonomous Data Streaming

Sampling multiple analog sensors via software polling wastes hundreds of microseconds of CPU time waiting for conversion flags. Modern microcontrollers configure the ADC in Scan Mode coupled with a Direct Memory Access (DMA) controller. A hardware timer triggers the ADC periodically; the ADC automatically converts channels 0 through 7 sequentially, and the DMA controller transfers each result directly into an SRAM array with zero CPU intervention.

Figure 1.5-4: Autonomous ADC Multi-Channel Scan and DMA Transfer Pipeline
Figure Parameters Explained:
  • Regular Channel Sequence: Configurable hardware sequencer (ADC_SQR1-SQR3) defining conversion order across arbitrary analog pins.
  • DMA Circular Mode: Continuously streams sensor data to RAM in an infinite ring buffer without CPU re-arming.
  • Zero CPU Overhead: The CPU remains in deep sleep or executes application algorithms while hardware acquires sensor telemetry.
  • Half-Transfer Interrupt: Signals that the first half of the DMA buffer is ready for processing while hardware fills the second half.

6.5 Digital-to-Analog Conversion (DAC) & Waveform Synthesis

The Digital-to-Analog Converter (DAC) executes the inverse of the ADC: it transforms 12-bit digital values into an authentic, continuous physical voltage on an output pin. Unlike PWM, which outputs a square wave that requires heavy low-pass filtering, a DAC produces genuine DC voltage levels capable of generating pure analog audio, servo reference voltages, or biomedical test signals.

Figure 1.5-5: DAC Sine Wave Synthesis with Timer Trigger and DMA
Figure Parameters Explained:
  • DAC Data Holding Register (DHR): Buffers 12-bit digital words before transferring to the active DAC output register.
  • Reconstruction Low-Pass Filter: Removes high-frequency image harmonics produced by discrete DAC voltage steps.
  • Output Buffer: Internal operational amplifier buffering DAC output to drive low-impedance external loads without sagging.
  • Settling Time: Time required for the DAC output voltage to settle within +/- 0.5 LSB of target (typically 3 to 6 microseconds on STM32).

6.6 Hands-On Code Implementations


#include <stdint.h>

#define RCC_AHB1ENR     (*(volatile uint32_t *)0x40023830UL)
#define RCC_APB2ENR     (*(volatile uint32_t *)0x40023844UL)

#define GPIOA_MODER     (*(volatile uint32_t *)0x40020000UL)

#define ADC1_BASE       0x40012000UL
#define ADC1_SR         (*(volatile uint32_t *)(ADC1_BASE + 0x00UL))
#define ADC1_CR1        (*(volatile uint32_t *)(ADC1_BASE + 0x04UL))
#define ADC1_CR2        (*(volatile uint32_t *)(ADC1_BASE + 0x08UL))
#define ADC1_SMPR2      (*(volatile uint32_t *)(ADC1_BASE + 0x10UL))
#define ADC1_SQR3       (*(volatile uint32_t *)(ADC1_BASE + 0x34UL))
#define ADC1_DR         (*(volatile uint32_t *)(ADC1_BASE + 0x4CUL))

void adc1_init_pa0(void) {
    /* 1. Enable clocks for GPIOA and ADC1 */
    RCC_AHB1ENR |= (1UL << 0);
    RCC_APB2ENR |= (1UL << 8);

    /* 2. Configure PA0 as Analog Mode (MODER0 = 0b11) */
    GPIOA_MODER |= (3UL << 0);

    /* 3. Set Sample Time for Channel 0 to 84 cycles (SMPR2 bits [2:0] = 0b100) */
    ADC1_SMPR2 |= (4UL << 0);

    /* 4. Sequence 1st conversion: Channel 0 (SQR3 bits [4:0] = 0) */
    ADC1_SQR3 &= ~0x1FUL;

    /* 5. Enable ADC peripheral (ADON = 1) */
    ADC1_CR2 |= (1UL << 0);
}

uint16_t adc1_read_single(void) {
    /* Start conversion by setting SWSTART bit in CR2 */
    ADC1_CR2 |= (1UL << 30);

    /* Poll End-of-Conversion (EOC) flag in SR */
    while (!(ADC1_SR & (1UL << 1))) {
        /* Busy wait */
    }

    /* Reading DR automatically clears EOC flag */
    return (uint16_t)(ADC1_DR & 0x0FFFUL);
}
Program 1.5-1: Single-Channel Polled ADC Reading on PA0 (ADC1_IN0) 

#include <stdint.h>
#include <math.h>

#define V_REF           3.30f       /* Volts */
#define R_FIXED         10000.0f    /* 10k ohm precision pull-up */
#define BETA            3950.0f     /* NTC Beta parameter (Kelvin) */
#define T0_KELVIN       298.15f     /* 25.0 degrees Celsius in Kelvin */
#define R0_THERMISTOR   10000.0f    /* 10k ohm at 25C */

float calculate_temperature_celsius(uint16_t raw_adc) {
    if (raw_adc == 0 || raw_adc >= 4095) return -999.0f; /* Fault */

    /* 1. Convert digital code to analog voltage */
    float v_out = ((float)raw_adc / 4095.0f) * V_REF;

    /* 2. Compute NTC resistance from voltage divider: V_out = V_DD * (R_NTC / (R_FIXED + R_NTC)) */
    float r_ntc = R_FIXED * (v_out / (V_REF - v_out));

    /* 3. Apply Steinhart-Hart Beta formula */
    float inv_t = (1.0f / T0_KELVIN) + (1.0f / BETA) * logf(r_ntc / R0_THERMISTOR);
    float temp_kelvin = 1.0f / inv_t;

    return temp_kelvin - 273.15f; /* Convert Kelvin to Celsius */
}
Program 1.5-2: NTC Thermistor Temperature Calculation via Steinhart-Hart Equation 

#include <stdint.h>

#define NUM_CHANNELS    4
static volatile uint16_t g_adc_buffer[NUM_CHANNELS];

/* Configures ADC1 in Scan Mode with DMA2 Stream 0 in Circular Mode */
void adc_dma_multichannel_init(void) {
    /* 1. Enable clocks for GPIOA, ADC1, DMA2 */
    /* 2. Configure PA0, PA1, PA2, PA3 in Analog Mode */
    /* 3. Configure ADC_CR1: SCAN mode enable */
    /* 4. Configure ADC_CR2: DMA enable, DDS (DMA requests continuous) */
    /* 5. Configure ADC_SQR1: Length = 4 channels */
    /* 6. Configure DMA2_Stream0:
          - Memory base address = &g_adc_buffer[0]
          - Peripheral base address = &ADC1->DR
          - Direction: Peripheral-to-Memory
          - Circular mode, 16-bit halfword transfers
          - Number of items = 4
    */
}
Program 1.5-3: Multi-Channel Autonomous ADC + DMA Data Streaming 

#include <stdint.h>

#define SINE_LUT_POINTS 32
static const uint16_t SINE_LUT[SINE_LUT_POINTS] = {
    2048, 2447, 2831, 3185, 3495, 3750, 3939, 4056,
    4095, 4056, 3939, 3750, 3495, 3185, 2831, 2447,
    2048, 1648, 1264,  910,  600,  345,  156,   39,
       0,   39,  156,  345,  600,  910, 1264, 1648
};

/* Configures TIM6 TRGO to update DAC1 Channel 1 (PA4) via DMA1 Stream 5 */
void dac_sine_init(void) {
    /* TIM6 configured at desired sample rate (e.g., 32 kHz -> 1 kHz output sine) */
    /* DAC configured in DMA trigger mode */
}
Program 1.5-4: DAC Sine Wave Synthesis via Timer TRGO and DMA 

#include <stdint.h>

/* Oversample 16 readings to gain 2 bits of effective resolution (12-bit -> 14-bit)
 * Formula: Oversampling Factor M = 4^k, where k is desired extra bits.
 * For 2 extra bits: M = 4^2 = 16 samples.
 * Resulting sum is right-shifted by k = 2 bits.
 */
uint16_t adc_read_oversampled_14bit(void) {
    uint32_t accumulator = 0;
    
    for (int i = 0; i < 16; i++) {
        /* In real systems, add small analog white dither noise */
        accumulator += adc1_read_single();
    }
    
    /* Decimation: Right shift accumulator by 2 bits */
    return (uint16_t)(accumulator >> 2);
}
Program 1.5-5: Software Oversampling & Decimation for Extended ADC Resolution

ADC Bit Resolution and Electrical Characteristics Comparison

ResolutionTotal Discrete Codes1 LSB at 3.30VTheoretical SNRQuantization Error BandTypical Application Area
8-Bit256 levels12.89 mV49.9 dB+/- 6.45 mVLow-cost battery indicators, coarse potentiometer dials
10-Bit1,024 levels3.22 mV61.9 dB+/- 1.61 mVLegacy 8-bit AVR Arduinos, joystick coordinate tracking
12-Bit4,096 levels0.806 mV74.0 dB+/- 0.403 mVStandard ARM Cortex-M MCUs, industrial 4-20mA current loops
14-Bit (Oversampled)16,384 levels0.201 mV86.0 dB+/- 0.100 mVPrecision thermistor telemetry, calibrated optical power sensors
16-Bit / 24-Bit (Sigma-Delta)65,536+ levels0.050 mV or lower98.0+ dB+/- 0.025 mVMedical ECG instrumentation, precision load cell scales (HX711)

Topic Quiz (10 Questions)

Test your conceptual understanding of today's embedded systems architecture, registers, and runtime behaviors.

1. What is the voltage value of 1 LSB for a 12-bit ADC with a Reference Voltage (VREF+) of 3.30 V?
  • 0.806 mV
  • 3.22 mV
  • 12.89 mV
  • 0.100 mV
1 LSB = 3.30 V / (2^12 - 1) = 3.30 V / 4095 ≈ 0.8058 mV (approx 0.806 mV).
2. How many clock cycles does a Successive Approximation Register (SAR) ADC require to complete a 12-bit conversion (excluding sampling time)?
  • 1 cycle
  • 12 cycles
  • 4096 cycles
  • 64 cycles
A SAR ADC resolves 1 bit per conversion clock cycle using a binary search algorithm. A 12-bit SAR ADC requires exactly 12 conversion clock cycles.
3. According to the Nyquist-Shannon sampling theorem, what is the minimum sampling frequency required to digitize an analog signal containing frequencies up to 4 kHz without aliasing?
  • 2 kHz
  • 4 kHz
  • 8 kHz
  • 16 kHz
The Nyquist criterion states that the sampling rate must be strictly greater than twice the highest frequency component (f_sample >= 2 * f_max = 8 kHz).
4. What is the role of an anti-aliasing low-pass RC filter placed in front of an ADC input pin?
  • To amplify microvolt signals
  • To attenuate frequencies above the Nyquist limit, preventing high-frequency noise from folding back into the digitized signal
  • To double the effective clock frequency
  • To provide galvanic isolation
Frequencies above half the sample rate reflect back into the measurement band as false low-frequency aliases unless eliminated by an analog low-pass filter.
5. To gain 2 additional bits of effective resolution (ENOB) via software oversampling and decimation, how many raw ADC samples must be accumulated?
  • 4 samples
  • 8 samples
  • 16 samples (4^2)
  • 64 samples
Oversampling requires M = 4^k samples, where k is the number of desired extra bits. For k = 2 bits, M = 4^2 = 16 samples.
6. Why is combining ADC Scan Mode with a DMA controller preferred over polling in multi-channel sensor acquisition?
  • DMA eliminates the need for reference voltages
  • DMA moves converted sensor words into SRAM autonomously without burning CPU cycles
  • DMA converts analog signals directly to floating point numbers
  • DMA doubles the sampling speed of silicon
DMA offloads memory transfer from the processor core, allowing multiple channels to be digitized and stored in RAM while the CPU sleeps.
7. What mathematical relationship describes the resistance variation of an NTC thermistor across temperature?
  • Ohm's Linear Law
  • The Steinhart-Hart / Beta Equation
  • Coulomb's Law
  • Faraday's Induction Equation
NTC thermistors exhibit a logarithmic, non-linear resistance decay modeled accurately by the Steinhart-Hart equation or its Beta parameter approximation.
8. What happens if the external source impedance driving an STM32 SAR ADC input pin is too high (> 50k ohm)?
  • The microcontroller resets
  • The internal sampling capacitor cannot charge fully during the sampling window, causing inaccurate, sagging readings
  • The ADC clock stops running
  • The flash memory becomes corrupted
The internal sampling switch connects an internal holding capacitor (~5-10 pF). If source resistance is too high, the RC time constant exceeds the sampling window.
9. What is the primary difference between a true DAC output and a filtered PWM output?
  • A true DAC produces a genuine, low-ripple continuous analog voltage level without high-frequency switching noise
  • A true DAC can only output AC square waves
  • Filtered PWM requires less CPU power than a DAC
  • DAC outputs cannot drive analog circuits
A true DAC uses an internal R-2R ladder or resistor string to generate pure DC voltage levels, avoiding the ripple and slow response of PWM filters.
10. In STM32 microcontrollers, which hardware peripheral event can automatically trigger the start of an ADC conversion without CPU software intervention?
  • Watchdog timeout
  • Timer TRGO (Trigger Output) event
  • Flash wait-state change
  • Brown-out reset
Timer TRGO outputs can be routed internally to trigger ADC conversions synchronously at deterministic sample rates.

Hands-On Assignments

Complete these 5 lab assignments to solidify your hands-on firmware engineering skills.

Assignment 1: Circular Buffer Multi-Channel Sensor Voltage Logger

Task: Configure ADC1 in continuous scan mode across 3 channels (Potentiometer, Thermistor, and Internal Temperature Sensor) using DMA in circular mode. Log 100 sets of samples and compute min/max/average over UART.

Assignment 2: Calibrated NTC Temperature Alarm with Visual LED Warning

Task: Build the NTC thermistor voltage divider circuit. Implement the Steinhart-Hart temperature solver. Light a Green LED when 20C < Temp < 30C, and flash a Red LED when Temp > 35C.

Assignment 3: Audio Waveform Synthesis via DAC + DMA

Task: Generate a 1 kHz audio sine wave using DAC1 and TIM6 TRGO DMA streaming from a 32-point look-up table. View the synthesized waveform on an oscilloscope and verify frequency accuracy.

Assignment 4: Software 16x Oversampling Accuracy Verification

Task: Sample a constant DC reference voltage using standard 12-bit single-conversion mode versus 16x oversampling with decimation. Compute standard deviation across 1,000 readings to quantify SNR improvement.

Assignment 5: Arbitrary Function Generator over UART Shell

Task: Build an arbitrary waveform generator: accept commands over UART ('sine', 'triangle', 'sawtooth', 'square') and update the DAC DMA buffer to synthesize the selected waveform dynamically.
