fields.title: Topic 5: Unit Testing Concepts
fields.content:
Topic 5

Unit Testing Concepts

Historically, embedded firmware testing was performed almost exclusively on physical target boards using flash programmers, logic analyzers, and oscilloscopes. While on-target hardware-in-the-loop (HIL) testing remains vital, relying on physical hardware for every minor code iteration creates crippling development bottlenecks: flashing takes seconds, setting up fault injection is difficult, and automated Continuous Integration (CI) test execution becomes complex and expensive.

Modern embedded engineering adopts the Embedded Testing Pyramid: 80% or more of firmware logic (state machines, ring buffers, communication packet parsers, PID algorithms, sensor filters) is compiled and verified natively on the developer's host workstation using native C unit test frameworks like Unity and CMock.

5.1 The Embedded Testing Pyramid

The embedded testing hierarchy balances execution speed, cost, and fidelity across three distinct layers:

Figure 5.1: The Embedded Software Testing Pyramid
Pyramid Tiers Explained:
  • Host Unit Tests (Unity): Compiled with native GCC/Clang on x86_64 or Apple Silicon. Mocks out hardware registers, executing thousands of test cases in milliseconds.
  • Integration Tests: Validates interactions between drivers, queues, and RTOS scheduler tasks in a simulated or target environment.
  • HIL (Hardware-in-the-Loop): The complete compiled firmware runs on physical silicon, validating crystal oscillator tolerances, ADC impedances, and electrical noise resilience.

5.2 The Unity Test Framework for C

Unity is a lightweight, pure-C testing framework specifically architected for embedded systems. It requires minimal RAM, avoids dynamic memory allocation, and produces clear, actionable test runner output.

A standard Unity test file contains three essential components:

  1. void setUp(void): Executed immediately before every single test function to initialize mock state and reset structures.
  2. void tearDown(void): Executed immediately after every test to clean up state and verify mock expectations.
  3. test_...() functions containing assertions like TEST_ASSERT_EQUAL_UINT32(expected, actual).

5.3 Decoupling Hardware Registers via Mocking

Firmware often fails unit testing because functions directly access silicon registers:
GPIOA->ODR |= (1 << 5);. When compiled on a host PC, this attempts to dereference address 0x40020014, immediately triggering a segmentation fault.

The professional architectural solution is Hardware Abstraction Layer (HAL) separation: business logic talks to interface functions, which are linked to hardware on target builds and linked to mock functions on host test builds.

5.4 Hands-On Code Implementations

The following self-contained implementation demonstrates a robust circular ring buffer paired with a full Unity-style test harness: 

/**
 * Program 5.1: Circular Ring Buffer with Unity-Style Unit Test Harness
 * File: test_ring_buffer.c
 * Target: Host Machine Native Execution (gcc -Wall test_ring_buffer.c)
 */

#include <stdio.h>
#include <stdint.h>
#include <stdbool.h>
#include <stddef.h>

/* ------------------- Production Ring Buffer Module ------------------- */

#define RING_BUF_CAPACITY 8U

typedef struct {
    uint8_t buffer[RING_BUF_CAPACITY];
    size_t  head;
    size_t  tail;
    size_t  count;
} RingBuffer_t;

void ring_buf_init(RingBuffer_t * const rb) {
    if (rb != NULL) {
        rb->head = 0U;
        rb->tail = 0U;
        rb->count = 0U;
    }
}

bool ring_buf_push(RingBuffer_t * const rb, const uint8_t byte) {
    if ((rb == NULL) || (rb->count >= RING_BUF_CAPACITY)) {
        return false; /* Buffer full or null */
    }
    rb->buffer[rb->head] = byte;
    rb->head = (rb->head + 1U) % RING_BUF_CAPACITY;
    rb->count++;
    return true;
}

bool ring_buf_pop(RingBuffer_t * const rb, uint8_t * const byte_out) {
    if ((rb == NULL) || (byte_out == NULL) || (rb->count == 0U)) {
        return false; /* Buffer empty or null */
    }
    *byte_out = rb->buffer[rb->tail];
    rb->tail = (rb->tail + 1U) % RING_BUF_CAPACITY;
    rb->count--;
    return true;
}

/* --------------------- Embedded Test Harness --------------------- */

static uint32_t s_tests_run = 0;
static uint32_t s_tests_passed = 0;
static RingBuffer_t s_test_rb;

#define TEST_ASSERT(cond, msg) \
    do { \
        if (!(cond)) { \
            printf("  [FAIL] Line %d: %s\n", __LINE__, msg); \
            return; \
        } \
    } while (0)

#define RUN_TEST(test_func) \
    do { \
        s_tests_run++; \
        ring_buf_init(&s_test_rb); /* setUp */ \
        printf("Running: %s...", #test_func); \
        test_func(); \
        s_tests_passed++; \
        printf(" PASSED\n"); \
    } while (0)

/* Test Case 1: Initial state after initialization */
void test_ring_buffer_init_is_empty(void) {
    TEST_ASSERT(s_test_rb.count == 0U, "Count should be zero on init");
    uint8_t byte = 0;
    TEST_ASSERT(!ring_buf_pop(&s_test_rb, &byte), "Pop on empty should return false");
}

/* Test Case 2: Push and Pop single byte */
void test_ring_buffer_push_pop_single(void) {
    TEST_ASSERT(ring_buf_push(&s_test_rb, 0x42), "Push should succeed");
    TEST_ASSERT(s_test_rb.count == 1U, "Count should be 1");
    uint8_t popped = 0;
    TEST_ASSERT(ring_buf_pop(&s_test_rb, &popped), "Pop should succeed");
    TEST_ASSERT(popped == 0x42, "Popped value mismatch");
    TEST_ASSERT(s_test_rb.count == 0U, "Buffer should be empty");
}

/* Test Case 3: Capacity overflow rejection */
void test_ring_buffer_overflow_rejected(void) {
    for (uint8_t i = 0; i < RING_BUF_CAPACITY; ++i) {
        TEST_ASSERT(ring_buf_push(&s_test_rb, i), "Push up to capacity must succeed");
    }
    TEST_ASSERT(!ring_buf_push(&s_test_rb, 0xFF), "Pushing past capacity must fail");
    TEST_ASSERT(s_test_rb.count == RING_BUF_CAPACITY, "Count must remain at max capacity");
}

int main(void) {
    printf("=== Starting Ring Buffer Unit Test Suite ===\n");
    RUN_TEST(test_ring_buffer_init_is_empty);
    RUN_TEST(test_ring_buffer_push_pop_single);
    RUN_TEST(test_ring_buffer_overflow_rejected);

    printf("\nTest Summary: %u / %u Passed (100%% Success)\n", s_tests_passed, s_tests_run);
    return (s_tests_passed == s_tests_run) ? 0 : 1;
}
Program 5.1: Circular Ring Buffer with Unity-Style Unit Test Harness

5.5 Buggy vs. Modern Safe Code Comparison

A catastrophic flaw in naive ring buffer implementations is neglecting to validate buffer count before updating indices, causing silent memory overwrite bugs when multiple calls occur.

View Buggy/Legacy Code

This unverified push function has no full-capacity check, overwriting unread data and desynchronizing head and tail indices: 

/* BUGGY: No capacity or pointer check, silent data loss */
void push_byte(uint8_t byte) {
    /* Bug: If buffer is full, head advances past tail and destroys unread data! */
    g_buf[g_head++] = byte;
    if (g_head >= 16) g_head = 0;
}
Program 5.2-A: Unvalidated Buffer Push with Silent Overwrite Hazard

The unit-tested production code rigorously verifies capacity, returns explicit status booleans, and cleanly manages atomic boundaries: 

/* SAFE / TESTED: Strict boundary check, status return */
bool safe_ring_buf_push(RingBuffer_t * const rb, const uint8_t byte) {
    if (rb == NULL) return false;
    if (rb->count >= RING_BUF_CAPACITY) return false; /* Reject overflow */
    
    rb->buffer[rb->head] = byte;
    rb->head = (rb->head + 1U) & (RING_BUF_CAPACITY - 1U);
    rb->count++;
    return true;
}
Program 5.2-B: Unit-Tested Safe Push Implementation

Topic Quiz (10 Questions)

Test your knowledge of host-based unit testing, mocking, and firmware TDD.

1. What is the primary advantage of executing firmware unit tests natively on a host PC rather than on target hardware?
  • Host PCs don't require C compilers.
  • Instant compilation and test execution speed (milliseconds vs seconds), enabling rapid TDD and automated CI pipelines.
  • Host PCs automatically test crystal oscillator tolerances.
  • Host testing eliminates the need for linker scripts.
Host unit testing executes thousands of tests in fractions of a second without waiting for JTAG flashing cycles, supercharging test iteration.
2. In the Unity test framework, what is the role of the 'setUp()' function?
  • To flash the microcontroller over UART.
  • To execute initialization code before every individual test function, ensuring each test begins in a known clean state.
  • To compile the assembly files.
  • To allocate heap memory for the test suite.
setUp() is invoked by Unity immediately prior to running each test case, resetting data structures to prevent inter-test side effects.
3. What is a 'Mock' in embedded unit testing?
  • A joke left in code comments.
  • A simulated replacement for a hardware driver or dependency that verifies how it was called and returns predetermined test responses.
  • A physical prototype PCB.
  • A hardware debugger probe.
Mocks emulate hardware peripherals (like I2C or Flash chips), allowing application logic to be tested thoroughly without physical hardware.
4. Why does direct register access (e.g. GPIOA->ODR = 0x01) cause a segmentation fault when compiled and run on a host PC?
  • Host PCs do not have a C compiler.
  • The physical memory address (e.g. 0x40020014) is invalid or protected in the host OS virtual memory space.
  • The host CPU cannot execute 32-bit instructions.
  • ODR is an illegal variable name on Linux.
Host operating systems enforce virtual memory page protection; dereferencing arbitrary microcontroller hardware addresses causes an instant SIGSEGV crash.
5. What is the fundamental cycle of Test-Driven Development (TDD)?
  • Code -> Flash -> Debug -> Document
  • Red (Write a failing test) -> Green (Write minimal code to pass) -> Refactor (Clean up architecture)
  • Compile -> Link -> Flash -> Ship
  • Plan -> Build -> Deploy -> Patch
TDD follows the Red-Green-Refactor cadence, verifying requirements with failing tests before writing production implementation code.
6. What code coverage metric requires verifying that every branch decision outcome and every Boolean condition within that decision independently affects the outcome?
  • Statement Coverage
  • Function Coverage
  • MC/DC (Modified Condition / Decision Coverage)
  • Line Coverage
MC/DC is required by DO-178C (avionics) and ISO 26262 ASIL D (automotive) for the highest levels of safety criticality.
7. Which tool in the Unity ecosystem automatically generates mock C functions and header stubs from existing interfaces?
  • Gcov
  • CMock
  • Valgrind
  • GDB
CMock parses C header files and automatically synthesizes mock functions capable of verifying expected parameters and returning canned data.
8. What is a 'Stub' in embedded testing?
  • A damaged PCB trace.
  • A simplified dummy implementation of a dependency that returns hardcoded values to satisfy linker requirements during testing.
  • A broken test assertion.
  • A hardware jumper cable.
Stubs provide simple canned return values so that code under test can link and execute without calling real hardware drivers.
9. Which GCC flag enables source code instrumentation to generate test execution coverage metrics (.gcda / .gcno files)?
  • -O3
  • --coverage (or -fprofile-arcs -ftest-coverage)
  • -Werror
  • -nostdlib
`--coverage` instructs GCC to emit branch and line execution counters, analyzed by gcov or lcov to generate coverage reports.
10. Why is achieving 100% statement coverage insufficient on its own to guarantee bug-free firmware?
  • Statement coverage only applies to C++ code.
  • Statement coverage does not test untested branch paths, missing edge cases (e.g. null inputs or buffer boundaries), or concurrency race conditions.
  • Compilers invert statement coverage calculations.
  • Statement coverage increases binary size.
Executing every line once does not verify what happens when conditions evaluate false, when boundary values are passed, or when timing interrupts interleave.

Hands-On Assignments

Execute these 5 laboratory assignments to build automated unit test suites for firmware components.

Assignment 1: Test-Driven Ring Buffer Development

Task: Clone or implement the Unity test harness. Write unit tests for a circular buffer verifying: (1) empty status on init, (2) push and pop FIFO sequence integrity, (3) wrap-around behavior across array bounds, and (4) rejection of null output pointers. Execute tests natively on your host PC with GCC.

Assignment 2: Hardware Register Mocking

Task: Create an abstract LED driver interface: led_set_state(led_id, state). Write a mock implementation on host PC that logs state changes into an array. Author unit tests verifying that an alert subsystem turns ON the warning LED when temperature exceeds 80 degrees.

Assignment 3: Code Coverage Analysis with Gcov

Task: Compile your unit test suite with gcc --coverage. Execute the test suite and run gcov. Inspect the annotated source file (.gcov) to identify any branches or defensive error checks that were never exercised. Add unit tests to achieve 100% branch coverage.

Assignment 4: State Machine Test Harness

Task: Design a 3-state connection finite-state machine (DISCONNECTED, CONNECTING, CONNECTED). Write unit tests verifying all valid transitions. Then write tests feeding unexpected events (e.g. timeout event while DISCONNECTED) to verify the state machine rejects illegal transitions gracefully.

Assignment 5: Packet Parser Fuzzing Test

Task: Implement a binary packet frame parser that validates a start-of-frame byte (0xAA), length byte, payload, and XOR checksum. Write an automated test feeder that generates 10,000 randomized corrupt byte streams. Verify that the parser never triggers a segmentation fault or buffer overflow.

Official References, Research Papers & Standards

Deepen your engineering foundation with canonical publications and official standard specifications:

Classic Textbook James W. Grenning

Test-Driven Development for Embedded C

The definitive guide to applying TDD, unit testing frameworks (Unity, CppUTest), and mocking to embedded software engineering.

View Official Resource →
Testing Framework ThrowTheSwitch.org

Unity: Embedded C Unit Testing Framework

Lightweight, portable C testing framework designed specifically for microcontrollers and safety-critical projects.

View Official Resource →
Aerospace Standard RTCA / EUROCAE

DO-178C: Software Considerations in Airborne Systems

International standard establishing verification, unit test, and structural coverage requirements (including MC/DC) for flight software.

fields.title: Day 7: UART, SPI & I2C Communication
fields.content:
Session 1.6

Day 7: UART, SPI & I2C Communication

Problem Statement: Sensors, displays, and host computers must exchange data reliably across printed circuit boards and cable harnesses. UART, SPI, and I2C each resolve trade-offs between wire count, clock speed, full-duplex concurrency, and multi-drop topologies. How do you implement and troubleshoot these foundational serial communication protocols from bare-metal registers?
📋 Daily Plan & Learning Architecture
Session 1.6 Module 1: Embedded C Foundations Estimated: 3.5 hrs

🎯 Today's Mission & Relevance

  • Master asynchronous UART framing, baud rate generation, and printf retargeting.
  • Implement high-speed 4-wire synchronous SPI Master drivers for Flash and sensors.
  • Understand I2C open-drain electrical dynamics, multi-drop addressing, and bus arbitration.

📐 Theoretical Milestones

  • Baud rate timing tolerances and oversampling clock recovery.
  • SPI Clock Polarity (CPOL) and Clock Phase (CPHA) operating modes 0-3.
  • I2C START/STOP conditions, 7-bit addressing, ACK/NACK signaling, and clock stretching.

💻 Hands-On Blueprint

  • Program 7.1: Bare-metal polled USART2 driver at 115200 baud.
  • Program 7.2: printf() redirection via Newlib C library _write() hook.
  • Program 7.3: SPI master Flash driver reading W25Q32 JEDEC device ID.
  • Program 7.4: I2C sensor communication reading BMP280 barometric chip registers.
  • Program 7.5: High-throughput UART transmission via DMA with TC interrupt.

🛡️ Production Failure Modes

  • Omitting external pull-up resistors on I2C bus, causing permanent line low lockup.
  • Selecting incorrect SPI CPOL/CPHA mode, resulting in shifted or inverted bit data.
  • Blocking CPU cores with polled UART writes instead of using DMA buffering.
🏁 Daily Milestone Deliverables: 5 Interactive Register-Level Programs • 5 Architecture Diagrams • 10 Practice MCQs • 5 Hands-On Assignments

7.1 Serial Communication in Embedded Systems

Microcontrollers cannot operate in isolation: they must stream telemetry to host computers, interrogate environmental sensor arrays, display graphics on LCD screens, and exchange packets with wireless modems. The three canonical embedded serial protocols are UART (Universal Asynchronous Receiver/Transmitter), SPI (Serial Peripheral Interface), and I2C (Inter-Integrated Circuit). Each protocol resolves trade-offs between wire count, transmission speed, bus topology, and silicon complexity.

Real World Example: In a modern quadcopter drone, the STM32 flight controller communicates simultaneously across all three buses: UART streams GPS NMEA coordinates and telemetries to the radio link at 115200 baud; SPI samples a 6-axis IMU gyro/accelerometer at 8 MHz for sub-millisecond PID stabilization; and I2C reads an external magnetic compass and barometric altimeter at 400 kHz over a shared 2-wire bus.
Figure 1.6-1: UART Asynchronous Frame Structure and Timing
Figure Parameters Explained:
  • Start Bit (Logic 0): Signals receiver hardware to synchronize its internal clock counter to the incoming frame.
  • Baud Rate Formula: Bit Duration = 1 / Baud Rate. At 115200 baud, each bit lasts exactly 8.68 microseconds.
  • Oversampling Receiver: Receivers sample each incoming bit 8x or 16x per bit period, taking majority votes at sample counts 7, 8, and 9 to reject line noise.
  • Clock Drift Tolerance: Asynchronous framing requires sender and receiver crystal clocks to match within +/- 2.5% to avoid bit slip errors.

7.2 SPI: Synchronous 4-Wire Master-Slave Protocol

SPI (Serial Peripheral Interface) is a high-speed, full-duplex, synchronous serial bus developed by Motorola. It utilizes four physical lines:

  • SCLK (Serial Clock): Driven exclusively by the Master device.
  • MOSI (Master Out, Slave In): Data transmission from Master to Slave.
  • MISO (Master In, Slave Out): Data transmission from Slave to Master.
  • CS / SS (Chip Select / Slave Select): Active-LOW line asserted by Master to address a specific slave on the bus.

SPI clocking is governed by two parameters: CPOL (Clock Polarity) and CPHA (Clock Phase), forming 4 distinct operating modes (Mode 0 through Mode 3).

Figure 1.6-2: SPI 4-Wire Topology and CPOL / CPHA Clock Timing Modes
Figure Parameters Explained:
  • CPOL = 0 / 1: Defines idle clock level: 0 = SCLK idles LOW; 1 = SCLK idles HIGH.
  • CPHA = 0 / 1: Defines capture edge: 0 = data sampled on first clock transition; 1 = data sampled on second transition.
  • High Throughput: SPI easily achieves 20 MHz to 80 MHz clock speeds, making it ideal for SPI Flash, SD cards, and TFT displays.
  • Independent Chip Selects: Adding multiple slaves requires a dedicated GPIO CS line per slave device.

7.3 I2C: Synchronous 2-Wire Multi-Device Bus with Open-Drain Architecture

Invented by Philips (now NXP), I2C (Inter-Integrated Circuit) reduces bus wiring to just two lines: SDA (Serial Data) and SCL (Serial Clock). Both lines operate in Open-Drain mode with external pull-up resistors to VDD. Key I2C protocol rules include:

  • START Condition: SDA transitions HIGH to LOW while SCL remains HIGH.
  • STOP Condition: SDA transitions LOW to HIGH while SCL remains HIGH.
  • Data Validity: SDA must remain stable while SCL is HIGH; SDA may only change when SCL is LOW.
  • ACK / NACK: Following every 8-bit byte transfer, the receiving device must pull SDA LOW during the 9th clock pulse to acknowledge receipt (ACK).
  • 7-Bit Device Addressing: The first byte transmitted by the Master contains the 7-bit slave address and bit 0 indicating Read ($1$) or Write ($0$).
Figure 1.6-3: I2C Bus Electrical Architecture and Packet Protocol Frame
Figure Parameters Explained:
  • Open-Drain + Pull-Ups: Enables wired-AND bus arbitration without short circuits when multiple nodes pull lines LOW.
  • ACK (Logic 0): Receiver pulls SDA LOW during 9th clock to confirm byte reception.
  • NACK (Logic 1): SDA remains HIGH (released to pull-up), signaling byte rejection or end of multi-byte read.
  • Bus Speed Grades: Standard Mode (100 kbps), Fast Mode (400 kbps), Fast Mode Plus (1 Mbps), High Speed (3.4 Mbps).

7.4 I2C Multi-Master Arbitration and Clock Stretching

Because I2C pins are open-drain, multiple master devices can share the same bus. When two masters transmit simultaneously, Non-Destructive Bus Arbitration occurs: both monitor SDA while transmitting. The first master attempting to send a 1 that reads back a 0 (because the other master drove a dominant 0) immediately detects that it lost arbitration, gracefully yielding the bus without corrupting the winning master's frame.

Additionally, slow slave devices can execute Clock Stretching by holding the SCL line LOW, temporarily pausing the master until the slave finishes internal processing.

Figure 1.6-4: I2C Multi-Master Bus Arbitration on Open-Drain SDA Line
Figure Parameters Explained:
  • Dominant State (0): Actively driven to ground by internal N-MOS transistor; overrides recessive state.
  • Recessive State (1): Line pulled HIGH by external resistor; can be pulled down by any other connected device.
  • Clock Stretching: Slave pulls SCL LOW to insert hardware wait-states while preparing data.
  • Bus Lockup Condition: If a slave crashes while pulling SDA LOW, the bus hangs; masters must toggle SCL 9 times to force a reset.

7.5 High-Throughput Serial Communication with DMA & printf Retargeting

Transmitting a 128-byte log message over UART at 115200 baud via software polling takes approximately 11 milliseconds—equivalent to nearly 2 million lost CPU cycles on a 168 MHz processor. By retargeting standard C library printf() functions through a circular UART DMA Controller, the processor initiates transmission in a single cycle and continues executing application tasks while DMA hardware streams bytes out the serial port.

Figure 1.6-5: UART DMA Streaming Pipeline vs. Polling Overhead
Figure Parameters Explained:
  • USART_DR to Memory DMA: Transfers bytes from RAM to transmit data register automatically as TXE flags assert.
  • Retargeting _write(): Newlib syscall hook that intercepts standard C library printf() and routes characters to UART.
  • Transfer Complete (TC) ISR: Fires only when the entire multi-byte buffer has completely cleared the UART shift register.

7.6 Hands-On Code Implementations


#include <stdint.h>

#define RCC_AHB1ENR     (*(volatile uint32_t *)0x40023830UL)
#define RCC_APB1ENR     (*(volatile uint32_t *)0x40023840UL)

#define GPIOA_MODER     (*(volatile uint32_t *)0x40020000UL)
#define GPIOA_AFRL      (*(volatile uint32_t *)0x40020020UL)

#define USART2_BASE     0x40004400UL
#define USART2_SR       (*(volatile uint32_t *)(USART2_BASE + 0x00UL))
#define USART2_DR       (*(volatile uint32_t *)(USART2_BASE + 0x04UL))
#define USART2_BRR      (*(volatile uint32_t *)(USART2_BASE + 0x08UL))
#define USART2_CR1      (*(volatile uint32_t *)(USART2_BASE + 0x0CUL))

/* Initialize USART2 on PA2 (TX) at 115200 baud (assuming 16 MHz APB1 clock) */
void usart2_init_115200(void) {
    /* 1. Enable clocks for GPIOA and USART2 */
    RCC_AHB1ENR |= (1UL << 0);
    RCC_APB1ENR |= (1UL << 17);

    /* 2. Configure PA2 as Alternate Function AF7 (MODER2 = 0b10) */
    GPIOA_MODER &= ~(3UL << 4);
    GPIOA_MODER |= (2UL << 4);
    GPIOA_AFRL &= ~(0xFUL << 8);
    GPIOA_AFRL |= (0x7UL << 8); /* AF7 = USART2_TX */

    /* 3. Configure Baud Rate: BRR = 16,000,000 / (16 * 115200) = 8.6805
          Mantissa = 8, Fraction = 0.6805 * 16 = 11 (0x8B) */
    USART2_BRR = 0x008B;

    /* 4. Enable Transmitter (TE) and USART peripheral (UE) */
    USART2_CR1 |= (1UL << 3) | (1UL << 13);
}

void uart2_send_char(char c) {
    /* Wait until Transmit Data Register Empty (TXE) flag is set */
    while (!(USART2_SR & (1UL << 7))) {
        /* Wait */
    }
    USART2_DR = (uint32_t)c;
}

void uart2_send_string(const char *str) {
    while (*str) {
        uart2_send_char(*str++);
    }
}
Program 1.6-1: Bare-Metal Polled UART Transmit Driver (USART2 @ 115200 Baud) 

#include <stdint.h>
#include <stdio.h>

void uart2_send_char(char c);

/* Retarget low-level Newlib system call to route printf output to UART */
int _write(int file, char *ptr, int len) {
    (void)file;
    for (int i = 0; i < len; i++) {
        /* Handle Unix newline to DOS CRLF conversion */
        if (ptr[i] == '\n') {
            uart2_send_char('\r');
        }
        uart2_send_char(ptr[i]);
    }
    return len;
}

void demo_printf(void) {
    uint32_t sensor_val = 1024;
    float voltage = 3.3f;
    printf("Telemetry Log: Sensor Raw = %lu, Voltage = %.2f V\n", sensor_val, voltage);
}
Program 1.6-2: Retargeting standard printf() via Newlib _write() Implementation 

#include <stdint.h>

#define SPI1_BASE       0x40013000UL
#define SPI1_CR1        (*(volatile uint32_t *)(SPI1_BASE + 0x00UL))
#define SPI1_SR         (*(volatile uint32_t *)(SPI1_BASE + 0x08UL))
#define SPI1_DR         (*(volatile uint32_t *)(SPI1_BASE + 0x0CUL))

#define GPIOA_BSRR      (*(volatile uint32_t *)0x40020018UL)
#define CS_PIN          4 /* PA4 as Software Chip Select */

static inline void spi_cs_low(void)  { GPIOA_BSRR = (1UL << (CS_PIN + 16)); }
static inline void spi_cs_high(void) { GPIOA_BSRR = (1UL << CS_PIN); }

uint8_t spi1_transfer(uint8_t tx_data) {
    /* Wait until TX buffer empty (TXE) */
    while (!(SPI1_SR & (1UL << 1)));
    SPI1_DR = tx_data;

    /* Wait until RX buffer full (RXNE) */
    while (!(SPI1_SR & (1UL << 0)));
    return (uint8_t)SPI1_DR;
}

/* Read 3-byte JEDEC Manufacturer and Device ID (0x9F command) */
uint32_t read_flash_jedec_id(void) {
    spi_cs_low();
    
    spi1_transfer(0x9F); /* JEDEC ID command */
    uint8_t mfg_id  = spi1_transfer(0x00); /* Manufacturer (0xEF for Winbond) */
    uint8_t mem_type = spi1_transfer(0x00); /* Memory Type */
    uint8_t capacity = spi1_transfer(0x00); /* Capacity (0x16 for 32Mb / 4MB) */
    
    spi_cs_high();
    
    return ((uint32_t)mfg_id << 16) | ((uint32_t)mem_type << 8) | capacity;
}
Program 1.6-3: SPI Master Flash Read: Reading JEDEC ID from W25Q32 

#include <stdint.h>
#include <stdbool.h>

#define I2C1_BASE       0x40005400UL
#define I2C1_CR1        (*(volatile uint32_t *)(I2C1_BASE + 0x00UL))
#define I2C1_CR2        (*(volatile uint32_t *)(I2C1_BASE + 0x04UL))
#define I2C1_DR         (*(volatile uint32_t *)(I2C1_BASE + 0x10UL))
#define I2C1_SR1        (*(volatile uint32_t *)(I2C1_BASE + 0x14UL))
#define I2C1_SR2        (*(volatile uint32_t *)(I2C1_BASE + 0x18UL))

#define BMP280_I2C_ADDR 0x76 /* 7-bit slave address */

/* Read single register from I2C slave */
uint8_t i2c_read_reg(uint8_t dev_addr, uint8_t reg_addr) {
    /* 1. Generate START condition */
    I2C1_CR1 |= (1UL << 8);
    while (!(I2C1_SR1 & (1UL << 0))); /* Wait for SB flag */

    /* 2. Send 7-bit Address with Write bit (0) */
    I2C1_DR = (dev_addr << 1);
    while (!(I2C1_SR1 & (1UL << 1))); /* Wait for ADDR flag */
    (void)I2C1_SR2; /* Clear ADDR by reading SR2 */

    /* 3. Send target register address */
    I2C1_DR = reg_addr;
    while (!(I2C1_SR1 & (1UL << 2))); /* Wait for BTF (Byte Transfer Finished) */

    /* 4. Repeated START for read */
    I2C1_CR1 |= (1UL << 8);
    while (!(I2C1_SR1 & (1UL << 0)));

    /* 5. Send 7-bit Address with Read bit (1) */
    I2C1_DR = (dev_addr << 1) | 1;
    while (!(I2C1_SR1 & (1UL << 1)));
    
    /* Disable ACK before reading single byte, generate STOP */
    I2C1_CR1 &= ~(1UL << 10);
    (void)I2C1_SR2;
    I2C1_CR1 |= (1UL << 9); /* STOP */

    while (!(I2C1_SR1 & (1UL << 6))); /* Wait for RXNE */
    return (uint8_t)I2C1_DR;
}
Program 1.6-4: I2C Sensor Interface: Reading BMP280 Barometer Chip ID 

#include <stdint.h>

#define DMA1_STREAM6_BASE   0x400260A0UL
#define DMA_SxCR(base)      (*(volatile uint32_t *)(base + 0x00UL))
#define DMA_SxNDTR(base)    (*(volatile uint32_t *)(base + 0x04UL))
#define DMA_SxPAR(base)     (*(volatile uint32_t *)(base + 0x08UL))
#define DMA_SxM0AR(base)    (*(volatile uint32_t *)(base + 0x0CUL))

void uart2_dma_transmit(const uint8_t *data, uint16_t length) {
    /* 1. Disable DMA stream to allow configuration */
    DMA_SxCR(DMA1_STREAM6_BASE) &= ~(1UL << 0);
    while (DMA_SxCR(DMA1_STREAM6_BASE) & (1UL << 0));

    /* 2. Set peripheral address to USART2->DR */
    DMA_SxPAR(DMA1_STREAM6_BASE) = 0x40004404UL;

    /* 3. Set memory buffer address and transfer length */
    DMA_SxM0AR(DMA1_STREAM6_BASE) = (uint32_t)data;
    DMA_SxNDTR(DMA1_STREAM6_BASE) = length;

    /* 4. Configure DMA: Channel 4, Memory Increment, Memory-to-Peripheral, TC Interrupt */
    DMA_SxCR(DMA1_STREAM6_BASE) = (4UL << 25) | (1UL << 10) | (1UL << 6) | (1UL << 4);

    /* 5. Enable DMA stream to begin transmission */
    DMA_SxCR(DMA1_STREAM6_BASE) |= (1UL << 0);
}
Program 1.6-5: High-Throughput UART Transmit via DMA with TC Interrupt

UART vs. SPI vs. I2C Serial Protocol Architectural Comparison

Metric / FeatureUART / USARTSPI (Serial Peripheral Interface)I2C (Inter-Integrated Circuit)
Physical Wires2 wires (TX, RX)4 wires (SCLK, MOSI, MISO, CS)2 wires (SDA, SCL)
Maximum SpeedUp to 10 Mbps (typically 115.2 kbps)Up to 80+ Mbps100 kbps, 400 kbps, 1 Mbps, 3.4 Mbps
Communication ModeAsynchronous, Full-DuplexSynchronous, Full-DuplexSynchronous, Half-Duplex
Bus TopologyPoint-to-Point (1 to 1)Master-Multi-Slave (dedicated CS lines)Multi-Master, Multi-Slave (shared 2-wire bus)
Addressing MechanismNone (Direct point-to-point)Hardware Chip Select line per slaveSoftware 7-bit or 10-bit address field
Hardware OverheadMedium (Baud clock recovery logic)Low (Simple shift registers)Medium (Open-drain buffers & arbitration logic)
Typical Use Cases
  • GPS receivers
  • Bluetooth / Cellular modems
  • Debug console shells
  • High-speed SPI Flash
  • SD card mass storage
  • Color TFT LCD displays
  • Temperature / Humidity sensors
  • RTC chips
  • EEPROM configuration memory

Topic Quiz (10 Questions)

Test your conceptual understanding of today's embedded systems architecture, registers, and runtime behaviors.

1. What is the primary function of the Start bit (Logic 0) in an asynchronous UART data frame?
  • To charge the receiver decoupling capacitors
  • To synchronize the receiver's internal bit-sampling clock to the incoming frame
  • To transmit the device hardware address
  • To clear the parity error flag
Because UART has no shared clock wire, the falling edge of the Start bit alerts the receiver to synchronize its oversampling timer.
2. In SPI communication, what does the configuration `CPOL = 0, CPHA = 1` define?
  • Clock idles LOW, data is captured on the second (falling) clock edge
  • Clock idles HIGH, data is captured on the first clock edge
  • Clock idles LOW, data is captured on the first (rising) clock edge
  • Clock idles HIGH, data is captured on the second clock edge
CPOL=0 means SCLK idles LOW. CPHA=1 specifies that data is sampled on the second clock transition (falling edge).
3. Why are external pull-up resistors mandatory on I2C SDA and SCL bus lines?
  • To protect against electrostatic discharge (ESD)
  • Because I2C pins operate in Open-Drain mode and can only pull the lines LOW, requiring resistors to pull HIGH
  • To step down 5V signals to 3.3V
  • To prevent high-frequency reflections on long cables
I2C drivers are open-drain (N-MOS only). They pull lines to ground (0) or float (Hi-Z). External pull-ups are required to pull lines to VDD (1).
4. How does an I2C slave acknowledge successful reception of an 8-bit data byte from the master?
  • By transmitting an ASCII 'OK' string
  • By pulling the SDA line LOW (ACK) during the 9th SCL clock pulse
  • By holding SCL LOW for 5 milliseconds
  • By asserting an external interrupt pin
During the 9th clock cycle, the master releases SDA and the receiver pulls SDA LOW to indicate ACK (0 = ACK, 1 = NACK).
5. What occurs during I2C multi-master arbitration if Master A transmits a 1 while Master B transmits a 0 on SDA?
  • A short-circuit condition destroys both transmitters
  • Master B drives the line LOW; Master A detects the collision, yields the bus, and Master B continues without error
  • The bus controller asserts a HardFault on both processors
  • Both masters immediately abort transmission and generate STOP conditions
In wired-AND open-drain logic, 0 dominates 1. Master A sees that it attempted to output a 1 but the line remained 0, detecting arbitration loss gracefully.
6. What is 'Clock Stretching' in the I2C protocol specification?
  • A method of overclocking the bus to 10 Mbps
  • An action where a slow slave pulls SCL LOW to pause the master while it processes data
  • A technique to reduce power by lowering the master PLL clock
  • An error condition caused by missing pull-up resistors
If a slave cannot keep up with master clocking, it holds SCL LOW. The master senses this and waits until the slave releases SCL before continuing.
7. Why is using UART with DMA vastly superior to polling for sending telemetry strings?
  • DMA automatically encrypts data packets
  • DMA transfers data from memory to the UART register autonomously, leaving 100% of CPU cycles free for other tasks
  • DMA doubles the baud rate of the UART transmitter
  • DMA eliminates the need for Start and Stop bits
Polling wastes millions of CPU cycles waiting for TXE flags. DMA streams entire buffers byte-by-byte in hardware without CPU involvement.
8. Which system call function in Newlib C library must be implemented to retarget `printf()` to a UART serial port?
  • _read()
  • _write()
  • _sbrk()
  • _exit()
Standard C runtime implementations route stdout through the low-level `_write(int fd, char *buf, int len)` syscall hook.
9. What is the standard JEDEC instruction byte sent over SPI to read manufacturer and memory density information from an SPI Flash chip?
  • 0x06 (Write Enable)
  • 0x03 (Read Data)
  • 0x9F (Read JEDEC ID)
  • 0xC7 (Chip Erase)
The JEDEC standard command 0x9F prompts all compliant SPI NOR flash devices (Winbond, Macronix, Micron) to return manufacturer, type, and capacity bytes.
10. If an I2C slave becomes desynchronized and locks the SDA line LOW indefinitely, how can the master recover the bus?
  • By generating an immediate STOP condition
  • By clocking the SCL line manually 9 times to force the slave to release SDA, then issuing a STOP condition
  • By shorting VDD to ground
  • By increasing the pull-up resistor values
Manually pulsing SCL up to 9 times gives the stuck slave enough clocks to finish sending its pending byte and release SDA.

Hands-On Assignments

Complete these 5 lab assignments to solidify your hands-on firmware engineering skills.

Assignment 1: Interactive UART Command-Line Shell Interpreter

Task: Build a responsive CLI over UART at 115200 baud. Implement an input line buffer parsing commands: 'led on', 'led off', 'temp', and 'status'. Handle backspaces and newline formatting gracefully.

Assignment 2: Automatic 7-Bit I2C Bus Address Scanner

Task: Write an I2C scanner that queries all 128 valid 7-bit addresses (0x00 to 0x7F). Check for slave ACK responses and print a formatted ASCII grid table of all detected peripherals to UART.

Assignment 3: SPI Flash Memory Identification and Sector Erase

Task: Connect a W25Q32 or similar SPI NOR flash. Write functions to read the 3-byte JEDEC ID, erase a 4 KB sector, program a 256-byte text string, and read it back to verify data retention across power cycles.

Assignment 4: Multi-Sensor BMP280 + MPU6050 Shared I2C Bus Driver

Task: Interface both a BMP280 pressure sensor (0x76) and an MPU-6050 accelerometer (0x68) on the exact same I2C bus pins. Read acceleration and barometric pressure alternately every 50 ms without bus collisions.

Assignment 5: UART RX DMA Circular Ring Buffer Engine

Task: Implement an asynchronous UART receiver using DMA in circular mode. Detect incoming line boundaries without polling using the UART Idle Line Detection (IDLE) interrupt to trigger packet parsing.

Official References, Research Papers & Standards

Deepen your engineering foundations with seminal reference manuals, processor architecture standards, and industry specifications:

Protocol Standard NXP Semiconductors

UM10204: I2C-Bus Specification and User Manual

The definitive international standard specification for I2C and SMBus protocols, detailing bus timings, open-drain electrical characteristics, and arbitration rules.

View Official Resource →
Hardware Standard Motorola / FreeScale

SPI Block Guide V04.01

Foundational technical paper defining the 4-wire serial peripheral interface, CPOL and CPHA clock phase definitions, and full-duplex shift register architectures.

View Official Resource →
Software Engineering Guide ARM Ltd.

Retargeting C Library I/O Functions to Serial Devices

Developer reference guide for implementing Newlib and ARM Compiler C runtime standard I/O hooks for printf redirection.

fields.title: Module 1 Project: C Foundations, Safety & Diagnostics
fields.content:
Module 1 Capstone Project

C Foundations, Safety & Hardware Diagnostics

Having mastered the foundational pillars of Embedded C—fixed-width types, memory boundaries, common compiler traps, assertions, defensive logging, and unit testing—it is time to consolidate this knowledge. This milestone features two complete, standalone engineering projects: one optimized for host simulation on Linux/WSL using GCC, sanitizers, and Unity; and one deployed bare-metal on an STM32 microcontroller using direct register access and hardware-level panic diagnostics.

Dimension Project 1: Linux / WSL Environment Project 2: Physical STM32 Board
Project Focus Safe Telemetry Packet Decoder & Assert Test Suite Bare-Metal Diagnostic Assert & LED Morse Blink Engine
Hardware / Target x86_64 / aarch64 Host Terminal (GCC, Valgrind, ASan) STM32F4 (Nucleo-F401RE / F411RE) or STM32F103 (BluePill)
Curriculum Synergy Fixed-width types, bitwise unpacking, endianness, Unity tests Volatile register pointers, hardware panic loops, zero-HAL GPIO
Verification Method Automated Unity test harness, AddressSanitizer runtime checks Logic analyzer / oscilloscope on LED pin, SWD GDB registers

Part 1: Linux / WSL Project — Safe Telemetry Packet Decoder

In distributed embedded systems (automotive CAN, avionics ARINC, IoT MQTT), sensor nodes transmit serialized binary frames over raw serial channels. A fundamental embedded programming skill is decoding packed frames into typed C structs safely—without buffer overruns, endianness bugs, or undefined behavior.

System Architecture & Frame Specification

The host simulator decodes binary packets structured according to a strict communication protocol:

[0xAA] [0x55] | [Msg_ID: 1B] | [Payload_Len: 1B] | [Data: N Bytes (Max 32)] | [CRC16: 2B (Little Endian)]
  • Sync Bytes: 0xAA, 0x55 (Must match or frame is rejected immediately).
  • Message ID: 0x01 (Battery Status), 0x02 (IMU Attitude), 0x03 (Motor Faults).
  • Payload Length: 1 to 32 bytes. Any length exceeding 32 triggers a length violation assert.
  • Data Integrity: CCITT-CRC16 checksum across Header + Payload bytes.

Step 1: Header Definition (telemetry.h)

Strict use of <stdint.h>, <stdbool.h>, defensive error codes, and macro assertions: 

/**
 * @file telemetry.h
 * @brief Defensive Telemetry Frame Decoder Interface
 */
#ifndef TELEMETRY_H
#define TELEMETRY_H

#include <stdint.h>
#include <stdbool.h>
#include <stddef.h>

#define TELEMETRY_SYNC_BYTE1      0xAAU
#define TELEMETRY_SYNC_BYTE2      0x55U
#define TELEMETRY_MAX_PAYLOAD_LEN 32U
#define TELEMETRY_MIN_FRAME_LEN   6U  /* 2 sync + 1 id + 1 len + 2 crc */

typedef enum {
    TELEM_OK = 0,
    TELEM_ERR_NULL_PTR,
    TELEM_ERR_FRAME_TOO_SHORT,
    TELEM_ERR_BAD_SYNC,
    TELEM_ERR_INVALID_LENGTH,
    TELEM_ERR_CRC_MISMATCH,
    TELEM_ERR_UNKNOWN_MSG_ID
} telem_status_t;

typedef struct {
    uint8_t  msg_id;
    uint8_t  payload_len;
    uint8_t  payload[TELEMETRY_MAX_PAYLOAD_LEN];
    uint16_t crc16;
} telem_frame_t;

/* Defensive Assertion with Return Code */
#define EMB_ASSERT_RETURN(cond, err_code) \
    do { \
        if (!(cond)) { \
            return (err_code); \
        } \
    } while (0)

/* API Prototypes */
uint16_t telem_compute_crc16(const uint8_t *data, size_t length);
telem_status_t telem_decode_frame(const uint8_t *raw_buf, size_t buf_len, telem_frame_t *out_frame);

#endif /* TELEMETRY_H */

Step 2: Robust Implementation (telemetry.c)

This decoder checks all boundaries before pointer dereferencing, calculates CRC16 dynamically, and unpacks multi-byte integers using explicit byte shifts (endian-neutral): 

/**
 * @file telemetry.c
 * @brief Defensive Frame Decoder Implementation
 */
#include "telemetry.h"

uint16_t telem_compute_crc16(const uint8_t *data, size_t length) {
    if (data == NULL || length == 0U) {
        return 0U;
    }
    uint16_t crc = 0xFFFFU;
    for (size_t i = 0; i < length; i++) {
        crc ^= (uint16_t)data[i];
        for (uint8_t bit = 0; bit < 8U; bit++) {
            if ((crc & 0x0001U) != 0U) {
                crc = (crc >> 1U) ^ 0x8408U; /* Reversed CCITT polynomial */
            } else {
                crc = crc >> 1U;
            }
        }
    }
    return crc;
}

telem_status_t telem_decode_frame(const uint8_t *raw_buf, size_t buf_len, telem_frame_t *out_frame) {
    EMB_ASSERT_RETURN(raw_buf != NULL, TELEM_ERR_NULL_PTR);
    EMB_ASSERT_RETURN(out_frame != NULL, TELEM_ERR_NULL_PTR);
    EMB_ASSERT_RETURN(buf_len >= TELEMETRY_MIN_FRAME_LEN, TELEM_ERR_FRAME_TOO_SHORT);

    /* 1. Verify Synchronization Header */
    if ((raw_buf[0] != TELEMETRY_SYNC_BYTE1) || (raw_buf[1] != TELEMETRY_SYNC_BYTE2)) {
        return TELEM_ERR_BAD_SYNC;
    }

    uint8_t msg_id = raw_buf[2];
    uint8_t payload_len = raw_buf[3];

    /* 2. Validate Payload Length */
    if (payload_len > TELEMETRY_MAX_PAYLOAD_LEN) {
        return TELEM_ERR_INVALID_LENGTH;
    }

    /* 3. Check Full Frame Length Boundary */
    size_t expected_total_len = 4U + (size_t)payload_len + 2U;
    if (buf_len < expected_total_len) {
        return TELEM_ERR_FRAME_TOO_SHORT;
    }

    /* 4. Extract Checksum (Little-Endian) */
    size_t crc_idx = 4U + (size_t)payload_len;
    uint16_t expected_crc = (uint16_t)raw_buf[crc_idx] | ((uint16_t)raw_buf[crc_idx + 1U] << 8U);

    /* 5. Compute CRC over Header & Payload */
    uint16_t calc_crc = telem_compute_crc16(&raw_buf[2], 2U + (size_t)payload_len);
    if (calc_crc != expected_crc) {
        return TELEM_ERR_CRC_MISMATCH;
    }

    /* 6. Populate Output Frame */
    out_frame->msg_id = msg_id;
    out_frame->payload_len = payload_len;
    out_frame->crc16 = expected_crc;
    for (uint8_t i = 0; i < payload_len; i++) {
        out_frame->payload[i] = raw_buf[4U + i];
    }

    return TELEM_OK;
}

Step 3: Automated Unit Test Suite (test_telemetry.c)

Writing tests for edge cases: null pointers, corrupted sync headers, truncated payloads, and CRC injection errors. 

/**
 * @file test_telemetry.c
 * @brief Host-Based Regression Suite using Unity
 */
#include <stdio.h>
#include <string.h>
#include <assert.h>
#include "telemetry.h"

/* Lightweight Host Test Harness */
static int tests_run = 0;
static int tests_passed = 0;

#define TEST_ASSERT(expr, msg) do { \
    tests_run++; \
    if (expr) { \
        tests_passed++; \
        printf("  [PASS] %s\n", msg); \
    } else { \
        printf("  [FAIL] %s (Line %d)\n", msg, __LINE__); \
    } \
} while(0)

void test_null_pointers(void) {
    telem_frame_t frame;
    uint8_t buf[16] = {0xAA, 0x55, 0x01, 0x01, 0x42, 0x00, 0x00};
    
    TEST_ASSERT(telem_decode_frame(NULL, sizeof(buf), &frame) == TELEM_ERR_NULL_PTR, "Rejects NULL input buffer");
    TEST_ASSERT(telem_decode_frame(buf, sizeof(buf), NULL) == TELEM_ERR_NULL_PTR, "Rejects NULL output frame");
}

void test_valid_packet(void) {
    /* Packet: Sync(0xAA, 0x55), ID(0x01), Len(0x02), Data(0x10, 0x20) */
    uint8_t buf[8] = {0xAA, 0x55, 0x01, 0x02, 0x10, 0x20, 0x00, 0x00};
    uint16_t crc = telem_compute_crc16(&buf[2], 4);
    buf[6] = (uint8_t)(crc & 0xFFU);
    buf[7] = (uint8_t)((crc >> 8U) & 0xFFU);

    telem_frame_t frame;
    telem_status_t status = telem_decode_frame(buf, sizeof(buf), &frame);

    TEST_ASSERT(status == TELEM_OK, "Decodes valid frame successfully");
    TEST_ASSERT(frame.msg_id == 0x01, "Correct message ID extracted");
    TEST_ASSERT(frame.payload_len == 2, "Correct payload length extracted");
    TEST_ASSERT(frame.payload[0] == 0x10 && frame.payload[1] == 0x20, "Payload data intact");
}

void test_bad_crc(void) {
    uint8_t buf[8] = {0xAA, 0x55, 0x01, 0x02, 0x10, 0x20, 0xDE, 0xAD};
    telem_frame_t frame;
    telem_status_t status = telem_decode_frame(buf, sizeof(buf), &frame);

    TEST_ASSERT(status == TELEM_ERR_CRC_MISMATCH, "Detects corrupted CRC checksum");
}

void test_oversized_payload_rejection(void) {
    uint8_t buf[64] = {0xAA, 0x55, 0x01, 35}; /* Len 35 > Max 32 */
    telem_frame_t frame;
    telem_status_t status = telem_decode_frame(buf, sizeof(buf), &frame);

    TEST_ASSERT(status == TELEM_ERR_INVALID_LENGTH, "Rejects packet with length > 32");
}

int main(void) {
    printf("=== RUNNING MODULE 1 TELEMETRY UNIT TESTS ===\n");
    test_null_pointers();
    test_valid_packet();
    test_bad_crc();
    test_oversized_payload_rejection();
    printf("Summary: %d / %d tests passed.\n", tests_passed, tests_run);
    return (tests_passed == tests_run) ? 0 : 1;
}

Step 4: Building with AddressSanitizer & Valgrind

Compile in your Linux terminal or WSL bash session with maximum diagnostic flags: 

# Compile with C11, all warnings as errors, and AddressSanitizer
gcc -std=c11 -Wall -Wextra -Werror -pedantic -fsanitize=address,undefined -g telemetry.c test_telemetry.c -o test_runner

# Execute the test suite
./test_runner

# Verify with Valgrind for zero memory leaks
valgrind --leak-check=full --show-leak-kinds=all ./test_runner

Part 2: Physical STM32 Board Project — Bare-Metal Diagnostics & Assert Engine

On an embedded target, when an assert fails, there is no terminal to print to and no OS to terminate the process. In safety-critical systems, an assert failure must trigger a controlled fail-safe halt: disabling motor drives, recording the source file and line to non-volatile RAM, and visually pulsing an error code on a diagnostic LED.

Hardware Mapping: STM32F401RE / STM32F411RE Nucleo

  • Target MCU: STM32F401RE (ARM Cortex-M4 @ 84MHz, 512KB Flash, 96KB SRAM).
  • Green User LED (LD2): Connected to GPIOA Pin 5 (Active High).
  • User Blue Pushbutton (B1): Connected to GPIOC Pin 13 (Active Low, Pull-Up).
  • Direct Memory Bus: AHB1 Peripheral Bus controls RCC (Base: 0x40023800) and GPIOA (Base: 0x40020000).

Bare-Metal Implementation (main.c)

The following pure C program requires zero vendor HAL or CubeMX libraries. It accesses hardware registers through strict volatile uint32_t * pointers and implements a hardware diagnostic assert handler: 

/**
 * @file main.c
 * @brief STM32F4 Bare-Metal Hardware Assert & GPIO Diagnostics
 * Target: STM32F401RE / STM32F411RE Nucleo-64
 */
#include <stdint.h>
#include <stdbool.h>

/* Base Addresses for STM32F4 Peripherals */
#define PERIPH_BASE       (0x40000000UL)
#define AHB1PERIPH_BASE   (PERIPH_BASE + 0x00020000UL)

/* RCC Register Map */
#define RCC_BASE          (AHB1PERIPH_BASE + 0x3800UL)
#define RCC_AHB1ENR       (*(volatile uint32_t *)(RCC_BASE + 0x30UL))
#define RCC_AHB1ENR_GPIOAEN (1UL << 0)
#define RCC_AHB1ENR_GPIOCEN (1UL << 2)

/* GPIOA (User LED on PA5) */
#define GPIOA_BASE        (AHB1PERIPH_BASE + 0x0000UL)
#define GPIOA_MODER       (*(volatile uint32_t *)(GPIOA_BASE + 0x00UL))
#define GPIOA_ODR         (*(volatile uint32_t *)(GPIOA_BASE + 0x14UL))
#define GPIOA_BSRR        (*(volatile uint32_t *)(GPIOA_BASE + 0x18UL))

/* GPIOC (User Button on PC13) */
#define GPIOC_BASE        (AHB1PERIPH_BASE + 0x0800UL)
#define GPIOC_MODER       (*(volatile uint32_t *)(GPIOC_BASE + 0x00UL))
#define GPIOC_IDR         (*(volatile uint32_t *)(GPIOC_BASE + 0x10UL))

#define LED_PIN           5UL
#define BUTTON_PIN        13UL

/* Diagnostic Error Record Stored in Uninitialized RAM */
typedef struct {
    const char *file;
    uint32_t    line;
    uint32_t    fault_code;
} diagnostic_record_t;

/* Global diagnostic block preserved across soft resets */
__attribute__((section(".noinit"))) diagnostic_record_t g_last_fault;

/* Software Delay Routine */
static void delay_cycles(volatile uint32_t count) {
    while (count > 0) {
        count--;
    }
}

/* Hardware Panic: Morse / Blink Error Code and Halt */
void hardware_assert_failed(const char *file, uint32_t line, uint32_t code) {
    /* 1. Disable all interrupts for atomic halt */
    __asm volatile ("cpsid i" : : : "memory");

    /* 2. Store fault telemetry for SWD/GDB debugger */
    g_last_fault.file = file;
    g_last_fault.line = line;
    g_last_fault.fault_code = code;

    /* 3. Infinite SOS / Blink Alarm on User LED */
    while (1) {
        /* Blink N times corresponding to error code */
        for (uint32_t i = 0; i < code; i++) {
            GPIOA_BSRR = (1UL << LED_PIN);          /* LED ON */
            delay_cycles(200000);
            GPIOA_BSRR = (1UL << (LED_PIN + 16UL)); /* LED OFF */
            delay_cycles(200000);
        }
        /* Long pause between code bursts */
        delay_cycles(1200000);
    }
}

/* Custom Embedded Assert Macro */
#define EMB_ASSERT(expr, err_code) \
    do { \
        if (!(expr)) { \
            hardware_assert_failed(__FILE__, __LINE__, (err_code)); \
        } \
    } while(0)

/* Initialize Clocks and GPIO Pins */
static void gpio_init(void) {
    /* Enable GPIOA and GPIOC Peripheral Clocks */
    RCC_AHB1ENR |= (RCC_AHB1ENR_GPIOAEN | RCC_AHB1ENR_GPIOCEN);

    /* Configure PA5 as General Purpose Output (MODER = 01) */
    GPIOA_MODER &= ~(3UL << (LED_PIN * 2));
    GPIOA_MODER |=  (1UL << (LED_PIN * 2));

    /* Configure PC13 as Input (MODER = 00) */
    GPIOC_MODER &= ~(3UL << (BUTTON_PIN * 2));
}

int main(void) {
    gpio_init();

    uint32_t loop_counter = 0;

    while (1) {
        /* Read Blue Button on PC13 (Active LOW on Nucleo) */
        bool button_pressed = ((GPIOC_IDR & (1UL << BUTTON_PIN)) == 0);

        /* Intentional Fault Injection: Pressing the button triggers Error Code 3 */
        EMB_ASSERT(!button_pressed, 3);

        /* Normal Heartbeat Blink */
        GPIOA_BSRR = (1UL << LED_PIN);
        delay_cycles(400000);
        GPIOA_BSRR = (1UL << (LED_PIN + 16UL));
        delay_cycles(400000);

        loop_counter++;
        /* Mathematical Invariant: Loop counter must never wrap negatively */
        EMB_ASSERT(loop_counter > 0, 1);
    }

    return 0;
}

Compiling, Flashing, and Debugging on Hardware

From your Linux/WSL terminal connected to the STM32 Nucleo via USB: 

# 1. Compile with arm-none-eabi-gcc targeting Cortex-M4
arm-none-eabi-gcc -mcpu=cortex-m4 -mthumb -mfloat-abi=hard -mfpu=fpv4-sp-d16 \
    -O2 -Wall -Wextra -Werror -g3 -c main.c -o main.o

# 2. Link with minimal startup and linker script (details in Module 2)
arm-none-eabi-gcc -mcpu=cortex-m4 -mthumb -T STM32F401RETx_FLASH.ld \
    main.o startup_stm32f401xe.o -o firmware.elf

# 3. Convert ELF to raw binary
arm-none-eabi-objcopy -O binary firmware.elf firmware.bin

# 4. Flash to STM32 board using ST-LINK CLI or st-flash
st-flash write firmware.bin 0x08000000

# 5. Connect GDB to inspect g_last_fault if an assert fires
arm-none-eabi-gdb firmware.elf
(gdb) target extended-remote :3333
(gdb) print g_last_fault

Module 1 Capstone Knowledge Check

Test your understanding of the concepts applied across both Linux and STM32 projects.

1. In telemetry.c, why is the 16-bit CRC reconstructed using explicit byte shifts (buf[0] | (buf[1] << 8)) rather than casting the buffer pointer directly to (uint16_t *)?

2. When hardware_assert_failed() is called on STM32, what is the critical purpose of __asm volatile ("cpsid i")?

3. What does __attribute__((section(".noinit"))) ensure for the g_last_fault variable?

4. Why is GPIOA_BSRR preferred over GPIOA_ODR for turning the LED on and off in embedded firmware?

5. Which GCC compiler flag flags out-of-bounds array reads and stack buffer overflows at runtime in our Linux project?

6. In EMB_ASSERT_RETURN(cond, err_code), why is the macro wrapped in do { ... } while(0)?

7. What is the danger of using int instead of uint32_t when creating bitmask shifts such as (1 << 31)?

8. When reading the user button state on PC13 with (GPIOC_IDR & (1UL << 13)) == 0, why does 0 indicate 'pressed'?

9. What happens if volatile is omitted from the hardware register pointers (e.g. #define GPIOA_ODR (*(uint32_t *)...))?

10. Why is Valgrind or ASan essential when verifying embedded C code on a Linux host?

Hands-on Engineering Challenges

Challenge 1 (Host)

Corrupted Packet Stream Fuzz Testing

Write a host-based fuzz tester in C that feeds 100,000 randomly corrupted byte sequences into telem_decode_frame(). Verify with AddressSanitizer that the function never crashes, leaks memory, or reads out-of-bounds.

Challenge 2 (Host)

Dynamic Payload Type Dispatcher

Extend telemetry.c with a message handler table: for msg_id = 0x01, unpack battery millivolts and temperature into a battery_telemetry_t struct; for msg_id = 0x02, unpack 3-axis accelerometer readings.

Challenge 3 (STM32)

Morse Code SOS Panic Generator

Modify hardware_assert_failed() on STM32 so that instead of simple N-blinks, it flashes international Morse code for "SOS" (... --- ...: 3 short, 3 long, 3 short) with precise timing intervals.

Challenge 4 (STM32)

Button Debounce Filter without Delay

fields.title: Day 8: Capstone: Sensor Logger with Serial Output
fields.content:
Session 1.7 — Capstone 1

Day 8: Capstone: Sensor Logger with Serial Output

Problem Statement: You have mastered GPIO, timers, ADC, and UART serial communication in isolation. Now prove your engineering mastery: design and construct a complete, interrupt-driven multi-sensor telemetry engine that samples sensors periodically, buffers records in a thread-safe circular queue, formats structured ASCII frames with XOR checksums, and streams data over UART via DMA while maintaining deep CPU sleep.
📋 Daily Plan & Learning Architecture
Session 1.7 — Capstone 1 Module 1: Embedded C Foundations Estimated: 3.5 hrs

🎯 Today's Mission & Relevance

  • Architect an end-to-end event-driven sensor telemetry system.
  • Implement a thread-safe power-of-two circular ring buffer (FIFO).
  • Integrate hardware timer triggers, ADC conversions, and autonomous UART DMA streaming.

📐 Theoretical Milestones

  • Power-of-two ring buffer bitwise wrap-around mathematics.
  • NMEA-0183 structured ASCII framing and 8-bit XOR checksum algorithms.
  • System clock tree scaling (168 MHz) and low-power Wait-For-Interrupt (WFI) sleep.

💻 Hands-On Blueprint

  • Program 8.1: System clock initialization to 168 MHz via HSE and PLL.
  • Program 8.2: Thread-safe circular telemetry ring buffer implementation.
  • Program 8.3: Sensor acquisition abstraction layer for NTC and BMP280.
  • Program 8.4: NMEA-style ASCII log frame serializer with XOR checksum.
  • Program 8.5: Master acquisition loop with WFI power-saving sleep.

🛡️ Production Failure Modes

  • Executing heavy string formatting (snprintf) inside ISRs instead of the main thread.
  • Failing to handle ring buffer overruns, silently corrupting unread telemetry records.
  • Missing Flash memory wait-state adjustments before boosting core clock to 168 MHz.
🏁 Daily Milestone Deliverables: 5 Interactive Register-Level Programs • 5 Architecture Diagrams • 10 Practice MCQs • 5 Hands-On Assignments

8.1 Module 1 Capstone: End-to-End System Architecture

Over the preceding seven days, we mastered individual hardware peripherals in isolation: clock tree configuration, bare-metal GPIO manipulation, atomic bitmask registers, interrupt handling via the NVIC, precision hardware timers, analog-to-digital conversion, and serial protocols. In this Module 1 Capstone Project, we integrate these disparate elements into an integrated, production-grade Interrupt-Driven Sensor Logging Engine.

The goal is to build an autonomous embedded data logger that samples an analog NTC thermistor and an I2C barometric pressure sensor periodically, buffers measurements inside a thread-safe circular ring buffer, serializes data into structured ASCII NMEA-style frames with checksum validation, and streams telemetry over UART using DMA—all while maximizing processor sleep time between acquisition cycles.

Real World Application: This architecture serves as the foundation for industrial condition-monitoring sensor pods installed on wind turbines and railroad wheel bearings. These pods monitor thermal decay and vibration signatures, streaming periodic time-stamped health frames over RS-485 serial buses to predictive maintenance gateways.
Figure 1.7-1: Capstone Autonomous Sensor Logger System Block Diagram
Figure Parameters Explained:
  • Analog Subsystem: Precision voltage divider with 10k 0.1% resistor and NTC thermistor feeding ADC1 with hardware RC anti-aliasing filter.
  • Digital Bus: I2C1 running at 400 kHz with 4.7k pull-up resistors reading temperature and pressure from BMP280.
  • Host Link: USART2 operating at 115200 baud (8-N-1) using DMA streaming for non-blocking packet transfer.
  • Power Management: CPU resides in Wait-For-Interrupt (WFI) sleep mode during inter-sample intervals, waking only on timer interrupts.

8.2 The Thread-Safe Circular Ring Buffer Design Pattern

When an interrupt-driven peripheral produces data faster than a communication channel can transmit it (or when transmission bursts require temporary staging), firmware engineers employ a Circular Ring Buffer (FIFO). The buffer uses fixed-size memory with two monotonic index pointers: head (where producers write new data) and tail (where consumers read old data).

By sizing the buffer to an exact power of two ($2^N$), index wrap-around is achieved using an ultra-fast bitwise AND mask (index = (index + 1) & (BUFFER_SIZE - 1)) rather than costly division or modulo operations. Furthermore, when single-byte indices are used, producer-consumer operations remain inherently atomic on 32-bit Cortex-M processors.

Figure 1.7-2: Power-of-Two Circular Ring Buffer (FIFO) Architecture
Figure Parameters Explained:
  • Head Pointer: Index where the Producer (Timer / ADC ISR) writes the next incoming sensor packet.
  • Tail Pointer: Index where the Consumer (UART DMA engine) reads the next pending packet for transmission.
  • Bitwise Wrap-Around: Buffer size = 16 (0x10); Mask = 15 (0x0F). Index 15 + 1 becomes (16 & 0x0F) = 0 automatically.
  • Buffer Full Condition: One slot is left empty to distinguish unambiguously between an empty buffer and a full buffer.

8.3 The Interrupt-Driven Sensor Acquisition Pipeline

To eliminate CPU busy-wait loops, the data acquisition pipeline is governed entirely by hardware events:

  1. Hardware Timer Trigger: General-purpose timer TIM2 fires an Update Event (UEV) every 100 milliseconds.
  2. ADC Conversion: TIM2 TRGO triggers ADC1 conversion of the NTC thermistor channel in hardware.
  3. ADC End of Conversion (EOC): ADC ISR reads the converted digital value, kicks off a rapid non-blocking I2C read of the BMP280 sensor, and calculates physical engineering units.
  4. Ring Buffer Push: The resulting sensor packet is pushed into the circular telemetry ring buffer.
  5. UART DMA Dispatch: If the UART DMA transmitter is idle, the next packet is serialized and DMA transmission begins immediately.
Figure 1.7-3: Data Pipeline: Hardware Timer Trigger to UART DMA Output
Figure Parameters Explained:
  • TIM2 TRGO Trigger: Hardware internal routing triggers ADC conversion without CPU software intervention.
  • Decoupled Producer/Consumer: ISRs quickly push raw readings into the ring buffer; serialization and formatting occur in background thread.
  • Non-Blocking Execution: No peripheral driver ever halts CPU execution with while-loop polling flags.

8.4 Structured ASCII Log Frame Format with XOR Checksum

To ensure robust data parsing on host systems (such as Python telemetry collectors or industrial PLCs), sensor readings are formatted into standardized ASCII frames modeled after the marine NMEA-0183 standard. Each frame incorporates a preamble header, sequence counter, comma-separated engineering values, and an 8-bit XOR checksum to detect line corruption:

$LOG,<seq>,<temp_c>,<pressure_pa>,<uptime_ms>*<XOR_HEX>

Example: $LOG,1042,24.85,101325,104200*5B
Figure 1.7-4: Structured ASCII Log Frame Packet Format and Checksum Verification
Figure Parameters Explained:
  • Preamble ($LOG): Enables the host parser to resynchronize immediately if serial bytes are dropped or garbled.
  • Sequence Counter: Monotonically increasing integer tracking packet loss over long deployment periods.
  • XOR Checksum: Computed by XOR-ing all ASCII character bytes between '$' and '*'. Guaranteed detection of single-bit bursts.
  • CRLF (\r\n): Standard end-of-frame packet delimiter for stream-based line buffering.

8.5 Overrun Detection and Fault Management

In real-world deployment, serial cables may be disconnected or transmission buffers may fill up if the baud rate is insufficient. A production-grade embedded logger must detect and report Buffer Overrun Faults. When a newly generated sensor reading cannot fit into the ring buffer, an overrun counter is incremented, an amber Error LED is illuminated, and a diagnostic fault flag is injected into the next successful log packet.

Figure 1.7-5: Sensor Logger Operational State Machine Flowchart
Figure Parameters Explained:
  • STATE_INIT: Configures PLL to 168 MHz, initializes GPIOs, Timers, ADC, I2C, and UART DMA.
  • STATE_SLEEP: Executes WFI instruction; CPU core halts clocking, saving up to 80% dynamic power.
  • FAULT_OVERRUN: Latches overrun event, sets diagnostic warning flag, and asserts hardware alert pin.

8.6 Hands-On Code Implementations


#include <stdint.h>

#define RCC_BASE        0x40023800UL
#define RCC_CR          (*(volatile uint32_t *)(RCC_BASE + 0x00UL))
#define RCC_PLLCFGR     (*(volatile uint32_t *)(RCC_BASE + 0x04UL))
#define RCC_CFGR        (*(volatile uint32_t *)(RCC_BASE + 0x08UL))
#define FLASH_ACR       (*(volatile uint32_t *)0x40023C00UL)

/* Configure STM32F4 clock tree: External 8MHz Crystal (HSE) -> PLL -> 168 MHz Core Clock */
void bsp_clock_init_168mhz(void) {
    /* 1. Enable HSE oscillator */
    RCC_CR |= (1UL << 16);
    while (!(RCC_CR & (1UL << 17))); /* Wait for HSE ready */

    /* 2. Configure Flash Latency: 5 wait states for 168 MHz operation at 3.3V */
    FLASH_ACR = (1UL << 9) | (1UL << 10) | (5UL << 0); /* Prefetch, I-Cache, D-Cache, 5 WS */

    /* 3. Configure PLL: PLL_M = 8, PLL_N = 336, PLL_P = 2 -> (8MHz / 8) * 336 / 2 = 168 MHz */
    RCC_PLLCFGR = (8UL << 0) | (336UL << 6) | (0UL << 16) | (1UL << 22);

    /* 4. Enable PLL */
    RCC_CR |= (1UL << 24);
    while (!(RCC_CR & (1UL << 25))); /* Wait for PLL ready */

    /* 5. Set AHB prescaler = 1 (168MHz), APB1 = 4 (42MHz), APB2 = 2 (84MHz) */
    RCC_CFGR |= (0UL << 4) | (5UL << 10) | (4UL << 13);

    /* 6. Switch System Clock source to PLL */
    RCC_CFGR |= (2UL << 0);
    while ((RCC_CFGR & (3UL << 2)) != (2UL << 2)); /* Wait for switch */
}
Program 1.7-1: System Clock and Board Support Package Initialization (bsp_init.c) 

#include <stdint.h>
#include <stdbool.h>

#define RING_BUFFER_SIZE    16 /* Must be power of two */
#define RING_BUFFER_MASK    (RING_BUFFER_SIZE - 1)

typedef struct {
    uint32_t timestamp_ms;
    float    temperature_c;
    float    pressure_pa;
    uint32_t sequence_num;
} SensorRecord_t;

typedef struct {
    SensorRecord_t records[RING_BUFFER_SIZE];
    volatile uint8_t head;
    volatile uint8_t tail;
    volatile uint32_t overrun_count;
} TelemetryRingBuffer_t;

void ring_buf_init(TelemetryRingBuffer_t *rb) {
    rb->head = 0;
    rb->tail = 0;
    rb->overrun_count = 0;
}

bool ring_buf_push(TelemetryRingBuffer_t *rb, const SensorRecord_t *item) {
    uint8_t next_head = (rb->head + 1) & RING_BUFFER_MASK;
    
    if (next_head == rb->tail) {
        /* Buffer is full! Record overrun event */
        rb->overrun_count++;
        return false;
    }
    
    rb->records[rb->head] = *item;
    rb->head = next_head;
    return true;
}

bool ring_buf_pop(TelemetryRingBuffer_t *rb, SensorRecord_t *item) {
    if (rb->head == rb->tail) {
        return false; /* Buffer empty */
    }
    
    *item = rb->records[rb->tail];
    rb->tail = (rb->tail + 1) & RING_BUFFER_MASK;
    return true;
}
Program 1.7-2: Thread-Safe Power-of-Two Circular Telemetry Ring Buffer 

#include <stdint.h>

/* Sensor acquisition API returning physical engineering units */
float sensor_read_ntc_temperature(void) {
    /* Reads PA0 ADC1 channel, computes Steinhart-Hart equation */
    uint16_t raw_adc = 2048; /* Simulated nominal reading */
    float voltage = (raw_adc / 4095.0f) * 3.3f;
    float resistance = 10000.0f * (voltage / (3.3f - voltage));
    
    /* Approximate linear conversion around 25C for demonstration */
    return 25.0f + (10000.0f - resistance) * 0.005f;
}

float sensor_read_bmp280_pressure(void) {
    /* Reads BMP280 via I2C1 registers, applies factory calibration */
    return 101325.0f; /* Standard atmospheric pressure in Pascals */
}
Program 1.7-3: Sensor Acquisition Abstraction Layer: NTC + Simulated BMP280 

#include <stdint.h>
#include <stdio.h>
#include <string.h>

uint8_t calculate_xor_checksum(const char *str) {
    uint8_t checksum = 0;
    /* Skip leading '$' if present */
    if (*str == '$') str++;
    
    while (*str && *str != '*') {
        checksum ^= (uint8_t)(*str++);
    }
    return checksum;
}

int serialize_log_frame(char *buffer, uint16_t max_len, uint32_t seq, float temp, float press, uint32_t time_ms) {
    char temp_buf[96];
    
    /* Format payload without checksum */
    int len = snprintf(temp_buf, sizeof(temp_buf), "$LOG,%lu,%.2f,%.0f,%lu*", 
                       seq, temp, press, time_ms);
                       
    if (len < 0 || len >= (int)sizeof(temp_buf)) return -1;
    
    /* Compute 8-bit XOR checksum */
    uint8_t chk = calculate_xor_checksum(temp_buf);
    
    /* Append checksum in two hex digits and CRLF */
    return snprintf(buffer, max_len, "%s%02X\r\n", temp_buf, chk);
}
Program 1.7-4: NMEA-Style Log Frame Serializer with XOR Checksum Calculation 

#include <stdint.h>
#include <stdbool.h>

static TelemetryRingBuffer_t g_telemetry_queue;
static volatile bool g_sample_trigger_flag = false;
static uint32_t g_sequence_counter = 0;

/* TIM2 Interrupt Service Routine: Sets trigger flag every 100 ms */
void TIM2_IRQHandler(void) {
    /* Clear update interrupt flag */
    *(volatile uint32_t *)0x40000010UL &= ~(1UL << 0);
    g_sample_trigger_flag = true;
}

int main(void) {
    bsp_clock_init_168mhz();
    ring_buf_init(&g_telemetry_queue);
    
    char tx_packet_buffer[128];

    while (1) {
        if (g_sample_trigger_flag) {
            g_sample_trigger_flag = false;
            
            /* Acquire sensor telemetry */
            SensorRecord_t record;
            record.timestamp_ms = g_sequence_counter * 100;
            record.temperature_c = sensor_read_ntc_temperature();
            record.pressure_pa = sensor_read_bmp280_pressure();
            record.sequence_num = ++g_sequence_counter;
            
            /* Push to circular buffer */
            if (!ring_buf_push(&g_telemetry_queue, &record)) {
                /* Hardware Error LED assertion on buffer overrun */
            }
        }
        
        /* Process pending queue records */
        SensorRecord_t pending_item;
        if (ring_buf_pop(&g_telemetry_queue, &pending_item)) {
            int frame_len = serialize_log_frame(tx_packet_buffer, sizeof(tx_packet_buffer),
                                               pending_item.sequence_num,
                                               pending_item.temperature_c,
                                               pending_item.pressure_pa,
                                               pending_item.timestamp_ms);
            if (frame_len > 0) {
                /* Initiate non-blocking UART DMA streaming */
            }
        }
        
        /* Sleep until next hardware interrupt */
        __asm__ volatile("wfi");
    }
    return 0;
}
Program 1.7-5: Master Capstone Main Acquisition Superloop with WFI Power Sleep

Industrial Sensor Logging Architectures Comparison

System ArchitectureCPU UtilizationPower Draw (Active/Sleep)Max Sample RateOverrun ResilienceIndustrial Suitability
Polled Superloop100% (No Sleep)High (35 mA continuous)Low (< 50 Hz)Very Poor (Data loss during delays)Toy projects, simple non-time-critical demos
Interrupt-Driven + Ring Buffer3% - 8%Low (< 3 mA average)High (1 kHz - 10 kHz)Excellent (Buffers burst loads safely)Industrial data loggers, environmental telemetry pods
Full RTOS (FreeRTOS) Multi-Tasking5% - 12%Low (Tickless Idle < 2 mA)Very High (10 kHz+)Superior (Prioritized queues & mailboxes)Safety-critical automotive ECUs, avionics flight recorders

Topic Quiz (10 Questions)

Test your conceptual understanding of today's embedded systems architecture, registers, and runtime behaviors.

1. Why is sizing a circular ring buffer to an exact power of two (e.g. 16, 32, 64) considered best practice in embedded firmware?
  • Because Cortex-M hardware requires RAM allocations in powers of two
  • Because index wrap-around can be executed using an ultra-fast bitwise AND mask instead of a costly division/modulo instruction
  • To prevent Flash memory wear
  • Because it doubles the serial baud rate
If BUFFER_SIZE is 2^N, `(idx + 1) & (BUFFER_SIZE - 1)` wraps around in a single CPU clock cycle, avoiding the 2-12 cycle hardware divide instruction.
2. In the NMEA-style checksum calculation `$LOG,...*XX\r\n`, which characters are included in the 8-bit XOR calculation?
  • All characters from the leading '$' through the trailing '\n'
  • Only characters situated strictly between '$' and '*' exclusive
  • Only numeric payload digits
  • The entire packet including the checksum itself
The standard NMEA XOR checksum calculates the cumulative XOR sum of all ASCII bytes appearing between the start delimiter '$' and the checksum delimiter '*'.
3. What happens when an interrupt-driven producer attempts to push a new sensor record into a completely full ring buffer?
  • The CPU halts and triggers a HardFault
  • A Buffer Overrun condition occurs; firmware must either drop the sample or overwrite oldest data while logging the fault
  • The timer frequency is automatically halved
  • The UART baud rate is doubled
A full buffer cannot accept new items without dropping them or overwriting unread data. Robust systems log the overrun count to alert supervisors.
4. What instruction is executed at the end of the main acquisition loop to put the ARM Cortex-M processor into low-power sleep until the next interrupt?
  • NOP
  • WFI (Wait For Interrupt)
  • SVC 0
  • BKPT 0
The WFI (Wait For Interrupt) instruction stops the CPU core clock, drastically cutting power consumption until any enabled interrupt wakes it.
5. Why is separating the raw data acquisition (in ISR) from the ASCII string formatting (in main loop) an essential architectural pattern?
  • Because string formatting functions like snprintf() are heavy and non-reentrant, and would severely inflate interrupt latency if executed inside an ISR
  • Because ISRs cannot access character arrays
  • Because snprintf() requires an external FPU coprocessor
  • Because ASCII characters cannot be stored in SRAM
String formatting consumes thousands of clock cycles and stack memory. Executing it inside an ISR starves other urgent hardware interrupts.
6. How does the ring buffer full condition `(head + 1) & MASK == tail` prevent ambiguous buffer states?
  • It leaves one buffer slot intentionally empty so `head == tail` always uniquely denotes an empty buffer
  • It doubles the buffer capacity automatically
  • It triggers a DMA interrupt
  • It reverses the queue direction
Reserving one empty slot guarantees that head == tail signifies an empty queue, while (head + 1) & MASK == tail uniquely identifies a full queue.
7. What clock configuration step must be executed before increasing the CPU core frequency from 16 MHz to 168 MHz on an STM32F4?
  • Disabling all GPIO pins
  • Increasing the Flash ACR wait states (latency) to 5 wait states to prevent memory read corruption
  • Enabling the software watchdog
  • Setting all UART ports to 9600 baud
Internal Flash memory cannot be read at 168 MHz. Software must increase Flash wait states (latency cycles) in FLASH_ACR before accelerating the clock.
8. What is the primary benefit of streaming telemetry packets via UART using a DMA controller instead of an interrupt-per-byte approach?
  • DMA eliminates electromagnetic interference
  • DMA requires zero CPU interrupts during the entire multi-byte packet transfer, firing only once when the transmission completes
  • DMA automatically verifies the XOR checksum
  • DMA converts ASCII characters to binary bytes
DMA offloads memory-to-peripheral transfers entirely, freeing the CPU core to sleep or compute sensor filters without taking 100+ context switches.
9. In the context of the sensor logger, why is a monotonically increasing sequence counter included in each transmitted frame?
  • To calibrate the ADC voltage reference
  • To allow the receiving host to immediately detect dropped packets or transmission dropouts
  • To set the real-time clock time
  • To synchronize SPI phase clocks
A missing sequence number (e.g. jumping from 104 to 106) immediately alerts the receiving system that a packet was lost over the communication channel.
10. What hardware peripheral trigger automatically initiates the ADC conversion in our Capstone pipeline without CPU software intervention?
  • TIM2 TRGO (Trigger Output) event
  • Watchdog reset
  • SysTick counter overflow
  • UART RXNE flag
Routing TIM2 TRGO directly into the ADC trigger input ensures microsecond-deterministic sampling rates independent of CPU software load.

Hands-On Assignments

Complete these 5 lab assignments to solidify your hands-on firmware engineering skills.

Assignment 1: Quad-Sensor Array Expansion with Ambient Light Sensing

Task: Wire an optical Light Dependent Resistor (LDR) to ADC1 Channel 1. Update the Capstone acquisition pipeline to sample temperature, barometric pressure, and ambient lux, serializing all four telemetry metrics into the ASCII log frame.

Assignment 2: Dual-Mode Compact Binary Telemetry Frame Mode

Task: Implement an alternative binary frame mode toggleable via a UART command. Define a packed C struct (Header 0xAA55, uint32_t seq, float temp, float press, CRC16) that reduces packet size by 65% compared to ASCII.

Assignment 3: Non-Volatile SD Card Logging with FatFS Staging

Task: Instead of merely streaming data over UART, stage sensor log packets inside the ring buffer and flush 512-byte blocks to an external micro-SD card formatted with FAT32 using the FatFS library over SPI.

Assignment 4: Buffer Overrun Injection & Recovery Validation

Task: Artificially stall the UART transmission engine for 2 seconds while the timer continues pushing sensor records. Verify that the overrun counter accurately increments, the Error LED lights up, and the system resumes without memory leaks.

Assignment 5: Python Host Live Telemetry Plotter and Checksum Verifier

Task: Write a Python script on your host PC using `pyserial` and `matplotlib`. Read serial frames, verify the XOR checksum of each packet, discard corrupted frames, and plot real-time temperature and pressure curves dynamically.

Official References, Research Papers & Standards

Deepen your engineering foundations with seminal reference manuals, processor architecture standards, and industry specifications:

Foundational specification for comma-separated ASCII serial telemetry frames, start delimiters, talker IDs, and XOR checksum verification algorithms.

Comprehensive architectural guide covering non-blocking state machines, event-driven pipelines, active object patterns, and ring buffer queues.

View Official Resource →

Application guide detailing circular memory streaming, FIFO threshold configurations, and multi-peripheral DMA priority arbitration.
