fields.title: Day 13: CAN Bus & Automotive Protocols
fields.content:
Session 2.4

Day 13: CAN Bus & Automotive Protocols

Problem Statement: In automotive, aerospace, and industrial automation, dozens of microcontrollers must exchange real-time control messages across high-noise environments without centralized switches. Point-to-point wiring is physically impossible. CAN bus provides a multi-drop, differential two-wire network with non-destructive arbitration and hardware fault confinement. How do you configure, transmit, and filter CAN frames in silicon?
📋 Daily Plan & Learning Architecture
Session 2.4 Module 2: RTOS, Peripherals & Communication Estimated: 3.5 hrs

🎯 Today's Mission & Relevance

  • Master CAN differential physical signaling, 120-ohm termination, and noise immunity.
  • Understand CAN 2.0A/B frame layouts and non-destructive CSMA/CR arbitration.
  • Configure STM32 bxCAN bit timing registers and hardware acceptance filters.

📐 Theoretical Milestones

  • Dominant (0) vs. Recessive (1) wired-AND bus arbitration dynamics.
  • Bit timing breakdown (Sync, Prop, Phase1, Phase2) and 87.5% sample point math.
  • Fault confinement: Error-Active, Error-Passive, and Bus-Off state machines.

💻 Hands-On Blueprint

  • Program 13.1: STM32 bxCAN initialization at 500 kbps (85.7% sample point).
  • Program 13.2: Transmitting multi-byte engine telemetry via CAN mailboxes.
  • Program 13.3: Hardware ID/Mask acceptance filter configuration for FIFO0.
  • Program 13.4: Host Linux SocketCAN raw packet transmission client in C.
  • Program 13.5: Promiscuous CAN bus sniffer and UART telemetry logger.

🛡️ Production Failure Modes

  • Missing 120-ohm termination resistors, causing high-frequency signal reflections.
  • Misconfiguring bit timing prescalers, drifting sample points outside acceptable windows.
  • Failing to clear FIFO output mailboxes, locking CAN reception permanently.
🏁 Daily Milestone Deliverables: 5 Interactive Register-Level Programs • 5 Architecture Diagrams • 10 Practice MCQs • 5 Hands-On Assignments

13.1 The Backbone of Automotive Electronics: CAN Bus Architecture

Modern automobiles contain between 70 and 150 independent Electronic Control Units (ECUs) controlling powertrain, braking, steering, battery management, climate control, and body lighting. Point-to-point wiring between all ECUs would create an unimaginably heavy, expensive, and fault-prone copper wiring harness weighing over 100 kilograms! In 1986, Robert Bosch GmbH invented the Controller Area Network (CAN Bus) to solve this crisis with a robust, multi-drop, two-wire differential serial network.

CAN operates with extreme noise immunity in harsh electromagnetic environments (such as proximity to ignition coils and electric traction inverters). The physical layer consists of two twisted-pair copper wires labeled CAN_H (High) and CAN_L (Low) terminated at both physical ends with 120-ohm resistors to prevent high-frequency transmission line signal reflections.

Automotive Reality: When you press the brake pedal in a car, the Hydraulic Brake ECU broadcasts a high-priority CAN message with ID 0x0C8. The Engine ECU, Transmission ECU, and Regenerative Inverter ECU all receive and act upon this exact same packet simultaneously within 500 microseconds over the vehicle CAN bus.
Figure 2.4-1: CAN Physical Layer Differential Signaling and Bus Voltage Levels
Figure Parameters Explained:
  • Recessive Bit (Logic 1): CANH = 2.5V, CANL = 2.5V (V_diff = 0V). Driven weakly; can be overridden by any transmitter.
  • Dominant Bit (Logic 0): CANH = 3.5V, CANL = 1.5V (V_diff = 2.0V). Actively driven; dominates the bus completely.
  • Common-Mode Noise Rejection: Electromagnetic noise couples equally into both twisted wires; the receiver differential amplifier (CANH - CANL) subtracts common-mode spikes perfectly.
  • 120 Ohm Termination Resistors: Placed across CANH and CANL at the two extreme cable ends to match the 120-ohm characteristic impedance of the twisted pair.

13.2 CAN Data Frame Architecture: 11-Bit Standard vs. 29-Bit Extended

Unlike Ethernet or IP packets, CAN messages do not contain source or destination node addresses. Instead, CAN messages are content-addressed: every frame contains an Arbitration Identifier (ID) that identifies the meaning and real-time urgency of the payload (e.g. ID 0x0C0 = Engine RPM). There are two standard framing formats:

  • CAN 2.0A (Standard Format): 11-bit identifier (allowing $2^{11} = 2048$ unique message IDs).
  • CAN 2.0B (Extended Format): 29-bit identifier (11-bit base ID + 18-bit extended ID, yielding over 536 million unique message IDs, standard in SAE J1939 heavy trucks).
Figure 2.4-2: CAN 2.0A Standard Data Frame Bit-Level Architecture
Figure Parameters Explained:
  • SOF (Start of Frame): Single dominant bit synchronizing all receiving node clocks on the bus.
  • Arbitration ID: 11-bit message identifier; also serves as the message priority during bus contention.
  • RTR (Remote Transmission Request): 0 for Data Frames; 1 for Remote Frames requesting data from another node.
  • DLC (Data Length Code): 4-bit binary field defining payload length from 0 to 8 bytes.
  • CRC (Cyclic Redundancy Check): 15-bit polynomial error detection code protecting frame integrity.
  • ACK Slot: Transmitter sends recessive 1; any receiver that decodes a valid CRC drives dominant 0 to acknowledge.

13.3 Non-Destructive Bitwise Arbitration (CSMA/CR)

CAN operates under Carrier Sense Multiple Access with Collision Resolution (CSMA/CR). Multiple nodes can begin transmitting simultaneously. While transmitting the arbitration ID, each node monitors the physical bus voltage. If Node A transmits a recessive 1 but reads back a dominant 0 (because Node B transmitted a 0), Node A realizes it lost arbitration. Node A immediately ceases transmission and switches to receiver mode, allowing Node B to continue uninterrupted with zero lost bus cycles!

Core Rule of CAN Arbitration: The lower the numerical ID value, the higher the message priority.

Figure 2.4-3: Non-Destructive Bitwise Bus Arbitration in Action
Figure Parameters Explained:
  • Bit-by-Bit Arbitration: Nodes transmit their ID MSB first; dominant bits (0) override recessive bits (1).
  • Zero Collisions: Unlike Ethernet CSMA/CD, no bandwidth is wasted on collision backoffs; the highest-priority message completes without delay.
  • Bus Latency Guarantee: Highest-priority frames (e.g. 0x000) experience zero arbitration delay regardless of total bus traffic load.

13.4 Bit Timing, Time Quanta, and Sample Point Configuration

Because CAN is asynchronous, every node must independently reconstruct bit boundaries. A single nominal bit time is divided into 4 non-overlapping segments composed of integer multiples of Time Quanta ($t_q$):

  • Sync_Seg (Synchronization Segment): 1 $t_q$. Edge transitions occur here.
  • Prop_Seg (Propagation Segment): Compensates for physical wire delays and transceiver delays.
  • Phase_Seg1 & Phase_Seg2: Compensate for oscillator phase errors; adjusted dynamically via the Synchronization Jump Width (SJW).

The point where the bit value is latched is the Sample Point. Automotive standards (CiA 303-1) mandate locating the sample point at exactly 87.5% of the bit time for 500 kbps powertrain networks.

Figure 2.4-4: CAN Bit Timing Segments and 87.5% Sample Point Location
Figure Parameters Explained:
  • Time Quantum (t_q): Basic unit of timer resolution derived from prescaled peripheral APB clock.
  • Baud Rate Formula: Baud Rate = 1 / (Nominal Bit Time) = f_clk / (BRP * (1 + TS1 + TS2)).
  • Sample Point Position: Sample Point (%) = ((1 + TS1) / (1 + TS1 + TS2)) * 100.
  • SJW (Sync Jump Width): Maximum number of time quanta by which Phase Segments can be lengthened or shortened to resynchronize.

13.5 Fault Confinement: Error State Machine & Bus-Off Recovery

CAN incorporates hardware fault confinement to prevent a malfunctioning ECU from bringing down the entire vehicle network. Each node maintains two internal error counters: Transmit Error Counter (TEC) and Receive Error Counter (REC). Based on error counts, a node transitions through three states:

  1. Error-Active (TEC < 128, REC < 128): Normal operation; transmits active error flags (dominant 0s).
  2. Error-Passive (TEC ≥ 128 or REC ≥ 128): Node is degraded; transmits passive error flags (recessive 1s) to avoid disrupting the bus.
  3. Bus-Off (TEC > 255): The node is completely disconnected from the bus by hardware; it cannot transmit or receive. Safe recovery requires explicit software reset or waiting for 128 occurrences of 11 consecutive recessive bits.
Figure 2.4-5: CAN Node Fault Confinement Finite State Machine
Figure Parameters Explained:
  • TEC / REC Counters: Incremented on transmit/receive errors (bit error, stuff error, CRC error, form error, ACK error).
  • Bus-Off State: Isolates a damaged ECU from the vehicle bus so it cannot jam communication.
  • Automatic Bus-Off Recovery: Requires software to clear the ABOM bit or monitor 128 occurrences of bus idle sequences.

13.6 Hands-On Code Implementations


#include <stdint.h>

#define RCC_APB1ENR     (*(volatile uint32_t *)0x40023840UL)
#define CAN1_BASE       0x40006400UL
#define CAN_MCR         (*(volatile uint32_t *)(CAN1_BASE + 0x00UL))
#define CAN_MSR         (*(volatile uint32_t *)(CAN1_BASE + 0x04UL))
#define CAN_BTR         (*(volatile uint32_t *)(CAN1_BASE + 0x1CUL))

/* Configure CAN1 at 500 kbps assuming 42 MHz APB1 peripheral clock:
 * Target: 500 kbps -> Bit Time = 2000 ns.
 * Total Time Quanta = 14 tq -> 1 tq = 142.85 ns -> Prescaler BRP = 6 (42MHz / 6 = 7 MHz).
 * Sync_Seg = 1 tq, TS1 = 11 tq, TS2 = 2 tq -> Total = 14 tq.
 * Sample Point = (1 + 11) / 14 = 85.7% (Meets ISO 11898 standard).
 */
void can1_init_500kbps(void) {
    /* 1. Enable CAN1 peripheral clock */
    RCC_APB1ENR |= (1UL << 25);

    /* 2. Request Initialization mode (INRQ = 1) and exit sleep (SLEEP = 0) */
    CAN_MCR |= (1UL << 0);
    CAN_MCR &= ~(1UL << 1);
    while (!(CAN_MSR & (1UL << 0))); /* Wait for INAK initialization acknowledge */

    /* 3. Configure Bit Timing: BRP=6, TS1=11, TS2=2, SJW=1 */
    /* Note: Register fields store (Value - 1) */
    CAN_BTR = ((1UL - 1UL) << 24)  |  /* SJW = 1 tq */
              ((2UL - 1UL) << 20)  |  /* TS2 = 2 tq */
              ((11UL - 1UL) << 16) |  /* TS1 = 11 tq */
              ((6UL - 1UL) << 0);     /* BRP = 6 */

    /* 4. Exit Initialization mode into Normal operating mode */
    CAN_MCR &= ~(1UL << 0);
    while (CAN_MSR & (1UL << 0));     /* Wait for INAK cleared */
}
Program 2.4-1: STM32 bxCAN Controller Initialization (500 kbps, 87.5% Sample Point) 

#include <stdint.h>
#include <stdbool.h>

#define CAN_TI0R        (*(volatile uint32_t *)0x40006580UL)
#define CAN_TDT0R       (*(volatile uint32_t *)0x40006584UL)
#define CAN_TDL0R       (*(volatile uint32_t *)0x40006588UL)
#define CAN_TDH0R       (*(volatile uint32_t *)0x4000658CUL)
#define CAN_TSR         (*(volatile uint32_t *)0x40006408UL)

/* Transmit 8-byte CAN message: ID 0x100 (Standard), Engine RPM + Throttle Position */
bool can_transmit_engine_frame(uint16_t rpm, uint8_t throttle_percent) {
    /* Check if Mailbox 0 is empty (TME0 = 1) */
    if (!(CAN_TSR & (1UL << 26))) {
        return false; /* All mailboxes busy */
    }

    /* 1. Set 11-bit Standard Identifier into bits [31:21] */
    CAN_TI0R = (0x100UL << 21);

    /* 2. Set Data Length Code (DLC = 8 bytes) */
    CAN_TDT0R = (8UL << 0);

    /* 3. Pack payload: Bytes 0-1 = RPM (big-endian), Byte 2 = Throttle % */
    uint32_t data_low = ((uint32_t)(rpm >> 8) << 0)  |
                        ((uint32_t)(rpm & 0xFF) << 8) |
                        ((uint32_t)throttle_percent << 16);
    CAN_TDL0R = data_low;
    CAN_TDH0R = 0x00000000; /* Remaining bytes */

    /* 4. Request transmission by setting TXRQ bit */
    CAN_TI0R |= (1UL << 0);
    return true;
}
Program 2.4-2: CAN Message Transmit Engine: Broadcasting Engine Telemetry 

#include <stdint.h>

#define CAN_FMR         (*(volatile uint32_t *)0x40006600UL)
#define CAN_FA1R        (*(volatile uint32_t *)0x4000661CUL)
#define CAN_FS1R        (*(volatile uint32_t *)0x4000660CUL)
#define CAN_FM1R        (*(volatile uint32_t *)0x40006604UL)
#define CAN_FFA1R       (*(volatile uint32_t *)0x40006614UL)
#define CAN_F0R1        (*(volatile uint32_t *)0x40006640UL)
#define CAN_F0R2        (*(volatile uint32_t *)0x40006644UL)

/* Configure Filter Bank 0: Accept only CAN IDs 0x100 through 0x1FF (Mask 0x700) */
void can_filter_config(void) {
    /* Enter Filter Initialization mode */
    CAN_FMR |= (1UL << 0);

    /* Deactivate Filter Bank 0 */
    CAN_FA1R &= ~(1UL << 0);

    /* 32-bit scale for Filter Bank 0 */
    CAN_FS1R |= (1UL << 0);

    /* Id/Mask mode (FM1R = 0) */
    CAN_FM1R &= ~(1UL << 0);

    /* Assign to FIFO 0 (FFA1R = 0) */
    CAN_FFA1R &= ~(1UL << 0);

    /* Filter ID: 0x100 (aligned to bits [31:21]) */
    CAN_F0R1 = (0x100UL << 21);

    /* Filter Mask: 0x700 (Matches upper 3 bits: only 0x100-0x1FF accepted) */
    CAN_F0R2 = (0x700UL << 21);

    /* Activate Filter Bank 0 */
    CAN_FA1R |= (1UL << 0);

    /* Exit Filter Initialization mode */
    CAN_FMR &= ~(1UL << 0);
}
Program 2.4-3: Hardware Acceptance Filter Configuration (Filter Bank 0) 

#include <stdio.h>
#include <string.h>
#include <unistd.h>
#include <net/if.h>
#include <sys/ioctl.h>
#include <sys/socket.h>
#include <linux/can.h>
#include <linux/can/raw.h>

int main(void) {
    int s;
    struct sockaddr_can addr;
    struct ifreq ifr;
    struct can_frame frame;

    /* 1. Open raw CAN socket */
    s = socket(PF_CAN, SOCK_RAW, CAN_RAW);
    strcpy(ifr.ifr_name, "can0");
    ioctl(s, SIOCGIFINDEX, &ifr);

    addr.can_family = AF_CAN;
    addr.can_ifindex = ifr.ifr_ifindex;
    bind(s, (struct sockaddr *)&addr, sizeof(addr));

    /* 2. Populate CAN 2.0A frame */
    frame.can_id = 0x100;
    frame.can_dlc = 8;
    frame.data[0] = 0x0A; /* RPM High */
    frame.data[1] = 0x28; /* RPM Low (2600 RPM) */
    frame.data[2] = 45;   /* Throttle 45% */

    /* 3. Send frame to virtual or physical CAN bus */
    write(s, &frame, sizeof(struct can_frame));
    printf("Transmitted CAN frame ID 0x%03X successfully over can0\n", frame.can_id);

    close(s);
    return 0;
}
Program 2.4-4: Linux SocketCAN Host Client in C (send_can.c) 

#include <stdint.h>
#include <stdio.h>

#define CAN_RI0R        (*(volatile uint32_t *)0x400065B0UL)
#define CAN_RDT0R       (*(volatile uint32_t *)0x400065B4UL)
#define CAN_RDL0R       (*(volatile uint32_t *)0x400065B8UL)
#define CAN_RDH0R       (*(volatile uint32_t *)0x400065BCUL)
#define CAN_RF0R        (*(volatile uint32_t *)0x4000640CUL)

void can_sniffer_poll(void) {
    /* Check if message pending in FIFO 0 */
    if ((CAN_RF0R & (3UL << 0)) != 0) {
        uint32_t id = (CAN_RI0R >> 21) & 0x7FF;
        uint8_t dlc = CAN_RDT0R & 0x0F;
        uint32_t data_l = CAN_RDL0R;
        uint32_t data_h = CAN_RDH0R;

        printf("CAN RX -> ID: 0x%03lX | DLC: %u | DATA: %02lX %02lX %02lX %02lX %02lX %02lX %02lX %02lX\r\n",
               id, dlc,
               (data_l >> 0) & 0xFF, (data_l >> 8) & 0xFF, (data_l >> 16) & 0xFF, (data_l >> 24) & 0xFF,
               (data_h >> 0) & 0xFF, (data_h >> 8) & 0xFF, (data_h >> 16) & 0xFF, (data_h >> 24) & 0xFF);

        /* Release FIFO 0 output mailbox */
        CAN_RF0R |= (1UL << 5);
    }
}
Program 2.4-5: Promiscuous CAN Bus Packet Sniffer over UART

CAN 2.0A vs. CAN 2.0B vs. CAN FD Protocol Evolution

Feature / SpecificationCAN 2.0A (Standard)CAN 2.0B (Extended)CAN FD (Flexible Data-rate)
Identifier Bit Length11-Bit Identifier29-Bit Identifier11-Bit or 29-Bit
Maximum Payload Length8 Bytes maximum8 Bytes maximumUp to 64 Bytes per frame
Arbitration Phase SpeedUp to 1.0 Mbps (typically 500 kbps)Up to 1.0 MbpsUp to 1.0 Mbps
Data Phase SpeedFixed at arbitration speedFixed at arbitration speedUp to 5.0 - 8.0 Mbps (Accelerated)
CRC Integrity Polynomial15-Bit CRC15-Bit CRC17-Bit (<=16B) or 21-Bit (>16B) CRC
Standard SpecificationISO 11898-1:2003ISO 11898-1:2003ISO 11898-1:2015
Primary Target Industry
  • Automotive Body & Chassis
  • Industrial Robotics
  • Heavy Trucks (SAE J1939)
  • Marine NMEA-2000
  • Electric Vehicle Powertrain
  • ADAS Radar & Cameras

Topic Quiz (10 Questions)

Test your conceptual understanding of today's embedded systems architecture, registers, and runtime behaviors.

1. What is the physical voltage level on the CAN_H and CAN_L lines during a Recessive (Logic 1) state?
  • CAN_H = 0V, CAN_L = 0V
  • CAN_H = 2.5V, CAN_L = 2.5V (Differential Voltage = 0V)
  • CAN_H = 5.0V, CAN_L = 0V
  • CAN_H = 3.5V, CAN_L = 1.5V
During recessive bits, both lines idle at half the transceiver supply (2.5V), yielding zero differential voltage across the termination resistors.
2. In CAN bus bitwise arbitration, which message wins bus access when two nodes transmit at the exact same instant?
  • The message with the larger payload size (DLC)
  • The message with the numerically lower Arbitration ID
  • The message with the numerically higher Arbitration ID
  • The node closest to the 120-ohm termination resistor
Dominant bits (0) override recessive bits (1). Therefore, frames with lower numerical IDs contain more leading zeroes and win arbitration.
3. Why are 120-ohm termination resistors mandatory at both ends of a high-speed CAN network?
  • To step down battery voltages
  • To match the characteristic impedance of the twisted-pair cable, preventing high-frequency signal reflections from corrupting bits
  • To power the microcontrollers
  • To invert the parity bits
Unterminated transmission lines cause signal edges to reflect back along the wire, causing destructive interference and bit corruption.
4. What happens when a CAN node's Transmit Error Counter (TEC) exceeds 255?
  • The node resets the baud rate to 10 kbps
  • The node enters the Bus-Off state, physically disconnecting its transmitter from the network to protect other nodes
  • The node begins transmitting at double frequency
  • A Non-Maskable Interrupt (NMI) is triggered
The CAN fault-confinement state machine forces defective nodes into Bus-Off (TEC > 255) to prevent a broken ECU from jamming traffic.
5. What is the maximum payload data length of a standard CAN 2.0A or 2.0B frame?
  • 4 Bytes
  • 8 Bytes
  • 64 Bytes
  • 1500 Bytes
Standard CAN 2.0 frames are limited to a maximum payload of 8 bytes (DLC = 8). CAN FD expands this to 64 bytes.
6. Where is the recommended bit Sample Point location for automotive 500 kbps powertrain CAN networks?
  • 50.0%
  • 75.0%
  • 87.5%
  • 99.0%
Automotive CiA 303-1 and ISO 11898 standards mandate placing the sample point at 87.5% of the bit duration to tolerate propagation delays.
7. How does an acknowledging node confirm successful receipt of a valid CAN frame?
  • By driving a dominant 0 during the ACK Slot bit on the bus
  • By replying with a 64-byte ACK frame
  • By toggling an external handshake line
  • By resetting its receive error counter
The transmitting node outputs a recessive 1 during the ACK bit; any receiver that computed a matching CRC pulls the bus dominant (0).
8. What feature distinguishes CAN FD from legacy CAN 2.0?
  • CAN FD uses fiber optic cables instead of copper
  • CAN FD supports larger payloads up to 64 bytes and switches to higher clock speeds (up to 8 Mbps) during the data phase
  • CAN FD eliminates the CRC checksum
  • CAN FD requires 6 physical wires
CAN Flexible Data-rate retains classical arbitration speeds (e.g. 500 kbps) but accelerates data phase clocks up to 5-8 Mbps with 64-byte payloads.
9. What is the role of the Linux SocketCAN kernel subsystem?
  • To emulate USB printers
  • To treat CAN controllers as network interfaces (like eth0), allowing applications to use standard Berkeley socket APIs
  • To convert CAN frames into Python scripts
  • To simulate analog battery degradation
SocketCAN integrates CAN natively into the Linux networking stack, allowing software to use standard socket(), bind(), and write() syscalls.
10. What is Bit Stuffing in CAN communication?
  • Padding payload data with random noise
  • An automatic rule where the transmitter inserts an opposite bit after 5 consecutive identical bits to guarantee clock synchronization edges
  • Compressing 16-bit integers into 8 bits
  • Overclocking the prescaler
To prevent receivers from losing clock synchronization during long runs of 1s or 0s, CAN inserts a stuffed bit of complementary polarity after 5 identical bits.

Hands-On Assignments

Complete these 5 lab assignments to solidify your hands-on firmware engineering skills.

Assignment 1: CAN Bit Timing Parameter Calculator

Task: Given a 42 MHz APB1 peripheral clock, write a C or Python script that computes the exact BRP, TS1, and TS2 register values required for 125 kbps, 250 kbps, 500 kbps, and 1 Mbps baud rates with sample points closest to 87.5%.

Assignment 2: Dual-Node Real-Time Engine RPM Broadcast Simulator

Task: Connect two STM32 boards (or an STM32 to a PC USB-CAN adapter). Node 1 broadcasts simulated engine RPM frames every 20 ms. Node 2 receives the frames via FIFO interrupt and controls a PWM tachometer needle.

Assignment 3: OBD-II Engine Coolant Temperature Requester

Task: Send an OBD-II diagnostic request frame (ID=0x7DF, Data=[02 01 05 00 00 00 00 00]). Parse the ECU response frame (ID=0x7E8), decode the temperature byte ($A - 40$), and display engine coolant in Celsius over UART.

Assignment 4: CAN Bus Fault Injection & Recovery Testbed

Task: Deliberately disconnect the CAN_H wire to trigger transmission errors. Monitor the CAN_ESR register: log the transition from Error-Active to Error-Passive and Bus-Off. Verify that automatic bus-off recovery restores operation upon reconnection.

Assignment 5: SocketCAN Linux Virtual Bus Simulation (vcan0)

Task: Set up a virtual CAN interface (`sudo ip link add dev vcan0 type vcan`). Write a Python script using `python-can` that streams synthetic vehicle telemetry and verify that `candump vcan0` captures all frames.

Official References, Research Papers & Standards

Deepen your engineering foundations with seminal reference manuals, processor architecture standards, and industry specifications:

International Standard International Organization for Standardization

ISO 11898-1:2015: Road Vehicles - Controller Area Network (CAN) - Part 1: Data Link Layer

The primary international standard for CAN 2.0 and CAN FD framing, arbitration rules, error confinement, and bit timing specifications.

View Official Resource →
Industry Specification CAN in Automation (CiA)

CiA 303-1: CANopen Cabling and Connector Recommendations

Engineering standard detailing differential physical layers, pinouts, bus line termination, and sample point placement for automotive networks.

View Official Resource →
Kernel Documentation Linux Kernel Documentation

SocketCAN - The Official Linux CAN Subsystem Documentation

Complete reference for Linux CAN networking architecture, raw sockets, broadcast managers, and CAN FD framing APIs.

fields.title: Module 2 Project: Toolchains, Linker Scripts & Binary Analysis
fields.content:
Module 2 Capstone Project

Toolchains, Linker Scripts & Binary Analysis

Firmware engineers cannot rely on black-box vendor IDEs to manage memory layouts and builds. A professional must understand the transition from source code to machine bits: configuring cross-compilers, orchestrating builds with Make/CMake, handcrafting custom linker scripts, inspecting ELF symbols, and automating memory budget enforcement in Git CI pipelines. This capstone guides you through building a complete cross-compilation pipeline on Linux/WSL and crafting a zero-IDE bare-metal firmware project with custom linker scripts on an STM32 microcontroller.

Dimension Project 1: Linux / WSL Environment Project 2: Physical STM32 Board
Project Focus Multi-Target Build Matrix & Binary Bloat Inspector CLI Zero-IDE Bare-Metal Firmware with Custom Linker Script
Key Artifacts Modular Makefile, bloat_check.sh, Git pre-commit hook stm32_flash.ld, startup_stm32.c, firmware.map
Toolchain Focus GCC, arm-none-eabi-size, arm-none-eabi-nm, objdump Cross-linker VMA/LMA mapping, CRT0 vector table, OpenOCD/GDB
Verification Automated memory budget gate halting builds on footprint bloat Section allocation audit in map file, GDB hardware reset verification

Part 1: Linux / WSL Project — Multi-Target Build Matrix & Binary Bloat Inspector

In commercial firmware development, builds must support both Host Simulation (for rapid automated unit testing on x86_64) and Target Cross-Compilation (for flashing to ARM Cortex-M). Furthermore, firmware teams use automated bloat gates to reject pull requests that exceed strict SRAM or Flash memory thresholds.

Step 1: Production Multi-Target Makefile

This Makefile cleanly decouples host native builds (make host) from target cross-compilation (make target), generates disassembly, symbol maps, and invokes our bloat inspector: 

# ==============================================================================
# Multi-Target Firmware Makefile
# Supports: Host Native (x86_64) & Cross-Target (ARM Cortex-M4)
# ==============================================================================

PROJECT_NAME := sensor_firmware
BUILD_DIR    := build

# Host Compilers
HOST_CC      := gcc
HOST_CFLAGS  := -std=c11 -Wall -Wextra -Werror -O2 -g

# Target Cross-Toolchain
TARGET_PREFIX := arm-none-eabi-
TARGET_CC     := $(TARGET_PREFIX)gcc
TARGET_OBJCOPY:= $(TARGET_PREFIX)objcopy
TARGET_OBJDUMP:= $(TARGET_PREFIX)objdump
TARGET_SIZE   := $(TARGET_PREFIX)size
TARGET_NM     := $(TARGET_PREFIX)nm

# Cortex-M4 Hardware Flags
TARGET_MCU_FLAGS := -mcpu=cortex-m4 -mthumb -mfloat-abi=hard -mfpu=fpv4-sp-d16
TARGET_CFLAGS    := $(TARGET_MCU_FLAGS) -std=c11 -Wall -Wextra -Werror -Os -g3 \
                    -ffunction-sections -fdata-sections -DSTM32F401xE
TARGET_LDFLAGS   := $(TARGET_MCU_FLAGS) -T stm32_flash.ld \
                    -Wl,-Map=$(BUILD_DIR)/$(PROJECT_NAME).map,--cref \
                    -Wl,--gc-sections --specs=nano.specs --specs=nosys.specs

# Sources
SRCS_COMMON := src/sensor.c
SRCS_HOST   := src/main_host.c $(SRCS_COMMON)
SRCS_TARGET := src/main_target.c src/startup_stm32.c $(SRCS_COMMON)

.PHONY: all host target clean bloat-check

all: target

# Target Cross-Compilation Rule
target: $(BUILD_DIR)/$(PROJECT_NAME).elf $(BUILD_DIR)/$(PROJECT_NAME).bin bloat-check

$(BUILD_DIR)/$(PROJECT_NAME).elf: $(SRCS_TARGET) stm32_flash.ld | $(BUILD_DIR)
	@echo "--> Cross-compiling target ELF for Cortex-M4..."
	$(TARGET_CC) $(TARGET_CFLAGS) $(SRCS_TARGET) $(TARGET_LDFLAGS) -o $@
	@echo "--> Generating Disassembly Listing..."
	$(TARGET_OBJDUMP) -d -S $@ > $(BUILD_DIR)/$(PROJECT_NAME).asm
	@echo "--> Generating Sorted Symbol Footprint..."
	$(TARGET_NM) --size-sort -C -r $@ > $(BUILD_DIR)/symbols_by_size.txt
	@echo "--> Memory Utilization Summary:"
	$(TARGET_SIZE) -B $@

$(BUILD_DIR)/$(PROJECT_NAME).bin: $(BUILD_DIR)/$(PROJECT_NAME).elf
	$(TARGET_OBJCOPY) -O binary $< $@

# Host Native Build Rule
host: $(SRCS_HOST) | $(BUILD_DIR)
	@echo "--> Compiling native host binary..."
	$(HOST_CC) $(HOST_CFLAGS) $(SRCS_HOST) -o $(BUILD_DIR)/$(PROJECT_NAME)_host
	@echo "--> Executing host simulator:"
	./$(BUILD_DIR)/$(PROJECT_NAME)_host

# Automated Binary Bloat Gate
bloat-check: $(BUILD_DIR)/$(PROJECT_NAME).elf
	@chmod +x scripts/bloat_check.sh
	@scripts/bloat_check.sh $(BUILD_DIR)/$(PROJECT_NAME).elf 524288 98304

$(BUILD_DIR):
	mkdir -p $(BUILD_DIR)

clean:
	rm -rf $(BUILD_DIR)

Step 2: Binary Bloat Inspector Script (scripts/bloat_check.sh)

This bash script parses the ELF output using arm-none-eabi-size and arm-none-eabi-nm. It halts the build if Flash or RAM thresholds are exceeded or if any single symbol exceeds budget: 

#!/usr/bin/env bash
# ==============================================================================
# scripts/bloat_check.sh: Embedded Binary Footprint & Memory Budget Gate
# Usage: ./bloat_check.sh <elf_file> <max_flash_bytes> <max_ram_bytes>
# ==============================================================================
set -euo pipefail

ELF_FILE="${1:-build/sensor_firmware.elf}"
MAX_FLASH="${2:-524288}" # 512 KB
MAX_RAM="${3:-98304}"    # 96 KB

if [ ! -f "$ELF_FILE" ]; then
    echo "ERROR: ELF file '$ELF_FILE' not found!"
    exit 1
fi

# Extract text, data, bss sections using size in Berkeley format
SIZE_OUTPUT=$(arm-none-eabi-size -B "$ELF_FILE" | tail -n 1)
TEXT=$(echo "$SIZE_OUTPUT" | awk '{print $1}')
DATA=$(echo "$SIZE_OUTPUT" | awk '{print $2}')
BSS=$(echo "$SIZE_OUTPUT"  | awk '{print $3}')

# Flash = .text + .data
TOTAL_FLASH=$((TEXT + DATA))
# RAM = .data + .bss
TOTAL_RAM=$((DATA + BSS))

FLASH_PERCENT=$(awk "BEGIN {printf \"%.2f\", ($TOTAL_FLASH / $MAX_FLASH) * 100}")
RAM_PERCENT=$(awk "BEGIN {printf \"%.2f\", ($TOTAL_RAM / $MAX_RAM) * 100}")

echo "================ MEMORY BUDGET REPORT ================"
echo "FLASH: ${TOTAL_FLASH} / ${MAX_FLASH} bytes (${FLASH_PERCENT}%)"
echo "  RAM: ${TOTAL_RAM} / ${MAX_RAM} bytes (${RAM_PERCENT}%)"
echo "  Breakdown: .text=${TEXT}B, .data=${DATA}B, .bss=${BSS}B"
echo "------------------------------------------------------"

# Audit Top 5 Largest Symbols
echo "Top 5 Memory-Consuming Symbols:"
arm-none-eabi-nm --size-sort -r -C "$ELF_FILE" | head -n 5

# Enforce Budgets
if [ "$TOTAL_FLASH" -gt "$MAX_FLASH" ]; then
    echo "ERROR: FLASH OVERFLOW! Exceeded budget by $((TOTAL_FLASH - MAX_FLASH)) bytes!"
    exit 2
fi

if [ "$TOTAL_RAM" -gt "$MAX_RAM" ]; then
    echo "ERROR: RAM OVERFLOW! Exceeded budget by $((TOTAL_RAM - MAX_RAM)) bytes!"
    exit 3
fi

echo "STATUS: Memory budget PASSED."
exit 0

Step 3: Git Pre-Commit Hook Integration

Integrate the bloat check directly into your local Git repository so no developer can commit code that breaks memory constraints: 

# Install Git pre-commit hook in .git/hooks/pre-commit
cat << 'EOF' > .git/hooks/pre-commit
#!/usr/bin/env bash
echo "Running firmware pre-commit verification..."
make clean
make target || { echo "Build failed! Commit aborted."; exit 1; }
echo "Pre-commit verification succeeded."
EOF

chmod +x .git/hooks/pre-commit

Part 2: Physical STM32 Board Project — Zero-IDE Bare-Metal Firmware with Custom Linker Script

Professional embedded firmware demands absolute control over the reset sequence and memory layout. Here, we discard vendor auto-generated code and build our own custom Linker Script (.ld) and C Startup Routine (startup_stm32.c) from first principles.

Step 1: Custom Linker Script (stm32_flash.ld)

This script defines the physical Flash (512K) and SRAM (96K) boundaries, maps the vector table to address 0x08000000, defines the VMA/LMA relocation mechanics for .data, zeroes .bss, and reserves top-of-RAM for the Main Stack Pointer (MSP): 

/* Entry Point symbol defined in startup code */
ENTRY(Reset_Handler)

/* Memory Layout for STM32F401RET6 */
MEMORY
{
    FLASH (rx)  : ORIGIN = 0x08000000, LENGTH = 512K
    RAM   (xrw) : ORIGIN = 0x20000000, LENGTH = 96K
}

/* Stack boundary calculation: Top of RAM */
_estack = ORIGIN(RAM) + LENGTH(RAM);

SECTIONS
{
    /* 1. Vector Table: Must reside at base of Flash */
    .isr_vector :
    {
        . = ALIGN(4);
        KEEP(*(.isr_vector))
        . = ALIGN(4);
    } > FLASH

    /* 2. Program Code and Read-Only Constants */
    .text :
    {
        . = ALIGN(4);
        *(.text)
        *(.text*)
        *(.rodata)
        *(.rodata*)
        . = ALIGN(4);
        _etext = .; /* Symbol marking end of code in Flash */
    } > FLASH

    /* 3. Initialized Data Section: VMA in RAM, LMA in Flash */
    _sidata = LOADADDR(.data);
    .data :
    {
        . = ALIGN(4);
        _sdata = .; /* Start of .data in RAM */
        *(.data)
        *(.data*)
        . = ALIGN(4);
        _edata = .; /* End of .data in RAM */
    } > RAM AT > FLASH

    /* 4. Zero-Initialized BSS Section in RAM */
    .bss :
    {
        . = ALIGN(4);
        _sbss = .;  /* Start of .bss in RAM */
        *(.bss)
        *(.bss*)
        *(COMMON)
        . = ALIGN(4);
        _ebss = .;  /* End of .bss in RAM */
    } > RAM

    /* Discard unused debugging metadata */
    /DISCARD/ :
    {
        *(.note.GNU-stack)
    }
}

Step 2: C Startup File & Vector Table (src/startup_stm32.c)

Rather than writing assembly, modern embedded practice implements CRT0 in pure C. The startup code copies initialized variables from Flash to RAM, fills .bss with zeros, and jumps to main(): 

/**
 * @file startup_stm32.c
 * @brief Bare-Metal C Startup Routine & Vector Table for STM32F4
 */
#include <stdint.h>

/* Symbols exported by the Linker Script */
extern uint32_t _estack;
extern uint32_t _etext;
extern uint32_t _sidata;
extern uint32_t _sdata;
extern uint32_t _edata;
extern uint32_t _sbss;
extern uint32_t _ebss;

/* Prototypes */
void Reset_Handler(void);
void Default_Handler(void);
extern int main(void);

/* Exception Handler Aliases pointing to Default_Handler */
void NMI_Handler(void)        __attribute__((weak, alias("Default_Handler")));
void HardFault_Handler(void)  __attribute__((weak, alias("Default_Handler")));
void MemManage_Handler(void)  __attribute__((weak, alias("Default_Handler")));
void BusFault_Handler(void)   __attribute__((weak, alias("Default_Handler")));
void UsageFault_Handler(void) __attribute__((weak, alias("Default_Handler")));
void SysTick_Handler(void)    __attribute__((weak, alias("Default_Handler")));

/* Vector Table placed in .isr_vector section */
__attribute__((section(".isr_vector"), used))
const uint32_t * const g_vector_table[] = {
    (uint32_t *)&_estack,        /* Initial Stack Pointer (MSP) */
    (uint32_t *)Reset_Handler,   /* Reset Handler */
    (uint32_t *)NMI_Handler,     /* NMI Handler */
    (uint32_t *)HardFault_Handler,/* HardFault Handler */
    (uint32_t *)MemManage_Handler,
    (uint32_t *)BusFault_Handler,
    (uint32_t *)UsageFault_Handler,
    0, 0, 0, 0,                  /* Reserved */
    (uint32_t *)Default_Handler, /* SVCall */
    (uint32_t *)Default_Handler, /* Debug Monitor */
    0,                           /* Reserved */
    (uint32_t *)Default_Handler, /* PendSV */
    (uint32_t *)SysTick_Handler  /* SysTick */
};

/* C Runtime Initialization (CRT0) */
void Reset_Handler(void) {
    /* 1. Copy initialized .data section from Flash (LMA) to RAM (VMA) */
    uint32_t *p_src = &_sidata;
    uint32_t *p_dest = &_sdata;
    while (p_dest < &_edata) {
        *p_dest++ = *p_src++;
    }

    /* 2. Zero-initialize the .bss section in RAM */
    uint32_t *p_bss = &_sbss;
    while (p_bss < &_ebss) {
        *p_bss++ = 0U;
    }

    /* 3. Call application entry point */
    main();

    /* 4. Safety trap if main ever returns */
    while (1) {
        __asm volatile ("wfi");
    }
}

/* Default Catch-All Exception Trap */
void Default_Handler(void) {
    while (1) {
        /* Hang in loop for debugger attachment */
    }
}

Step 3: Target Application (src/main_target.c)

A clean firmware application demonstrating global variables (in .data and .bss) to verify our startup initialization: 

/**
 * @file main_target.c
 * @brief Hardware Demonstration of Linker Sections & Startup
 */
#include <stdint.h>

/* Hardware Register Definitions */
#define RCC_AHB1ENR   (*(volatile uint32_t *)(0x40023830UL))
#define GPIOA_MODER   (*(volatile uint32_t *)(0x40020000UL))
#define GPIOA_BSRR    (*(volatile uint32_t *)(0x40020018UL))

/* Variable in .data (Initialized, must be copied from Flash to RAM) */
uint32_t g_blink_period_ticks = 400000UL;

/* Variable in .bss (Uninitialized, must be zeroed by Reset_Handler) */
uint32_t g_heartbeat_counter;

static void delay(volatile uint32_t count) {
    while (count > 0) {
        count--;
    }
}

int main(void) {
    /* Enable GPIOA Clock */
    RCC_AHB1ENR |= (1UL << 0);

    /* Configure PA5 (LD2) as Output */
    GPIOA_MODER &= ~(3UL << (5 * 2));
    GPIOA_MODER |=  (1UL << (5 * 2));

    /* Verification check: If CRT0 failed to copy .data, period would be 0! */
    if (g_blink_period_ticks == 0UL) {
        g_blink_period_ticks = 50000UL; /* Fast error blink */
    }

    while (1) {
        GPIOA_BSRR = (1UL << 5);       /* LED ON */
        delay(g_blink_period_ticks);
        GPIOA_BSRR = (1UL << (5 + 16)); /* LED OFF */
        delay(g_blink_period_ticks);

        g_heartbeat_counter++;
    }

    return 0;
}

Module 2 Capstone Knowledge Check

Test your mastery of the build pipeline, linker mechanics, and memory budget enforcement.

1. In stm32_flash.ld, what is the distinction between VMA (Virtual/Run Address) and LMA (Load Memory Address) for the .data section?

2. Why are the GCC flags -ffunction-sections and -fdata-sections combined with -Wl,--gc-sections?

3. What is the very first entry at index 0 of the ARM Cortex-M vector table?

4. Which flag in arm-none-eabi-nm sorts symbols by their memory size in descending order?

5. Why is --specs=nano.specs commonly passed to the linker in embedded ARM GCC projects?

6. What happens if the startup code fails to initialize .bss memory?

7. What information does the .map file provide to an embedded engineer?

8. In stm32_flash.ld, why is KEEP(*(.isr_vector)) necessary?

9. What is the role of LOADADDR(.data) in the linker script?

10. Why should a firmware project track binary sizes in a Git pre-commit hook or CI pipeline?

Hands-on Engineering Challenges

Challenge 1 (Host)

Symbol Bloat Regression CLI

Extend bloat_check.sh to compare the newly compiled ELF against the previous Git commit's ELF (using git show HEAD:build/firmware.elf). Fail the build if any individual function grew by more than 15%.

Challenge 2 (Host)

CMake Multi-Toolchain Target Matrix

Write a single CMakeLists.txt that uses a CMake toolchain file (arm-gcc.cmake) to build the target firmware when passed -DCMAKE_TOOLCHAIN_FILE=arm-gcc.cmake, and builds a host simulator when omitted.

Challenge 3 (STM32)

Custom Flash Sector for Calibration Data

Modify stm32_flash.ld to carve out a dedicated 16KB Flash sector named .calib_data at address 0x0807C000. Place a const calibration_t struct into this section using GCC __attribute__((section(".calib_data"))) and verify in the .map file.

Challenge 4 (STM32)

Stack Watermarking & Overflow Guard

In startup_stm32.c, fill the RAM region between _ebss and _estack - 1024 with a watermark pattern (0xDEADBEEF). In main(), count how many words of the watermark were overwritten to determine peak stack usage.

Challenge 5 (Toolchain Automation)

Disassembly Annotation Automation

Add a Makefile target make annotate that generates mixed C and assembly listings using arm-none-eabi-objdump -S -l, highlighting compiler optimization differences between -O0, -O2, and -Os.

Further Technical Reading

GNU Toolchain Free Software Foundation

GNU Linker (ld) Command Language Manual

Official specification of linker scripts, section commands, memory regions, and symbol assignments.

Architecture Arm Developer

Arm Cortex-M4 Generic User Guide

Defines exception model, vector table offsets, core registers (MSP/PSP), and memory architecture.

fields.title: Day 14: USB, Ethernet & Wireless (BLE/Wi-Fi)
fields.content:
Session 2.5

Day 14: USB, Ethernet & Wireless (BLE/Wi-Fi)

Problem Statement: Embedded systems must communicate beyond local circuit boards to host PCs, enterprise LANs, smartphones, and cloud databases. Implementing USB descriptors, lightweight TCP/IP stacks (lwIP), Bluetooth Low Energy GATT services, and asynchronous AT command parsers requires mastering complex protocol abstractions on resource-constrained microcontrollers.
📋 Daily Plan & Learning Architecture
Session 2.5 Module 2: RTOS, Peripherals & Communication Estimated: 3.5 hrs

🎯 Today's Mission & Relevance

  • Master USB descriptor trees and implement USB CDC virtual serial ports.
  • Deploy embedded TCP/IP networking via the open-source lwIP stack.
  • Structure wireless telemetry using BLE GATT profiles and MQTT Wi-Fi modems.

📐 Theoretical Milestones

  • USB descriptor hierarchy (Device, Config, Interface, Endpoint).
  • Zero-copy packet buffer (pbuf) architectures in embedded TCP/IP.
  • BLE GAP advertising channels vs GATT hierarchical Service/Characteristic topologies.

💻 Hands-On Blueprint

  • Program 14.1: USB CDC virtual COM port echo loopback driver.
  • Program 14.2: USB HID consumer keyboard report generator via button inputs.
  • Program 14.3: lwIP TCP client connecting and streaming JSON telemetry.
  • Program 14.4: ESP-AT non-blocking state machine for cloud MQTT publishing.
  • Program 14.5: BLE peripheral custom GATT service with temperature notifications.

🛡️ Production Failure Modes

  • Violating USB 64-byte Full-Speed packet boundaries, stalling bulk endpoints.
  • Blocking RTOS threads inside synchronous AT command parsing loops.
  • Allocating large TCP buffers that exceed internal microcontroller SRAM limits.
🏁 Daily Milestone Deliverables: 5 Interactive Register-Level Programs • 5 Architecture Diagrams • 10 Practice MCQs • 5 Hands-On Assignments

14.1 Connectivity Beyond the Circuit Board

While I2C, SPI, and CAN interconnect chips on a single board or vehicle harness, modern IoT and embedded systems must bridge to the wider digital world. They must connect directly to host PCs via USB (Universal Serial Bus), interface with industrial local area networks via Ethernet, communicate with consumer smartphones via Bluetooth Low Energy (BLE), and stream telemetry to cloud databases via Wi-Fi and MQTT.

Integrating these complex protocol stacks on resource-constrained microcontrollers without a desktop operating system requires understanding descriptor hierarchies, lightweight TCP/IP stacks (lwIP), and asynchronous AT command state machines.

Real World Application: Modern hospital patient monitors communicate simultaneously across these layers: a USB CDC port provides local technician diagnostics; an isolated Ethernet port streams vital signs over hospital LANs via lwIP; and a BLE transceiver links to wearable pulse oximeter finger rings.
Figure 2.5-1: USB 2.0 Descriptor Tree Hierarchy
Figure Parameters Explained:
  • Device Descriptor: Root metadata identifying the device VID (Vendor ID) and PID (Product ID).
  • Configuration Descriptor: Specifies bus-powered vs self-powered status and maximum current draw (in 2mA units).
  • Interface Descriptor: Declares functional class (e.g. Class 0x02 = CDC Communications, Class 0x03 = HID).
  • Endpoint Descriptors: Configure hardware FIFOs for Control (EP0), Bulk, Interrupt, or Isochronous transfers.

14.2 USB Device Classes: Communication Device Class (CDC) vs. Human Interface Device (HID)

To avoid writing custom operating system kernel drivers, embedded engineers design USB firmware conforming to standard USB Classes recognized natively by Windows, macOS, and Linux:

  • USB CDC (Communications Device Class): Emulates an RS-232 serial COM port over high-speed USB bulk endpoints. The host OS automatically assigns a virtual serial port (e.g. /dev/ttyACM0 or COM3), allowing standard terminal programs to communicate at over 1 Megabyte/sec.
  • USB HID (Human Interface Device): Used for keyboards, mice, and gamepads. Transmits structured HID Reports over low-latency Interrupt endpoints. Requires zero host driver installation and works in BIOS pre-boot environments.
Figure 2.5-2: USB CDC Virtual COM Port Architecture and Data Flow
Figure Parameters Explained:
  • Bulk Transfer Endpoints: Guarantees error-free data delivery with hardware CRC and retries; utilizes spare bus bandwidth.
  • Control Endpoint (EP0): Handles standard USB enumeration, descriptor requests, and line coding parameters (baud rate, parity).
  • Throughput Advantage: Bypasses physical UART baud rate dividers; USB Full-Speed transmits at up to 12 Mbps wire speed.

14.3 Embedded TCP/IP Networking: The lwIP Architecture

Connecting a microcontroller to an Ethernet LAN requires an operating system networking stack. Because standard Linux socket stacks require megabytes of virtual memory, microcontrollers utilize lwIP (Lightweight IP), an open-source TCP/IP stack designed by Adam Dunkels. lwIP implements full IPv4/IPv6, TCP, UDP, DHCP, and ARP protocols while fitting inside less than 40 KB of ROM and a few kilobytes of RAM through zero-copy packet buffer (pbuf) chaining.

Figure 2.5-3: lwIP Lightweight Embedded TCP/IP Stack Protocol Layers
Figure Parameters Explained:
  • Ethernet PHY (Physical Layer): Transceiver chip (e.g. LAN8742) converting differential cable voltages to digital RMII signals.
  • RMII (Reduced Media Independent Interface): High-speed 50 MHz 7-wire digital interface connecting MAC to PHY.
  • pbuf (Packet Buffer): lwIP memory structure chaining fragmented network packets without copying data.
  • Zero-Copy Architecture: DMA transfers Ethernet frames directly into lwIP pbufs, avoiding multiple CPU memory copies.

14.4 Bluetooth Low Energy (BLE): GAP Advertising & GATT Data Hierarchy

Unlike classic Bluetooth designed for continuous audio streaming, Bluetooth Low Energy (BLE) is engineered for extreme power conservation, allowing sensor nodes to operate for years on a single coin cell. BLE software architecture is divided into two operational models:

  • GAP (Generic Access Profile): Controls device discovery, advertising, and connection establishment. A Broadcaster / Peripheral sends periodic 31-byte Advertising Packets; an Observer / Central (e.g. a smartphone) scans for advertisements.
  • GATT (Generic Attribute Profile): Organizes data once a connection is formed. Data is structured hierarchically into Services (logical functional groups identified by 16-bit or 128-bit UUIDs) containing Characteristics (individual data values supporting Read, Write, and Notify operations).
Figure 2.5-4: BLE GATT Data Structure and Smartphone Notification Flow
Figure Parameters Explained:
  • UUID (Universally Unique Identifier): 16-bit numbers for standard Bluetooth SIG profiles; 128-bit UUIDs for custom vendor profiles.
  • Notify Operation: The peripheral pushes data to the central smartphone asynchronously without waiting for host polling.
  • Connection Interval: Configurable period (e.g. 50 ms to 4000 ms) controlling how frequently radio transceivers exchange synchronization pulses.

14.5 Wireless IoT via Cellular & Wi-Fi: The AT Command State Machine

Many industrial embedded systems pair a host microcontroller with an external co-processor modem (such as an Espressif ESP32 or a Quectel 4G LTE module) over a high-speed UART interface. Communication is managed via standardized Haynes AT Commands. Firmware must implement an asynchronous, non-blocking Parser State Machine to transmit AT strings, handle variable-latency responses (OK, ERROR), and stream telemetry over MQTT.

Figure 2.5-5: STM32 to ESP32 AT Command Flow for Cloud MQTT Publishing
Figure Parameters Explained:
  • Asynchronous AT Parser: Parses incoming ASCII response lines in real-time without blocking the CPU in delay loops.
  • MQTT (Message Queuing Telemetry Transport): Lightweight publish-subscribe protocol ideal for high-latency, low-bandwidth wireless links.
  • Unsolicited Result Codes (URCs): Spontaneous notifications from modem (e.g. '+MQTTRCV') handled by interrupt ring buffers.

14.6 Hands-On Code Implementations


#include <stdint.h>
#include <string.h>

/* Prototype hooks matching STM32 USB Device CDC Class Library */
int8_t CDC_Receive_FS(uint8_t* Buf, uint32_t *Len);
uint8_t CDC_Transmit_FS(uint8_t* Buf, uint16_t Len);

/* Called by USB interrupt when a packet arrives from host PC */
int8_t CDC_Receive_FS(uint8_t* Buf, uint32_t *Len) {
    uint32_t rx_bytes = *Len;

    /* Echo received bytes back to host PC immediately */
    CDC_Transmit_FS(Buf, (uint16_t)rx_bytes);

    return 0; /* USBD_OK */
}

/* Transmit log string over USB CDC at native 12 Mbps wire speed */
void usb_cdc_print_string(const char *str) {
    uint16_t len = (uint16_t)strlen(str);
    CDC_Transmit_FS((uint8_t *)str, len);
}
Program 2.5-1: USB CDC Virtual COM Port Echo Loopback Driver 

#include <stdint.h>

/* Standard USB HID Keyboard Report Format (8 bytes) */
typedef struct __attribute__((packed)) {
    uint8_t modifiers;      /* Bit 0=LCTRL, 1=LSHIFT, 2=LALT, 3=LGUI */
    uint8_t reserved;       /* 0x00 */
    uint8_t keycodes[6];    /* Up to 6 simultaneous pressed keys */
} USB_HID_KeyboardReport_t;

extern void USBD_HID_SendReport(uint8_t *report, uint16_t len);

#define HID_KEY_A           0x04
#define HID_KEY_RETURN      0x28

void send_keystroke_a(void) {
    USB_HID_KeyboardReport_t report = {0};

    /* Step 1: Press 'A' */
    report.keycodes[0] = HID_KEY_A;
    USBD_HID_SendReport((uint8_t *)&report, sizeof(report));

    /* Simple delay before releasing key */
    for (volatile int i = 0; i < 100000; i++);

    /* Step 2: Release all keys (all zeroes report) */
    report.keycodes[0] = 0x00;
    USBD_HID_SendReport((uint8_t *)&report, sizeof(report));
}
Program 2.5-2: USB HID Keyboard Report Generator via GPIO Button Trigger 

#include <string.h>
#include <stdio.h>
#include "lwip/netconn.h"
#include "lwip/ip_addr.h"

void tcp_telemetry_task(void *pvParameters) {
    (void)pvParameters;
    struct netconn *conn;
    ip_addr_t server_ip;
    
    /* Target server IP: 192.168.1.100, Port 8080 */
    IP4_ADDR(&server_ip, 192, 168, 1, 100);

    for (;;) {
        /* Create TCP socket connection */
        conn = netconn_new(NETCONN_TCP);
        if (conn != NULL) {
            if (netconn_connect(conn, &server_ip, 8080) == ERR_OK) {
                char payload[128];
                snprintf(payload, sizeof(payload), 
                         "{\"temp\": 24.5, \"pressure\": 101325}\r\n");

                /* Send data over TCP socket */
                netconn_write(conn, payload, strlen(payload), NETCONN_COPY);
                
                netconn_close(conn);
            }
            netconn_delete(conn);
        }
        vTaskDelay(pdMS_TO_TICKS(5000)); /* Repeat every 5 seconds */
    }
}
Program 2.5-3: lwIP TCP Client Connecting and Sending JSON Telemetry 

#include <stdint.h>
#include <stdbool.h>
#include <stdio.h>

typedef enum {
    AT_STATE_TEST,
    AT_STATE_JOIN_WIFI,
    AT_STATE_CONNECT_MQTT,
    AT_STATE_PUBLISH,
    AT_STATE_IDLE
} AT_ClientState_t;

static AT_ClientState_t g_at_state = AT_STATE_TEST;

void send_uart_command(const char *cmd);

void at_modem_state_machine_step(void) {
    switch (g_at_state) {
        case AT_STATE_TEST:
            send_uart_command("AT\r\n");
            g_at_state = AT_STATE_JOIN_WIFI;
            break;

        case AT_STATE_JOIN_WIFI:
            /* Connect to Access Point */
            send_uart_command("AT+CWJAP=\"LabNetwork\",\"SecurePassword\"\r\n");
            g_at_state = AT_STATE_CONNECT_MQTT;
            break;

        case AT_STATE_CONNECT_MQTT:
            /* Connect to Cloud Broker */
            send_uart_command("AT+MQTTCONN=0,\"broker.hivemq.com\",1883,1\r\n");
            g_at_state = AT_STATE_PUBLISH;
            break;

        case AT_STATE_PUBLISH:
            /* Publish telemetry payload */
            send_uart_command("AT+MQTTPUB=0,\"sensors/telemetry\",\"{\\"status\\":\\"OK\\"}\",0,0\r\n");
            g_at_state = AT_STATE_IDLE;
            break;

        case AT_STATE_IDLE:
            break;
    }
}
Program 2.5-4: ESP-AT Non-Blocking State Machine for Wi-Fi and MQTT Publishing 

#include <stdint.h>

/* Custom 128-bit Service and Characteristic UUIDs */
#define SERVICE_UUID_ENVIRONMENTAL  0x181A
#define CHAR_UUID_TEMPERATURE       0x2A6E

typedef struct {
    uint16_t service_handle;
    uint16_t char_temp_handle;
    uint16_t client_config_handle;
} BLE_GattDatabase_t;

/* Push temperature notification to connected smartphone */
void ble_notify_temperature(uint16_t temp_centidegrees) {
    /* Pack 16-bit signed integer (0.01 deg C resolution) */
    uint8_t notification_data[2];
    notification_data[0] = (uint8_t)(temp_centidegrees & 0xFF);
    notification_data[1] = (uint8_t)(temp_centidegrees >> 8);

    /* Transmit over active BLE connection handle */
    /* Prototype: aci_gatt_update_char_value(service, char, 0, 2, notification_data); */
}
Program 2.5-5: BLE Peripheral Custom GATT Service with Temperature Notification

Embedded External Communication Technologies Comparison

TechnologyPhysical LayerMax Practical SpeedTypical RangePower ConsumptionPrimary Application Domain
USB 2.0 (Full-Speed)Differential D+ / D- copper wire12 MbpsUp to 5 metersModerate (10 - 50 mA)PC diagnostics, firmware flashing, high-speed data export
100Base-TX EthernetTwisted-pair copper (RJ-45)100 MbpsUp to 100 metersHigh (80 - 200 mA)Industrial PLCs, factory automation, building gateways
Bluetooth Low Energy (BLE)2.4 GHz ISM RF Wireless1 - 2 Mbps10 - 50 metersUltra-Low (5 - 15 mA active, uA sleep)Wearables, medical sensors, smartphone configuration
Wi-Fi (802.11 b/g/n)2.4 GHz RF Wireless15 - 72 Mbps50 - 100 metersHigh (100 - 300 mA active)Smart home appliances, cloud IoT cameras, OTA downloads

Topic Quiz (10 Questions)

Test your conceptual understanding of today's embedded systems architecture, registers, and runtime behaviors.

1. What is the primary role of the USB Device Descriptor?
  • To configure PWM frequencies
  • To define root device metadata including Vendor ID (VID), Product ID (PID), and supported USB revision
  • To establish Wi-Fi credentials
  • To allocate dynamic heap memory
The Device Descriptor is the initial 18-byte structure read by the host upon plug-in to identify the hardware vendor and product class.
2. Why is the USB Human Interface Device (HID) class widely used for custom embedded PC communication?
  • It supports multi-gigabit throughput
  • Standard OS kernels (Windows, Linux, macOS) include built-in generic HID drivers, eliminating the need to write custom kernel drivers
  • It requires zero RAM on the microcontroller
  • It can only transmit text strings
HID devices require no custom host driver installation. Operating systems natively provide user-space APIs to read/write HID reports.
3. In the lwIP embedded TCP/IP stack, what is a `pbuf`?
  • A hardware register inside the Ethernet PHY
  • A packet buffer data structure that chains network memory blocks without copying data, enabling zero-copy network processing
  • A floating point math coprocessor
  • A persistent configuration sector in Flash
pbufs (packet buffers) allow network layers to add headers and route frames by linking memory pointers rather than allocating and copying buffers.
4. What is the difference between BLE GAP and BLE GATT?
  • GAP manages broadcast advertising and connections; GATT structures data into services and characteristics once connected
  • GAP is used for audio; GATT is used for sensors
  • GAP requires 5V power; GATT operates at 3.3V
  • GATT operates over Wi-Fi only
GAP (Generic Access Profile) governs discovery and pairing. GATT (Generic Attribute Profile) organizes application data into readable/notifiable characteristics.
5. What property must a BLE GATT Characteristic possess to push data asynchronously to a smartphone without being polled?
  • Read Property
  • Write Property
  • Notify (or Indicate) Property
  • Broadcast Property
The Notify property enables the peripheral server to push value updates to the client central device immediately upon data change.
6. What physical interface is commonly used to connect a microcontroller Ethernet MAC to an external Ethernet PHY chip using only 7 digital pins?
  • I2C
  • RMII (Reduced Media Independent Interface)
  • UART
  • 1-Wire
RMII reduces the pin count from 16 (in classical MII) down to 7 lines while clocking at 50 MHz to achieve 100 Mbps data throughput.
7. What does the USB CDC class emulate when connected to a host computer?
  • A SCSI Hard Disk Drive
  • A Virtual COM (Serial) Port
  • An HDMI Display Monitor
  • An Audio Microphone
CDC ACM (Abstract Control Model) presents itself to the operating system as a standard virtual RS-232 serial port.
8. Why is MQTT preferred over HTTP for battery-powered wireless IoT sensor telemetry?
  • MQTT packets have minimal overhead (as small as 2 bytes), reducing radio transmit time and power consumption
  • MQTT requires gigabit Ethernet
  • MQTT cannot be encrypted
  • MQTT requires full web browsers
HTTP headers consume hundreds of bytes per request. MQTT uses compact binary headers, minimizing active radio duration and conserving battery life.
9. In an AT command parser, what are 'Unsolicited Result Codes' (URCs)?
  • Hardware syntax errors
  • Spontaneous messages transmitted by the modem without a prior request (e.g. incoming call, network disconnect, or received MQTT message)
  • Compiler linker errors
  • Parity bit mismatch flags
URCs are sent asynchronously by modems to notify the host MCU of external network events (e.g. '+RECEIVE: 10 bytes').
10. What is the maximum payload size of a single Full-Speed USB Bulk Transfer packet?
  • 8 Bytes
  • 64 Bytes
  • 512 Bytes
  • 1024 Bytes
Under the USB 2.0 specification for Full-Speed (12 Mbps) endpoints, the maximum packet size for Bulk endpoints is exactly 64 bytes.

Hands-On Assignments

Complete these 5 lab assignments to solidify your hands-on firmware engineering skills.

Assignment 1: USB CDC High-Speed Binary Telemetry Streamer

Task: Configure STM32 USB in CDC Virtual COM port mode. Write an application that streams simulated 3-axis accelerometer and gyro data at 500 Hz to a PC Python receiver script, measuring throughput and packet loss.

Assignment 2: USB HID Custom Multi-Media Keypad Controller

Task: Build a 3-button USB HID device: Button 1 sends Volume Up; Button 2 sends Volume Down; Button 3 sends Play/Pause media consumer keys. Test on your workstation without installing any drivers.

Assignment 3: lwIP Embedded HTTP Web Status Dashboard

Task: Deploy lwIP on an Ethernet-enabled microcontroller (or simulator). Serve a responsive HTML status page displaying CPU uptime, free heap memory, and live ADC sensor voltages over local LAN.

Assignment 4: ESP-AT Non-Blocking Cloud MQTT Telemetry Publisher

Task: Write a robust C state machine driving an ESP8266 or ESP32 Wi-Fi modem over UART. Automatically connect to an AP, handle disconnects with exponential backoff, and publish sensor JSON to test.mosquitto.org.

Assignment 5: Smartphone-Controlled BLE Environmental Sensor Node

Task: Create a BLE Peripheral advertising an Environmental Sensing service. Expose Temperature and Humidity characteristics. Connect using a smartphone BLE scanner app (e.g. nRF Connect) and verify live push notifications.

Official References, Research Papers & Standards

Deepen your engineering foundations with seminal reference manuals, processor architecture standards, and industry specifications:

Industry Standard USB Implementers Forum (USB-IF)

Universal Serial Bus Specification Revision 2.0

The foundational standard specification detailing packet framing, descriptor layouts, token transactions, and endpoint electrical signaling.

View Official Resource →
Wireless Specification Bluetooth Special Interest Group (SIG)

Bluetooth Core Specification Version 5.3 - Vol 3: Host Architecture (GATT/GAP)

Official specification defining Bluetooth Low Energy advertising packets, GATT service/characteristic hierarchies, and UUID definitions.

View Official Resource →
Open-Source Networking Adam Dunkels / Swedish Institute of Computer Science

lwIP: A Lightweight TCP/IP Stack Implementation Guide

Technical paper detailing zero-copy pbuf architectures, memory footprint optimization, and raw API callback integration for microcontrollers.

fields.title: Topic 11: Events & Event Handling
fields.content:
Topic 11

Events & Event Handling

Novice firmware is typically written as a sequential script: read sensor, delay 500 ms, toggle LED, transmit UART, repeat. In modern real-time systems, external inputs (button clicks, packet reception, timer expirations, fault conditions) occur asynchronously and unpredictably. A system that blocks waiting for one event misses all other inputs.

The event-driven paradigm fundamentally reorganizes firmware: instead of polling hardware in tight blocking loops, system components react asynchronously to discrete events. Hardware Interrupt Service Routines (ISRs) act as rapid event producers, posting structured event messages into a FIFO queue. The main background superloop acts as an event pump, dispatching events to registered handlers without ever blocking CPU cycles.

11.1 The Anatomy of an Embedded Event

In C, an event is modeled as a lightweight, fixed-size structure carrying an event type identifier, timestamp, and optional data payload:

Figure 11.1: Structured Event Layout in C

11.2 The Producer-Consumer Event Queue Pattern

The heart of reactive firmware is the decoupled Producer-Consumer Queue:

  • Producers (Hardware ISRs & Drivers): Detect physical events (GPIO edge, UART byte received, timer tick). They package an Event_t and push it into the queue in under 2 microseconds, then exit immediately.
  • Consumer (Main Superloop): Runs continuously. Pops events from the queue one at a time and dispatches them to state machines or application logic.

11.3 Hands-On Code Implementations

The following complete, thread-safe module implements an event queue, event signals, and an event pump in pure C: 

/**
 * Program 11.1: Interrupt-Safe Event Queue & Dispatcher Engine
 * File: event_engine.c
 */

#include <stdint.h>
#include <stdbool.h>
#include <stdio.h>

/* Event signal enumeration */
typedef enum {
    EVT_NONE = 0,
    EVT_TIMER_TICK,
    EVT_BUTTON_PRESSED,
    EVT_UART_PACKET_RX,
    EVT_BATTERY_LOW,
    EVT_CRITICAL_FAULT
} EventSignal_t;

/* Event message structure */
typedef struct {
    EventSignal_t signal;
    uint32_t      timestamp_ms;
    uint32_t      parameter;
} Event_t;

#define EVENT_QUEUE_CAPACITY 16U

typedef struct {
    Event_t  queue[EVENT_QUEUE_CAPACITY];
    volatile uint8_t head;
    volatile uint8_t tail;
    volatile uint8_t count;
} EventQueue_t;

static EventQueue_t s_event_queue = { .head = 0, .tail = 0, .count = 0 };

/**
 * @brief Thread-safe push of an event into the queue (Invoked from ISR or main).
 */
bool event_post(EventSignal_t sig, uint32_t param) {
    /* Critical section start: disable interrupts briefly if multi-threaded */
    __asm volatile ("cpsid i" : : : "memory");

    if (s_event_queue.count >= EVENT_QUEUE_CAPACITY) {
        __asm volatile ("cpsie i" : : : "memory");
        return false; /* Queue full */
    }

    s_event_queue.queue[s_event_queue.head].signal = sig;
    s_event_queue.queue[s_event_queue.head].timestamp_ms = 12000UL; /* In real MCU: get_sys_tick() */
    s_event_queue.queue[s_event_queue.head].parameter = param;

    s_event_queue.head = (s_event_queue.head + 1U) % EVENT_QUEUE_CAPACITY;
    s_event_queue.count++;

    __asm volatile ("cpsie i" : : : "memory");
    return true;
}

/**
 * @brief Pops the oldest event from the queue.
 */
bool event_get(Event_t * const evt_out) {
    if ((evt_out == NULL) || (s_event_queue.count == 0U)) {
        return false;
    }

    __asm volatile ("cpsid i" : : : "memory");
    *evt_out = s_event_queue.queue[s_event_queue.tail];
    s_event_queue.tail = (s_event_queue.tail + 1U) % EVENT_QUEUE_CAPACITY;
    s_event_queue.count--;
    __asm volatile ("cpsie i" : : : "memory");

    return true;
}

/* Event Dispatcher Handlers */
void handle_button_event(uint32_t button_id) {
    printf("[DISPATCH] Button %lu pressed! Toggling state.\n", (unsigned long)button_id);
}

void handle_battery_event(uint32_t millivolts) {
    printf("[DISPATCH] WARNING: Battery low (%lu mV)!\n", (unsigned long)millivolts);
}

/**
 * @brief The Central Event Pump: dispatches events to business logic.
 */
void event_pump_dispatch(void) {
    Event_t evt;
    if (event_get(&evt)) {
        switch (evt.signal) {
            case EVT_BUTTON_PRESSED:
                handle_button_event(evt.parameter);
                break;
            case EVT_BATTERY_LOW:
                handle_battery_event(evt.parameter);
                break;
            default:
                break;
        }
    }
}
Program 11.1: Interrupt-Safe Event Queue & Dispatcher Engine in C

11.4 Buggy vs. Modern Safe Code Comparison

Polling hardware pins inside a slow superloop causes missed user inputs because human button presses occur between slow polling iterations.

View Buggy/Legacy Code

This linear loop blocks for 500 ms on every iteration. Any button press that begins and ends during the delay is completely lost: 

/* BUGGY: Blocking loop misses asynchronous user inputs */
while (1) {
    /* If button is pressed during this 500ms sleep, it is MISSED! */
    delay_ms(500); 
    
    if (READ_BUTTON_PIN() == 0) {
        toggle_led();
    }
}
Program 11.2-A: Blocking Polling Loop with Missed Events

The event-driven solution captures button presses instantly via an external interrupt (EXTI) and dispatches them in the background without delay loops: 

/* SAFE / EVENT-DRIVEN: Hardware interrupt captures edge, superloop dispatches */
void EXTI0_IRQHandler(void) {
    /* 1. Clear hardware flag */
    EXTI->PR = (1U << 0);
    /* 2. Post event in < 2 microseconds */
    event_post(EVT_BUTTON_PRESSED, 1);
}

void main_loop(void) {
    while (1) {
        event_pump_dispatch(); /* Non-blocking event pump */
        /* CPU enters low-power sleep until next interrupt */
        __asm volatile ("wfi");
    }
}
Program 11.2-B: Event-Driven Interrupt Capture and Dispatch

Topic Quiz (10 Questions)

Test your understanding of event-driven architectures, queues, and reactive execution.

1. What is the fundamental principle of event-driven programming compared to traditional linear programming?
  • Event-driven code uses recursion instead of loops.
  • System execution flow is determined by asynchronous events (sensor edges, timers, packets) rather than a rigid sequential script.
  • It eliminates the need for C header files.
  • It requires an operating system.
Event-driven systems react to events as they arrive, preserving CPU responsiveness and eliminating busy-waiting.
2. In an event-driven microcontroller architecture, who typically acts as the event 'producer'?
  • The compiler
  • Hardware Interrupt Service Routines (ISRs) and peripheral drivers
  • The linker script
  • The terminal screen
ISRs detect hardware occurrences (timer ticks, GPIO edges, UART byte ready) and post events into the event queue.
3. What data structure is universally used to decouple event producers from event consumers?
  • A binary search tree
  • A FIFO (First-In, First-Out) circular ring buffer
  • A dynamic heap linked list
  • A hash map
A statically allocated circular FIFO ring buffer provides O(1) deterministic insertion and retrieval without dynamic memory allocation.
4. Why must an event queue's push operation be protected by a critical section (e.g. disabling interrupts)?
  • To increase CPU clock speed.
  • To prevent race conditions where a higher-priority interrupt preempts the main loop while it is updating queue indices.
  • To erase Flash memory.
  • To enable C++ exceptions.
Updating shared head/tail/count variables non-atomically allows an ISR to interleave, corrupting queue indices and losing events.
5. What happens when an event queue overflows (is full and a new event arrives)?
  • The microcontroller automatically reboots.
  • The queue must drop the event (or oldest event) gracefully and record an error telemetry counter without hanging.
  • Memory is allocated from the heap.
  • The compiler throws a warning.
Robust embedded queues reject additions when full, return false, and increment an overflow counter for diagnostics.
6. What is the role of the 'Event Pump' (or Event Dispatcher)?
  • It cools down the CPU.
  • A loop in the background thread that continuously pops events from the queue and routes them to appropriate handler functions.
  • It flashes the firmware over JTAG.
  • It generates random numbers.
The event pump is the central engine that drains the queue and executes corresponding state machine actions.
7. What low-power ARM instruction is called in the event pump when the event queue is empty?
  • NOP
  • WFI (Wait For Interrupt)
  • BKPT
  • SVC
WFI halts the CPU clock, entering sleep mode until an interrupt occurs, dramatically cutting battery power consumption when idle.
8. Why is keeping ISR execution time under a few microseconds critical in event-driven systems?
  • To prevent the crystal from drifting.
  • To ensure the CPU is immediately available to service subsequent high-priority interrupts without latency jitter.
  • To save RAM space.
  • To avoid triggering compiler optimizations.
Short ISRs package events and defer heavy processing to the main loop, minimizing interrupt latency across all peripherals.
9. What design pattern combines an event queue, a private thread/loop, and a finite state machine?
  • Singleton Pattern
  • Active Object Pattern (Actor Model)
  • Factory Pattern
  • Observer Pattern
The Active Object pattern encapsulates a dedicated event queue and state machine, ensuring message-passing concurrency without shared-memory locks.
10. In C, what is the best way to associate event signals with specific data payloads without wasting memory?
  • Use an array of void pointers with malloc().
  • Use a tagged union inside the event structure, sharing memory across different event data types.
  • Store everything as an ASCII string.
  • Use global variables for each event.
A tagged union allows different event types (e.g. keyboard char vs ADC 32-bit int) to share the same payload byte space efficiently.

Hands-On Assignments

Execute these 5 laboratory assignments to master event-driven architecture and message passing.

Assignment 1: Event Queue Saturation Test

Task: Implement an event queue with a capacity of 8 events. Write a test loop that attempts to post 12 consecutive events without draining the queue. Verify that the queue gracefully rejects the final 4 events, returns false, and increments an overflow_count metric.

Assignment 2: EXTI Push Button Event Producer

Task: Configure a push button on GPIO pin PA0 to generate an external interrupt (EXTI0). In the ISR, clear the pending flag and post an EVT_BUTTON_PRESS event to the event queue. In the main superloop, pop and handle the event by toggling an LED.

Assignment 3: Tagged Union Event Structure

Task: Create an event structure containing a tagged union supporting three payload types: (1) 32-bit ADC voltage, (2) 8-bit keypad character, and (3) an enum error code. Author a dispatcher that uses a switch statement on the signal to decode the correct union field.

Assignment 4: Low-Power WFI Event Pump

Task: In your main loop, drain and handle all pending events in the queue. When the queue is completely empty, invoke __WFI(). Connect an oscilloscope or current probe to measure the board's power consumption drop when waiting in sleep mode.

Assignment 5: Multi-Priority Event Queues

Task: Expand the engine to maintain two separate queues: a High-Priority Queue (for emergency stop faults and over-temperature alerts) and a Normal-Priority Queue (for user UI and routine telemetry). Ensure the event pump always exhausts all high-priority events before servicing normal events.
