fields.title: Day 15: Bootloaders & Firmware Update (OTA)
fields.content:
Session 2.6

Day 15: Bootloaders & Firmware Update (OTA)

Problem Statement: After deployment, your firmware will have bugs. How do you update it safely in the field without a hardware debugger and guarantee that a bad update or mid-transfer power loss never bricks the device?
📋 Daily Plan & Learning Architecture
Session 2.6 Module 2: Peripherals & FreeRTOS Estimated: 3.5 hrs

🎯 Today's Mission & Relevance

  • Master internal Flash partitioning between Bootloader, Application Slots, and NVM Metadata.
  • Implement low-level Vector Table Offset Register (SCB->VTOR) relocation and MSP jumping.
  • Construct a resilient A/B dual-partition state machine with automatic golden-image rollback.

📐 Theoretical Milestones

  • NOR Flash physics: Erase-before-write constraints and high-voltage sector bulk erasing.
  • ARM Cortex-M vector table layout and Thumb execution state requirements.
  • Hardware CRC32 polynomial computation vs software checksumming.

💻 Hands-On Blueprint

  • Program 15.1: Bare-metal jump to application routine setting MSP and branch vector.
  • Program 15.2: Bare-metal STM32 Flash memory controller driver (unlock, erase, write).
  • Program 15.3: Hardware CRC32 engine firmware integrity checker.
  • Program 15.4: Packetized UART DFU receiver with sector auto-erase and write.
  • Program 15.5: A/B dual partition metadata handler with safe rollback counter.

🛡️ Production Failure Modes

  • Failing to disable active peripheral interrupts before jumping, causing HardFault in the application.
  • Neglecting to clear bit 0 of the target Reset Handler address in assembly branch instructions.
  • Single-slot flash updates failing mid-write due to power loss, permanently bricking hardware.
🏁 Daily Milestone Deliverables: 5 Interactive Register-Level Programs • 5 Architecture Diagrams • 10 Practice MCQs • 5 Hands-On Assignments

15.1 Bootloader vs Application Architectural Separation

In production embedded engineering, deploying firmware to devices operating in remote field installations—such as automotive engine controllers, smart utility meters, or orbital satellites—demands the ability to update firmware without physical access via JTAG or SWD debuggers. This is achieved through a dedicated secondary program stored permanently in internal non-volatile memory: the In-System Programming (ISP) Bootloader.

The internal Flash memory is divided into distinct physical memory regions: a small, immutable Bootloader Partition located at the physical reset address (e.g., 0x08000000), an active Application Slot A, an update staging Application Slot B, and a persistent Metadata / NVM Configuration Sector.

Figure 15.0-1: Flash Memory Partitioning for Safe In-Field and OTA Firmware Updates
Figure Parameters Explained:
  • Bootloader Slot (0x08000000): Protected, non-volatile initial execution target executed upon every power-on reset (POR).
  • Metadata Partition (0x08004000): Contains boot state machines, firmware version numbers, execution counters, and 32-bit CRC signatures.
  • Dual-Bank Slots A & B: Permits atomic background download into inactive bank while the current bank continues real-time execution.
  • Golden Image Rollback: Allows immediate recovery to a known operational image if the newly flashed application crashes or fails watchdog health checks.

15.2 The Boot Decision Flow and Vector Relocation (VTOR)

Upon power-on reset, the microcontroller core executes the bootloader. The bootloader performs hardware sanity checks, samples a physical DFU recovery pin or UART command byte, and reads the metadata partition to determine which application slot is active and valid.

To transfer control to the user application, the bootloader must perform two low-level hardware procedures:

  1. Relocate the CPU Vector Table Offset Register (SCB->VTOR) to the base address of the application slot (e.g., 0x08008000).
  2. Load the Main Stack Pointer (MSP) from the first 32-bit word of the application's vector table, and jump to the function address specified in the second 32-bit word (the Application Reset Handler).

Figure 15.0-2: Bootloader Execution Flow and Application Branching State Machine
Figure Parameters Explained:
  • Hardware Pin Sampling: Samples a designated external switch or UART header within 50 ms of boot to permit emergency recovery.
  • CRC32 Integrity Validation: Computes polynomial checksum across application flash boundaries before permitting vector jump.
  • SCB->VTOR Relocation: Repoints CPU exception entry points to application interrupt handlers so peripherals fire correctly.
  • DFU Recovery Loop: Waits indefinitely for incoming firmware packets if application flash is corrupted or blank.

15.3 Vector Table Jump and Stack Pointer Initialization in C

Executing a jump to an embedded application requires direct assembly instructions or inline C function pointers. Because the ARM Cortex-M architecture places the initial stack pointer at address AppBase + 0x00 and the Reset Handler vector at AppBase + 0x04, the bootloader reads these memory words directly.


#include <stdint.h>

#define APP_START_ADDRESS   0x08008000U
#define SCB_VTOR            (*(volatile uint32_t *)0xE000ED08U)

typedef void (*pFunction)(void);

void jump_to_application(uint32_t app_address) {
    /* 1. Verify application stack pointer is located in valid internal SRAM */
    uint32_t app_stack = *(volatile uint32_t *)app_address;
    if ((app_stack & 0x2FFE0000U) != 0x20000000U) {
        /* Invalid stack pointer; abort jump to avoid HardFault */
        return;
    }

    /* 2. Disable all interrupts and clear pending flags */
    __asm volatile ("cpsid i" : : : "memory");
    for (int i = 0; i < 8; i++) {
        *(volatile uint32_t *)(0xE000E180U + (i * 4)) = 0xFFFFFFFFU; /* NVIC ICER */
        *(volatile uint32_t *)(0xE000E280U + (i * 4)) = 0xFFFFFFFFU; /* NVIC ICPR */
    }

    /* 3. Relocate Vector Table Offset Register (VTOR) */
    SCB_VTOR = app_address;

    /* 4. Extract application Reset Handler address (offset +4) */
    uint32_t reset_handler_addr = *(volatile uint32_t *)(app_address + 4U);
    pFunction app_entry = (pFunction)reset_handler_addr;

    /* 5. Set Main Stack Pointer (MSP) and branch to application */
    __asm volatile ("msr msp, %0" : : "r" (app_stack) : );
    __asm volatile ("cpsie i" : : : "memory");

    app_entry();

    /* Never reached */
    while (1);
}
Program 15.1: Bare-Metal Jump to Application Routine on ARM Cortex-M

15.4 Bare-Metal Flash Memory Driver: Sector Erasing and Word Programming

Embedded NOR Flash memory exhibits physical constraints fundamentally distinct from RAM: bits can only be cleared from 1 to 0 during a write operation. Transitioning bits back from 0 to 1 requires an erase operation, which can only be performed on entire multi-kilobyte flash sectors. Furthermore, the microcontroller Flash controller requires a strict cryptographic key unlock sequence to prevent spurious writes during power dips.


#include <stdint.h>

#define FLASH_BASE_ADDR     0x40023C00U
#define FLASH_KEYR          (*(volatile uint32_t *)(FLASH_BASE_ADDR + 0x04U))
#define FLASH_SR            (*(volatile uint32_t *)(FLASH_BASE_ADDR + 0x0CU))
#define FLASH_CR            (*(volatile uint32_t *)(FLASH_BASE_ADDR + 0x10U))

#define FLASH_KEY1          0x45670123U
#define FLASH_KEY2          0xCDEF89ABU
#define FLASH_SR_BSY        (1U << 16)
#define FLASH_CR_LOCK       (1U << 31)
#define FLASH_CR_PG         (1U << 0)
#define FLASH_CR_SER        (1U << 1)
#define FLASH_CR_STRT       (1U << 16)

void flash_unlock(void) {
    if (FLASH_CR & FLASH_CR_LOCK) {
        FLASH_KEYR = FLASH_KEY1;
        FLASH_KEYR = FLASH_KEY2;
    }
}

void flash_lock(void) {
    FLASH_CR |= FLASH_CR_LOCK;
}

void flash_wait_busy(void) {
    while (FLASH_SR & FLASH_SR_BSY);
}

void flash_erase_sector(uint8_t sector_num) {
    flash_wait_busy();
    flash_unlock();

    /* Configure Sector Erase and select sector (bits 3:6) */
    FLASH_CR &= ~(0x1FU << 3);
    FLASH_CR |= FLASH_CR_SER | ((uint32_t)sector_num << 3);
    FLASH_CR |= FLASH_CR_STRT;

    flash_wait_busy();
    FLASH_CR &= ~FLASH_CR_SER;
    flash_lock();
}

void flash_write_word(uint32_t address, uint32_t data) {
    flash_wait_busy();
    flash_unlock();

    /* Enable programming mode */
    FLASH_CR |= FLASH_CR_PG;

    /* Write 32-bit word */
    *(volatile uint32_t *)address = data;

    flash_wait_busy();
    FLASH_CR &= ~FLASH_CR_PG;
    flash_lock();
}
Program 15.2: Bare-Metal STM32 Flash Controller Driver (Unlock, Erase, Write)

15.5 Hardware CRC32 Firmware Integrity Verification

Before launching a newly written application, firmware integrity must be verified mathematically to ensure transmission corruption or premature power loss during flashing does not execute invalid opcodes. Microcontrollers integrate a dedicated Hardware CRC Peripheral implementing the standard Ethernet / ISO 3309 CRC-32 polynomial (0x04C11DB7) to verify hundreds of kilobytes of Flash in under 5 milliseconds.


#include <stdint.h>
#include <stdbool.h>

#define CRC_BASE            0x40023000U
#define CRC_DR              (*(volatile uint32_t *)(CRC_BASE + 0x00U))
#define CRC_CR              (*(volatile uint32_t *)(CRC_BASE + 0x08U))
#define RCC_AHB1ENR         (*(volatile uint32_t *)(0x40023830U))

void crc_peripheral_init(void) {
    /* Enable CRC peripheral clock in RCC */
    RCC_AHB1ENR |= (1U << 12);
    /* Reset CRC computation unit */
    CRC_CR |= 1U;
}

uint32_t compute_firmware_crc(const uint32_t *p_data, uint32_t num_words) {
    CRC_CR |= 1U; /* Reset computation */
    for (uint32_t i = 0; i < num_words; i++) {
        CRC_DR = p_data[i];
    }
    return CRC_DR;
}

bool verify_application_integrity(uint32_t app_base_addr, uint32_t app_size_bytes, uint32_t expected_crc) {
    crc_peripheral_init();
    uint32_t num_words = app_size_bytes / 4U;
    uint32_t computed = compute_firmware_crc((const uint32_t *)app_base_addr, num_words);
    return (computed == expected_crc);
}
Program 15.3: Hardware CRC32 Engine Firmware Integrity Checker

15.6 UART Packetized Device Firmware Upgrade (DFU) Protocol

When the bootloader detects an active update session, it runs a packetized transport protocol over UART, CAN, or USB. The protocol receives binary chunks, verifies frame checksums, writes words into Flash memory, and sends acknowledgments (ACK/NACK) back to the host programmer.


#include <stdint.h>
#include <stdbool.h>

#define DFU_PACKET_SIZE     128U
#define DFU_SOF             0x02U  /* Start of Frame */
#define DFU_ACK             0x06U  /* Acknowledge */
#define DFU_NACK            0x15U  /* Negative Acknowledge */

typedef struct {
    uint8_t  sof;
    uint16_t packet_id;
    uint8_t  payload[DFU_PACKET_SIZE];
    uint16_t checksum;
} __attribute__((packed)) DfuPacket_t;

extern void uart_send_byte(uint8_t b);
extern uint8_t uart_receive_byte(void);
extern void flash_erase_sector(uint8_t sec);
extern void flash_write_word(uint32_t addr, uint32_t data);

bool dfu_process_next_packet(uint32_t target_flash_addr) {
    DfuPacket_t packet;
    uint8_t *raw_ptr = (uint8_t *)&packet;

    /* Receive entire frame over UART */
    for (uint32_t i = 0; i < sizeof(DfuPacket_t); i++) {
        raw_ptr[i] = uart_receive_byte();
    }

    if (packet.sof != DFU_SOF) {
        uart_send_byte(DFU_NACK);
        return false;
    }

    /* Compute 16-bit additive checksum */
    uint16_t sum = 0;
    for (uint32_t i = 0; i < DFU_PACKET_SIZE; i++) {
        sum += packet.payload[i];
    }

    if (sum != packet.checksum) {
        uart_send_byte(DFU_NACK);
        return false;
    }

    /* Program verified 128 bytes (32 words) into Flash */
    uint32_t *p_data = (uint32_t *)packet.payload;
    for (uint32_t w = 0; w < (DFU_PACKET_SIZE / 4U); w++) {
        flash_write_word(target_flash_addr + (w * 4U), p_data[w]);
    }

    uart_send_byte(DFU_ACK);
    return true;
}
Program 15.4: Packetized UART DFU Receiver with Sector Auto-Erase and Write

15.7 Non-Volatile A/B Dual-Bank Partitioning State Machine

To prevent bricking during over-the-air (OTA) updates, industrial systems implement an A/B Partitioning Scheme. While Slot A executes the active firmware, the network stack writes incoming packets into Slot B. Once verified, a persistent boot flag designates Slot B as pending trial. If Slot B fails to confirm successful startup within 3 reboots, the bootloader automatically rolls back to Slot A.


#include <stdint.h>
#include <stdbool.h>

#define NVM_METADATA_ADDR   0x08004000U
#define MAX_BOOT_ATTEMPTS   3U

typedef enum {
    SLOT_A = 0,
    SLOT_B = 1
} ActiveSlot_t;

typedef struct {
    uint32_t magic_header;       /* 0x55AA55AA */
    ActiveSlot_t active_slot;
    uint32_t boot_attempts;
    uint32_t slot_a_crc;
    uint32_t slot_b_crc;
    uint32_t slot_a_size;
    uint32_t slot_b_size;
} BootMetadata_t;

ActiveSlot_t bootloader_select_slot(BootMetadata_t *meta) {
    if (meta->magic_header != 0x55AA55AAU) {
        /* Default fallback */
        return SLOT_A;
    }

    if (meta->boot_attempts >= MAX_BOOT_ATTEMPTS) {
        /* Candidate failed to confirm operational status; rollback */
        meta->active_slot = (meta->active_slot == SLOT_A) ? SLOT_B : SLOT_A;
        meta->boot_attempts = 0;
        /* Note: Write updated metadata to NVM sector here */
    } else {
        meta->boot_attempts++;
    }

    return meta->active_slot;
}
Program 15.5: A/B Dual Partition Metadata Handler with Safe Rollback Counter

Device Firmware Upgrade (DFU) Transport Protocols Comparison

TransportPhysical LayerTypical ThroughputTransfer RangeHardware OverheadIndustrial Application
UART / RS-485Asynchronous serial copper115.2 kbps - 1 MbpsUp to 1200 meters (RS-485)Minimal (1 UART port)Factory automation, diagnostic ports, smart energy meters
CAN Bus (ISO 14229 UDS)Differential CAN_H / CAN_L500 kbps - 2 Mbps (CAN-FD)Up to 40 metersLow (on-chip CAN controller)Automotive ECU flashing, industrial machinery
USB DFU ClassDifferential D+ / D-12 Mbps (Full-Speed)Up to 5 metersModerate (USB core required)Bench flashing, commercial USB consumer electronics
Bluetooth Low Energy (BLE)2.4 GHz RF ISM band100 - 800 kbps10 - 30 metersModerate (BLE coprocessor)Wearables, medical implants, smart lock updates
Wi-Fi / Cellular OTAIP Socket / HTTPS1 - 10 MbpsGlobal cloud reachHigh (TCP/IP stack + TLS crypto)Autonomous vehicle telemetry, smart home gateways

Intel HEX Record Types Reference

Record TypeNameDescriptionData LengthTypical Usage
0x00Data RecordContains raw binary opcodes or data bytes to be programmed1 - 32 bytes (typically 16)Standard machine code payload
0x01End of File (EOF)Marks the termination of the HEX binary file0 bytesAlways the final record in the file
0x02Extended Segment AddressSpecifies upper 4 bits for 20-bit real-mode addressing2 bytesLegacy 16-bit x86 architectures
0x04Extended Linear AddressSpecifies upper 16 bits of 32-bit absolute address2 bytesMandatory for ARM Cortex 32-bit linear address space
0x05Start Linear AddressSpecifies 32-bit execution entry point address4 bytesDirects programmer to Reset Handler vector

Topic Quiz (10 Questions)

Test your conceptual understanding of today's embedded systems architecture, registers, and runtime behaviors.

1. What is the primary function of the Vector Table Offset Register (SCB->VTOR) during a jump to application?
  • To increase CPU core clock frequency
  • To repoint the base address of the exception vector table so interrupts invoke application handlers rather than bootloader handlers
  • To disable flash memory sector write protection
  • To reset the SysTick timer counter
SCB->VTOR contains the base physical address of the vector table. When an interrupt fires, the CPU looks up handlers relative to VTOR. Failing to update VTOR causes interrupts to jump into obsolete bootloader addresses.
2. Why must NOR Flash sectors be erased prior to writing new data words?
  • Because NOR Flash writes can only clear bits from 1 to 0; transitioning from 0 to 1 requires an erase cycle
  • Because NOR Flash behaves exactly like dynamic RAM
  • To reduce power consumption during programming
  • Because the compiler optimizer removes un-erased instructions
Floating-gate NOR flash cells are charged to represent 0 and discharged to represent 1. Write operations only inject charge (1->0); removing charge (0->1) requires high-voltage sector bulk erasing.
3. What are the first two 32-bit words stored at the base address of any ARM Cortex-M application binary?
  • Initial Main Stack Pointer (MSP) value and Reset Handler function address
  • CRC32 checksum and firmware version string
  • UART baud rate register and clock divider settings
  • Heap pointer base and FreeRTOS task count
The ARM Cortex-M hardware vector table specification mandates that word 0 (offset 0x00) is loaded into the MSP register and word 1 (offset 0x04) is loaded into the Program Counter (PC).
4. In an A/B dual-partition update scheme, what is the purpose of the 'boot_attempts' counter in the metadata sector?
  • To limit how many times the user can plug in USB devices
  • To detect an application crash loop and automatically roll back to the previously operational image
  • To calculate the CPU clock cycle count
  • To verify the serial number of the microcontroller
If a newly flashed candidate image crashes or triggers a watchdog reset before marking itself as 'healthy', the boot_attempts counter increments. Exceeding the threshold triggers an automatic rollback to the known-good partition.
5. Which Intel HEX record type defines the upper 16 bits of a 32-bit linear memory address on ARM Cortex-M microcontrollers?
  • Record Type 0x00 (Data)
  • Record Type 0x01 (EOF)
  • Record Type 0x04 (Extended Linear Address Record)
  • Record Type 0x02 (Extended Segment Record)
Intel HEX record type 04 supplies the upper 16 address bits (base address), enabling addressing across the entire 4 GB 32-bit address space.
6. Why should interrupts be globally disabled before jumping from a bootloader to an application?
  • To prevent an in-flight peripheral interrupt from executing an ISR in the wrong memory context during vector table transition
  • To prevent flash memory from discharging
  • Because Cortex-M cores do not support interrupts in applications
  • To preserve battery power during the jump
If an interrupt fires during the transition between the bootloader stack pointer configuration and the application VTOR update, the core will branch using indeterminate vector table pointers, causing an immediate HardFault.
7. What is the primary vulnerability of updating firmware in-place in a single flash slot without an A/B dual bank or golden image?
  • SRAM becomes too fast for CPU execution
  • A sudden power outage or connection drop mid-write leaves the device permanently unbootable (bricked)
  • The serial baud rate doubles automatically
  • The compiler optimization flag drops from -O2 to -O0
Single-slot in-place updating erases the running application before writing the new image. If power fails mid-erase, no valid application exists on flash, requiring physical SWD/JTAG intervention.
8. How does the hardware CRC32 engine compare in throughput to a software bitwise CRC calculation?
  • Hardware CRC executes in 1 clock cycle per 32-bit word, outperforming software loops by 10x to 50x
  • Hardware CRC is slower because it requires network access
  • Hardware CRC consumes more Flash memory than software lookup tables
  • They operate at identical speeds
The integrated hardware CRC engine computes polynomial division in combinational hardware at 1 word per clock cycle, verifying multi-hundred-kilobyte images in milliseconds.
9. What does the Thumb instruction bit (bit 0) in an ARM function address indicate?
  • Whether the core operates in 16/32-bit Thumb state (must be 1 for Cortex-M processors)
  • Whether the memory is cached
  • Whether the function was compiled with -O3
  • Whether floating point hardware is present
Cortex-M microcontrollers exclusively execute the Thumb instruction set. Bit 0 of function pointer addresses must be set to 1; branching to an even address clears EPSR.T and triggers a UsageFault.
10. In automotive diagnostics, which protocol standard governs firmware reprogramming over the CAN bus?
  • ISO 14229 Unified Diagnostic Services (UDS)
  • Bluetooth SIG GAP Spec
  • IEEE 802.11 Wi-Fi
  • I2C Fast Mode Plus
ISO 14229 (UDS) specifies the diagnostic services (such as 0x34 RequestDownload, 0x36 TransferData, and 0x37 RequestTransferExit) used by automotive OEMs to flash ECUs over CAN.

Hands-On Assignments

Complete these 5 lab assignments to solidify your hands-on firmware engineering skills.

Assignment 1: Non-Volatile Boot Flag Sector Manager

Task: Implement a persistent boot flag driver in the dedicated metadata flash sector. Implement functions to read, erase, and write the active partition index and boot attempt counter, surviving 10 consecutive simulated power-loss events.

Assignment 2: Dual-Bank Automatic Rollback Engine

Task: Develop an A/B partition switcher that increments an attempt counter upon booting Candidate Slot B. If the candidate fails to call app_mark_healthy() within 3 boots, the bootloader automatically sets active partition back to Slot A.

Assignment 3: Host-Side Python DFU Packetizer

Task: Write a host Python script that parses a compiled .bin firmware binary, packetizes it into 128-byte Xmodem frames with 16-bit additive checksums, and transmits frames over serial COM/tty port while processing target ACK/NACK responses.

Assignment 4: Cryptographic Firmware Signature Verification

Task: Append a 32-byte HMAC-SHA256 signature to the firmware binary header. In the bootloader, compute the HMAC over the application image using a pre-shared secret key stored in protected flash; reject the jump if the signature fails.

Assignment 5: USB Device Firmware Upgrade (DFU) Class Integration

Task: Implement a USB DFU 1.1 class driver on an STM32 development board. Connect the board to a Linux host PC and execute a complete firmware update cycle using the standard open-source dfu-util utility.

fields.title: Topic 12: Polling vs Interrupts
fields.content:
Topic 12

Polling vs Interrupts

Every embedded peripheral interaction boils down to a fundamental architectural choice: should the processor repeatedly query the hardware status register (Polling), or should the hardware alert the processor asynchronously when an event occurs (Interrupts)?

While polling is conceptually simple and requires zero vector table configuration, it wastes millions of CPU cycles in busy-wait loops and burns battery power. Interrupts unlock high CPU utilization and microsecond reaction times, but introduce the hazards of asynchronous preemption: race conditions, shared memory corruption, priority inversion, and stack blowouts.

12.1 Comparative Analysis Matrix

Selecting between polling and interrupts requires evaluating latency, throughput, power consumption, and code complexity:

Evaluation Metric Polling (Busy-Wait) Interrupt-Driven Architecture
CPU Utilization 100% busy-wait during transactions; wastes CPU cycles. Near 0% idle; CPU computes background tasks or sleeps.
Response Latency Variable and high; depends on main loop execution period. Deterministic and immediate (~12 clock cycles on ARM Cortex-M).
Power Consumption High; core runs active clock cycles continuously. Ultra-low; CPU sleeps in WFI until an interrupt awakens it.
Software Complexity Trivial; linear code execution, no race conditions. Higher; requires volatile qualifiers, critical sections, and NVIC tuning.

12.2 Hardware Interrupt Mechanics & NVIC

On ARM Cortex-M microcontrollers, interrupt handling is governed by the Nested Vectored Interrupt Controller (NVIC). When a hardware peripheral asserts an interrupt line:

  1. Hardware Stacking: The processor automatically pushes 8 core registers onto the active stack: R0, R1, R2, R3, R12, LR, PC, xPSR in just 12 CPU clock cycles.
  2. Vector Fetch: Simultaneously, the NVIC reads the 32-bit ISR function address directly from the Vector Table in Flash memory.
  3. Execution: The CPU jumps directly to the C ISR function.
  4. Unstacking: Upon executing the special return code in LR (EXC_RETURN), hardware automatically pops the registers and restores the interrupted code.

12.3 Critical Sections & Atomic Access

Whenever a variable wider than the CPU data bus (e.g. a 64-bit millisecond counter on a 32-bit ARM, or a 16-bit int on an 8-bit AVR) or a multi-field structure is shared between the main loop and an ISR, a critical section is mandatory.

Figure 12.1: Non-Atomic Multi-Word Read Corruption Hazard

12.4 Hands-On Code Implementations

The following C implementation demonstrates atomic reading of a 64-bit shared timestamp counter using ARM assembly critical section primitives: 

/**
 * Program 12.1: Atomic 64-Bit Timekeeper with Nested Interrupt Protection
 * File: atomic_timer.c
 */

#include <stdint.h>
#include <stdbool.h>

/* 64-bit system tick counter updated asynchronously in SysTick ISR */
static volatile uint64_t s_system_uptime_ticks = 0ULL;

/**
 * @brief Enter Critical Section: saves previous interrupt mask state and disables IRQs.
 */
static inline uint32_t enter_critical_section(void) {
    uint32_t primask;
    /* Read active PRIMASK interrupt state */
    __asm volatile ("mrs %0, primask" : "=r" (primask));
    /* Disable interrupts */
    __asm volatile ("cpsid i" : : : "memory");
    return primask;
}

/**
 * @brief Exit Critical Section: restores previous interrupt mask state.
 */
static inline void exit_critical_section(uint32_t primask) {
    /* Restore saved PRIMASK */
    __asm volatile ("msr primask, %0" : : "r" (primask) : "memory");
}

/**
 * @brief Thread-safe atomic read of 64-bit uptime counter.
 * @return uint64_t Snapshot of uptime in ticks
 */
uint64_t get_system_uptime_atomic(void) {
    uint32_t mask = enter_critical_section();
    /* Atomic 64-bit copy: completely immune to ISR interleaving */
    uint64_t snapshot = s_system_uptime_ticks;
    exit_critical_section(mask);
    return snapshot;
}

/**
 * @brief 1 kHz Hardware SysTick Timer Interrupt Handler.
 */
void SysTick_Handler(void) {
    /* Incremented asynchronously every 1 millisecond */
    s_system_uptime_ticks++;
}
Program 12.1: Atomic 64-Bit Timekeeper with Nested Interrupt Protection in C

12.5 Buggy vs. Modern Safe Code Comparison

Directly disabling interrupts globally using __enable_irq() breaks nested calls if an outer function had intentionally disabled interrupts.

View Buggy/Legacy Code

Calling __enable_irq() unconditionally re-enables interrupts even if the outer calling function was inside its own critical section: 

/* BUGGY: Unconditionally enables interrupts, breaking outer critical sections */
void write_shared_data(uint32_t val) {
    __disable_irq();
    g_shared_reg = val;
    __enable_irq(); /* DANGER: Re-enables interrupts even if caller disabled them! */
}
Program 12.2-A: Broken Unconditional Interrupt Re-Enable

The modern pattern captures and restores the original PRIMASK register, cleanly supporting arbitrary critical section nesting: 

/* SAFE / PRODUCTION-GRADE: Nestable PRIMASK state capture */
void write_shared_data_safe(uint32_t val) {
    uint32_t primask = enter_critical_section();
    g_shared_reg = val;
    exit_critical_section(primask); /* Restores previous state cleanly */
}
Program 12.2-B: Nestable Critical Section Implementation

Topic Quiz (10 Questions)

Test your understanding of polling limitations, interrupt mechanics, and critical sections.

1. What is the primary drawback of using busy-wait polling to wait for a UART character to arrive?
  • UART baud rates drift.
  • The CPU is 100% tied up executing tight loops, burning battery power and preventing other tasks from executing.
  • The compiler emits an error on polling loops.
  • It disables SRAM memory reads.
Polling monopolizes the processor in unproductive spin-loops, preventing sleep modes and wasting power.
2. On an ARM Cortex-M processor, how many core registers are automatically pushed onto the stack by hardware upon interrupt entry?
  • 4 registers
  • 8 registers (R0, R1, R2, R3, R12, LR, PC, xPSR)
  • 16 registers
  • 0 (all stacking is done by software)
Hardware automatically pushes the 8 caller-saved registers in 12 clock cycles, enabling standard C functions to act directly as ISRs without assembly wrappers.
3. What does the Nested Vectored Interrupt Controller (NVIC) enable on ARM Cortex-M processors?
  • Direct execution of Python scripts.
  • Hardware-managed interrupt prioritization, dynamic preemption of lower-priority ISRs, and tail-chaining.
  • Automatic Flash memory wear leveling.
  • Wireless communication over Wi-Fi.
The NVIC handles prioritized preemption and tail-chaining optimization in hardware without software overhead.
4. What is 'tail-chaining' in the ARM Cortex-M interrupt architecture?
  • Daisy chaining multiple microcontroller chips over SPI.
  • An optimization where the processor transitions directly to a pending interrupt without restoring and re-stacking registers, saving 24 clock cycles.
  • A software algorithm for linking lists.
  • A compiler warning.
Tail-chaining avoids redundant unstacking and re-stacking when another interrupt is pending as an ISR finishes, reducing switch latency to just 6 cycles.
5. Why is an atomic read required when reading a 64-bit variable on a 32-bit ARM Cortex-M processor?
  • 64-bit integers are illegal in C99.
  • The CPU requires two separate 32-bit load instructions; an interrupt can fire between the two instructions, resulting in corrupted data.
  • Flash cannot store 64-bit variables.
  • The compiler forces a hard fault.
A 32-bit CPU cannot read 64 bits in a single cycle. An ISR interleaving between the lower and upper word reads reads desynchronized halves.
6. What is the role of the PRIMASK register in ARM Cortex-M CPUs?
  • It stores the processor serial number.
  • A 1-bit register that masks all configurable interrupts when set to 1 (except HardFault and NMI).
  • It controls the PLL clock multiplier.
  • It holds the baud rate divider.
Setting PRIMASK via 'cpsid i' disables all interrupts with configurable priority, creating an atomic critical section.
7. What is 'Interrupt Jitter'?
  • Physical vibration of the PCB.
  • The timing variation between when a hardware interrupt request is asserted and when the first instruction of the ISR actually executes.
  • A bug in the linker script.
  • Fluctuation in supply voltage.
Jitter is caused by critical sections holding interrupts disabled or higher-priority ISRs executing when the event occurs.
8. What happens if an ISR does not clear its peripheral's hardware interrupt pending flag before exiting?
  • The peripheral is permanently powered off.
  • The interrupt controller immediately re-triggers the ISR upon exit, locking the CPU in an infinite interrupt loop and starving the main loop.
  • The compiler reports a warning.
  • The vector table is erased.
If the hardware status bit remains high, the NVIC observes an active interrupt condition and re-invokes the ISR endlessly.
9. What special return value placed in the Link Register (LR) by ARM hardware signals an exception return?
  • 0x00000000
  • EXC_RETURN (e.g. 0xFFFFFFFD or 0xFFFFFFF9)
  • 0xDEADBEEF
  • 0x08000000
When the CPU branches to an EXC_RETURN value (0xFFFFFFFx), hardware automatically initiates exception unstacking and mode restoration.
10. What is priority grouping in the ARM Cortex-M NVIC?
  • Grouping multiple C source files into an archive.
  • Splitting the 8-bit priority register into 'Preemption Priority' (which determines who preempts whom) and 'Subpriority' (which resolves simultaneous pending requests).
  • Sorting variables in SRAM.
  • A feature exclusive to Linux.
Priority grouping allows system architects to partition priority bits between preemption levels and tie-breaker subpriorities.

Hands-On Assignments

Execute these 5 laboratory assignments to master interrupt control, latency analysis, and atomic protection.

Assignment 1: Interrupt Response Latency Benchmarking

Task: Configure a GPIO input interrupt. In the ISR, set an output pin high as the very first line of code. Using an oscilloscope or logic analyzer, measure the time elapsed from the input pin rising edge to the output pin rising edge. Calculate the total latency in nanoseconds and CPU cycles.

Assignment 2: Nestable Critical Section Implementation

Task: Implement the nestable critical section functions enter_critical_section() and exit_critical_section() using inline assembly to save and restore PRIMASK. Write a test case with nested function calls and verify that interrupts remain disabled until the outermost function exits.

Assignment 3: NVIC Priority Preemption Experiment

Task: Configure two hardware timers: Timer 2 with priority 2 and Timer 3 with priority 1. In Timer 2's ISR, toggle a pin and enter a delay loop. Trigger Timer 3 during this delay. Using an oscilloscope, demonstrate that Timer 3 immediately preempts Timer 2 mid-execution.

Assignment 4: Polling vs. Interrupt CPU Utilization Audit

Task: Write a UART receive driver in polling mode. Count how many iterations of a background compute loop execute per second while receiving 100 bytes/sec. Then refactor to an interrupt-driven circular buffer and measure the 10x increase in background iterations.

Assignment 5: Infinite Interrupt Lockup Reproduction

Task: Configure an external GPIO interrupt. In the ISR, deliberately omit the code line that clears the pending flag in EXTI->PR. Run the program and observe in GDB how the processor becomes permanently trapped in the ISR, starving the main loop.

Official References, Research Papers & Standards

Deepen your engineering foundation with canonical publications and official standard specifications:

ARM Architecture Spec ARM Ltd.

ARMv7-M Architecture Reference Manual (NVIC Chapter)

Complete specification of NVIC priority grouping, tail-chaining, exception entry stacking, and PRIMASK/FAULTMASK registers.

View Official Resource →
Technical Book Joseph Yiu

The Definitive Guide to ARM Cortex-M3 and Cortex-M4

Authoritative hardware reference explaining interrupt latency measurements, fault escalation, and low-power WFI wakeups.

View Official Resource →
Industry Practice Barr Group

Interrupt Latency and Jitter Optimization

Engineering methodologies for minimizing critical section durations and avoiding race conditions in real-time firmware.

View Official Resource →

fields.title: Day 16: Capstone: Multi-Tasking RTOS Sensor Hub
fields.content:
Session 2.7

Day 16: Capstone: Multi-Tasking RTOS Sensor Hub

Problem Statement: Integrate FreeRTOS tasks, thread-safe queues, mutexes, DMA ADC, I2C environmental sensing, CAN telemetry, and a serial command shell into one cohesive, production-grade embedded hub.
📋 Daily Plan & Learning Architecture
Session 2.7 Module 2: Peripherals & FreeRTOS Estimated: 3.5 hrs

🎯 Today's Mission & Relevance

  • Architect a 6-task production FreeRTOS firmware application with strict separation of concerns.
  • Implement non-blocking inter-task communication using FreeRTOS Queues and Mutexes.
  • Build a multi-thread heartbeat supervision system driving a hardware Independent Watchdog (IWDG).

📐 Theoretical Milestones

  • Priority inheritance mechanics for preventing unbounded priority inversion.
  • Determinism and jitter elimination using vTaskDelayUntil() vs vTaskDelay().
  • Stack high-water mark calculation and heap management strategies (Heap_4 vs Static).

💻 Hands-On Blueprint

  • Program 16.1: Centralized FreeRTOS task descriptor table and stack allocation.
  • Program 16.2: Periodic sensor task reading BMP280 and posting to FreeRTOS queue.
  • Program 16.3: CAN telemetry task packing and transmitting CAN frame.
  • Program 16.4: Mutex-guarded serial CLI command shell.
  • Program 16.5: Multi-task heartbeat aggregator and hardware IWDG supervisor.

🛡️ Production Failure Modes

  • Calling blocking FreeRTOS API functions (xQueueReceive with portMAX_DELAY) inside ISRs.
  • Failing to protect shared data structures with mutexes, leading to race conditions and tearing.
  • Kicking the watchdog unconditionally inside a low-priority thread while high-priority loops hang.
🏁 Daily Milestone Deliverables: 5 Interactive Register-Level Programs • 5 Architecture Diagrams • 10 Practice MCQs • 5 Hands-On Assignments

16.1 Industrial Multi-Tasking RTOS System Architecture

Modern embedded IoT gateways, automotive sensor nodes, and avionics flight computers require multi-rate, concurrent processing with microsecond determinism. Combining independent peripherals—such as I2C barometric sensors, ADC DMA converters, CAN-bus automotive transceivers, and CLI serial consoles—into a single bare-metal loop creates fragile coupling where any slow bus transaction stalls critical control loops.

By leveraging FreeRTOS, we partition system responsibilities into six decoupled, priority-driven tasks communicating strictly through thread-safe FreeRTOS Queues and protected by binary/mutex semaphores. A central Health Watchdog Monitor continuously tracks task heartbeats, enforcing system reliability and triggering graceful recovery if any thread deadlocks.

Figure 16.0-1: Industrial Multi-Tasking RTOS Sensor Hub Architecture
Figure Parameters Explained:
  • Sensor Task (Priority 4): Acquires I2C pressure/temperature and ADC DMA thermistor data every 100 ms; publishes to sensor_queue.
  • Control Task (Priority 4): Consumes sensor packets and computes PID heater control commands driving high-resolution PWM outputs.
  • CAN Telemetry Task (Priority 3): Packs sensor metrics into standard 8-byte CAN frames (ID 0x301) and pushes them onto the automotive bus.
  • CLI Command Task (Priority 2): Parses incoming ASCII commands over UART; accesses system parameters protected by a shared Mutex.
  • Health Watchdog (Priority 5): Highest priority supervisor; verifies all task heartbeat flags before resetting hardware Independent Watchdog (IWDG).

16.2 Task Configuration Table and Thread Allocation

In safety-conscious firmware development, task definitions, stack depths, and priorities should never be scattered across ad-hoc code blocks. Instead, they are consolidated into a centralized Task Configuration Descriptor Table. This allows compile-time stack allocation audits and systematic priority tuning to prevent priority inversion.


#include <stdint.h>
#include "FreeRTOS.h"
#include "task.h"

typedef struct {
    const char *task_name;
    TaskFunction_t task_func;
    configSTACK_DEPTH_TYPE stack_words;
    UBaseType_t priority;
    TaskHandle_t *task_handle;
} TaskDescriptor_t;

/* Task function declarations */
extern void vSensorTask(void *pvParams);
extern void vControlTask(void *pvParams);
extern void vCanTxTask(void *pvParams);
extern void vCliTask(void *pvParams);
extern void vHealthTask(void *pvParams);

/* Task handles */
TaskHandle_t hSensorTask;
TaskHandle_t hControlTask;
TaskHandle_t hCanTxTask;
TaskHandle_t hCliTask;
TaskHandle_t hHealthTask;

static const TaskDescriptor_t g_task_table[] = {
    {"HealthMon", vHealthTask,  configMINIMAL_STACK_SIZE * 2, 5, &hHealthTask},
    {"SensorAcq", vSensorTask,  configMINIMAL_STACK_SIZE * 3, 4, &hSensorTask},
    {"ControlPID",vControlTask, configMINIMAL_STACK_SIZE * 2, 4, &hControlTask},
    {"CanTelem",  vCanTxTask,   configMINIMAL_STACK_SIZE * 2, 3, &hCanTxTask},
    {"SerialCLI", vCliTask,     configMINIMAL_STACK_SIZE * 4, 2, &hCliTask},
};

#define NUM_TASKS (sizeof(g_task_table) / sizeof(TaskDescriptor_t))

void system_tasks_init(void) {
    for (size_t i = 0; i < NUM_TASKS; i++) {
        BaseType_t status = xTaskCreate(
            g_task_table[i].task_func,
            g_task_table[i].task_name,
            g_task_table[i].stack_words,
            NULL,
            g_task_table[i].priority,
            g_task_table[i].task_handle
        );
        configASSERT(status == pdPASS);
    }
}
Program 16.1: Centralized FreeRTOS Task Descriptor Table and Stack Allocation

16.3 High-Rate Sensor Acquisition Task (I2C + ADC DMA)

The Sensor Acquisition Task executes periodically every 100 milliseconds. It queries the digital BMP280 environmental sensor via hardware I2C and samples the analog temperature thermistor via circular ADC DMA buffers. It packs these readings into an immutable SensorData_t struct and pushes copies into the inter-task queues.

Figure 16.0-2: Telemetry Pipeline from Physical Transducers to Transmission
Figure Parameters Explained:
  • I2C Sensor Interface: Synchronous I2C transaction reads raw 20-bit calibration registers and temperature words.
  • ADC DMA Interface: Direct Memory Access controller continuously updates analog thermistor values in SRAM without CPU load.
  • FreeRTOS Queue Dispatch: Non-blocking xQueueSend() copies structured telemetry into thread-safe message queues.
  • CAN TX Mailbox: Transmits standard CAN 2.0B frames with automatic hardware retransmission upon arbitration loss.

#include <stdint.h>
#include "FreeRTOS.h"
#include "task.h"
#include "queue.h"

typedef struct {
    uint32_t timestamp_ms;
    int16_t  temperature_degc_x10;  /* e.g., 255 = 25.5 C */
    uint32_t pressure_pa;           /* e.g., 101325 Pa */
    uint16_t ntc_raw_adc;
    uint8_t  sensor_fault_flags;
} SensorData_t;

extern QueueHandle_t g_sensor_queue;
extern void record_heartbeat(uint32_t task_id);

void vSensorTask(void *pvParams) {
    TickType_t xLastWakeTime = xTaskGetTickCount();
    const TickType_t xFrequency = pdMS_TO_TICKS(100); /* 10 Hz */

    SensorData_t sample;

    for (;;) {
        vTaskDelayUntil(&xLastWakeTime, xFrequency);

        /* 1. Sample physical transducers */
        sample.timestamp_ms = (uint32_t)(xTaskGetTickCount() * portTICK_PERIOD_MS);
        sample.temperature_degc_x10 = 245; /* 24.5 C from BMP280 */
        sample.pressure_pa = 101350;       /* 1013.5 hPa */
        sample.ntc_raw_adc = 2048;         /* 12-bit ADC mid-scale */
        sample.sensor_fault_flags = 0x00;

        /* 2. Broadcast sample to CAN and telemetry tasks */
        if (g_sensor_queue != NULL) {
            /* Non-blocking write: overwrite oldest if queue is full */
            xQueueOverwrite(g_sensor_queue, &sample);
        }

        /* 3. Report heartbeat to health supervisor */
        record_heartbeat(1); /* Task ID 1 = Sensor */
    }
}
Program 16.2: Periodic Sensor Task Reading BMP280 and Posting to FreeRTOS Queue

16.4 CAN Bus Telemetry Transmission Task

The CAN Telemetry Task wakes when new telemetry arrives in the sensor queue. It extracts the sensor struct, translates engineering values into standard CAN data frame fields, and queues them into the microcontroller CAN mailbox for transmission onto the automotive bus at 500 kbps.


#include <stdint.h>
#include "FreeRTOS.h"
#include "task.h"
#include "queue.h"

#define CAN_TELEMETRY_ID    0x301U

typedef struct {
    uint32_t id;
    uint8_t  dlc;
    uint8_t  data[8];
} CanTxFrame_t;

extern QueueHandle_t g_sensor_queue;
extern void can_hardware_send(const CanTxFrame_t *frame);
extern void record_heartbeat(uint32_t task_id);

void vCanTxTask(void *pvParams) {
    SensorData_t current_data;
    CanTxFrame_t frame;

    for (;;) {
        /* Block until new sensor data arrives in queue (timeout: 250 ms) */
        if (xQueueReceive(g_sensor_queue, &current_data, pdMS_TO_TICKS(250)) == pdPASS) {
            frame.id = CAN_TELEMETRY_ID;
            frame.dlc = 8;

            /* Pack Temperature (16-bit signed, offset 0) */
            frame.data[0] = (uint8_t)(current_data.temperature_degc_x10 & 0xFF);
            frame.data[1] = (uint8_t)(current_data.temperature_degc_x10 >> 8);

            /* Pack Pressure (24-bit unsigned, offset 2) */
            frame.data[2] = (uint8_t)(current_data.pressure_pa & 0xFF);
            frame.data[3] = (uint8_t)((current_data.pressure_pa >> 8) & 0xFF);
            frame.data[4] = (uint8_t)((current_data.pressure_pa >> 16) & 0xFF);

            /* Pack ADC and status */
            frame.data[5] = (uint8_t)(current_data.ntc_raw_adc & 0xFF);
            frame.data[6] = (uint8_t)(current_data.ntc_raw_adc >> 8);
            frame.data[7] = current_data.sensor_fault_flags;

            can_hardware_send(&frame);
        }

        record_heartbeat(2); /* Task ID 2 = CAN TX */
    }
}
Program 16.3: CAN Telemetry Task Packing and Transmitting CAN Frame

16.5 Mutex-Protected Command-Line Interface (CLI) Task

The Serial CLI Task enables engineers to calibrate sensor offsets, change CAN broadcast frequencies, and dump runtime task statistics over UART. Because configuration parameters are shared between tasks, modifications are strictly guarded using a FreeRTOS Mutex with Priority Inheritance.


#include <stdint.h>
#include <string.h>
#include <stdio.h>
#include "FreeRTOS.h"
#include "task.h"
#include "semphr.h"

extern SemaphoreHandle_t g_config_mutex;
extern void uart_write_string(const char *str);
extern char uart_read_char_blocking(void);
extern void record_heartbeat(uint32_t task_id);

typedef struct {
    uint32_t can_period_ms;
    int16_t  temp_offset_degc_x10;
    uint8_t  logging_enabled;
} SystemConfig_t;

extern SystemConfig_t g_system_config;

void vCliTask(void *pvParams) {
    char rx_buf[64];
    uint8_t idx = 0;

    uart_write_string("
=== Industrial Sensor Hub CLI Ready ===
> ");

    for (;;) {
        char c = uart_read_char_blocking();

        if (c == '
' || c == '
') {
            rx_buf[idx] = '�';
            idx = 0;

            if (strcmp(rx_buf, "stats") == 0) {
                char stats_buf[256];
                vTaskList(stats_buf);
                uart_write_string("
Name          State  Prio  Stack  Num
");
                uart_write_string(stats_buf);
            } else if (strcmp(rx_buf, "log start") == 0) {
                if (xSemaphoreTake(g_config_mutex, pdMS_TO_TICKS(100)) == pdPASS) {
                    g_system_config.logging_enabled = 1;
                    xSemaphoreGive(g_config_mutex);
                    uart_write_string("
Logging Enabled.
");
                }
            } else {
                uart_write_string("
Unknown command.
");
            }
            uart_write_string("> ");
        } else if (idx < sizeof(rx_buf) - 1) {
            rx_buf[idx++] = c;
        }

        record_heartbeat(3); /* Task ID 3 = CLI */
    }
}
Program 16.4: Mutex-Guarded Serial CLI Command Shell

16.6 System Health Monitor and Hardware Watchdog (IWDG)

Relying on a single thread to kick the hardware watchdog is dangerous: if a high-priority task deadlocks while the watchdog thread continues running, the system will never reset. The Health Monitor Task checks an atomic bitmask where every active thread must register its heartbeat. Only if all five tasks report healthy execution within the 500 ms supervisor window is the hardware IWDG refreshed.

Figure 16.0-3: Multi-Task Heartbeat Supervised Watchdog Subsystem
Figure Parameters Explained:
  • Atomic Heartbeat Mask: Each task sets its dedicated bit (1<<0 through 1<<4) upon completing its periodic cycle.
  • Evaluation Window (500 ms): Health task evaluates the mask twice per second against the expected mask (0x1F).
  • Hardware IWDG Reload: Writes 0xAAAA to IWDG_KR only upon 100% thread compliance.
  • Black-Box Fault Logging: If a thread starves or deadlocks, the identity of the hung task is preserved in backup registers before reboot.

#include <stdint.h>
#include "FreeRTOS.h"
#include "task.h"

#define EXPECTED_HEARTBEATS ((1U << 1) | (1U << 2) | (1U << 3)) /* Tasks 1, 2, 3 */
#define IWDG_KR             (*(volatile uint32_t *)0x40003000U)
#define IWDG_REFRESH_KEY    0x0000AAAAU

static volatile uint32_t g_heartbeat_mask = 0;

void record_heartbeat(uint32_t task_id) {
    taskENTER_CRITICAL();
    g_heartbeat_mask |= (1U << task_id);
    taskEXIT_CRITICAL();
}

void vHealthTask(void *pvParams) {
    TickType_t xLastWakeTime = xTaskGetTickCount();
    const TickType_t xCheckPeriod = pdMS_TO_TICKS(500);

    for (;;) {
        vTaskDelayUntil(&xLastWakeTime, xCheckPeriod);

        taskENTER_CRITICAL();
        uint32_t current_mask = g_heartbeat_mask;
        g_heartbeat_mask = 0; /* Reset for next cycle */
        taskEXIT_CRITICAL();

        if ((current_mask & EXPECTED_HEARTBEATS) == EXPECTED_HEARTBEATS) {
            /* All supervised tasks are alive and responsive: kick hardware IWDG */
            IWDG_KR = IWDG_REFRESH_KEY;
        } else {
            /* Fault detected: one or more tasks hung or starved! */
            /* Do NOT kick watchdog; allow hardware reset to recover system */
        }
    }
}
Program 16.5: Multi-Task Heartbeat Aggregator and Hardware IWDG Supervisor

Sensor Hub Inter-Task Communication and Synchronization Matrix

Task NamePriorityPeriod / TriggerInput MechanismsOutput MechanismsShared Resource Guard
Health Supervisor5 (Highest)Periodic 500 msg_heartbeat_mask bitmaskHardware IWDG kickCritical Section (taskENTER_CRITICAL)
Sensor Acquisition4 (High)Periodic 100 msI2C registers, ADC DMA buffersensor_data_queue (overwrite)DMA Hardware Ring Buffer
Closed-Loop Control4 (High)Queue Triggeredsensor_data_queuePWM Timer registers (TIM1)Direct Register Access
CAN Telemetry TX3 (Medium)Queue Triggeredsensor_data_queueCAN Hardware Mailbox (0x301)CAN Mailbox Status Semaphores
Serial CLI Shell2 (Low)UART RX InterruptUART RX Circular Ring BufferUART TX Streamg_config_mutex (Priority Inheritance)
Idle Daemon0 (Lowest)BackgroundNoneLow-Power WFI sleep modeKernel Internal

Topic Quiz (10 Questions)

Test your conceptual understanding of today's embedded systems architecture, registers, and runtime behaviors.

1. Why is it unsafe to refresh the hardware watchdog timer (IWDG) inside the low-priority Idle Task?
  • Because the Idle Task runs only when no other tasks are ready; if a higher priority task starves or hangs in a loop, the watchdog will never be fed, causing an unwanted reset
  • Because the Idle Task has no access to microcontroller hardware registers
  • Because the watchdog timer only works when interrupts are disabled
  • Because FreeRTOS does not provide an Idle Task by default
If a high-priority task enters an infinite loop, the Idle task will never execute, correctly triggering a watchdog reset. However, if a medium-priority task deadlocks while higher priority tasks keep the CPU busy, the Idle task also starves. A dedicated supervisor monitoring explicit heartbeats is far safer.
2. What is the advantage of using xQueueOverwrite() over xQueueSend() for real-time sensor telemetry?
  • It always succeeds without blocking, replacing obsolete samples so consumer tasks always read the freshest measurement
  • It encrypts the payload using AES-128
  • It allows multiple items to be stored in a zero-length queue
  • It automatically converts integers to floating-point numbers
In telemetry streaming, holding onto old samples is counterproductive. xQueueOverwrite() on a queue of length 1 guarantees that slow consumers never block the sensor task, and always receive the most up-to-date data.
3. Which FreeRTOS synchronization primitive should be chosen to protect a shared configuration struct accessed by both a CLI task and a Control task?
  • A FreeRTOS Mutex with Priority Inheritance (xSemaphoreCreateMutex)
  • A simple global volatile boolean flag
  • A binary semaphore without ownership
  • Disabling the global SysTick timer permanently
Mutexes implement priority inheritance: if a low-priority CLI task holds the mutex and a high-priority Control task requests it, the CLI task temporarily inherits high priority, avoiding unbounded priority inversion.
4. What does the FreeRTOS vTaskList() API function output?
  • A text table detailing all created tasks, their execution states, priorities, remaining stack high-water marks, and task numbers
  • The assembly disassembly of the bootloader
  • A list of active CAN message identifiers
  • The microcontroller Flash sector allocation map
vTaskList() provides a diagnostic snapshot of system threads, showing stack high-water marks (minimum remaining stack words since task creation) to diagnose stack overflows.
5. Why should task stack sizes be specified in words rather than bytes in FreeRTOS on 32-bit ARM cores?
  • Because configSTACK_DEPTH_TYPE represents 32-bit words on Cortex-M; allocating 100 words reserves 400 bytes of SRAM
  • Because bytes cannot be stored in SRAM
  • Because words allow faster network transfers
  • To satisfy MISRA-C memory alignment rules
In FreeRTOS for 32-bit architectures, the stack depth parameter represents 32-bit (4-byte) words. Specifying 128 words allocates 512 bytes.
6. What is the primary role of the CAN Bus Identifier (e.g., 0x301) in automotive communication?
  • It defines both the message priority on the physical bus and the identity/type of the data payload
  • It specifies the physical MAC address of the receiving node
  • It sets the baud rate for that specific frame
  • It serves as a cryptographic session token
CAN arbitration uses the 11-bit or 29-bit message ID: lower numerical IDs have higher priority during bus contention, and receivers use acceptance filters on this ID to accept relevant data.
7. What happens if a FreeRTOS task exceeds its allocated stack space?
  • It silently overwrites adjacent memory (such as other task TCBs or global variables), leading to erratic HardFaults or memory corruption
  • The microcontroller automatically reallocates heap memory
  • The compiler issues an immediate error during cross-compilation
  • The FreeRTOS scheduler doubles the CPU clock frequency
Microcontrollers lack hardware virtual memory paging (MMUs). Stack overflows directly corrupt memory. Enabling configCHECK_FOR_STACK_OVERFLOW hooks helps catch these corruptions during debugging.
8. How does vTaskDelayUntil() differ from vTaskDelay()?
  • vTaskDelayUntil() guarantees a fixed periodic execution frequency regardless of how long the task body took to execute
  • vTaskDelayUntil() sleeps for microsecond intervals using SysTick
  • vTaskDelayUntil() can only be called from an ISR
  • They are completely identical functions with different names
vTaskDelay(N) delays for N ticks relative to the call moment, causing cumulative timing drift if task execution time varies. vTaskDelayUntil() calculates delay relative to the previous wake time, maintaining rigid periodicity.
9. What is the purpose of entering a critical section (taskENTER_CRITICAL) when modifying the global heartbeat mask?
  • To disable interrupts and context switching, guaranteeing an atomic read-modify-write on the shared bitmask
  • To put the processor into deep STOP low-power mode
  • To trigger an immediate CAN transmission
  • To erase a flash sector safely
Read-modify-write operations (g_mask |= val) require multiple machine instructions (LDR, ORR, STR). A context switch in between would lead to lost updates. Critical sections ensure atomicity.
10. In production embedded systems, what should happen if a required task fails to report its heartbeat to the supervisor task?
  • The supervisor logs the stalled task's ID and halts watchdog refreshing, allowing the hardware IWDG to reset the system safely
  • The supervisor dynamically deletes the task and ignores the error
  • The supervisor writes a panic message to the active CAN bus indefinitely
  • The supervisor switches the CPU from 32-bit to 8-bit mode
Failing to refresh the hardware IWDG forces a hardware reset, returning the system to a known good state while preserving fault records in non-volatile registers.

Hands-On Assignments

Complete these 5 lab assignments to solidify your hands-on firmware engineering skills.

Assignment 1: Closed-Loop PID Temperature Control Task

Task: Implement a discrete PID control task running at 50 Hz. The task consumes temperature data from the sensor queue, calculates error relative to a setpoint (target: 35.0 C), and modulates a TIM1 PWM channel driving an external power MOSFET heater.

Assignment 2: FatFS CAN Bus Black-Box Logger

Task: Add a dedicated SD card logging task. Using FatFS, create a CSV log file ('can_log.csv') and append timestamped records of every transmitted and received CAN frame using a high-throughput 512-byte block buffer.

Assignment 3: Thread-Safe Remote Parameter Configuration via CAN

Task: Configure CAN message filter for ID 0x200 (Config Command). When a valid frame arrives, extract new PID gain parameters (Kp, Ki, Kd) and update the active control parameters safely using g_config_mutex.

Assignment 4: Inactivity-Driven Low-Power Sleep Task

Task: Implement a power management supervisor task that monitors CAN bus traffic. If no CAN frames are detected for 10 consecutive seconds, put the MCU into STM32 STOP mode, waking upon CAN RX or EXTI button interrupt.

Assignment 5: Host PC Python Real-Time Telemetry Dashboard

Task: Write a Python application utilizing PyQtGraph or Matplotlib. Connect to the sensor hub via serial port or CAN-USB adapter; parse incoming live telemetry packets and plot real-time temperature, pressure, and CPU utilization.

Deepen your engineering foundations with seminal reference manuals, processor architecture standards, and industry specifications:

Official engineering reference for task management, queue IPC, priority inheritance mutexes, and tickless idle operations.

Details hardware exception context stacking, tail-chaining latency, and PendSV software interrupt scheduling.

View Official Resource →

Defines physical bit-timing, non-destructive bitwise arbitration, error containment, and cyclic redundancy checking.

View Official Resource →

International benchmark for designing multi-task watchdog supervision and defensive embedded software architectures.

fields.title: Topic 13: Callbacks & Timers
fields.content:
Topic 13

Callbacks & Timers

A modular firmware driver should never have hardcoded dependencies on application business logic. A UART driver, button debouncer, or hardware timer module should not directly call update_motor_speed() or turn_on_heater(); doing so couples the peripheral driver to a specific application, preventing reuse across projects.

The standard architectural solution in C is the Callback Pattern utilizing Function Pointers. A driver provides registration APIs allowing higher-level application components to register callback functions that are invoked automatically when hardware events occur. Paired with hardware timer interrupts, this pattern enables building flexible, multi-instance Software Timer Services that manage dozens of independent periodic tasks from a single hardware timer.

13.1 Function Pointers in C: Syntax & Usage

A function pointer stores the physical entry point address of executable code in Flash memory. In C, declaring a function pointer type requires explicit parentheses around the pointer name to differentiate it from a function returning a pointer: 

/* Typedef for a callback taking a void* context pointer and uint32_t event data */
typedef void (*TimerCallback_t)(void *context, uint32_t elapsed_ms);

/* Declaration of a function pointer variable */
TimerCallback_t on_timer_expire = NULL;
Program 13.1: Defining and Declaring Typed Function Pointers in C
Defensive Tip: Never invoke a function pointer without an explicit NULL check! Invoking a NULL function pointer attempts to execute address 0x00000000, instantly triggering an ARM Cortex-M HardFault or executing the vector table as code!

13.2 Hardware Timers to Software Timers

A typical microcontroller contains 4 to 8 physical hardware timers. However, real-world firmware often requires dozens of concurrent periodic intervals: blinking an LED at 1 Hz, sampling a temperature sensor at 10 Hz, polling a keypad at 50 Hz, and sending a telemetry heartbeat every 5 seconds.

Figure 13.1: Multiplexing a Single Hardware Tick into Multiple Software Timers

13.3 Hands-On Code Implementations

The following complete module provides a production-grade Software Timer Engine supporting one-shot and periodic callback execution: 

/**
 * Program 13.2: Multi-Instance Software Timer Service with Callbacks
 * File: soft_timer.c
 */

#include <stdint.h>
#include <stdbool.h>
#include <stddef.h>
#include <stdio.h>

typedef void (*SoftTimerCallback_t)(void *context);

typedef struct {
    uint32_t            period_ticks;
    uint32_t            remaining_ticks;
    SoftTimerCallback_t callback;
    void               *context;
    bool                is_periodic;
    bool                is_active;
} SoftTimer_t;

#define MAX_SOFT_TIMERS 8U
static SoftTimer_t s_timers[MAX_SOFT_TIMERS];

void soft_timer_init(void) {
    for (size_t i = 0; i < MAX_SOFT_TIMERS; ++i) {
        s_timers[i].is_active = false;
        s_timers[i].callback  = NULL;
    }
}

int32_t soft_timer_start(uint32_t period_ticks, bool periodic, SoftTimerCallback_t cb, void *ctx) {
    if ((cb == NULL) || (period_ticks == 0U)) return -1;

    for (size_t i = 0; i < MAX_SOFT_TIMERS; ++i) {
        if (!s_timers[i].is_active) {
            s_timers[i].period_ticks    = period_ticks;
            s_timers[i].remaining_ticks = period_ticks;
            s_timers[i].is_periodic     = periodic;
            s_timers[i].callback        = cb;
            s_timers[i].context         = ctx;
            s_timers[i].is_active       = true;
            return (int32_t)i; /* Return timer handle */
        }
    }
    return -2; /* Out of timer slots */
}

/**
 * @brief Called every 1 ms from hardware SysTick ISR or timer tick.
 */
void soft_timer_tick_isr(void) {
    for (size_t i = 0; i < MAX_SOFT_TIMERS; ++i) {
        if (s_timers[i].is_active) {
            s_timers[i].remaining_ticks--;
            if (s_timers[i].remaining_ticks == 0U) {
                /* Execute registered callback */
                if (s_timers[i].callback != NULL) {
                    s_timers[i].callback(s_timers[i].context);
                }
                
                if (s_timers[i].is_periodic) {
                    s_timers[i].remaining_ticks = s_timers[i].period_ticks;
                } else {
                    s_timers[i].is_active = false; /* One-shot expired */
                }
            }
        }
    }
}
Program 13.2: Multi-Instance Software Timer Service with Callbacks in C

13.4 Buggy vs. Modern Safe Code Comparison

Invoking heavy business logic directly from an ISR callback violates real-time deadlines and causes unpredictable interrupt preemption lockups.

View Buggy/Legacy Code

The callback executes heavy mathematics, Flash erasing, and serial I/O directly in the hardware timer ISR context, locking the CPU: 

/* BUGGY: Heavy blocking computation inside timer callback */
void on_timer_expire_bad(void *ctx) {
    /* Runs in ISR context! Blocking for 250 ms will starve all other hardware! */
    spi_flash_sector_erase(0x1000); 
    printf("Erase finished\n");
}
Program 13.3-A: Heavy Blocking Execution Inside Timer Callback

The safe pattern sets a lightweight atomic event flag or posts an event, deferring heavy computation to the non-interrupt background thread: 

/* SAFE / PRODUCTION-GRADE: Non-blocking flag setting in ISR callback */
static volatile bool s_erase_requested = false;

void on_timer_expire_safe(void *ctx) {
    /* Fast non-blocking flag: takes 2 clock cycles in ISR */
    s_erase_requested = true;
}

void main_superloop(void) {
    while (1) {
        if (s_erase_requested) {
            s_erase_requested = false;
            /* Heavy operation executes safely in background thread */
            spi_flash_sector_erase(0x1000);
        }
    }
}
Program 13.3-B: Deferred Background Execution Pattern

Topic Quiz (10 Questions)

Test your understanding of function pointers, callback architectures, and timer services.

1. In C, what does the typedef 'typedef void (*ButtonCallback_t)(uint8_t pin);' declare?
  • A function returning a pointer to a button.
  • A pointer type to a function that accepts an 8-bit unsigned integer argument and returns void.
  • A struct containing an 8-bit integer.
  • An array of 8 buttons.
The syntax defines ButtonCallback_t as a function pointer type matching signatures: void func(uint8_t pin).
2. What happens if firmware invokes a function pointer that holds a NULL address?
  • The function returns 0.
  • The CPU attempts to fetch instructions from address 0x00000000, triggering an instant HardFault exception.
  • The compiler emits a warning at runtime.
  • Execution pauses for 1 ms.
Branching to NULL (0x0) executes memory outside valid code regions, causing the processor to generate an invalid instruction or memory fault.
3. Why do professional callback registration interfaces accept a 'void *context' user parameter?
  • To enable dynamic memory allocation.
  • To allow callers to pass instance-specific state data to the callback without relying on messy global variables.
  • To measure execution time.
  • It is required by the C standard.
Passing a context pointer provides an object-oriented 'this' pointer in C, allowing a single callback function to manage multiple hardware instances.
4. What is the role of a hardware timer Prescaler (PSC) register?
  • It scales the display contrast.
  • It divides the high-frequency CPU/bus clock down to a slower, manageable counter frequency.
  • It measures battery temperature.
  • It stores the interrupt vector address.
The prescaler clock divider slows down timer clock ticks, allowing microsecond or millisecond tick intervals from multi-MHz system clocks.
5. What is the Auto-Reload Register (ARR) in an embedded hardware timer?
  • A register that reloads Flash memory.
  • The register defining the maximum count value at which the timer counter resets to zero and generates an update/overflow interrupt.
  • A backup battery register.
  • The program counter.
The ARR defines timer period: when the counter matches ARR, it resets to 0 and asserts the periodic overflow interrupt flag.
6. What is the fundamental difference between a 'One-Shot' timer and a 'Periodic' timer?
  • One-shot timers run in hardware; periodic timers run in software.
  • A one-shot timer fires its callback once upon expiration and stops; a periodic timer automatically reloads its countdown and fires repeatedly.
  • Periodic timers require 64-bit integers.
  • One-shot timers ignore interrupts.
One-shot timers are used for timeouts and delays; periodic timers drive cyclic tasks like LED blinking and sensor sampling.
7. Why is it dangerous to execute long or blocking operations inside a timer callback that runs in ISR context?
  • The timer hardware melts.
  • It monopolizes CPU time at interrupt priority, blocking lower-priority interrupts and causing timing jitter or missed deadlines across the system.
  • Flash memory cannot be read during callbacks.
  • It disables compiler optimizations.
Callbacks called directly from ISRs inherit interrupt priority; blocking operations inside them starve other critical real-time subsystems.
8. What is a 'Timer Wheel' algorithm?
  • A mechanical dial on the microcontroller.
  • An efficient circular buffer data structure that schedules and fires thousands of software timers with O(1) tick complexity.
  • A motor control algorithm.
  • A debugger GUI widget.
Hashed timer wheels organize timers into circular buckets, enabling O(1) insertion and expiration checking even with hundreds of active timers.
9. Which standard ARM Cortex-M hardware peripheral provides an integrated 24-bit down-counter timer designed for RTOS and software ticks?
  • Watchdog Timer (WDT)
  • SysTick (System Tick Timer)
  • RTC (Real-Time Clock)
  • CRC Engine
SysTick is an integral core peripheral in every ARM Cortex-M CPU, providing a universal periodic 1 ms tick source across all silicon vendors.
10. Why should an array of function pointer callbacks be declared 'const' if the table is known at compile time?
  • To make the callbacks execute faster.
  • To place the dispatch table into Flash memory (.rodata), preventing RAM consumption and protecting pointers from memory corruption.
  • It enables thread locking.
  • It disables interrupts automatically.
Placing dispatch tables in Flash protects function pointers from accidental corruption by wild pointers or stack overflows.

Hands-On Assignments

Execute these 5 laboratory assignments to master function pointers, callbacks, and software timer multiplexing.

Assignment 1: Multi-Rate LED Blinker via Software Timers

Task: Using the software timer service from Program 13.2 driven by a 1 ms SysTick tick, register three periodic callbacks: (1) Green LED toggling at 500 ms, (2) Red LED toggling at 200 ms, and (3) Blue LED toggling at 1000 ms. Verify simultaneous multi-rate execution.

Assignment 2: Hardware Prescaler Calculation

Task: Given an MCU core running at 84 MHz, calculate the exact 16-bit Prescaler (PSC) and Auto-Reload (ARR) register values needed to generate an exact 1.000 kHz timer interrupt. Implement the register configuration and verify the frequency on an oscilloscope.

Assignment 3: Dynamic Callback Cancellation

Task: Implement a soft_timer_stop(int32_t handle) function. Create a one-shot communication timeout timer (3000 ms). If a simulated packet acknowledgment arrives before the timeout, stop the timer. Verify that the timeout error callback is never invoked.

Assignment 4: Button Debounce State Callback

Task: Implement a digital debouncing module for a mechanical push button. When a state change persists stably for 20 ms, fire an on_button_change(uint8_t state) callback. Verify that noisy mechanical contact bounce does not trigger false callbacks.

Assignment 5: Context-Aware Callback Structure

Task: Create a struct representing a PID heater controller. Register a periodic timer callback passing the address of this struct as the void *context argument. Inside the callback, cast the context back to the PID struct and update heater PWM output without using global variables.

Official References, Research Papers & Standards

Deepen your engineering foundation with canonical publications and official standard specifications:

Classic Paper George Varghese & Tony Lauck

Hashed and Hierarchical Timing Wheels

Seminal ACM paper introducing efficient O(1) timer management algorithms used in network stacks and real-time operating systems.

View Official Resource →
Architecture Standard ARM Ltd.

Cortex-M SysTick Timer Architecture Specification

Hardware technical reference defining the SysTick CSR, RVR, and CVR registers and clock source division modes.

View Official Resource →
Design Patterns Addison-Wesley

Design Patterns in C (Embedded Architecture)

Architectural guide to implementing function pointer tables, callbacks, and polymorphic interfaces in procedural C.
