fields.title: Day 17: Low-Power Design & Sleep Modes
fields.content:
Session 3.0

Day 17: Low-Power Design & Sleep Modes

Problem Statement: Battery-powered IoT devices must last years on a tiny coin cell where every single microampere matters. How do you transition a microcontroller into deep sleep and wake it deterministically using hardware timers?
📋 Daily Plan & Learning Architecture
Session 3.0 Module 3: Advanced Embedded Architecture Estimated: 3.5 hrs

🎯 Today's Mission & Relevance

  • Understand the physics of dynamic vs static CMOS power consumption.
  • Master STM32 power mode hierarchies: Run, Sleep, Stop 0/1/2, Standby, and Shutdown.
  • Implement FreeRTOS Tickless Idle and low-power RTC timer wakeups.

📐 Theoretical Milestones

  • Dynamic switching power (P = C * V^2 * f) vs static transistor channel leakage.
  • GPIO analog mode conditioning to prevent floating input pin leakage.
  • Coin cell internal resistance (ESR) and brownout risks during RF pulse currents.

💻 Hands-On Blueprint

  • Program 17.1: ARM Cortex-M sleep mode entry with __WFI() in idle superloop.
  • Program 17.2: Entering STM32 Stop 2 mode with RTC wakeup timer.
  • Program 17.3: Peripheral clock gating and GPIO analog low-power conditioning.
  • Program 17.4: Tickless idle implementation hook for FreeRTOS.
  • Program 17.5: Python battery lifetime and average current simulator.

🛡️ Production Failure Modes

  • Leaving unused GPIO pins configured as floating inputs, causing hundreds of microamps of leakage.
  • Allowing the 1 ms SysTick interrupt to run in FreeRTOS, preventing true deep sleep.
  • Failing to account for internal battery ESR, causing brown-out resets on radio transmissions.
🏁 Daily Milestone Deliverables: 5 Interactive Register-Level Programs • 5 Architecture Diagrams • 10 Practice MCQs • 5 Hands-On Assignments

17.1 The Physics of Microcontroller Power Dissipation

In battery-operated embedded engineering—such as wilderness wildlife trackers, smart utility water meters, and wearable medical monitors—devices must operate unattended for up to 10 years powered exclusively by a miniature primary cell (e.g., a 225 mAh CR2032 coin cell or a 2.4 Ah Li-SOCl2 battery). At this operational frontier, power dissipation is governed by two fundamental physical components:

  • Dynamic (Active) Power ($P_{\text{dyn}} = C \cdot V^2 \cdot f$): Dissipated when internal transistors switch states, charging and discharging parasitic gate capacitance $C$ at supply voltage $V$ and clock frequency $f$.
  • Static (Leakage) Power ($P_{\text{static}} = V \cdot I_{\text{leak}}$): Dissipated even when the clock is completely stopped, caused by quantum sub-threshold leakage currents flowing through silicon transistor channels.

Figure 17.0-1: STM32 Ultra-Low-Power Operating Modes Hierarchy
Figure Parameters Explained:
  • Run Mode (80 MHz): Full computational performance; maximum dynamic current draw (approx. 100 uA/MHz).
  • Sleep Mode (WFI): CPU core instruction clock stopped; peripheral DMA and interrupts continue running autonomously.
  • Stop 2 Mode: Main internal voltage regulator powered down; high-speed oscillators halted; full SRAM1/SRAM2 data retention.
  • Standby Mode: Core logic powered down; almost all SRAM lost; woke up via RTC alarm or dedicated WKUP pins.
  • Shutdown Mode: Ultra-low leakage state (30 nA); only power-on reset circuitry and dedicated tamper pins remain operational.

17.2 Duty Cycling and Average Current Profile Engineering

Ultra-low-power devices survive not by operating continuously at low speed, but through Aggressive Duty Cycling. The microcontroller remains in an ultra-deep sleep state (consuming $1 \,\mu\text{A}$) for 99.9% of its operational life, wakes rapidly within microseconds to capture sensor samples and transmit an RF packet (consuming $30 \,\text{mA}$ for $50 \,\text{ms}$), and immediately plunges back into sleep.

Figure 17.0-2: Periodic Duty-Cycle Current Consumption Waveform
Figure Parameters Explained:
  • Baseline Sleep Floor (1.5 uA): Dominated by RTC counter and silicon sub-threshold transistor leakage.
  • Wakeup Latency Penalty: Transient current consumed while internal PLLs stabilize and voltage regulators ramp up.
  • Sensor Acquisition Window: Active ADC sampling and sensor bus transactions with peripherals clock-gated.
  • RF Transmission Peak: High peak current draw during PA (Power Amplifier) packet transmission.

17.3 Core Sleep Mode Entry with Wait For Interrupt (__WFI)

The simplest low-power mechanism is the ARM Cortex-M __WFI() (Wait For Interrupt) assembly instruction. In standard Sleep mode, the CPU halts instruction execution while peripheral clocks remain running. Any active peripheral interrupt (such as a Timer or UART RX) immediately wakes the core with zero wake-up latency.


#include <stdint.h>

#define SCB_SCR             (*(volatile uint32_t *)0xE000ED10U)
#define SCB_SCR_SLEEPDEEP   (1U << 2)
#define SCB_SCR_SLEEPONEXIT (1U << 1)

void enter_light_sleep(void) {
    /* 1. Ensure deep-sleep bit is cleared for standard light sleep */
    SCB_SCR &= ~SCB_SCR_SLEEPDEEP;

    /* 2. Optional: enable Sleep-on-Exit to sleep immediately after ISR finishes */
    /* SCB_SCR |= SCB_SCR_SLEEPONEXIT; */

    /* 3. Execute Data Synchronization Barrier to complete pending memory writes */
    __asm volatile ("dsb" : : : "memory");

    /* 4. Execute Wait For Interrupt instruction */
    __asm volatile ("wfi");

    /* 5. Instruction Synchronization Barrier after waking up */
    __asm volatile ("isb" : : : "memory");
}
Program 17.1: ARM Cortex-M Sleep Mode Entry with __WFI() in Idle Superloop

17.4 STM32 Stop 2 Mode with Hardware RTC Periodic Wakeup

In Stop 2 Mode, the microcontroller achieves sub-microampere static current while preserving full SRAM retention. The high-speed internal oscillators (HSI, HSE, PLL) are gated off. A low-power 32.768 kHz quartz crystal clock (LSE) drives the internal Real-Time Clock (RTC), which triggers an external interrupt line (EXTI Line 20) to wake the microcontroller periodically.

Figure 17.0-3: RTC Wakeup Timer Subsystem Driving EXTI Line
Figure Parameters Explained:
  • LSE 32.768 kHz Clock: Ultra-low-power quartz crystal running permanently with less than 200 nA power draw.
  • 20-bit Downcounter: Configurable auto-reload register sets periodic wakeup intervals from 122 us to 36 hours.
  • EXTI Line 20: Asynchronous interrupt line capable of waking the core even when peripheral bus clocks are stopped.
  • Regulator Transition: PWR switches from low-power regulator (LPR) to main regulator (MR) in 5 microseconds.

#include <stdint.h>

#define PWR_CR1             (*(volatile uint32_t *)0x40007000U)
#define PWR_SCR             (*(volatile uint32_t *)0x40007008U)
#define SCB_SCR             (*(volatile uint32_t *)0xE000ED10U)
#define EXTI_IMR1           (*(volatile uint32_t *)0x40010400U)
#define EXTI_RTSR1          (*(volatile uint32_t *)0x40010408U)

#define SCB_SCR_SLEEPDEEP   (1U << 2)
#define PWR_CR1_LPMS_STOP2  (2U << 0)  /* Select Stop 2 mode */
#define PWR_SCR_CWUF        (0x1FU << 0) /* Clear wakeup flags */

void rtc_wakeup_init_10s(void) {
    /* Enable EXTI Line 20 (RTC Wakeup) rising edge and event */
    EXTI_IMR1 |= (1U << 20);
    EXTI_RTSR1 |= (1U << 20);
}

void enter_stop2_mode(void) {
    /* 1. Clear all power wakeup flags */
    PWR_SCR |= PWR_SCR_CWUF;

    /* 2. Configure Power Control Register for Stop 2 */
    PWR_CR1 &= ~(0x7U << 0);
    PWR_CR1 |= PWR_CR1_LPMS_STOP2;

    /* 3. Set ARM SLEEPDEEP bit in System Control Block */
    SCB_SCR |= SCB_SCR_SLEEPDEEP;

    /* 4. Memory barriers and sleep */
    __asm volatile ("dsb" : : : "memory");
    __asm volatile ("wfi");
    __asm volatile ("isb" : : : "memory");

    /* 5. Upon waking: re-enable high-speed clocks (PLL/HSI) */
    /* Hardware automatically resets clock source to MSI/HSI */
}
Program 17.2: Entering STM32 Stop 2 Mode with RTC Wakeup Timer

17.5 Dynamic Clock Gating and Unused Peripheral Power Isolation

Every peripheral connected to the microcontroller AHB and APB buses consumes dynamic current if its clock tree is enabled—even if the peripheral is idle. Furthermore, floating GPIO input pins act like antennas, repeatedly toggling high-impedance CMOS inputs and leaking microamperes. Before sleeping, unused GPIOs must be configured into Analog Mode and bus clocks disabled.


#include <stdint.h>

#define RCC_AHB1ENR         (*(volatile uint32_t *)0x40021048U)
#define RCC_AHB2ENR         (*(volatile uint32_t *)0x4002104CU)
#define RCC_APB1ENR1        (*(volatile uint32_t *)0x40021058U)
#define RCC_APB2ENR         (*(volatile uint32_t *)0x40021060U)
#define GPIOA_MODER         (*(volatile uint32_t *)0x48000000U)
#define GPIOB_MODER         (*(volatile uint32_t *)0x48000400U)

void configure_pins_for_low_power(void) {
    /* Configure all non-essential GPIO pins to Analog Mode (0b11) */
    /* This disables input Schmitt triggers, preventing parasitic leakage */
    GPIOA_MODER = 0xFFFFFFFFU;
    GPIOB_MODER = 0xFFFFFFFFU;
}

void gate_off_peripheral_clocks(void) {
    /* Disable DMA, CRC, and Crypto peripheral clocks */
    RCC_AHB1ENR &= ~((1U << 0) | (1U << 12)); /* DMA1, CRC */

    /* Disable Timers, SPI, and I2C clocks */
    RCC_APB1ENR1 &= ~((1U << 0) | (1U << 14) | (1U << 21)); /* TIM2, SPI2, I2C1 */

    /* Disable ADC and UART clocks */
    RCC_AHB2ENR &= ~(1U << 13); /* ADC */
    RCC_APB2ENR &= ~(1U << 14); /* USART1 */
}
Program 17.3: Peripheral Clock Gating and GPIO Analog Low-Power Conditioning

17.6 FreeRTOS Tickless Idle Architecture

In standard FreeRTOS configurations, the SysTick interrupt fires every 1 millisecond (1000 Hz) to maintain the kernel tick count. If the microcontroller attempts to sleep, SysTick forces the core awake 1000 times per second, obliterating battery life. FreeRTOS solves this with Tickless Idle (configUSE_TICKLESS_IDLE = 1), which calculates the expected idle duration, disables SysTick, sets a low-power timer (LPTIM), and sleeps undisturbed for seconds or minutes.


#include <stdint.h>
#include "FreeRTOS.h"
#include "task.h"

extern void enter_stop2_mode(void);
extern void lptim_start_timeout(uint32_t ticks);
extern uint32_t lptim_get_elapsed_ticks(void);

void vPortSuppressTicksAndSleep(TickType_t xExpectedIdleTicks) {
    /* 1. Cap maximum sleep time to low-power timer counter capacity */
    if (xExpectedIdleTicks > 5000) {
        xExpectedIdleTicks = 5000;
    }

    /* 2. Stop SysTick interrupt to prevent 1 ms wakeups */
    *(volatile uint32_t *)0xE000E010U &= ~1U; /* Disable SysTick */

    /* 3. Configure low-power timer (LPTIM) to wake after expected ticks */
    lptim_start_timeout((uint32_t)xExpectedIdleTicks);

    /* 4. Enter Stop 2 low-power mode */
    enter_stop2_mode();

    /* 5. Execution resumes here after wakeup! */
    uint32_t ulElapsed = lptim_get_elapsed_ticks();

    /* 6. Step FreeRTOS tick counter forward by the actual elapsed time */
    vTaskStepTick((TickType_t)ulElapsed);

    /* 7. Restart SysTick timer */
    *(volatile uint32_t *)0xE000E010U |= 1U;
}
Program 17.4: Tickless Idle Implementation Hook for FreeRTOS

17.7 System Power Budgeting and Battery Lifetime Calculator

Firmware architects must validate power profiles against battery chemistry limits. Lithium coin cells (CR2032) suffer severe voltage droop if pulsed with peak currents exceeding 15 mA due to high internal equivalent series resistance (ESR ~ 10-30 $\Omega$). A mathematical budget models each phase to predict lifetime in days and years.


def calculate_battery_lifetime(battery_capacity_mah, phases, sleep_phase):
    """
    phases: list of dicts [{'name': 'RF TX', 'current_ma': 25.0, 'duration_s': 0.05}]
    sleep_phase: dict {'current_ma': 0.0015, 'duration_s': 9.95}
    """
    total_cycle_time_s = sum(p['duration_s'] for p in phases) + sleep_phase['duration_s']
    
    # Calculate energy consumed in milliamp-seconds (mAs) per cycle
    total_mas = sum(p['current_ma'] * p['duration_s'] for p in phases)
    total_mas += sleep_phase['current_ma'] * sleep_phase['duration_s']
    
    avg_current_ma = total_mas / total_cycle_time_s
    avg_current_ua = avg_current_ma * 1000.0
    
    # Derate battery by 20% for self-discharge and temperature losses
    usable_capacity_mah = battery_capacity_mah * 0.80
    lifetime_hours = usable_capacity_mah / avg_current_ma
    lifetime_days = lifetime_hours / 24.0
    lifetime_years = lifetime_days / 365.25

    print(f"Total Cycle Period:   {total_cycle_time_s:.2f} s")
    print(f"Average Current Draw: {avg_current_ua:.2f} uA")
    print(f"Estimated Lifetime:   {lifetime_days:.1f} days ({lifetime_years:.2f} years)")
    return avg_current_ua, lifetime_years

# Sample usage for a CR2032 environmental node
phases = [
    {'name': 'Sensor Sample', 'current_ma': 3.5,  'duration_s': 0.010},
    {'name': 'BLE Advertising', 'current_ma': 18.0, 'duration_s': 0.030}
]
sleep = {'current_ma': 0.0012, 'duration_s': 9.960}
calculate_battery_lifetime(225.0, phases, sleep)

Topic Quiz (10 Questions)

Test your conceptual understanding of today's embedded systems architecture, registers, and runtime behaviors.

1. What is the primary physical cause of static (leakage) power consumption in sub-micron silicon microcontrollers?
  • Sub-threshold conduction and gate-oxide tunneling leakage flowing through transistors even when clocks are stopped
  • The resistance of external PCB copper traces
  • Electrons evaporating into the air from the IC package
  • The speed of the USB transceiver
Even when the clock is stopped ($f=0$), static leakage current ($I_{\text{leak}}$) flows due to finite sub-threshold channel conduction and quantum tunneling across ultra-thin gate oxides.
2. Why should unused microcontroller GPIO pins be configured into Analog Mode before entering deep sleep?
  • To disconnect the internal digital input Schmitt triggers, preventing parasitic floating voltages from inducing cross-conduction current
  • To allow the pins to generate analog voltages during sleep
  • To increase the speed of the ADC when waking up
  • Because digital pins cannot be woken by interrupts
A floating digital input hovers between logic 0 and logic 1, causing both the P-channel and N-channel CMOS input transistors to partially conduct, leaking up to tens of microamperes per pin. Analog mode completely isolates the input buffer.
3. How does FreeRTOS Tickless Idle mode improve battery lifetime?
  • It suppresses the 1 ms periodic SysTick interrupt, allowing the MCU to remain in deep sleep for seconds or minutes until a real event occurs
  • It deletes all tasks and restarts the microcontroller
  • It halves the required RAM memory size
  • It replaces FreeRTOS with a Linux kernel
Standard FreeRTOS wakes every 1 ms due to SysTick. Tickless idle reprograms a low-power timer for the expected idle duration and disables SysTick, allowing prolonged deep sleep.
4. What is the key retention difference between STM32 Stop 2 mode and Standby mode?
  • Stop 2 retains the full contents of SRAM1 and SRAM2; Standby mode powers off internal SRAM, losing RAM contents unless backup SRAM is powered
  • Stop 2 erases Flash memory
  • Standby mode consumes more current than Run mode
  • Stop 2 cannot be woken by the RTC timer
In Stop 2, internal low-power regulators maintain SRAM cell bias, ensuring variables are preserved upon waking. In Standby, core SRAM is unpowered; waking triggers a reset-like initialization.
5. What frequency crystal is standard for running the real-time clock (RTC) in ultra-low-power embedded devices?
  • 32.768 kHz (because dividing by 2^15 yields exactly 1 Hz)
  • 8.000 MHz
  • 100.000 MHz
  • 1.000 kHz
32.768 kHz is the global standard for horology and RTCs. An asynchronous 15-bit binary ripple counter divides 32,768 by $2^{15}$ to produce exactly one 1-second tick with minimal power.
6. Which ARM assembly instruction halts the CPU core until an interrupt occurs?
  • WFI (Wait For Interrupt)
  • NOP (No Operation)
  • SVC (Supervisor Call)
  • BKPT (Breakpoint)
The WFI instruction suspends CPU instruction fetching and core clocks until any unmasked NVIC or EXTI interrupt event is detected.
7. What happens if a battery-powered device draws high peak currents (e.g., 40 mA) from a standard CR2032 coin cell?
  • The high internal Equivalent Series Resistance (ESR) of the cell causes a severe voltage drop that can trigger the MCU Brown-Out Reset (BOR)
  • The coin cell immediately catches fire
  • The MCU clock doubles in frequency automatically
  • The battery capacity increases due to chemical agitation
CR2032 coin cells have a high internal resistance (10 to 30 ohms). A 40 mA pulse produces an internal drop of $V = IR = 0.04 \times 25 = 1.0 \,\text{V}$. A 3.0V cell drops to 2.0V, crossing the BOR threshold.
8. What is the purpose of the Low-Power UART (LPUART) in ultra-low-power microcontrollers?
  • It can receive incoming serial data and wake the microcontroller from deep Stop mode using a low-frequency clock (LSE)
  • It encrypts UART data using quantum keys
  • It converts UART to gigabit Ethernet
  • It eliminates the need for TX and RX pins
LPUART operates from the 32.768 kHz LSE or a dedicated low-speed oscillator, remaining active while main bus clocks are off. It wakes the core upon detecting a valid start bit or address match.
9. What is the mathematical equation governing dynamic power dissipation in digital CMOS circuitry?
  • P = C * V^2 * f
  • P = V / I
  • P = I^2 / R
  • P = C * f / V
Dynamic power is quadratically proportional to supply voltage ($V^2$) and linearly proportional to switching frequency ($f$) and switched capacitance ($C$).
10. Why is it important to execute Data Synchronization Barrier (DSB) and Instruction Synchronization Barrier (ISB) around WFI?
  • To guarantee all outstanding memory write transactions complete before entering sleep, and that prefetched instructions are flushed upon waking
  • To unlock the Flash memory write controller
  • To force the compiler to use assembly optimizations
  • To calibrate the crystal oscillator
ARM pipeline architecture requires DSB to ensure all queued memory accesses finish before clocks stop, and ISB after waking to purge the instruction pipeline of obsolete instructions.

Hands-On Assignments

Complete these 5 lab assignments to solidify your hands-on firmware engineering skills.

Assignment 1: Nordic PPK2 Current Waveform Profiling

Task: Connect a development board to a Nordic Power Profiler Kit II (PPK2) or INA219 current sensor. Capture current consumption during: (a) busy superloop, (b) WFI sleep, and (c) Stop 2 mode with RTC wakeup. Calculate exact average power over a 1-minute trace.

Assignment 2: Hierarchical Inactivity Sleep Escalator

Task: Implement an adaptive power governor: if no button or sensor events occur for 100 ms, enter Sleep; after 2 seconds of inactivity, escalate to Stop 1; after 10 seconds, escalate to Stop 2 with periodic 5-second RTC wakeups.

Assignment 3: LPUART Asynchronous Wakeup on Command Token

Task: Configure LPUART1 on STM32 to run from the 32.768 kHz LSE crystal. Enter Stop 2 mode. Send ASCII character 'W' from a host PC; verify the LPUART detects the start bit, wakes the MCU, and prints a greeting over serial.

Assignment 4: CR2032 IoT Sensor Node Life Optimization

Task: Take the Day 16 Sensor Hub project. Implement Tickless Idle and configure GPIO conditioning. Measure and optimize the firmware to achieve an average current consumption below 45 uA on a 3.0V supply.

Assignment 5: LoRaWAN Class A Power Budget Model

Task: Write a Python script that models a LoRaWAN Class A sensor node transmitting an 18-byte payload at Spreading Factor 10 every 15 minutes. Include TX burst (120 mA, 350 ms), RX1/RX2 windows, and sleep leakage; compute battery life on a 1200 mAh cell.

fields.title: Topic 14: Non-Blocking Firmware Design
fields.content:
Topic 14

Non-Blocking Firmware Design

In novice firmware, timing is frequently achieved through busy-wait loops such as delay_ms(500) or spin loops polling a status flag: while (!(USART1->SR & USART_SR_TXE));. While superficially simple, blocking code paralyzes the microcontroller core. For hundreds of thousands or even millions of CPU clock cycles, the processor burns power executing dummy instructions while completely blind to user input, incoming bus communications, and scheduled sensor readings.

Professional bare-metal and real-time firmware enforces a strict design law: Never Block the CPU. Every task executed by the main superloop must adhere to the Run-to-Completion (RTC) principle: execute immediate deterministic work, inspect timestamps or hardware flags without waiting, update internal state variables, and promptly return control to the scheduler.

14.1 The Pathology of Blocking Delays

Consider an embedded system running on an ARM Cortex-M4 clocked at 168 MHz. When a developer inserts delay_ms(100) to pause between sensor readings, the CPU executes exactly:

168,000,000 cycles/sec × 0.100 sec = 16,800,000 CPU Clock Cycles Wasted

During those 16.8 million clock cycles, the following catastrophic failure modes occur in a multi-functional system:

  • Button Latency and Missed Inputs: A mechanical button pressed for 80 ms during the 100 ms delay is completely missed unless tied to an edge-triggered hardware interrupt.
  • UART / SPI Buffer Overrun: If high-speed incoming UART bytes (e.g., 115200 baud, 1 byte every 86.8 μs) arrive faster than the hardware FIFO can store them (often only 1 to 4 bytes deep), characters are overwritten and lost (Overrun Error: ORE).
  • Watchdog Timer (WDT) Starvation: The hardware independent watchdog timer (IWDG) requires regular refresh pulses. Blocking functions starve the watchdog feeder, causing spontaneous system resets under peak load.
  • Increased Power Consumption: A spinning CPU draws maximum dynamic switching current ($I_{dynamic} \propto C \cdot V^2 \cdot f$). A non-blocking architecture allows the CPU to enter low-power sleep (__WFI() - Wait For Interrupt) whenever tasks are waiting for future deadlines.

14.2 Non-Blocking Timekeeping & The Wraparound Proof

To replace blocking delays, we establish a monotonic millisecond timebase driven by the ARM Cortex-M SysTick hardware interrupt incrementing a global volatile counter: 

/* systick.h / systick.c */
static volatile uint32_t g_system_ticks = 0U;

void SysTick_Handler(void) {
    g_system_ticks++;
}

uint32_t millis(void) {
    uint32_t ticks;
    /* Atomic read on 32-bit Cortex-M architecture */
    ticks = g_system_ticks;
    return ticks;
}
Program 14.1: Monotonic Millisecond Counter Implementation

The Unsigned Difference Rule

A 32-bit unsigned counter incremented every 1 millisecond overflows back to zero after:

(232 - 1) milliseconds ≈ 4,294,967,295 ms ≈ 49.71 days

Novice engineers often write deadline comparisons using addition: 

/* DANGEROUS BUG: Subject to catastrophic overflow failure! */
if (millis() >= target_time) { ... }

If millis() is currently 0xFFFFFFF0 (16 ms before overflow) and we schedule a task for +30 ms, target_time becomes 0x0000000E (14). Because 0xFFFFFFF0 >= 0x0000000E evaluates to TRUE immediately, the task executes instantly without waiting!

The mathematically sound, immune-to-wraparound method relies strictly on unsigned subtraction: 

/* CORRECT: Fully immune to 32-bit unsigned integer overflow! */
if ((millis() - previous_time) >= INTERVAL_MS) {
    previous_time += INTERVAL_MS; /* Or previous_time = millis(); */
    execute_task();
}

Mathematical Proof of Unsigned Subtraction Wraparound

In two's complement unsigned 32-bit arithmetic, all operations are implicitly modulo $2^{32}$.
Suppose previous_time = 0xFFFFFFF0 (-16 in decimal relative to overflow).
Suppose current now = 0x0000000A (+10 in decimal past overflow).
The true elapsed time is $16 + 10 = 26\text{ ms}$.
Calculating now - previous_time in C:
0x0000000A - 0xFFFFFFF0 = 0x0000000A + (~0xFFFFFFF0 + 1) = 0x0000000A + 0x00000010 = 0x0000001A = 26!
The subtraction yields the exact elapsed duration without any branching or conditional logic, provided the interval is less than $2^{31} - 1$ ms (≈ 24.8 days).

14.3 The Cooperative Superloop Architecture

A non-blocking architecture replaces monolithic sequential loops with a structured Cooperative Task Superloop. Every subsystem (display, keypad, communication, sensor acquisition, motor control) exposes an asynchronous _process() or _task() function.

Figure 14.1: Cooperative Non-Blocking Superloop Execution Flow

Notice the crucial engineering requirement: Every individual task must guarantee a bounded Worst-Case Execution Time (WCET). If Task 3 takes 50 ms to poll a slow I2C temperature sensor, Tasks 1, 2, and 4 will suffer 50 ms of jitter. Therefore, slow hardware transactions must be broken down into finite-state machine steps.

14.4 Converting Monolithic Routines to State Steps

Let us analyze a common real-world problem: communicating with an environmental sensor (e.g., SHT31 or BMP280) that requires a 20 ms conversion delay between triggering a measurement and reading the data registers.

The Naive Blocking Approach (Anti-Pattern)

/* BAD: Blocks the entire microcontroller for 20 ms every second */
float read_temperature_blocking(void) {
    i2c_write_command(CMD_START_CONVERSION);
    delay_ms(20); /* COMPLETE CPU PARALYSIS! */
    uint16_t raw = i2c_read_word();
    return calculate_celsius(raw);
}

The Professional Non-Blocking State-Step Pattern

By introducing an enumeration of sensor states and storing the timestamp when the conversion command was launched, the function transforms into a zero-wait non-blocking worker: 

/* sensor_fsm.h / sensor_fsm.c */
#include <stdint.h>
#include <stdbool.h>

typedef enum {
    SENSOR_STATE_IDLE,
    SENSOR_STATE_CONVERTING,
    SENSOR_STATE_DATA_READY,
    SENSOR_STATE_ERROR
} SensorState_t;

typedef struct {
    SensorState_t state;
    uint32_t      conversion_start_ms;
    uint32_t      last_poll_ms;
    float         latest_temperature;
    bool          new_data_available;
} TempSensor_t;

static TempSensor_t g_temp_sensor = {
    .state = SENSOR_STATE_IDLE,
    .conversion_start_ms = 0U,
    .last_poll_ms = 0U,
    .latest_temperature = 0.0f,
    .new_data_available = false
};

void temp_sensor_step(void) {
    uint32_t now = millis();

    switch (g_temp_sensor.state) {
        case SENSOR_STATE_IDLE:
            /* Poll every 1000 ms */
            if ((now - g_temp_sensor.last_poll_ms) >= 1000U) {
                g_temp_sensor.last_poll_ms = now;
                i2c_start_async_conversion(); /* Non-blocking I2C transmit */
                g_temp_sensor.conversion_start_ms = now;
                g_temp_sensor.state = SENSOR_STATE_CONVERTING;
            }
            break;

        case SENSOR_STATE_CONVERTING:
            /* Check if 20 ms conversion deadline has elapsed without blocking */
            if ((now - g_temp_sensor.conversion_start_ms) >= 20U) {
                if (i2c_is_bus_ready()) {
                    uint16_t raw = i2c_read_raw_word();
                    g_temp_sensor.latest_temperature = (float)raw * 0.01f;
                    g_temp_sensor.new_data_available = true;
                    g_temp_sensor.state = SENSOR_STATE_IDLE;
                }
            }
            break;

        case SENSOR_STATE_ERROR:
        default:
            i2c_reset_bus();
            g_temp_sensor.state = SENSOR_STATE_IDLE;
            break;
    }
}
Program 14.2: Asynchronous Non-Blocking Sensor Acquisition Engine

When temp_sensor_step() is called in the main loop, it executes in less than 2.4 microseconds. During the 20 ms conversion window, the function simply exits immediately, allowing the superloop to service serial ports, buttons, and display screens thousands of times.

14.5 Full Production Example: Multi-Rate Task Scheduler

The following complete C module implements a lightweight, static cooperative task table scheduler with execution time tracking and overrun detection. 

#include <stdint.h>
#include <stdbool.h>

typedef void (*TaskFunction_t)(void);

typedef struct {
    const char       *task_name;
    TaskFunction_t    function;
    uint32_t          period_ms;
    uint32_t          last_run_ms;
    uint32_t          execution_count;
    uint32_t          max_duration_us;
} CooperativeTask_t;

/* Forward task prototypes */
static void task_heartbeat_led(void);
static void task_button_scan(void);
static void task_sensor_acquire(void);
static void task_comm_service(void);

static CooperativeTask_t g_task_registry[] = {
    { "ButtonScan",    task_button_scan,     10U,   0U, 0U, 0U },
    { "CommService",   task_comm_service,    20U,   0U, 0U, 0U },
    { "SensorAcquire", task_sensor_acquire,  100U,  0U, 0U, 0U },
    { "HeartbeatLED",  task_heartbeat_led,   500U,  0U, 0U, 0U }
};

#define TASK_COUNT (sizeof(g_task_registry) / sizeof(g_task_registry[0]))

void scheduler_dispatch(void) {
    uint32_t now = millis();

    for (size_t i = 0; i < TASK_COUNT; ++i) {
        CooperativeTask_t *task = &g_task_registry[i];

        /* Unsigned subtraction guarantees correct wraparound handling */
        if ((now - task->last_run_ms) >= task->period_ms) {
            task->last_run_ms = now;
            
            /* Execute task run-to-completion */
            task->function();
            task->execution_count++;
        }
    }
}

int main(void) {
    hardware_clock_init();
    systick_init();
    watchdog_init(1000U); /* 1.0 second watchdog window */

    while (1) {
        scheduler_dispatch();
        
        /* Kick watchdog in the superloop idle point */
        watchdog_feed();

        /* Optional: Enter Sleep Mode until SysTick or external IRQ wakes CPU */
        __WFI();
    }
}
Program 14.3: Table-Driven Cooperative Multi-Rate Task Scheduler

14.6 Code Comparison: Blocking Spin-Loop vs. Non-Blocking Delta Timer

Observe the dramatic difference in system responsiveness when comparing a blocking implementation with an event-driven non-blocking alternative.

Compare Implementations: Button Debounce & LED Pulse

❌ Buggy: Blocking delay_ms()

void handle_user_interface(void) {
    if (GPIO_Read(BUTTON_PIN) == LOW) {
        /* Blocking debounce */
        delay_ms(50);
        if (GPIO_Read(BUTTON_PIN) == LOW) {
            /* Turn on LED for 1 second */
            GPIO_SetHigh(LED_PIN);
            delay_ms(1000); /* FREEZES ALL OTHER WORK! */
            GPIO_SetLow(LED_PIN);
        }
    }
}

Flaw: During the 1050 ms total delay, UART buffers overflow, sensor readings halt, and the watchdog is starved.

✔ Safe: Non-Blocking State Machine

typedef enum { UI_IDLE, UI_DEBOUNCING, UI_PULSING } UiState_t;
static UiState_t s_state = UI_IDLE;
static uint32_t  s_timer = 0U;

void handle_user_interface(void) {
    uint32_t now = millis();
    switch (s_state) {
        case UI_IDLE:
            if (GPIO_Read(BUTTON_PIN) == LOW) {
                s_timer = now;
                s_state = UI_DEBOUNCING;
            }
            break;
        case UI_DEBOUNCING:
            if ((now - s_timer) >= 50U) {
                if (GPIO_Read(BUTTON_PIN) == LOW) {
                    GPIO_SetHigh(LED_PIN);
                    s_timer = now;
                    s_state = UI_PULSING;
                } else { s_state = UI_IDLE; }
            }
            break;
        case UI_PULSING:
            if ((now - s_timer) >= 1000U) {
                GPIO_SetLow(LED_PIN);
                s_state = UI_IDLE;
            }
            break;
    }
}

Safety: Returns instantly every call (WCET < 1 μs). Communication and watchdog servicing never miss a beat.

14.7 Interactive Knowledge Check

Test your mastery of non-blocking firmware mechanics and integer wraparound arithmetic.

1. Why does the expression (millis() - previous_time) >= INTERVAL work correctly across a 32-bit unsigned overflow?
  • Because the C compiler automatically casts unsigned integers to floating point doubles during subtraction.
  • Because standard unsigned binary subtraction is performed modulo 2^32, producing the exact circular distance between timestamps.
  • Because SysTick automatically pauses counting during the subtraction operation.
  • It does not work; an explicit conditional check for overflow is always mandated by MISRA-C.
Explanation: Under two's complement unsigned integer arithmetic, (now - previous) wraps naturally modulo $2^{32}$. Even if now has rolled over to 2 and previous was 0xFFFFFFFE, 2 - 0xFFFFFFFE = 4, accurately representing elapsed time.
2. What is the fundamental requirement for all tasks executed within a cooperative superloop scheduler?
  • Every task must execute in its own preemptive FreeRTOS thread.
  • Every task must run to completion (RTC) rapidly with a strictly bounded Worst-Case Execution Time (WCET).
  • Every task must disable global interrupts upon entry and re-enable them upon exit.
  • Every task must include at least one delay_ms(1) to allow the CPU to cool down.
Explanation: In a cooperative system, tasks cannot preempt each other. If any task blocks or runs for a long period, it delays all other tasks by that exact duration.
3. What is the fatal flaw in scheduling a periodic task using: next_deadline = millis() + INTERVAL; followed by if (millis() >= next_deadline)?
  • When millis() + INTERVAL wraps around zero, millis() >= next_deadline evaluates to TRUE prematurely, firing immediately.
  • The compiler optimizes out the variable because it is not marked register.
  • Addition takes twice as many clock cycles as subtraction on Cortex-M processors.
  • The SysTick interrupt vector is invalidated.
Explanation: If millis() is near 0xFFFFFFFF, adding INTERVAL wraps to a tiny number (e.g. 50). Since 0xFFFFFFF0 >= 50 is TRUE, the task fires without waiting.
4. What occurs when a sensor takes 25 ms to convert data, and the firmware uses delay_ms(25) inside the main loop?
  • The sensor will deliver higher resolution measurements.
  • All other main-loop operations (buttons, serial communication, displays) are completely blocked for 25 ms.
  • The SysTick interrupt stops firing until the delay finishes.
  • The flash memory wear level increases.
Explanation: Busy-waiting holds CPU control exclusively, delaying every other peer task in the superloop and causing UI sluggishness and communication overruns.
5. To achieve cumulative drift-free periodic execution every 100 ms, how should previous_time be updated?
  • previous_time = millis();
  • previous_time += 100U;
  • previous_time = 0;
  • previous_time = SysTick->VAL;
Explanation: Setting previous_time = millis() discards any loop latency or processing delay that occurred before the task was scheduled, causing cumulative timing drift over minutes or hours. previous_time += PERIOD preserves the exact timeline.
6. What is the purpose of placing the ARM Cortex-M __WFI() instruction at the end of a cooperative superloop?
  • To reset the microcontroller when an error occurs.
  • To put the core into low-power sleep mode until the next interrupt (e.g. SysTick) wakes it up, saving power.
  • To flush the CPU instruction cache.
  • To trigger a software interrupt trap.
Explanation: __WFI() (Wait For Interrupt) halts the core clock until an interrupt arrives. If no tasks have work to do, the MCU sleeps, slashing power consumption.
7. If a task requires 500 ms to erase a sector of external SPI Flash memory, how should it be implemented in non-blocking firmware?
  • By executing while (flash_is_busy()); inside the function.
  • By sending the Sector Erase command, entering a FLASH_ERASING state, and polling the status register non-blockingly across subsequent loop iterations.
  • By increasing the MCU clock speed to 10 GHz so 500 ms becomes instantaneous.
  • By disabling the watchdog timer permanently.
Explanation: Flash erases take hundreds of milliseconds. Sending the erase command and non-blockingly querying the WIP (Write In Progress) bit in an FSM state allows other tasks to run smoothly.
8. What maximum timing interval can be safely measured using 32-bit unsigned millisecond subtraction?
  • Exactly 255 milliseconds.
  • Exactly 65,535 milliseconds (65.5 seconds).
  • Up to 2^31 - 1 milliseconds (~24.8 days) if signed comparisons are used, or 2^32 - 1 (~49.7 days) for pure unsigned intervals.
  • Infinite duration without limitation.
Explanation: Pure unsigned difference (now - prev) >= INTERVAL accurately measures periods up to $2^{32} - 1$ ms (~49.7 days). Any single interval greater than 49.7 days would be indistinguishable from a recent timestamp.
9. What is a "heartbeat LED" task in non-blocking embedded design?
  • An LED that pulses only when a human touch sensor detects a physical pulse.
  • A periodic non-blocking task that toggles an LED (e.g., 1 Hz) to provide visual proof that the superloop is actively scheduling and not locked in a freeze or fault.
  • An LED driven directly by the MCU crystal oscillator circuit.
  • A high-priority hardware interrupt that flashes the LED in hardware.
Explanation: A heartbeat LED toggled by the main superloop serves as a visual health indicator: if the LED freezes, the developer immediately knows a task blocked or a HardFault occurred.
10. In a non-blocking architecture, where should the Hardware Watchdog Timer (IWDG) refresh call watchdog_feed() be located?
  • Inside the SysTick interrupt service routine.
  • Exclusively inside the main superloop, ensuring the watchdog resets the chip if any cooperative task blocks.
  • Inside an external timer ISR running at 10 kHz.
  • Inside every driver initialization function.
Explanation: Kicking the watchdog inside an ISR is a cardinal sin: the ISR will continue happily feeding the watchdog even if the main loop hangs completely! Feeding the watchdog only from the main superloop verifies that all cooperative tasks are executing.

14.8 Hands-On Engineering Laboratories

Execute these 5 laboratory assignments to eliminate blocking delays and master cooperative real-time architecture.

Assignment 1: Drift-Free Dual LED Flasher

Task: Implement two independent non-blocking LED blinkers without using delay_ms(). LED 1 must toggle at exactly 100 ms period, and LED 2 must toggle at 333 ms period. Use last_time += INTERVAL. Run for 1 hour and verify using an oscilloscope or logic analyzer that zero cumulative drift occurs.

Assignment 2: Non-Blocking Button Debounce Engine

Task: Write a state-based button debouncer (states: RELEASED, MAYBE_PRESSED, PRESSED, MAYBE_RELEASED). When a transition is detected, require the input to remain stable for 25 ms before accepting the state change. Confirm that holding or releasing the button never halts the superloop.

Assignment 3: 32-bit Wraparound Simulator

Task: Write a host test program where g_system_ticks is initialized to 0xFFFFFFF0 (16 ms prior to 32-bit overflow). Schedule tasks for 10 ms, 25 ms, and 100 ms intervals. Simulate tick advancement through 0x00000050 and verify that every task executes at the exact expected timestamp across the boundary.

Assignment 4: Non-Blocking UART Command Prompt

Task: Implement an interactive CLI over UART. Incoming characters are collected non-blockingly into a line buffer. While typing commands, the superloop must concurrently service an ADC sampler at 100 Hz. If the user stops typing mid-command, the ADC sampler must continue without disruption.

Assignment 5: Task Execution Time Profiler

Task: Instrument the cooperative scheduler from Program 14.3 using the ARM Cortex-M DWT->CYCCNT (Data Watchpoint and Trace Cycle Counter). Measure the execution duration of each task in microseconds. If any task exceeds a 1.0 ms budget, print an alert to UART indicating a WCET violation.

Official References, Research Papers & Standards

Deepen your engineering foundation with canonical publications and official standard specifications:

Patterns for Time-Triggered Embedded Systems

The definitive textbook on cooperative schedulers, run-to-completion tasks, and jitter management for safety-critical microcontrollers.

View Official Resource →

Formal industry requirements prohibiting blocking spin-loops and establishing rules for hardware watchdog placement.

View Official Resource →

Authoritative guide on using the Wait-For-Interrupt instruction to achieve dynamic power savings in event-driven systems.

fields.title: Day 18: Flash Memory, EEPROM & File Systems (FatFS)
fields.content:
Session 3.1

Day 18: Flash Memory, EEPROM & File Systems (FatFS)

Problem Statement: You need to store configuration, logs, and firmware images persistently across power cycles. Flash memory has limited write cycles, erase-before-write constraints, and wear. How do you manage it safely?
📋 Daily Plan & Learning Architecture
Session 3.1 Module 3: Advanced Embedded Architecture Estimated: 3.5 hrs

🎯 Today's Mission & Relevance

  • Master NOR Flash vs NAND Flash vs true EEPROM architectural and physical tradeoffs.
  • Implement dual-sector EEPROM emulation to store parameters with zero power-cut data loss.
  • Integrate ChaN's FatFS to read and write FAT32 filesystems on microSD cards and SPI flash.

📐 Theoretical Milestones

  • Floating-gate charge trapping physics and erase-before-write constraints.
  • FAT32 File Allocation Table cluster chains and power-loss corruption prevention.
  • Wear leveling algorithms for distributing write stress across silicon sectors.

💻 Hands-On Blueprint

  • Program 18.1: EEPROM emulation variable write and page transfer in C.
  • Program 18.2: Bare-metal SPI driver for W25Q32 external NOR flash.
  • Program 18.3: Mounting FatFS, creating directory, and appending sensor CSV log.
  • Program 18.4: Power-safe high-throughput FatFS block logger with periodic sync.
  • Program 18.5: Wear-leveling block map with write count tracking in C.

🛡️ Production Failure Modes

  • Writing beyond a 256-byte NOR flash page boundary, causing silent address wraparound.
  • Omitting f_sync() or f_close(), leaving uncommitted FAT allocation records in volatile RAM.
  • Logging directly to a single flash sector in a tight loop, destroying the sector in days.
🏁 Daily Milestone Deliverables: 5 Interactive Register-Level Programs • 5 Architecture Diagrams • 10 Practice MCQs • 5 Hands-On Assignments

18.1 Solid-State Non-Volatile Memory: NOR, NAND, and EEPROM

Persistent storage is foundational for embedded engineering: calibration offsets, encryption credentials, event logs, and firmware update images must survive complete power loss. However, non-volatile solid-state memory exhibits physical and metallurgical constraints fundamentally distinct from RAM:

  • Endurance Limits: Every flash write/erase cycle stresses the microscopic dielectric oxide layer insulating floating-gate or charge-trap transistors. After 10,000 to 100,000 cycles, the oxide breaks down, permanently trapping charge and creating bad blocks.
  • Asymmetric Granularity: Flash memory allows byte or word-level reading, page-level writing (programming), but requires sector or block-level erasing. You cannot overwrite a byte without erasing an entire multi-kilobyte block.

Figure 18.0-1: Solid-State Flash Memory Cell Architectures (NOR vs NAND)
Figure Parameters Explained:
  • NOR Flash Architecture: Parallel bit-cell connections provide ultra-fast random read access, allowing the CPU to execute code directly from flash (eXecute-In-Place / XIP).
  • NAND Flash Architecture: Serial cell strings maximize silicon density for massive mass storage (SD cards, eMMC, SSDs), but require software bad-block management and Error Correction Code (ECC).
  • True EEPROM: Dual-transistor bit cell allows single-byte erasing and writing with extreme endurance (> 1,000,000 cycles), but possesses low storage density.

18.2 EEPROM Emulation in Microcontroller Flash

Because true on-chip EEPROM increases silicon fabrication wafer costs, modern microcontrollers emulate EEPROM using internal NOR Flash. By designating two identical Flash sectors (e.g., Page 0 and Page 1), the firmware writes key-value parameter pairs sequentially. When the active page fills up, valid parameters are copied to the alternate page, and the old page is erased in the background.

Figure 18.0-2: Dual-Sector EEPROM Emulation State Machine
Figure Parameters Explained:
  • Page Header (Valid / Erased): First 32-bit word in sector declares its state (0xFFFF=Erased, 0x0000=Receiving, 0x1111=Valid).
  • Key-Value Element Format: Each variable is written as a 16-bit Virtual Address + 16-bit Data Value.
  • Append-Only Updates: Modifying a parameter simply writes a new entry at the next free address without erasing.
  • Atomic Page Swap: Garbage collection only moves the latest version of each variable, minimizing flash wear.

#include <stdint.h>
#include <stdbool.h>

#define PAGE0_BASE          0x08010000U
#define PAGE1_BASE          0x08014000U
#define PAGE_SIZE           0x4000U  /* 16 KB */

#define STATE_ERASED        0xFFFFFFFFU
#define STATE_RECEIVING     0xEEEEEEEEU
#define STATE_VALID         0x00000000U

typedef struct {
    uint16_t virt_addr;
    uint16_t data;
} EepromVar_t;

extern void flash_erase_sector_by_addr(uint32_t addr);
extern void flash_write_word(uint32_t addr, uint32_t data);

bool eeprom_write_variable(uint16_t var_id, uint16_t value) {
    uint32_t active_page = PAGE0_BASE;
    uint32_t page_state = *(volatile uint32_t *)active_page;

    if (page_state != STATE_VALID) {
        active_page = PAGE1_BASE;
    }

    /* Scan for the first blank word (0xFFFFFFFF) in active page */
    uint32_t write_addr = active_page + 4U;
    while (write_addr < (active_page + PAGE_SIZE)) {
        if (*(volatile uint32_t *)write_addr == 0xFFFFFFFFU) {
            /* Pack 16-bit ID and 16-bit Data into single 32-bit word */
            uint32_t packed = ((uint32_t)var_id << 16) | value;
            flash_write_word(write_addr, packed);
            return true;
        }
        write_addr += 4U;
    }

    /* Page full: Trigger garbage collection and page swap here */
    return false;
}
Program 18.1: EEPROM Emulation Variable Write and Page Transfer in C

18.3 External SPI NOR Flash Driver (Winbond W25Q32 / W25Q128)

When firmware data logging exceeds internal MCU flash (e.g., audio clips, high-rate flight data, local web assets), embedded systems interface external SPI or Quad-SPI (QSPI) NOR flash chips. Operating over SPI mode 0 or 3, commands follow a rigid sequence: Write Enable (0x06), Sector Erase (0x20), and Page Program (0x02).


#include <stdint.h>

#define W25Q_CMD_WRITE_ENABLE   0x06U
#define W25Q_CMD_READ_STATUS1   0x05U
#define W25Q_CMD_PAGE_PROGRAM   0x02U
#define W25Q_CMD_SECTOR_ERASE   0x20U
#define W25Q_CMD_READ_DATA      0x03U
#define W25Q_STATUS1_BUSY       (1U << 0)

extern void spi_cs_low(void);
extern void spi_cs_high(void);
extern uint8_t spi_transfer_byte(uint8_t byte);

void w25q_wait_busy(void) {
    uint8_t status;
    do {
        spi_cs_low();
        spi_transfer_byte(W25Q_CMD_READ_STATUS1);
        status = spi_transfer_byte(0xFF);
        spi_cs_high();
    } while (status & W25Q_STATUS1_BUSY);
}

void w25q_erase_4k_sector(uint32_t sector_addr) {
    /* 1. Send Write Enable command */
    spi_cs_low();
    spi_transfer_byte(W25Q_CMD_WRITE_ENABLE);
    spi_cs_high();

    /* 2. Issue 4KB Sector Erase with 24-bit address */
    spi_cs_low();
    spi_transfer_byte(W25Q_CMD_SECTOR_ERASE);
    spi_transfer_byte((uint8_t)(sector_addr >> 16));
    spi_transfer_byte((uint8_t)(sector_addr >> 8));
    spi_transfer_byte((uint8_t)(sector_addr & 0xFF));
    spi_cs_high();

    w25q_wait_busy();
}

void w25q_write_page(uint32_t page_addr, const uint8_t *data, uint16_t len) {
    if (len > 256) len = 256; /* Page boundary limit */

    spi_cs_low();
    spi_transfer_byte(W25Q_CMD_WRITE_ENABLE);
    spi_cs_high();

    spi_cs_low();
    spi_transfer_byte(W25Q_CMD_PAGE_PROGRAM);
    spi_transfer_byte((uint8_t)(page_addr >> 16));
    spi_transfer_byte((uint8_t)(page_addr >> 8));
    spi_transfer_byte((uint8_t)(page_addr & 0xFF));

    for (uint16_t i = 0; i < len; i++) {
        spi_transfer_byte(data[i]);
    }
    spi_cs_high();

    w25q_wait_busy();
}
Program 18.2: Bare-Metal SPI Driver for W25Q32 External NOR Flash

18.4 Chan's FatFS Architecture on Embedded Media

To read and write files compatible with standard desktop operating systems (Windows, macOS, Linux), embedded systems integrate FatFS (developed by ChaN). FatFS separates the FAT12/FAT16/FAT32/exFAT filesystem algorithms from physical hardware via an abstraction layer called diskio.c.

Figure 18.0-3: FatFS Modular Layer Stack and DiskIO Abstraction
Figure Parameters Explained:
  • Application Layer: Calls high-level POSIX-like file operations (f_mount, f_open, f_printf).
  • FatFS Library: Manages cluster chains, FAT directory tables, LFN (Long File Names), and caching.
  • DiskIO Abstraction: Standard 5-function interface translating sector requests to hardware reads/writes.
  • Physical Storage: Interchangeable storage medium: microSD card via 4-bit SDMMC, or external SPI flash chip.

#include <stdio.h>
#include <string.h>
#include "ff.h"

static FATFS g_fatfs;
static FIL   g_logfile;

FRESULT log_sensor_sample_csv(uint32_t timestamp, float temp, float press) {
    FRESULT fr;
    UINT bytes_written;
    char line_buf[64];

    /* 1. Mount logical drive 0 */
    fr = f_mount(&g_fatfs, "0:", 1);
    if (fr != FR_OK) {
        return fr;
    }

    /* 2. Open or create file with Read/Write and Append flags */
    fr = f_open(&g_logfile, "0:/log.csv", FA_WRITE | FA_OPEN_ALWAYS);
    if (fr != FR_OK) {
        f_mount(NULL, "0:", 0);
        return fr;
    }

    /* 3. Seek to end of file to append new records */
    f_lseek(&g_logfile, f_size(&g_logfile));

    /* 4. Format CSV line: timestamp, temperature, pressure */
    snprintf(line_buf, sizeof(line_buf), "%lu,%.2f,%.2f
", timestamp, temp, press);

    /* 5. Write buffer to SD card */
    fr = f_write(&g_logfile, line_buf, (UINT)strlen(line_buf), &bytes_written);

    /* 6. Flush cache buffers and close file */
    f_sync(&g_logfile);
    f_close(&g_logfile);

    /* Unmount drive */
    f_mount(NULL, "0:", 0);
    return fr;
}
Program 18.3: Mounting FatFS, Creating Directory, and Appending Sensor CSV Log

18.5 FAT32 Cluster Allocation and Power-Loss Corruption

A FAT32 filesystem organizes storage into Clusters (typically 4 KB, consisting of eight 512-byte sectors). The File Allocation Table (FAT) acts as a linked list: entry $N$ contains the index of the next cluster in the file. If power fails while f_write() has updated directory entries but not the FAT table, file cross-linking and corruption occurs. Embedded firmware must issue periodic f_sync() calls to commit metadata.


#include "ff.h"

#define SYNC_INTERVAL_SAMPLES   50U

static FIL g_file;
static uint32_t g_sample_count = 0;

void power_safe_logger_append(const void *record_bytes, UINT record_size) {
    UINT bw;
    f_write(&g_file, record_bytes, record_size, &bw);

    g_sample_count++;

    /* Commit cached FAT tables to physical non-volatile media periodically */
    if ((g_sample_count % SYNC_INTERVAL_SAMPLES) == 0) {
        f_sync(&g_file);
    }
}
Program 18.4: Power-Safe High-Throughput FatFS Block Logger with Periodic Sync

18.6 Wear-Leveling and Flash Longevity Auditing

Unlike rotating magnetic hard disks, flash sectors will physically degrade if written repeatedly. A circular logging task writing 100 bytes every second directly to sector 0 will destroy the sector in under 3 days ($100\text{K cycles} / 86400\text{s} \approx 1.15\text{ days}$). Wear leveling distributes write cycles evenly across all available sectors.


#include <stdint.h>
#include <stdbool.h>

#define TOTAL_LOG_BLOCKS    16U
#define MAX_ALLOWED_ERASES  100000U

typedef struct {
    uint32_t physical_block_addr;
    uint32_t erase_count;
    bool is_bad_block;
} BlockWearEntry_t;

static BlockWearEntry_t g_wear_table[TOTAL_LOG_BLOCKS];

uint32_t get_optimal_wear_level_block(void) {
    uint32_t min_erases = 0xFFFFFFFFU;
    uint32_t best_index = 0;

    for (uint32_t i = 0; i < TOTAL_LOG_BLOCKS; i++) {
        if (!g_wear_table[i].is_bad_block && g_wear_table[i].erase_count < min_erases) {
            min_erases = g_wear_table[i].erase_count;
            best_index = i;
        }
    }

    /* Audit endurance limit */
    if (g_wear_table[best_index].erase_count >= (MAX_ALLOWED_ERASES * 8U / 10U)) {
        /* Warning: Sector has reached 80% of rated endurance */
    }

    g_wear_table[best_index].erase_count++;
    return g_wear_table[best_index].physical_block_addr;
}
Program 18.5: Wear-Leveling Block Map with Write Count Tracking in C

Non-Volatile Solid-State Storage Technologies Comparison

AttributeInternal MCU FlashExternal SPI NOR FlashNAND Flash (eMMC/SD)True EEPROM
Erase Granularity1 KB - 128 KB Sector4 KB Sector / 64 KB Block128 KB - 2 MB Block1 Byte
Write Granularity32-bit Word or 64-bit Double256-byte Page2 KB - 8 KB Page1 Byte
Write Endurance10,000 - 100,000 cycles100,000 cycles3,000 - 10,000 (TLC/QLC)1,000,000 - 4,000,000 cycles
Read Access TimeSingle-cycle (15-30 ns)Fast SPI (50-133 MHz)Slow bus transfer (~25 us)Fast byte read (~100 ns)
XIP (Execute-In-Place)Yes (Native)Yes (via QSPI Memory Mapped)No (Must load into RAM)No
Primary Use CaseApplication Code & VectorsAsset storage, OTA stagingMass logging, Linux rootfsCalibration & board IDs

ChaN FatFS Core API Functions Reference

FunctionDescriptionParametersReturn TypeKey Failure Modes
f_mount()Registers / unregisters logical drive work areaFATFS* fs, const TCHAR* path, BYTE optFRESULTFR_NOT_READY (no card detected)

Topic Quiz (10 Questions)

Test your conceptual understanding of today's embedded systems architecture, registers, and runtime behaviors.

1. Why cannot a single byte in NOR Flash memory be overwritten from 0x00 back to 0xFF without an erase operation?
  • Because programming flash only adds electrons to floating gates (turning 1s into 0s); removing charge (turning 0s to 1s) requires a high-voltage block erase
  • Because the SPI bus clock is too slow to reverse the byte
  • Because the compiler flags forbid writing 0xFF
  • Because NOR Flash only supports read operations
Flash programming operates unidirectionally: Fowler-Nordheim tunneling or hot-carrier injection traps charge to clear bits from 1 to 0. Quantum discharge requires high reverse voltage applied across the entire sector.
2. What is the primary function of the f_sync() API call in Chan's FatFS library?
  • To flush internal sector cache buffers and write updated file size and cluster allocation metadata to the physical media
  • To format the SD card as ext4
  • To encrypt the file using AES-256
  • To synchronize the microcontroller clock with an NTP server
f_write() buffers data in RAM caches to maximize throughput. If power cuts out before f_sync() or f_close(), unwritten data and directory allocation updates remain in RAM, causing file truncation.
3. What is 'wear leveling' in solid-state flash memory management?
  • An algorithmic technique that distributes erase and write cycles evenly across all physical flash blocks to prevent premature localized sector wear
  • A physical polishing process applied to silicon wafers during manufacturing
  • A circuit that regulates supply voltage to the flash chip
  • A method to increase SPI clock frequencies
Because flash blocks endure only 10K to 100K erases before oxide degradation causes bit errors, wear leveling maps logical addresses dynamically to ensure all physical blocks wear at equal rates.
4. What is Execute-In-Place (XIP) in the context of external Quad-SPI (QSPI) NOR Flash?
  • The CPU core fetches and executes instructions directly from external flash over memory-mapped QSPI without copying the code into SRAM first
  • The microcontroller executes code only inside the bootloader
  • Executing Python scripts directly in hardware
  • Running code without compiling it first
Using Memory-Mapped Mode on QSPI controllers, external serial flash appears directly inside the 32-bit physical address space (e.g., 0x90000000), allowing instruction execution with transparent cache.
5. How does Dual-Sector EEPROM Emulation handle variable updates without constantly erasing flash sectors?
  • It appends new key-value pairs sequentially into blank words in the active sector; full sector erase only occurs during periodic page transfers
  • It stores all data in volatile CPU core registers
  • It writes data into the microcontroller analog comparator
  • It relies on an external lithium battery to hold RAM states
EEPROM emulation writes new records to consecutive blank addresses. Searching for a variable reads backwards to find the newest entry, deferring sector erasure until the page is 100% exhausted.
6. What is the typical page size limit for a single SPI write operation on standard NOR flash chips like the W25Q32?
  • 256 bytes (writing beyond a 256-byte page wraps around to the beginning of the same page)
  • 16 megabytes
  • 4 kilobytes
  • 1 single bit
SPI NOR flash chips incorporate internal 256-byte SRAM page latches. Writing more than 256 bytes in one command causes the internal address pointer to wrap to the page start, overwriting earlier bytes.
7. What does a cluster in the FAT32 filesystem represent?
  • The fundamental unit of disk allocation composed of a fixed number of contiguous 512-byte sectors
  • A group of networked microcontrollers
  • A collection of 32-bit CPU registers
  • A set of FreeRTOS tasks
FAT32 allocates files in clusters (e.g., 4 KB = 8 sectors). The File Allocation Table tracks files as linked chains of cluster numbers.
8. Why is true EEPROM preferred over Flash for storing real-time automotive odometer values?
  • True EEPROM supports single-byte modification and millions of write cycles without sector erasing overhead
  • True EEPROM is completely immune to high temperatures
  • True EEPROM has larger gigabyte capacities
  • True EEPROM consumes zero current during write cycles
Odometers write frequently (e.g., every 0.1 km). Flash would quickly burn out its 100K endurance limit, whereas true EEPROM withstands 1M to 4M cycles with single-byte granularity.
9. What error occurs if an application attempts to write to a Winbond W25Q flash chip without first issuing command 0x06 (Write Enable)?
  • The chip silently ignores the programming command because its internal Write Enable Latch (WEL) bit is 0
  • The microcontroller triggers a BusFault exception
  • The chip permanently locks its SPI port
  • The Flash chip explodes
NOR flash requires an explicit Write Enable (WREN, 0x06) command before any program or erase command to prevent accidental writes caused by electrical noise on the SPI bus.
10. Which FatFS return code indicates that physical communication with the SD card or flash chip failed at the hardware level?
  • FR_DISK_ERR
  • FR_OK
  • FR_NO_FILE
  • FR_INVALID_NAME
FR_DISK_ERR indicates that the low-level diskio driver returned an error (such as an SPI timeout or CRC check failure) during physical sector read or write operations.

Hands-On Assignments

Complete these 5 lab assignments to solidify your hands-on firmware engineering skills.

Assignment 1: Flash Sector Wear Leveling Auditor

Task: Implement an in-memory block allocation table tracking erase counts across 8 sectors. Reject writes to any sector whose erase count exceeds 80,000 cycles; redirect incoming records to the least-worn sector.

Assignment 2: Dual-Page EEPROM Emulation Configuration Engine

Task: Construct a complete eeprom_set(id, val) and eeprom_get(id, *val) library using two 16 KB MCU flash sectors. Include an automatic page swap garbage collector that survives 100 simulated power cuts.

Assignment 3: Pre-Allocated Circular File Ring Buffer on FatFS

Task: Create a pre-allocated 1 MB binary file on an SD card ('ring_buffer.bin'). Implement a circular FIFO pointer mechanism that continuously appends 64-byte records, wrapping around seamlessly without fragmenting the filesystem.

Assignment 4: Post-Write Flash CRC32 Guardian

Task: After every flash page program operation, read back the newly written bytes and compute their hardware CRC32. Store the CRC in an integrity header; verify all flash blocks during boot before executing application logic.

Assignment 5: MicroSD File System Throughput Benchmark

Task: Write a benchmarking application measuring FatFS write throughput (KB/sec) on a microSD card across varying block sizes: 512 bytes, 2 KB, 8 KB, and 32 KB. Print the results over UART in tabular format.

Official References, Research Papers & Standards

Deepen your engineering foundations with seminal reference manuals, processor architecture standards, and industry specifications:

Official documentation for ChaN's FatFS, covering cluster mapping, diskio hardware interface, and reentrancy configuration.

Technical guide explaining dual-sector page swap algorithms, atomic state flags, and wear reduction.
