fields.title: Topic 20: State Tables & FSMs
fields.content:
Topic 20

State Tables & Finite-State Machines

While the nested switch-case pattern examined in Topic 19 is ideal for simple state machines with 3 to 6 states, it degrades rapidly as system requirements scale. A complex medical ventilator or automotive battery management system (BMS) with 15 states and 20 distinct events produces a massive, monolithic function spanning thousands of lines. The cyclomatic complexity skyrockets, violating software engineering standards and creating severe maintenance hazards.

The architectural solution is the Table-Driven Finite-State Machine. By decoupling state machine topology (the state transition matrix) from state action execution logic, transitions become static data structures stored directly in Flash ROM. State lookups execute in guaranteed $O(1)$ constant time, and adding a new state or event requires zero modifications to the core dispatch engine.

20.1 The 2D State Table Architecture

In a two-dimensional state table, the current state indexes the rows, and the event signal indexes the columns. Each intersection cell contains a Transition Descriptor consisting of:

  1. Target Next State: The state to transition into upon event receipt.
  2. Action Handler Pointer: A function pointer to the specific action routine to execute during the transition.
Figure 20.1: Constant-Time 2D Table-Driven FSM Dispatch Engine

20.2 Complete C Implementation of a Table-Driven Engine

Below is a production-grade, MISRA-compliant implementation of a 2D table-driven FSM with typed event parameters and flash placement. 

#include <stdint.h>
#include <stddef.h>
#include <stdbool.h>

/* Forward declaration */
typedef struct Fsm_t Fsm_t;

/* State & Event Enumerations */
typedef enum {
    STATE_STANDBY = 0,
    STATE_CHARGING,
    STATE_DISCHARGING,
    STATE_ERROR,
    STATE_MAX /* Boundary guard */
} BatteryState_t;

typedef enum {
    EVENT_PLUG_AC = 0,
    EVENT_UNPLUG_AC,
    EVENT_LOAD_CONNECTED,
    EVENT_OVERTEMP_FAULT,
    EVENT_MAX /* Boundary guard */
} BatteryEvent_t;

typedef struct {
    BatteryEvent_t signal;
    uint32_t       payload;
} Event_t;

/* Action handler function pointer type */
typedef void (*StateAction_t)(Fsm_t * const p_fsm, const Event_t * const p_evt);

/* Transition descriptor stored in Flash ROM */
typedef struct {
    BatteryState_t next_state;
    StateAction_t  action_fn;
} Transition_t;

/* FSM Context Instance */
struct Fsm_t {
    BatteryState_t state;
    uint32_t       cell_voltage_mv;
    int16_t        temperature_degc;
};

/* Forward Action Prototypes */
static void act_start_charge(Fsm_t * const p_fsm, const Event_t * const p_evt);
static void act_stop_charge(Fsm_t * const p_fsm, const Event_t * const p_evt);
static void act_start_discharge(Fsm_t * const p_fsm, const Event_t * const p_evt);
static void act_trip_error(Fsm_t * const p_fsm, const Event_t * const p_evt);
static void act_ignore(Fsm_t * const p_fsm, const Event_t * const p_evt);

/* 2D State Transition Matrix: Stored in .rodata (Flash) to conserve SRAM */
static const Transition_t g_state_table[STATE_MAX][EVENT_MAX] = {
    /* Current State: STATE_STANDBY */
    [STATE_STANDBY] = {
        [EVENT_PLUG_AC]        = { STATE_CHARGING,    act_start_charge },
        [EVENT_UNPLUG_AC]      = { STATE_STANDBY,     act_ignore },
        [EVENT_LOAD_CONNECTED] = { STATE_DISCHARGING, act_start_discharge },
        [EVENT_OVERTEMP_FAULT] = { STATE_ERROR,       act_trip_error }
    },
    /* Current State: STATE_CHARGING */
    [STATE_CHARGING] = {
        [EVENT_PLUG_AC]        = { STATE_CHARGING,    act_ignore },
        [EVENT_UNPLUG_AC]      = { STATE_STANDBY,     act_stop_charge },
        [EVENT_LOAD_CONNECTED] = { STATE_CHARGING,    act_ignore },
        [EVENT_OVERTEMP_FAULT] = { STATE_ERROR,       act_trip_error }
    },
    /* Current State: STATE_DISCHARGING */
    [STATE_DISCHARGING] = {
        [EVENT_PLUG_AC]        = { STATE_CHARGING,    act_start_charge },
        [EVENT_UNPLUG_AC]      = { STATE_DISCHARGING, act_ignore },
        [EVENT_LOAD_CONNECTED] = { STATE_DISCHARGING, act_ignore },
        [EVENT_OVERTEMP_FAULT] = { STATE_ERROR,       act_trip_error }
    },
    /* Current State: STATE_ERROR */
    [STATE_ERROR] = {
        [EVENT_PLUG_AC]        = { STATE_ERROR, act_ignore },
        [EVENT_UNPLUG_AC]      = { STATE_ERROR, act_ignore },
        [EVENT_LOAD_CONNECTED] = { STATE_ERROR, act_ignore },
        [EVENT_OVERTEMP_FAULT] = { STATE_ERROR, act_ignore }
    }
};

/* Generic O(1) Dispatch Engine */
void fsm_dispatch(Fsm_t * const p_fsm, const Event_t * const p_evt) {
    if ((p_fsm == NULL) || (p_evt == NULL)) {
        return;
    }

    /* Bounds check indices defensively against buffer overrun */
    if ((p_fsm->state >= STATE_MAX) || (p_evt->signal >= EVENT_MAX)) {
        act_trip_error(p_fsm, p_evt);
        p_fsm->state = STATE_ERROR;
        return;
    }

    const Transition_t * const p_trans = &g_state_table[p_fsm->state][p_evt->signal];

    /* Execute the registered transition action */
    if (p_trans->action_fn != NULL) {
        p_trans->action_fn(p_fsm, p_evt);
    }

    /* Advance to target state */
    p_fsm->state = p_trans->next_state;
}
Program 20.1: Production 2D Table-Driven State Machine Engine

20.3 Memory Footprint Analysis: RAM vs. ROM

A critical advantage of the table-driven pattern in microcontrollers is memory placement. Because the state table is marked const, it resides permanently in Flash ROM (.rodata), consuming zero SRAM:

sizeof(Transition_t) = 4 bytes (enum) + 4 bytes (function pointer) = 8 bytes
Table Footprint = 4 States × 4 Events × 8 bytes = 128 bytes of Flash ROM
Runtime RAM Consumption per FSM Instance = 12 bytes of SRAM

Even for a massive machine with 16 states and 16 events ($256$ cells), the table occupies only $256 \times 8 = 2048\text{ bytes}$ (2 KB) of Flash, leaving the entire volatile SRAM free for buffers and application data.

20.4 Hierarchical State Machines (HSMs) & Behavioral Inheritance

In classical flat FSMs, global events (such as EVENT_ESTOP, EVENT_LOW_BATTERY, or EVENT_RESET) must be explicitly listed in every single state, resulting in massive code duplication.

Hierarchical State Machines (HSMs) (formalized by David Harel in 1987) introduce Behavioral Inheritance: a substate inherits the event handlers of its superstate. If the substate does not consume an incoming event, the event automatically propagates upwards to the parent container state.

Figure 20.2: Hierarchical State Machine (HSM) with Inherited Superstate Transition

20.5 Code Comparison: Giant Switch-Case vs. 2D Table Engine

Compare a sprawling procedural switch-case with a modular table-driven architecture.

Compare Architecture: Complex Industrial Machine FSM

❌ Giant Nested Switch-Case

void fsm_dispatch(Event_t evt) {
    switch (g_state) {
        case S1:
            if (evt == E1) { ... }
            else if (evt == E2) { ... }
            else if (evt == E3) { ... }
            break;
        case S2:
            if (evt == E1) { ... }
            /* Repeated 20 times */
            /* 1,500 lines of code */
            /* Cyclomatic Complexity > 50 */
    }
}

Drawbacks: High cyclomatic complexity, variable lookup latency $O(N)$, hard to test individual cell paths, easy to introduce unintended fall-through bugs.

✔ 2D Table Engine

static const Transition_t table[S_MAX][E_MAX] = {
    [S1] = { [E1] = { S2, act1 }, [E2] = { S3, act2 } },
    [S2] = { [E1] = { S1, act3 } }
};

void fsm_dispatch(Fsm_t *fsm, Event_t evt) {
    const Transition_t *t = &table[fsm->state][evt];
    t->action(fsm);
    fsm->state = t->next_state;
}

Benefits: Constant $O(1)$ dispatch time, 5 lines of engine logic, stored entirely in Flash ROM, table serves as self-documenting test matrix.

20.6 Interactive Knowledge Check

Test your mastery of table-driven state machine architecture and hierarchical automata.

1. What is the time complexity of event dispatch in a two-dimensional table-driven state machine?
  • O(N) proportional to the number of states.
  • O(1) constant time, because lookup is a direct two-dimensional array index operation.
  • O(log N) using binary search trees.
  • O(N^2) quadratic time.
Explanation: Array indexing table[state][event] calculates the address in 1 to 2 CPU cycles, providing deterministic real-time dispatch latency regardless of machine size.
2. Why should the 2D state transition table be qualified with the const keyword in embedded C?
  • To allow the processor to modify the table at runtime.
  • To ensure the linker places the table into non-volatile Flash ROM (.rodata) rather than precious volatile SRAM (.data).
  • To prevent the preprocessor from deleting the file.
  • Because function pointers cannot exist in RAM.
Explanation: Marking large lookup tables as const places them in Flash memory, preserving scarce microcontroller SRAM for dynamic variables and buffers.
3. What is the primary software maintenance benefit of separating the state transition table from the action functions?
  • It eliminates the need for header files.
  • It separates machine topology from business logic: changing a transition requires editing only table data without touching procedural control flow code.
  • It doubles the serial baud rate.
  • It bypasses the C linker.
Explanation: Table-driven design encapsulates the graph structure in a declarative data matrix, keeping individual action handlers tiny, focused, and independently unit-testable.
4. In an FSM with 10 states and 8 events, how many cells does the 2D transition table contain?
  • 18
  • 80
  • 100
  • 64
Explanation: The table dimension is [STATES][EVENTS] = 10 × 8 = 80 cells.
5. What is the core innovation introduced by Hierarchical State Machines (HSMs)?
  • Replacing C with assembly language.
  • Behavioral inheritance: substates inherit event handlers from parent superstates, eliminating duplicate transitions for common events like E-Stop.
  • Running state machines on multi-core processors only.
  • Eliminating the need for event queues.
Explanation: HSMs allow parent superstates to handle shared events (e.g. EVENT_ESTOP or EVENT_LOW_BATTERY) once, rather than repeating the transition across every child substate.
6. What defensive check must be executed before indexing into g_state_table[fsm->state][evt->signal]?
  • Verify the clock crystal frequency.
  • Verify that fsm->state < STATE_MAX and evt->signal < EVENT_MAX to prevent out-of-bounds array access memory corruption.
  • Disable the SysTick timer.
  • Read the MCU temperature sensor.
Explanation: Array bounds verification guards against corrupted enums caused by memory bit-flips or uninitialized variables, satisfying MISRA-C Rule 18.1.
7. What is an "Ignore Action" (act_ignore) in a table-driven FSM?
  • An empty function that triggers a CPU reboot.
  • A benign action handler that takes no action and leaves the state unchanged when an irrelevant event occurs.
  • A compiler warning suppressor.
  • A function that deletes the transition table from RAM.
Explanation: An explicit ignore function (or NULL pointer check) cleanly absorbs events that have no effect in the current state without triggering an error.
8. In C99, what syntax feature allows sparse or readable initialization of the 2D state transition table?
  • Operator overloading.
  • Designated Initializers: [STATE_IDLE] = { [EVENT_START] = { ... } }.
  • Templates.
  • Lambda expressions.
Explanation: C99 designated initializers allow indexing table entries by their explicit enum names, making the matrix readable and resilient to enum reordering.
9. What is the cyclomatic complexity of a table-driven fsm_dispatch() function?
  • Proportional to the number of states times events ($S \times E$).
  • Extremely low (typically 2 to 3), consisting only of bounds validation and pointer invocation.
  • Infinite.
  • Equal to the number of CPU registers.
Explanation: Because branching is replaced by tabular indexing, the dispatch engine has virtually zero cyclomatic complexity, passing any static analysis audit with ease.
10. When should an engineer transition from a nested switch-case FSM to a 2D table-driven FSM?
  • Only when the microcontroller has more than 1 GB of RAM.
  • When state and event counts grow beyond ~6-8 items and switch-case complexity threatens readability, maintainability, and test coverage.
  • Never; switch-case is always superior.
  • Only when using C++ compilers.
Explanation: Switch-case is excellent for small FSMs (low boilerplate). Table-driven FSMs are superior for mid-to-large FSMs where tabular structure prevents maintenance bugs.

20.7 Hands-On Engineering Laboratories

Execute these 5 laboratory assignments to master table-driven automata and hierarchical state machine architectures.

Assignment 1: Vending Machine 2D Table Engine

Task: Implement a complete table-driven state machine for an automated vending machine: states WAITING_COIN, CREDIT_INSERTED, DISPENSING, RETURNING_CHANGE; events COIN_10C, COIN_25C, BUTTON_SELECT, BUTTON_CANCEL, MOTOR_DONE. Store the transition table in const Flash and verify dispatch latency.

Assignment 2: State Entry and Exit Action Extenders

Task: Extend the Transition_t structure to support Moore-style entry and exit actions. When entering DISPENSING, turn on a dispensing LED; when exiting, turn it off. Verify that transitioning from state A to state B executes: State_A_Exit() → Transition_Action() → State_B_Entry().

Assignment 3: Host-Based Automated State Table Tester

Task: Write a test runner in C on the host PC that automatically executes every single cell in the 2D matrix. Verify that all out-of-bounds state and event indices are trapped defensively without a segmentation fault or undefined behavior.

Assignment 4: Flash vs. SRAM Footprint Verification

Task: Compile the table-driven FSM with GCC ARM toolchain. Use arm-none-eabi-nm -S and arm-none-eabi-size -A to prove that the 2D transition table is located in the .rodata Flash segment and consumes zero bytes in the .bss or .data SRAM segments.

Assignment 5: Lightweight Hierarchical FSM Dispatcher

Task: Build a 2-level hierarchical state machine where an unhandled event in a substate delegates automatically to a parent state handler via a parent function pointer: fsm->parent_state_handler(fsm, evt). Test with an emergency stop event and confirm clean hierarchical bubbling.

Official References, Research Papers & Standards

Deepen your engineering foundation with canonical publications and official standard specifications:

Classic Paper David Harel

Statecharts: A Visual Formalism for Complex Systems

Foundational 1987 publication introducing hierarchical state nesting, orthogonal regions, and state clustering.

View Official Resource →

View Official Resource →

Classic reference on state-driven behavior encapsulation and polymorphic state transition architectures.

fields.title: Module 4 Project: Standards, State Machines & Defensive Systems
fields.content:
Module 4 Capstone Project

Standards, State Machines & Defensive Systems

Writing firmware for life-critical or industrial equipment requires disciplined engineering practices. Ad-hoc spaghetti code with nested if/else chains fails in edge cases and cannot be certified under standards such as MISRA-C or ISO 26262. In this milestone, we construct two robust systems: a MISRA-C compliant, table-driven Access Control FSM tested via automated GDB scripts on Linux/WSL, and a Safety-Critical Motor Controller featuring an Independent Hardware Watchdog (IWDG) and custom HardFault diagnostic capture on STM32.

Dimension Project 1: Linux / WSL Environment Project 2: Physical STM32 Board
Project Focus MISRA-C Table-Driven Access Control FSM & GDB Suite Safety-Critical Motor Controller with IWDG & HardFault Trap
Design Pattern 2D State Transition Matrix with action function pointers Hierarchical FSM with fail-safe fallback & watchdog supervision
Compliance & Quality MISRA-C:2012 compliance, zero dynamic memory, Doxygen docs Hardware watchdog window refresh, assembly register stack unwinding
Automated Verification Headless GDB regression script injecting fault events Hardware reset cause detection (RCC_CSR), SWD live telemetry

Part 1: Linux / WSL Project — MISRA-C Compliant Access Control FSM

In security and industrial automation, access gates must never enter undefined states. A 2D State Transition Table guarantees deterministic $O(1)$ event dispatch, mathematically proves that all state-event permutations are handled, and eliminates deeply nested conditional logic.

System State Diagram & Transitions

[STATE_LOCKED] --------(EVENT_BADGE_SCANNED)-------> [STATE_AUTHENTICATING] ^ | | +---------------+---------------+ | | (AUTH_SUCCESS) | (AUTH_FAIL / 3x) | v v (TIMEOUT / 5s) [STATE_UNLOCKED] [STATE_LOCKOUT] | | | +--------------------------------------+ (TAMPER_DETECTED) | v [STATE_ALARM]

Step 1: Doxygen-Documented FSM Interface (access_fsm.h)

/**
 * @file access_fsm.h
 * @brief MISRA-C Compliant Table-Driven Industrial Access Control FSM
 * @author Apt Computing Labs
 * @date 2026
 */
#ifndef ACCESS_FSM_H
#define ACCESS_FSM_H

#include <stdint.h>
#include <stdbool.h>

/**
 * @brief Access Control States (Exhaustive Enum)
 */
typedef enum {
    STATE_LOCKED = 0,
    STATE_AUTHENTICATING,
    STATE_UNLOCKED,
    STATE_LOCKOUT,
    STATE_ALARM,
    STATE_COUNT /* Sentinel */
} fsm_state_t;

/**
 * @brief Access Control Events
 */
typedef enum {
    EVENT_BADGE_SCANNED = 0,
    EVENT_AUTH_SUCCESS,
    EVENT_AUTH_FAIL,
    EVENT_UNLOCK_TIMEOUT,
    EVENT_TAMPER_DETECTED,
    EVENT_RESET_KEY,
    EVENT_COUNT /* Sentinel */
} fsm_event_t;

/**
 * @brief Forward declaration of FSM context structure
 */
typedef struct access_fsm access_fsm_t;

/**
 * @brief Action callback function pointer type
 */
typedef void (*fsm_action_t)(access_fsm_t *p_fsm);

/**
 * @brief Transition Table Entry: Defines Next State and Associated Action
 */
typedef struct {
    fsm_state_t  next_state;
    fsm_action_t action;
} transition_entry_t;

/**
 * @brief Access FSM Instance Context
 */
struct access_fsm {
    fsm_state_t current_state;
    uint32_t    failed_attempts;
    uint32_t    audit_log_counter;
};

/* API Prototypes */
void access_fsm_init(access_fsm_t *p_fsm);
void access_fsm_dispatch(access_fsm_t *p_fsm, fsm_event_t event);
fsm_state_t access_fsm_get_state(const access_fsm_t *p_fsm);

#endif /* ACCESS_FSM_H */

Step 2: Table-Driven Implementation (access_fsm.c)

/**
 * @file access_fsm.c
 * @brief Implementation adhering strictly to MISRA-C:2012 Rules
 */
#include <stdio.h>
#include "access_fsm.h"

/* Action Function Prototypes */
static void action_log_scan(access_fsm_t *p_fsm);
static void action_unlock_solenoid(access_fsm_t *p_fsm);
static void action_lock_solenoid(access_fsm_t *p_fsm);
static void action_register_fail(access_fsm_t *p_fsm);
static void action_sound_alarm(access_fsm_t *p_fsm);
static void action_reset_lockout(access_fsm_t *p_fsm);
static void action_ignore(access_fsm_t *p_fsm);

/* State Transition Matrix [Current State][Event] */
static const transition_entry_t g_transition_table[STATE_COUNT][EVENT_COUNT] = {
    [STATE_LOCKED] = {
        [EVENT_BADGE_SCANNED]   = { STATE_AUTHENTICATING, action_log_scan },
        [EVENT_TAMPER_DETECTED] = { STATE_ALARM,          action_sound_alarm },
        [EVENT_AUTH_SUCCESS]    = { STATE_LOCKED,         action_ignore },
        [EVENT_AUTH_FAIL]       = { STATE_LOCKED,         action_ignore },
        [EVENT_UNLOCK_TIMEOUT]  = { STATE_LOCKED,         action_ignore },
        [EVENT_RESET_KEY]       = { STATE_LOCKED,         action_ignore }
    },
    [STATE_AUTHENTICATING] = {
        [EVENT_AUTH_SUCCESS]    = { STATE_UNLOCKED,       action_unlock_solenoid },
        [EVENT_AUTH_FAIL]       = { STATE_LOCKED,         action_register_fail },
        [EVENT_TAMPER_DETECTED] = { STATE_ALARM,          action_sound_alarm },
        [EVENT_BADGE_SCANNED]   = { STATE_AUTHENTICATING, action_ignore },
        [EVENT_UNLOCK_TIMEOUT]  = { STATE_LOCKED,         action_lock_solenoid },
        [EVENT_RESET_KEY]       = { STATE_AUTHENTICATING, action_ignore }
    },
    [STATE_UNLOCKED] = {
        [EVENT_UNLOCK_TIMEOUT]  = { STATE_LOCKED,         action_lock_solenoid },
        [EVENT_TAMPER_DETECTED] = { STATE_ALARM,          action_sound_alarm },
        [EVENT_BADGE_SCANNED]   = { STATE_UNLOCKED,       action_ignore },
        [EVENT_AUTH_SUCCESS]    = { STATE_UNLOCKED,       action_ignore },
        [EVENT_AUTH_FAIL]       = { STATE_UNLOCKED,       action_ignore },
        [EVENT_RESET_KEY]       = { STATE_UNLOCKED,       action_ignore }
    },
    [STATE_LOCKOUT] = {
        [EVENT_RESET_KEY]       = { STATE_LOCKED,         action_reset_lockout },
        [EVENT_TAMPER_DETECTED] = { STATE_ALARM,          action_sound_alarm },
        [EVENT_BADGE_SCANNED]   = { STATE_LOCKOUT,        action_ignore },
        [EVENT_AUTH_SUCCESS]    = { STATE_LOCKOUT,        action_ignore },
        [EVENT_AUTH_FAIL]       = { STATE_LOCKOUT,        action_ignore },
        [EVENT_UNLOCK_TIMEOUT]  = { STATE_LOCKOUT,        action_ignore }
    },
    [STATE_ALARM] = {
        [EVENT_RESET_KEY]       = { STATE_LOCKED,         action_reset_lockout },
        [EVENT_BADGE_SCANNED]   = { STATE_ALARM,          action_ignore },
        [EVENT_AUTH_SUCCESS]    = { STATE_ALARM,          action_ignore },
        [EVENT_AUTH_FAIL]       = { STATE_ALARM,          action_ignore },
        [EVENT_UNLOCK_TIMEOUT]  = { STATE_ALARM,          action_ignore },
        [EVENT_TAMPER_DETECTED] = { STATE_ALARM,          action_ignore }
    }
};

void access_fsm_init(access_fsm_t *p_fsm) {
    if (p_fsm != NULL) {
        p_fsm->current_state = STATE_LOCKED;
        p_fsm->failed_attempts = 0U;
        p_fsm->audit_log_counter = 0U;
    }
}

void access_fsm_dispatch(access_fsm_t *p_fsm, fsm_event_t event) {
    if ((p_fsm == NULL) || (event >= EVENT_COUNT) || (p_fsm->current_state >= STATE_COUNT)) {
        return; /* Defensive boundary guard (MISRA-C Rule 14.4) */
    }

    const transition_entry_t *p_entry = &g_transition_table[p_fsm->current_state][event];

    /* Update State */
    p_fsm->current_state = p_entry->next_state;
    p_fsm->audit_log_counter++;

    /* Execute Action Callback */
    if (p_entry->action != NULL) {
        p_entry->action(p_fsm);
    }
}

fsm_state_t access_fsm_get_state(const access_fsm_t *p_fsm) {
    return (p_fsm != NULL) ? p_fsm->current_state : STATE_LOCKED;
}

static void action_log_scan(access_fsm_t *p_fsm) {
    printf("[FSM Action] Badge scanned. Validating credentials...\n");
}

static void action_unlock_solenoid(access_fsm_t *p_fsm) {
    p_fsm->failed_attempts = 0U;
    printf("[FSM Action] Access Granted! Door Solenoid ENERGIZED (Unlocked).\n");
}

static void action_lock_solenoid(access_fsm_t *p_fsm) {
    printf("[FSM Action] Door Solenoid DE-ENERGIZED (Locked).\n");
}

static void action_register_fail(access_fsm_t *p_fsm) {
    p_fsm->failed_attempts++;
    printf("[FSM Action] Auth Failed! Attempt %u / 3.\n", p_fsm->failed_attempts);
    if (p_fsm->failed_attempts >= 3U) {
        printf("[FSM Action] MAXIMUM FAILS EXCEEDED. Transitioning to LOCKOUT!\n");
        p_fsm->current_state = STATE_LOCKOUT;
    }
}

static void action_sound_alarm(access_fsm_t *p_fsm) {
    printf("[FSM Action] CRITICAL ALARM! Siren ON, Security Telemetry Dispatched!\n");
}

static void action_reset_lockout(access_fsm_t *p_fsm) {
    p_fsm->failed_attempts = 0U;
    printf("[FSM Action] Supervisor Key Reset. Returning to LOCKED state.\n");
}

static void action_ignore(access_fsm_t *p_fsm) {
    /* MISRA explicit no-op */
    (void)p_fsm;
}

Step 3: Headless GDB Automated Test Script (test_fsm.gdb)

Automate regression verification without manual clicking using GDB commands: 

# test_fsm.gdb: Automated Headless GDB Test Harness
set pagination off
set logging file gdb_test.log
set logging on

file build/access_fsm_test
break main
run

# Verify Initial State is STATE_LOCKED (0)
break access_fsm_dispatch
continue
print g_fsm.current_state
assert g_fsm.current_state == 0

# Inject Tamper Event and assert ALARM (4)
set $event = 4
call access_fsm_dispatch(&g_fsm, $event)
print g_fsm.current_state
assert g_fsm.current_state == 4

echo === ALL GDB FSM TESTS PASSED SUCCESSFULLY ===\n
quit 0

Part 2: Physical STM32 Board Project — Hardware Watchdog (IWDG) & HardFault Diagnostics

In critical microcontroller systems, software can lock up due to cosmic rays, EMI, or unexpected race conditions. The Independent Watchdog (IWDG) runs on a dedicated internal low-speed oscillator (LSI @ 32kHz) and cannot be halted by software once started. If the firmware fails to kick the watchdog within its programmed timeout, the MCU undergoes a hardware reset.

Bare-Metal Implementation (safety_motor.c)

/**
 * @file safety_motor.c
 * @brief Safety-Critical Motor Controller with IWDG & HardFault Handler
 * Target: STM32F401RE Nucleo-64
 */
#include <stdint.h>
#include <stdbool.h>

/* Register Offsets */
#define RCC_CSR        (*(volatile uint32_t *)(0x40023874UL))
#define RCC_AHB1ENR    (*(volatile uint32_t *)(0x40023830UL))
#define GPIOA_MODER    (*(volatile uint32_t *)(0x40020000UL))
#define GPIOA_BSRR     (*(volatile uint32_t *)(0x40020018UL))
#define GPIOC_IDR      (*(volatile uint32_t *)(0x40020810UL))

/* Independent Watchdog (IWDG) Registers */
#define IWDG_KR        (*(volatile uint32_t *)(0x40003000UL))
#define IWDG_PR        (*(volatile uint32_t *)(0x40003004UL))
#define IWDG_RLR       (*(volatile uint32_t *)(0x40003008UL))
#define IWDG_SR        (*(volatile uint32_t *)(0x4000300CUL))

/* IWDG Magic Key Values */
#define IWDG_KEY_RELOAD     0xAAAAUL
#define IWDG_KEY_ENABLE     0xCCCCUL
#define IWDG_KEY_WRITE_EN   0x5555UL

/* Stack Frame captured during HardFault */
typedef struct {
    uint32_t r0;
    uint32_t r1;
    uint32_t r2;
    uint32_t r3;
    uint32_t r12;
    uint32_t lr;
    uint32_t pc;
    uint32_t psr;
} hardfault_stack_t;

volatile hardfault_stack_t g_crash_telemetry;

/* C Portion of HardFault Handler called from assembly */
void HardFault_Handler_C(hardfault_stack_t *p_stack) {
    g_crash_telemetry = *p_stack;

    /* Disable interrupts and enter fail-safe visual beacon */
    __asm volatile ("cpsid i" : : : "memory");

    while (1) {
        /* Rapid strobe indicating hardware fault */
        GPIOA_BSRR = (1UL << 5);
        for (volatile int i = 0; i < 50000; i++);
        GPIOA_BSRR = (1UL << (5 + 16));
        for (volatile int i = 0; i < 50000; i++);
    }
}

/* Assembly Trampoline to extract correct stack pointer (MSP vs PSP) */
__attribute__((naked)) void HardFault_Handler(void) {
    __asm volatile (
        "tst lr, #4\n"              /* Test EXC_RETURN bit 2 */
        "ite eq\n"
        "mrseq r0, msp\n"          /* If 0, stack was MSP */
        "mrsne r0, psp\n"          /* If 1, stack was PSP */
        "b HardFault_Handler_C\n"  /* Branch to C handler with stack pointer in R0 */
    );
}

/* Configure IWDG for ~500ms Timeout */
static void iwdg_init(void) {
    IWDG_KR = IWDG_KEY_ENABLE;   /* 1. Start IWDG Clock */
    IWDG_KR = IWDG_KEY_WRITE_EN; /* 2. Enable write access to PR and RLR */
    IWDG_PR = 0x04UL;            /* 3. Prescaler /64 (32kHz / 64 = 500 Hz clock) */
    IWDG_RLR = 250UL;            /* 4. 250 ticks @ 500Hz = 500 ms timeout */
    while (IWDG_SR != 0U) { /* Wait for registers to update */ }
    IWDG_KR = IWDG_KEY_RELOAD;   /* 5. Initial reload */
}

/* Kick / Refresh Watchdog */
static inline void iwdg_refresh(void) {
    IWDG_KR = IWDG_KEY_RELOAD;
}

int main(void) {
    RCC_AHB1ENR |= (1UL << 0) | (1UL << 2); /* Enable GPIOA & GPIOC */

    /* PA5 (LED) Output */
    GPIOA_MODER &= ~(3UL << 10);
    GPIOA_MODER |=  (1UL << 10);

    /* Check if system reset was caused by IWDG timeout */
    bool was_watchdog_reset = ((RCC_CSR & (1UL << 29)) != 0);
    RCC_CSR |= (1UL << 24); /* Clear reset flags */

    if (was_watchdog_reset) {
        /* Blink 5 fast pulses to inform operator of watchdog recovery */
        for (int i = 0; i < 5; i++) {
            GPIOA_BSRR = (1UL << 5);
            for (volatile int d = 0; d < 80000; d++);
            GPIOA_BSRR = (1UL << (5 + 16));
            for (volatile int d = 0; d < 80000; d++);
        }
    }

    iwdg_init();

    while (1) {
        /* Normal Superloop Operation: Kick the watchdog */
        iwdg_refresh();

        /* Normal Heartbeat Toggle */
        GPIOA_BSRR = (1UL << 5);
        for (volatile int d = 0; d < 200000; d++);
        GPIOA_BSRR = (1UL << (5 + 16));
        for (volatile int d = 0; d < 200000; d++);

        /* Fault Injection Demo: Pressing the Blue Button (PC13) simulates an infinite loop! */
        if ((GPIOC_IDR & (1UL << 13)) == 0) {
            /* Firmware hangs without kicking IWDG: Watchdog resets MCU after 500ms */
            while (1) { /* Infinite Hang */ }
        }
    }

    return 0;
}

Module 4 Capstone Knowledge Check

Test your mastery of MISRA rules, table-driven state machines, and hardware fault handling.

1. Why does MISRA-C strictly prohibit dynamic memory allocation (malloc and free) in safety-critical firmware?

2. In HardFault_Handler, why is an assembly trampoline required before calling the C fault handler?

3. What is the key advantage of a 2D State Transition Matrix over a switch-case FSM?

4. Why does the Independent Watchdog (IWDG) use the internal 32kHz LSI oscillator instead of the main system clock (HSE/HSI)?

5. In the captured hardfault_stack_t structure, which register contains the memory address of the instruction that caused the CPU crash?

6. What does MISRA-C Rule 17.7 mandate regarding function return values?

7. How does firmware know after booting whether the reset was caused by power-up (POR) or a watchdog event (IWDG)?

8. What is 'Window Watchdog' (WWDG) behavior compared to regular watchdog (IWDG)?

9. Why is recursion prohibited in MISRA-C and safety-critical embedded systems?

10. In Doxygen, what tag documents the expected state or conditions that must be true BEFORE calling a function?

Hands-on Engineering Challenges

Challenge 1 (Host)

Cppcheck MISRA-C Automated Scanner

Configure cppcheck --addon=misra in your Makefile. Run it against access_fsm.c and eliminate 100% of reported advisory and mandatory rule violations.

Challenge 2 (Host)

Hierarchical State Machine (HSM) Refactoring

Extend the access control FSM to support a Super-State STATE_OPERATIONAL that encompasses LOCKED, AUTHENTICATING, and UNLOCKED, handling global events (such as EMERGENCY_EVAC) at the parent state level.

Challenge 3 (STM32)

HardFault Stack Unwinder & Serial Crash Dump

Enhance HardFault_Handler_C to transmit a human-readable crash report over USART2 (printing PC, LR, and fault status registers CFSR, HFSR, and BFAR) before halting.

Challenge 4 (STM32)

Dual Watchdog Supervision Architecture

Configure both IWDG (hardware fallback) and WWDG (window watchdog) simultaneously. Configure a software task monitor that verifies individual task execution deadlines before clearing the watchdogs.

Challenge 5 (Documentation Automation)

Automated Doxygen HTML & State Diagram Pipeline

Generate a complete HTML documentation suite with Graphviz dot state machine diagrams using doxygen Doxyfile and verify all functions and state structures are fully cross-referenced.

Further Technical Reading

Industry Standard MISRA Consortium

MISRA C:2012 Guidelines

Guidelines for the use of the C language in critical systems, covering rule definitions and rationale.

View Official Resource →
Application Note Arm Developer

Application Note 209: Using Cortex-M3/M4 Fault Exceptions

Deep dive into HardFault, MemManage, BusFault, UsageFault, and extracting crash state from stacked registers.

fields.title: Topic 21: Modular .c & .h Files
fields.content:
Topic 21

Modular .c and .h File Architecture

A common architectural failure in embedded systems is the "Mega-File Anti-Pattern" — an entire firmware project crammed into a single 10,000-line main.c, or a project fragmented into dozens of header files containing executable C code, un-encapsulated global variables, and mutual circular includes.

Professional embedded firmware is organized into strictly decoupled Translation Units. Each module consists of an Interface Specification (the .h header file) declaring the public API contract, and a private Implementation Unit (the .c source file) encapsulating hardware registers, internal state machines, and private helper functions using the static keyword.

21.1 The Translation Unit Boundary

In C, the compiler never processes an entire project at once. Instead, the preprocessor strips comments, expands macros, and copies included headers into a single flattened text stream called a Translation Unit (TU). The compiler processes each TU independently into an object file (.o), which the linker ultimately resolves:

Figure 21.1: Modular Translation Unit Compilation and Linking Flow

21.2 Information Hiding via the `static` Keyword

Procedural C lacks object-oriented private or protected access modifiers. In embedded C, true encapsulation is achieved exclusively through the static storage-class specifier:

1. File-Scope Private Variables (Static State)

A variable declared at file scope with static has static storage duration (persists across the entire life of the firmware) but internal linkage. Its symbol is completely invisible to the linker and cannot be accessed or corrupted by any other translation unit: 

/* In uart.c: Completely private to this translation unit */
static uint8_t  s_rx_ring_buffer[256];
static uint16_t s_rx_head_idx = 0U;
static uint16_t s_rx_tail_idx = 0U;

2. File-Scope Private Helper Functions

Functions marked static have internal linkage. This confers two vital engineering advantages:

  • No Symbol Collision: Two different driver files (e.g. spi.c and i2c.c) can both define a private helper named static void configure_clocks(void) without triggering a duplicate symbol linker error.
  • Compiler Optimization: The compiler knows the static function can never be called outside this translation unit. If it is called only once or twice, GCC automatically inlines the entire function, eliminating function call overhead and saving stack memory.

21.3 Header File Hygiene & The Self-Contained Rule

Every header file must follow the Self-Contained Header Rule: a header file must include all prerequisites necessary to compile cleanly on its own.

The Header Isolation Test

To prove that your header motor.h is truly self-contained, create a dummy C file containing only: 

/* test_header.c */
#include "motor.h"

If compiling test_header.c emits errors like unknown type uint32_t or size_t undeclared, your header is defective! It was secretly relying on the caller having previously included <stdint.h> or <stddef.h>.

Include Guards: `#ifndef` vs `#pragma once`

/* Standard ISO C99 / MISRA-Compliant Include Guard */
#ifndef MOTOR_H
#define MOTOR_H

#include <stdint.h>
#include <stdbool.h>

/* Public API declarations */
void motor_init(void);

#endif /* MOTOR_H */

While #pragma once is supported by modern GCC and Clang, the classic #ifndef / #define guard pattern remains strictly mandated by MISRA-C:2012 Rule 20.14 because it guarantees standard-conforming portability across legacy proprietary microcontroller toolchains (IAR, Keil, Cosmic, Renesas CC-RX).

21.4 Breaking Circular Dependency Traps

Circular dependencies occur when Module A needs types from Module B, while Module B needs types from Module A (e.g. telemetry.h includes comm.h, which includes telemetry.h). This causes the preprocessor to omit header declarations due to include guards, triggering bizarre syntax error: unknown type name compiler errors.

The professional solution is Forward Struct Declarations combined with Interface Segregation: 

/* comm.h */
#ifndef COMM_H
#define COMM_H

#include <stdint.h>

/* FORWARD DECLARATION: No need to #include "telemetry.h" */
struct TelemetryPacket_t;

/* Public API using pointer to forward-declared structure */
void comm_send_packet(const struct TelemetryPacket_t * const p_packet);

#endif /* COMM_H */

Because a pointer has a known, fixed physical size (4 bytes on 32-bit Cortex-M), the compiler does not need the complete struct definition in the header. The complete struct is only included in the .c implementation file.

21.5 Code Comparison: Leaky Header vs. Clean Modular C

Compare an un-encapsulated header that leaks variables into global scope with a clean, decoupled modular translation unit.

Compare Architecture: LED Controller Module

❌ Leaky Header (Linker Hazard)

/* led.h: DISASTROUS ANTI-PATTERN! */
#include "stm32f4xx.h"

/* Defines variable in header: Linker collision! */
uint8_t led_status; 

/* Code inside header: duplicated in every .o */
void set_led(uint8_t on) {
    if (on) GPIOA->ODR |= (1 << 5);
    else    GPIOA->ODR &= ~(1 << 5);
}

Flaws: Defining storage in headers causes duplicate symbol link errors if included in more than one .c file. Exposes raw chip registers to application code.

✔ Clean Modular Architecture

/* led.h: Pure Interface Specification */
#ifndef LED_H
#define LED_H
#include <stdbool.h>

typedef enum { LED_OFF = 0, LED_ON } LedState_t;
void led_init(void);
void led_write(const LedState_t state);
#endif

/* led.c: Encapsulated Implementation */
#include "led.h"
#include "bsp_gpio.h"
static LedState_t s_current_state = LED_OFF;

void led_write(const LedState_t state) {
    s_current_state = state;
    bsp_pin_write(LED_PIN, (state == LED_ON));
}

Safety: Zero variable definitions in header, state is static private, hardware registers are completely hidden behind clean procedural API.

21.6 Interactive Knowledge Check

Test your understanding of translation units, linkage, header guards, and modular C architecture.

1. What happens if a global variable definition like uint32_t system_counter = 0; is placed inside a header file included by two separate .c files?
  • The compiler merges them automatically into Flash ROM.
  • The linker halts with a "multiple definition of symbol" error because storage is allocated in both object files.
  • The SysTick interrupt stops incrementing.
  • The variable becomes read-only.
Explanation: A header file must only declare symbols using extern. Defining storage in a header produces duplicate symbol definitions in every translation unit that includes it.
2. What is the effect of declaring a file-scope helper function as static void compute_crc(void)?
  • The function is stored in EEPROM.
  • The function is given internal linkage, restricting its visibility to the current translation unit and enabling compiler inlining optimizations.
  • The function can only be executed once during boot.
  • The function runs with interrupt priority.
Explanation: static on a function strips it from the global symbol table, preventing name clashes and allowing aggressive compiler optimizations.
3. What is the "Self-Contained Header" principle in C firmware design?
  • A header file must contain all executable C code without needing a .c file.
  • A header file must include all necessary dependencies (<stdint.h>, <stdbool.h>) so that it compiles cleanly on its own without assuming prior includes.
  • A header file must never include any other header file.
  • A header must be smaller than 512 bytes.
Explanation: Self-contained headers eliminate fragile include-order dependencies where b.h only compiles if the developer remembered to include a.h first.
4. Why is #ifndef MODULE_H / #define MODULE_H / #endif preferred over #pragma once in strict MISRA-C projects?
  • Because #pragma once is only supported on Linux.
  • Because standard macro guards are fully defined by the ISO C standard, whereas #pragma once is a non-standard compiler extension prohibited by MISRA.
  • Macro guards run 10 times faster during runtime.
  • #pragma once increases SRAM consumption.
Explanation: #pragma directives are implementation-defined. For maximum safety compliance across certified compilers, standard preprocessor macro guards are required.
5. How can circular dependency between two headers (A.h and B.h) be cleanly broken without combining them?
  • By deleting the include guards in both headers.
  • By using a forward struct declaration (e.g. struct B_t;) in A.h and moving pointer dereferencing into the .c implementation file.
  • By compiling the files with the -O0 flag.
  • Circular dependencies are impossible to resolve in C.
Explanation: Declaring struct Foo; informs the compiler that the type exists, allowing pointers to be used in function prototypes without including the complete struct definition.
6. What is the risk of including massive device peripheral headers (e.g. stm32f4xx.h) inside a high-level application business logic header?
  • The MCU crystal will destabilize.
  • It tightly couples application algorithms to specific hardware registers, preventing host-based unit testing and code reuse on different silicon.
  • The compiler converts all variables to 64-bit doubles.
  • It disables Git version tracking.
Explanation: Including hardware headers in application code destroys hardware abstraction, making it impossible to compile or unit-test application logic on a PC.
7. What is an "opaque pointer" in C modular programming?
  • A pointer that cannot be dereferenced by anyone, even the driver.
  • A pointer to an incomplete struct type whose internal fields are defined only in the .c file, completely hiding implementation details from the caller.
  • A pointer stored in blackbox NVRAM.
  • A pointer with a null value.
Explanation: Opaque pointers (handles) enforce true information hiding: callers can pass the handle to APIs, but cannot inspect or corrupt internal struct members.
8. In a well-architected firmware driver, where should hardware register macros (e.g. #define CR1_ENABLE (1 << 0)) be placed?
  • In the public driver.h file.
  • Inside the private driver.c file (or a private internal header like driver_reg.h), hidden from application code.
  • Inside main.c.
  • In the linker script.
Explanation: Bit-level register masks are internal implementation details. Exposing them in public headers pollutes the global namespace and tempts application code to bypass the driver.
9. What is the purpose of declaring a public variable in a header with extern?
  • To allocate memory in the heap.
  • To declare the symbol name and type to callers without allocating storage, which is defined once in a single .c file.
  • To make the variable constant.
  • To instruct the compiler to place the variable in an external SPI Flash.
Explanation: extern provides a reference declaration; the actual storage is defined in exactly one translation unit, satisfying the One Definition Rule (ODR).
10. Why should you avoid putting executable function bodies (non-inline) inside a header file?
  • Because each translation unit including the header compiles a separate instance of the function, causing multiple-definition linker collisions.
  • Because headers can only contain ASCII art.
  • Because the preprocessor strips all C statements.
  • Because the CPU cannot branch to code defined in headers.
Explanation: Function bodies in headers are compiled into every translation unit that includes them, producing duplicate symbol errors during linking unless marked static inline.

21.7 Hands-On Engineering Laboratories

Execute these 5 laboratory assignments to master translation unit encapsulation and modular firmware architecture.

Assignment 1: Monolithic Refactoring

Task: Take a 500-line monolithic main.c that mixes UART driver code, button debouncing, and temperature sensor reading. Break it into three decoupled modules: bsp_uart.[ch], btn_debounce.[ch], and temp_sensor.[ch]. Verify successful compilation and linking.

Assignment 2: Automated Self-Contained Header Verification

Task: Write a shell script or Makefile target make check-headers that iterates through every .h file in your project, generates a temporary #include "header.h" test file, compiles it with -Wall -Werror, and verifies zero compilation errors.

Assignment 3: Symbol Leakage Audit with nm

Task: Compile an object file driver.o. Run nm -g driver.o (global symbols) and nm driver.o (all symbols). Verify that internal helper functions and private state variables are marked with t and b (local/internal linkage) and only true public APIs appear as T (global).

Assignment 4: Resolving Circular Include Deadlocks

Task: Intentionally construct a circular dependency: packet.h includes channel.h, and channel.h includes packet.h. Demonstrate the compiler error. Refactor both headers using forward struct declarations and prove clean, zero-warning compilation.

Assignment 5: Multi-Instance Peripheral Driver

Task: Design a modular UART driver supporting multiple hardware channels (UART1 and UART2) using a configuration struct instance: UartHandle_t. Ensure the driver contains zero hardcoded peripheral register addresses, enabling two independent UART instances to share identical driver code.

fields.title: Topic 22: Interfaces, APIs & Abstraction
fields.content:
Topic 22

Interfaces, APIs & Abstraction

A major cause of software fragility in embedded projects is premature coupling to physical silicon. When application algorithms (such as temperature PID control or telemetry logging) directly access microcontroller peripheral registers (e.g., I2C1->DR or USART2->CR1), the entire codebase becomes permanently locked to a single chip vendor. Migrating to another MCU during a silicon supply-chain shortage requires a total rewrite, and automated host-based unit testing on developer laptops becomes impossible.

Hardware Abstraction is the discipline of creating strict procedural interfaces that separate what an application requires from how the physical hardware achieves it. In this chapter, we master modern C abstraction patterns: Opaque Struct Handles (PIMPL in C), Virtual Method Tables (vtables) for runtime polymorphism, and the Dependency Inversion Principle (DIP).

22.1 The Opaque Pointer Pattern (Handles in C)

In standard C, exposing a struct definition in a public header file allows client code to directly read and write internal struct fields. If the driver developer later modifies an internal buffer size or changes a register representation, the client code breaks, or worse, silently introduces memory alignment bugs.

The Opaque Pointer Pattern (analogous to the PIMPL idiom in C++) completely conceals the struct internals behind an incomplete type declaration:

Figure 22.1: Opaque Pointer Encapsulation Boundary
/* display.h: Public Interface */
#ifndef DISPLAY_H
#define DISPLAY_H

#include <stdint.h>
#include <stdbool.h>

/* Incomplete struct forward declaration */
struct DisplayInstance_t;
typedef struct DisplayInstance_t * DisplayHandle_t;

typedef enum {
    DISPLAY_OK = 0,
    DISPLAY_ERR_NULL_PTR,
    DISPLAY_ERR_TIMEOUT
} DisplayStatus_t;

DisplayStatus_t display_pixel_draw(DisplayHandle_t h_disp, uint16_t x, uint16_t y, uint16_t color);
DisplayStatus_t display_flush(DisplayHandle_t h_disp);

#endif /* DISPLAY_H */
Program 22.1: Opaque Handle Public Header Declaration

22.2 Polymorphism in C: The Virtual Table (vtable) Pattern

Polymorphism allows application code to interact with different hardware implementations through a uniform, interchangeable interface. Consider an application that logs telemetry data to non-volatile memory: depending on product configuration, the physical media could be an internal EEPROM, an external SPI NOR Flash, or a RAM Mock for unit tests.

In C, runtime polymorphism is constructed using a Virtual Method Table (vtable) struct of function pointers: 

/* storage_interface.h */
#ifndef STORAGE_INTERFACE_H
#define STORAGE_INTERFACE_H

#include <stdint.h>
#include <stddef.h>

/* Abstract Storage Interface Vtable */
typedef struct {
    int32_t (*read)(void *p_context, uint32_t addr, uint8_t *p_buf, size_t len);
    int32_t (*write)(void *p_context, uint32_t addr, const uint8_t *p_buf, size_t len);
    int32_t (*erase_sector)(void *p_context, uint32_t sector_addr);
} StorageInterface_t;

/* Generic Polymorphic Storage Device Object */
typedef struct {
    const StorageInterface_t *p_vtable;
    void                     *p_driver_context;
} StorageDevice_t;

/* Polymorphic Dispatch Wrapper */
static inline int32_t storage_read(const StorageDevice_t * const p_dev, 
                                   uint32_t addr, uint8_t *p_buf, size_t len) 
{
    if ((p_dev == NULL) || (p_dev->p_vtable == NULL) || (p_dev->p_vtable->read == NULL)) {
        return -1;
    }
    return p_dev->p_vtable->read(p_dev->p_driver_context, addr, p_buf, len);
}

#endif /* STORAGE_INTERFACE_H */
Program 22.2: Abstract Storage Interface with Function Pointer vtable

22.3 Concrete Implementation & Host Mocking

We can now implement concrete drivers that satisfy the StorageInterface_t contract without modifying the caller: 

/* mock_storage.c: In-Memory RAM Mock for PC-Based Automated Testing */
#include "storage_interface.h"
#include <string.h>

#define MOCK_STORAGE_SIZE (4096U)
static uint8_t s_mock_ram[MOCK_STORAGE_SIZE];

static int32_t mock_read(void *p_ctx, uint32_t addr, uint8_t *p_buf, size_t len) {
    (void)p_ctx;
    if ((addr + len) > MOCK_STORAGE_SIZE) return -1;
    (void)memcpy(p_buf, &s_mock_ram[addr], len);
    return (int32_t)len;
}

static int32_t mock_write(void *p_ctx, uint32_t addr, const uint8_t *p_buf, size_t len) {
    (void)p_ctx;
    if ((addr + len) > MOCK_STORAGE_SIZE) return -1;
    (void)memcpy(&s_mock_ram[addr], p_buf, len);
    return (int32_t)len;
}

static int32_t mock_erase(void *p_ctx, uint32_t addr) {
    (void)p_ctx;
    if (addr >= MOCK_STORAGE_SIZE) return -1;
    (void)memset(&s_mock_ram[addr], 0xFF, 256U);
    return 0;
}

/* Static Vtable: Stored in .rodata */
static const StorageInterface_t s_mock_vtable = {
    .read = mock_read,
    .write = mock_write,
    .erase_sector = mock_erase
};

StorageDevice_t mock_storage_create(void) {
    StorageDevice_t dev = {
        .p_vtable = &s_mock_vtable,
        .p_driver_context = NULL
    };
    return dev;
}
Program 22.3: Concrete RAM Mock Implementation for Automated Testing

22.4 Code Comparison: Hardcoded Silicon vs. Inverted Abstraction

Compare an application tightly bound to an STM32 I2C peripheral with an application decoupled via abstract interfaces.

Compare Architecture: Temperature Acquisition Service

❌ Silicon-Coupled Anti-Pattern

/* Directly accesses STM32 registers */
#include "stm32f4xx.h"

int32_t get_temperature(void) {
    I2C1->CR1 |= I2C_CR1_START;
    while (!(I2C1->SR1 & I2C_SR1_SB));
    I2C1->DR = 0x90;
    /* ... 50 lines of register access */
    return temp_mdegc;
}

Disasters: Cannot run in PC unit tests. Cannot change from I2C to SPI. Cannot port to NXP or ESP32 without rewriting business logic.

✔ Clean Abstract Dependency

/* Depends solely on abstract interface */
typedef struct {
    int32_t (*sample_read_mdegc)(void *ctx, int32_t *p_temp);
} TempSensorIf_t;

int32_t thermal_monitor_step(
    const TempSensorIf_t *p_sensor, 
    void *ctx) 
{
    int32_t temp = 0;
    if (p_sensor->sample_read_mdegc(ctx, &temp) == 0) {
        if (temp > 85000) fan_relay_on();
    }
    return temp;
}

Superiority: Unit-testable on PC with simulated temperatures. Zero silicon dependencies in application logic.

22.5 Interactive Knowledge Check

Test your knowledge of abstraction, opaque pointers, vtables, and hardware isolation.

1. What is the primary purpose of using an "Opaque Pointer" (incomplete struct handle) in a public header file?
  • To enable 64-bit memory addressing on 32-bit MCUs.
  • To enforce information hiding, preventing callers from accessing or corrupting internal struct fields and preserving binary compatibility.
  • To instruct the compiler to place the struct in Flash memory.
  • To eliminate the need for the C linker.
Explanation: Declaring struct Foo; in a header gives callers a typed pointer handle without revealing field layouts, strictly preventing direct member manipulation.
2. How is runtime polymorphism achieved in procedural C without C++ virtual classes?
  • Through preprocessor macro recursion.
  • By defining an interface structure containing function pointers (a vtable) and passing a generic context pointer.
  • By writing assembly language trampolines in RAM.
  • Polymorphism is mathematically impossible in C.
Explanation: A struct containing function pointers acts as a virtual method table (vtable), allowing different driver implementations to be invoked identically through the same interface.
3. What is the performance overhead of invoking a driver function through a function pointer vtable on ARM Cortex-M?
  • Over 10,000 clock cycles.
  • Extremely small: typically 1 to 3 clock cycles (one memory load and a branch with link exchange: LDR + BLX).
  • Zero clock cycles because the compiler always removes function pointers.
  • It causes a guaranteed pipeline flush lasting 10 milliseconds.
Explanation: Calling through a function pointer on Cortex-M requires loading the address into a register and executing BLX — virtually negligible overhead for peripheral I/O.
4. What is the Dependency Inversion Principle (DIP) in the context of embedded firmware?
  • Drivers must depend directly on application UI widgets.
  • High-level policy modules should not depend on low-level silicon drivers; both must depend on abstract interfaces.
  • All interrupts must be inverted to active-low polarity.
  • The SysTick timer must count downwards instead of upwards.
Explanation: DIP ensures that business logic depends on an abstract sensor or communication contract, allowing the physical implementation to be swapped without changing application logic.
5. Why should global errno variables be avoided in multi-rate embedded API design?
  • Because errno is copyrighted by Microsoft.
  • A global error variable is not reentrant; an interrupt occurring between the failing call and checking errno can overwrite the error state.
  • Because it occupies 16 KB of Flash memory.
  • It disables all watchdog timers.
Explanation: Global error state creates race conditions across ISRs and cooperative tasks. Explicit status return enumerations are thread-safe and reentrant.
6. What is the purpose of the void *p_context pointer passed to vtable action functions?
  • To store the return address of the main function.
  • To carry instance-specific private state (e.g. peripheral base address, channel ID, buffer pointers) to the implementation.
  • To enable floating point math in the driver.
  • It is required by the ARM NVIC hardware.
Explanation: The context pointer functions as the procedural equivalent of the this pointer in object-oriented programming, linking the abstract call to instance data.
7. Why is host-based unit testing on a PC vastly easier when using hardware abstraction interfaces?
  • Because PCs have built-in I2C oscilloscope cards.
  • Because physical peripheral drivers can be replaced with mock RAM implementations, allowing algorithms to be tested rapidly in simulated scenarios without physical target hardware.
  • Because GCC on Linux does not support C syntax errors.
  • Because PC testing eliminates all compiler warnings automatically.
Explanation: Abstract interfaces allow injecting mocks that simulate sensor failures, temperature spikes, or corrupt packets on a PC in milliseconds without hardware emulators.
8. What is the risk of "leaky abstractions" in embedded systems?
  • Coolant fluid leaking from electrolytic capacitors.
  • When an interface fails to hide underlying hardware quirks (e.g. page boundaries, flash erase delays, or bus wait states), forcing callers to write hardware-specific workaround code.
  • Memory leaks in the heap.
  • DMA buffers overflowing into the stack.
Explanation: A leaky abstraction exposes implementation details (like requiring callers to pause for 5 ms after an EEPROM write), defeating the purpose of hardware independence.
9. In MISRA-C:2012, what rule governs function pointer casting?
  • Function pointers may be freely cast to void *.
  • A function pointer shall not be converted to any type other than an integral type or a pointer to a function of compatible signature (Rule 11.1).
  • Function pointers are completely forbidden.
  • Function pointers must always point to address 0.
Explanation: MISRA-C Rule 11.1 prohibits casting function pointers to object pointers (like void*) or incompatible signatures, preventing undefined branching behavior.
10. When should an architect prefer static compile-time interface binding (via linking or header aliasing) over runtime vtables?
  • When the system has more than 16 MB of Flash.
  • When the product hardware is fixed at build time and zero indirect call overhead or maximum compiler inlining is required for high-frequency control loops.
  • When using C++ instead of C.
  • Static binding is never used in embedded systems.
Explanation: If a board will only ever have one specific ADC chip, binding the interface at compile-time allows the compiler to inline driver calls with zero indirect branch overhead.

22.6 Hands-On Engineering Laboratories

Execute these 5 laboratory assignments to master opaque handles, vtables, and hardware decoupling in embedded C.

Assignment 1: Opaque Handle Refactoring

Task: Take a UART driver where struct Uart_t is currently exposed in uart.h. Refactor the header to declare an opaque handle typedef struct UartInstance_t* UartHandle_t;. Move the struct definition into uart.c. Verify that attempting to access struct fields in main.c produces a compile-time "dereferencing pointer to incomplete type" error.

Assignment 2: Polymorphic Digital Temperature Sensor API

Task: Create an abstract TemperatureSensor_t interface with a vtable: init(), read_mdegc(). Implement two concrete drivers: (1) An I2C sensor driver (e.g. LM75) and (2) An SPI sensor driver (e.g. MAX31855). Write application code that logs temperature from either sensor interchangeably.

Assignment 3: Host PC Mock Storage Unit Test

Task: Implement the StorageInterface_t and mock_storage_create() from Program 22.2 and 22.3. Write a host-based Unity test suite that writes a telemetry packet, re-reads it, verifies CRC checksums, and tests boundary errors without any physical target microcontroller.

Assignment 4: Function Pointer Call Overhead Measurement

Task: Write a benchmark comparing direct function calls versus indirect vtable calls. Use the ARM Cortex-M DWT->CYCCNT cycle counter to measure the exact execution duration of 1,000,000 iterations of both approaches. Calculate the precise CPU cycle overhead per indirect call.

Assignment 5: Dependency Inversion Architecture Audit

Task: Inspect an existing firmware repository. Draw the module dependency graph. Identify any instances where high-level application modules directly include vendor register headers (e.g. #include <stm32f4xx.h>). Refactor the dependency using an abstract Hardware Abstraction Layer (HAL) interface.

Official References, Research Papers & Standards

Deepen your engineering foundation with canonical publications and official standard specifications:

Classic Architecture David R. Hanson

C Interfaces and Implementations (Chapter 2: Interfaces)

Authoritative guide on constructing opaque abstract data types, handles, and clean contract boundaries in ANSI C.

View Official Resource →
Engineering Standard Robert C. Martin

The Dependency Inversion Principle (DIP)

Foundational paper explaining why architectural abstractions must isolate high-level business rules from low-level I/O.

View Official Resource →
Coding Guidelines Barr Group

Embedded C Coding Standard: Information Hiding & Interfaces

Rules mandating encapsulation of driver hardware details behind procedural and opaque pointer interfaces.

fields.title: Topic 23: Reusable Components
fields.content:
Topic 23

Reusable Software Components in Embedded C

In typical embedded engineering organizations, firmware developers reinvent the wheel on every project: rewriting circular ring buffers, button debouncers, CRC generators, and packet parsers from scratch. Invariably, subtle race conditions, off-by-one errors, and buffer overflow bugs are reintroduced each time.

A Reusable Embedded Component is a hardened, self-contained software module designed to operate seamlessly across different microcontroller families (ARM Cortex-M, RISC-V, AVR, ESP32) and host test environments. It enforces zero reliance on dynamic memory allocation, operates without global variables, and achieves mathematical reentrancy.

23.1 The 4 Laws of Reusable Firmware Architecture

For a C component to achieve true portability and reusability, it must strictly comply with four architectural rules:

Figure 23.1: The Four Pillars of Reusable Embedded Component Design

23.2 Canonical Component 1: The Lock-Free SPSC Ring Buffer

A Circular Ring Buffer is the primary data structure bridging asynchronous hardware Interrupt Service Routines (ISRs) to background superloop tasks.

Power-of-Two Masking Optimization

Standard ring buffers compute index advancement using the modulo operator: head = (head + 1) % capacity. On microcontroller cores lacking hardware integer division (such as ARM Cortex-M0 and Cortex-M0+), integer division requires an expensive software runtime routine consuming 40 to 80 CPU clock cycles!

By enforcing that buffer capacity is strictly a power of two ($2^N$), modulo division is replaced by a lightning-fast bitwise AND operation executing in 1 single clock cycle:

index = (index + 1U) & (capacity - 1U); /* Power of Two Optimization */

Production Implementation (MISRA-Compliant)

/* ring_buffer.h */
#ifndef RING_BUFFER_H
#define RING_BUFFER_H

#include <stdint.h>
#include <stddef.h>
#include <stdbool.h>

typedef struct {
    uint8_t *p_buffer;
    size_t   capacity;
    size_t   mask;
    volatile size_t head; /* Modified only by Producer */
    volatile size_t tail; /* Modified only by Consumer */
} RingBuffer_t;

typedef enum {
    RING_BUF_OK = 0,
    RING_BUF_ERR_NULL_PTR,
    RING_BUF_ERR_INVALID_SIZE,
    RING_BUF_FULL,
    RING_BUF_EMPTY
} RingBufStatus_t;

RingBufStatus_t ring_buffer_init(RingBuffer_t * const p_rb, uint8_t * const p_storage, const size_t capacity);
RingBufStatus_t ring_buffer_put(RingBuffer_t * const p_rb, const uint8_t data);
RingBufStatus_t ring_buffer_get(RingBuffer_t * const p_rb, uint8_t * const p_data);
size_t          ring_buffer_get_count(const RingBuffer_t * const p_rb);
bool            ring_buffer_is_empty(const RingBuffer_t * const p_rb);
bool            ring_buffer_is_full(const RingBuffer_t * const p_rb);

#endif /* RING_BUFFER_H */
Program 23.1: Reusable SPSC Ring Buffer Header Interface
/* ring_buffer.c */
#include "ring_buffer.h"

static bool is_power_of_two(const size_t val) {
    return ((val > 0U) && ((val & (val - 1U)) == 0U));
}

RingBufStatus_t ring_buffer_init(
    RingBuffer_t * const p_rb, 
    uint8_t * const      p_storage, 
    const size_t         capacity) 
{
    if ((p_rb == NULL) || (p_storage == NULL)) {
        return RING_BUF_ERR_NULL_PTR;
    }
    if (!is_power_of_two(capacity)) {
        return RING_BUF_ERR_INVALID_SIZE;
    }

    p_rb->p_buffer = p_storage;
    p_rb->capacity = capacity;
    p_rb->mask     = capacity - 1U;
    p_rb->head     = 0U;
    p_rb->tail     = 0U;

    return RING_BUF_OK;
}

RingBufStatus_t ring_buffer_put(RingBuffer_t * const p_rb, const uint8_t data) {
    if (p_rb == NULL) return RING_BUF_ERR_NULL_PTR;

    const size_t current_head = p_rb->head;
    const size_t next_head = (current_head + 1U) & p_rb->mask;

    /* If next head reaches tail, buffer is full */
    if (next_head == p_rb->tail) {
        return RING_BUF_FULL;
    }

    p_rb->p_buffer[current_head] = data;
    __DMB(); /* ARM Cortex Data Memory Barrier ensures data write finishes */
    p_rb->head = next_head;

    return RING_BUF_OK;
}

RingBufStatus_t ring_buffer_get(RingBuffer_t * const p_rb, uint8_t * const p_data) {
    if ((p_rb == NULL) || (p_data == NULL)) return RING_BUF_ERR_NULL_PTR;

    const size_t current_tail = p_rb->tail;

    /* If tail equals head, buffer is empty */
    if (current_tail == p_rb->head) {
        return RING_BUF_EMPTY;
    }

    *p_data = p_rb->p_buffer[current_tail];
    __DMB();
    p_rb->tail = (current_tail + 1U) & p_rb->mask;

    return RING_BUF_OK;
}
Program 23.2: Lock-Free Single-Producer Single-Consumer FIFO Implementation

Single-Producer Single-Consumer (SPSC) Lock-Free Safety

In Program 23.2, the Producer (e.g. UART RX ISR) only modifies head and only reads tail. The Consumer (e.g. main loop) only modifies tail and only reads head. Because 32-bit aligned reads and writes are atomic on ARM Cortex-M processors and memory barriers (__DMB()) prevent CPU pipeline reordering, no critical section (disabling interrupts) is required!

23.3 Canonical Component 2: Hardware-Agnostic CRC-16 Engine

Data integrity verification over communication links (UART, SPI, CAN) requires Cyclic Redundancy Checks (CRC). Below is a fast table-driven CRC-16-CCITT ($x^{16} + x^{12} + x^5 + 1$) engine: 

#include <stdint.h>
#include <stddef.h>

/* 256-word Lookup Table in Flash ROM (.rodata) */
static const uint16_t s_crc16_table[256] = {
    0x0000U, 0x1021U, 0x2042U, 0x3063U, 0x4084U, 0x50A5U, 0x60C6U, 0x70E7U,
    0x8108U, 0x9129U, 0xA14AU, 0xB16BU, 0xC18CU, 0xD1ADU, 0xE1CEU, 0xF1EFU,
    /* ... 240 additional precomputed polynomial coefficients ... */
};

uint16_t crc16_ccitt_compute(
    const uint8_t * const p_data, 
    const size_t          len_bytes, 
    uint16_t              seed) 
{
    if (p_data == NULL) return 0U;

    uint16_t crc = seed;
    for (size_t i = 0; i < len_bytes; ++i) {
        const uint8_t tbl_idx = (uint8_t)((crc >> 8) ^ p_data[i]);
        crc = (uint16_t)((crc << 8) ^ s_crc16_table[tbl_idx]);
    }

    return crc;
}
Program 23.3: High-Speed Reusable CRC-16 Calculation Engine

23.4 Canonical Component 3: Parallel Bit-Shift Debouncer

Mechanical push buttons bounce for 5 to 20 ms. While novice code uses blocking delays, a professional reusable debouncer uses an 8-bit shift register integrator sampled periodically (e.g. every 5 ms): 

#include <stdint.h>
#include <stdbool.h>

typedef struct {
    uint8_t shift_reg;
    bool    stable_state;
    bool    edge_pressed;
    bool    edge_released;
} DebounceChannel_t;

void debouncer_update(DebounceChannel_t * const p_btn, const bool raw_pin_level) {
    if (p_btn == NULL) return;

    /* Shift history and insert latest raw physical sample */
    p_btn->shift_reg = (uint8_t)((p_btn->shift_reg << 1) | (raw_pin_level ? 1U : 0U));

    /* Reset edge flags */
    p_btn->edge_pressed  = false;
    p_btn->edge_released = false;

    /* 8 consecutive identical samples confirm state transition */
    if ((p_btn->shift_reg == 0xFFU) && (!p_btn->stable_state)) {
        p_btn->stable_state  = true;
        p_btn->edge_pressed  = true;  /* Clean debounced rising edge */
    } else if ((p_btn->shift_reg == 0x00U) && (p_btn->stable_state)) {
        p_btn->stable_state  = false;
        p_btn->edge_released = true; /* Clean debounced falling edge */
    }
}
Program 23.4: Reusable Shift-Register Debounce Engine

23.5 Code Comparison: Hardcoded vs. Reusable Component

Compare a hardcoded UART ring buffer with a reusable, multi-instance component.

Compare Architecture: Circular Buffer Implementation

❌ Hardcoded & Non-Reusable

/* Fixed buffer inside C file */
static uint8_t buf[100];
static int head = 0;
static int tail = 0;

void uart_put(uint8_t c) {
    /* Slow division modulo */
    head = (head + 1) % 100;
    buf[head] = c;
}

Flaws: Cannot be reused for UART2 or SPI (only 1 global instance exists). Uses slow division modulo. Fixed 100-byte size cannot be adjusted without editing driver code.

✔ Reusable Multi-Instance Component

/* Unlimited instances; caller injects storage */
RingBuffer_t uart1_rb;
RingBuffer_t uart2_rb;
uint8_t mem1[256];
uint8_t mem2[64];

ring_buffer_init(&uart1_rb, mem1, 256);
ring_buffer_init(&uart2_rb, mem2, 64);

ring_buffer_put(&uart1_rb, 0x55);
ring_buffer_put(&uart2_rb, 0xAA);

Safety: Supports multiple independent channels, zero heap allocation, power-of-two bitwise masking, verified lock-free reentrancy.

23.6 Interactive Knowledge Check

Test your understanding of reusable embedded components, buffer math, and reentrant data structures.

1. Why should circular ring buffer capacities always be sized to a power of two (e.g. 64, 128, 256)?
  • Because silicon Flash sectors are always 64 bytes.
  • It allows replacing slow software integer division modulo (%) with a 1-cycle bitwise AND operation: (idx + 1) & (cap - 1).
  • Because C compilers reject arrays that are not powers of two.
  • To enable DMA burst transfers of 1024 bytes.
Explanation: On Cortex-M0/M0+ cores without a hardware divide instruction, modulo % requires a multi-cycle subroutine. Bitwise masking executes in 1 clock cycle.
2. What does "Storage Injection" mean in reusable component design?
  • Writing directly to external SD cards.
  • The component allocates no internal buffers or heap; instead, the caller passes an allocated memory buffer and size during initialization.
  • Injecting SQL queries into EEPROM.
  • Using the linker script to erase RAM.
Explanation: Storage injection allows the caller to determine buffer sizing and memory placement (e.g. fast DTCM RAM vs slow external SRAM) without modifying component code.
3. In a lock-free Single-Producer Single-Consumer (SPSC) ring buffer, why are mutexes or interrupt disables unnecessary?
  • Because Cortex-M CPUs execute all code in parallel.
  • Because the Producer only modifies head and only reads tail, while the Consumer only modifies tail and only reads head, with atomic 32-bit index access.
  • Because interrupts are automatically masked by the C preprocessor.
  • Ring buffers are never used in interrupts.
Explanation: SPSC separation ensures neither context ever writes to the other's pointer, eliminating write races and avoiding expensive interrupt disabling.
4. What is the role of the ARM __DMB() (Data Memory Barrier) instruction inside the ring buffer put and get functions?
  • To flush the display screen.
  • To ensure that payload data is completely written into memory before the index pointer is updated and observed by the other context.
  • To clear the watchdog timer.
  • To put the CPU into deep sleep.
Explanation: Out-of-order execution or write buffering could update the head pointer before the byte is physically written to RAM. __DMB() enforces strict memory ordering.
5. How many distinct switch press events does an 8-bit shift register debouncer require before confirming a state change?
  • 1 sample.
  • 8 consecutive identical samples (register equals 0xFF for press, 0x00 for release).
  • 256 samples.
  • Exactly 1000 samples.
Explanation: Shifting pin states into an 8-bit register requires 8 consecutive high samples (0xFF) to accept a press, cleanly rejecting contact chatter.
6. What is the primary difference between a checksum (like Fletcher-16) and a CRC (like CRC-16)?
  • Checksums are 64-bit; CRCs are 8-bit.
  • CRCs use polynomial division, providing superior mathematical detection of burst bit errors compared to additive checksums.
  • Checksums can only be computed in hardware.
  • CRCs require floating point math.
Explanation: CRCs treat data as binary polynomial coefficients, providing strong guarantees against burst noise errors common in industrial electrical environments.
7. Why must reusable C components avoid defining variables with static storage duration inside functions?
  • Because static variables are placed in Flash ROM.
  • Function-local static variables make the function non-reentrant, preventing multiple instances from functioning independently.
  • Because the GCC compiler deletes static local variables.
  • To reduce MCU clock speed.
Explanation: A local static variable is shared across all callers. If two instances call the function, they corrupt each other's state.
8. What framing technique replaces delimiter bytes (like 0x00) with offset pointers to guarantee zero-overhead packet demarcation?
  • Base64 encoding.
  • Consistent Overhead Byte Stuffing (COBS).
  • Manchester encoding.
  • RSA encryption.
Explanation: COBS encodes packets so that byte 0x00 never appears inside the payload, allowing 0x00 to serve as an unambiguous end-of-packet delimiter with minimal overhead.
9. In the ring buffer in Program 23.2, why is one slot reserved as empty (usable capacity is $N - 1$)?
  • To store the buffer checksum.
  • To unambiguously distinguish between the buffer being completely EMPTY (head == tail) and completely FULL ((head + 1) == tail).
  • To prevent stack collisions.
  • Because ARM architecture requires odd memory addresses.
Explanation: Without an explicit count variable, reserving one empty slot differentiates the empty condition (head == tail) from the full condition.
10. How should a reusable component report operational errors to the caller?
  • By printing error text directly to the UART console.
  • By returning an explicit enumeration status code (e.g. STATUS_OK, STATUS_FULL) allowing the caller to decide the recovery policy.
  • By calling exit(1).
  • By asserting a hardware CPU reset.
Explanation: A library component must never dictate recovery policy or assume a UART console exists; it must return typed status codes to the calling application.

23.7 Hands-On Engineering Laboratories

Execute these 5 laboratory assignments to construct a verified repository of reusable embedded firmware components.

Assignment 1: Multi-Channel Ring Buffer Stress Harness

Task: Instantiate four independent ring buffers (sizes: 16, 64, 128, 512 bytes). Write a host test program with two threads (one simulated ISR producer, one background consumer) pushing and pulling 10,000,000 random bytes. Verify zero data corruption, zero lost bytes, and correct boundary flags.

Assignment 2: Bit-Parallel 8-Button Debounce Engine

Task: Implement vertical counter debouncing where an entire 8-bit GPIO port (8 mechanical pushbuttons) is sampled and debounced simultaneously in parallel using bitwise logic (AND, OR, XOR) in less than 10 CPU clock cycles.

Assignment 3: CRC-16 Table Generator & Benchmark

Task: Write a C utility that generates the 256-entry lookup table for the CRC-16-CCITT polynomial and outputs it as formatted C code. Benchmark the table-driven algorithm against bit-by-bit calculation on an ARM microcontroller and record the execution speedup.

Assignment 4: Reusable COBS Packet Framer

Task: Implement a pair of reusable functions: cobs_encode(dst, src, len) and cobs_decode(dst, src, len). Verify with test packets containing arbitrary binary data (including multiple 0x00 bytes) and confirm that encoded frames are cleanly separated by 0x00 delimiters.

Assignment 5: Fixed-Block Memory Pool Allocator

Task: Build a reusable, deterministic block pool manager: pool_init(pool, storage, block_size, num_blocks), pool_alloc(pool), and pool_free(pool, p_block). Guarantee $O(1)$ constant allocation time, zero fragmentation, and MISRA-C Rule 21.3 compliance.
