fields.title: Ref 4: 20 Industrial Architectures
fields.content:
Engineering Reference 4

20 Mission-Critical Real-World Embedded Architectures

Below is an exhaustive engineering compendium profiling 20 real-world devices across four core industrial verticals: Automotive & Transportation, Medical & Healthcare, Industrial Automation & Smart Grid, and Aerospace & Connected IoT.

Domain 1: Automotive & Transportation

1. Engine Control Unit (ECU) — ISO 26262 ASIL D

Regulates direct fuel injection and ignition spark timing relative to top-dead-center piston position.

  • Silicon: Infineon AURIX TC397 (Triple 300 MHz TriCore in lock-step) or NXP S32S24.
  • Sensors: Hall crankshaft 60-2 tooth input capture, cam phase, wideband O2, MAP, knock sensors.
  • Actuators: 65V peak-and-hold GDI direct fuel injectors, ignition coils, electronic throttle H-bridge.
  • Real-Time Constraint: Spark pulse timing determinism within ±10 μs at 7,000 RPM.

2. Anti-Lock Braking (ABS) & Electronic Stability (ESC) — ISO 26262 ASIL D

Modulates individual wheel hydraulic brake line pressure to counteract skidding and wheel lockup.

  • Silicon: TI TMS570LS3137 (Dual Cortex-R4F lock-step) + redundant supervisor IC.
  • Sensors: 4× active magneto-resistive wheel speed sensors, central 6-DoF yaw rate IMU, steering angle.
  • Actuators: 12× high-speed hydraulic solenoid valves, 40A brushless hydraulic return pump.
  • Real-Time Constraint: Main slip control cycle executes at 100 Hz (10 ms); 3 ms valve response.

3. EV High-Voltage Battery Management System (BMS) — ISO 26262 ASIL C/D

Monitors 800V pack cell voltages, temperatures, SoC/SoH, and activates safety disconnect contactors.

  • Silicon: NXP S32K344 + daisy-chained TI BQ79616 / ADI ADBMS6815 isoSPI AFEs.
  • Sensors: 96–192 cell voltage monitors (±1 mV), 40+ NTC thermistors, isolated fluxgate current transducer.
  • Actuators: Pyro-fuse emergency disconnect trigger, 800V DC vacuum contactors, cell balancing MOSFETs.
  • Real-Time Constraint: Short-circuit trip contactor disconnect within 2 milliseconds.

4. 77 GHz ADAS Radar / Camera Perception Fusion Unit — ISO 26262 ASIL B/D

Fuses millimeter-wave radar point clouds and HDR optical video for Autonomous Emergency Braking (AEB).

  • Silicon: TI AWR2944 (77 GHz Transceiver + 4× Cortex-R5F + FFT Engine) + NXP S32G3.
  • Sensors: 4Tx/4Rx 77 GHz radar channels, 8-Megapixel automotive HDR CMOS sensor over MIPI CSI-2.
  • Actuators: Windshield defrost heater, CAN-FD / 100BASE-T1 Ethernet brake command packet dispatch.
  • Real-Time Constraint: Radar chirp-sequence FFT processing within 50 milliseconds per frame.

5. Digital Cockpit Domain Controller & Cluster — ISO 26262 ASIL B

Renders safety-critical warning telltales alongside Android Automotive OS infotainment.

  • Silicon: NXP i.MX 8M QuadMax (Linux/Android) + dedicated Cortex-M4F safety cluster core.
  • Sensors: Dual CAN-FD buses (speed, battery, gear), ambient cabin light photo-sensor.
  • Actuators: Dual 4K MIPI DSI displays, haptic touch console drivers, audio chime amplifier.
  • Real-Time Constraint: Safety cluster telltales must render within 1,200 ms of vehicle unlock.

Domain 2: Medical & Healthcare Devices

6. Implantable Cardiac Pacemaker — IEC 62304 Class C

Monitors intrinsic cardiac depolarizations and delivers calibrated pacing pulses under bradycardia.

  • Silicon: Custom ultra-low-power ASIC containing ARM Cortex-M0+ (<2 μA total current).
  • Sensors: Sub-mV intracardiac lead electrodes, 3-axis accelerometer for rate-adaptive exercise pacing.
  • Actuators: Capacitive multiplier delivering 0.5V–5V stimulation pulses across myocardial leads.
  • Real-Time Constraint: ±2 ms pacing timing accuracy; 10+ year battery lifespan on 1.2 Ah cell.

7. Insulin Patch Pump & Continuous Glucose Monitor (CGM) — IEC 62304 Class C

Measures interstitial glucose every 5 minutes and dispenses micro-units of insulin automatically.

  • Silicon: Nordic nRF52840 (Cortex-M4F + BLE 5.3) + TI MSP430FR safety supervisor MCU.
  • Sensors: Enzymatic glucose-oxidase potentiostat probe, syringe lead-screw occlusion strain gauge.
  • Actuators: Piezoelectric micro-pump or precision stepper motor delivering 0.025-microliter doses.
  • Real-Time Constraint: 500 ms independent dual-core verification of dose before motor enablement.

8. Critical Care ICU Mechanical Ventilator — IEC 62304 Class C

Maintains patient respiration through closed-loop airway pressure and volume regulation.

  • Silicon: Dual STM32H743 (480 MHz Cortex-M7: Control + Safety) + NXP i.MX 8M for touch GUI.
  • Sensors: Dual differential pressure mass flow sensors, proximal airway piezoresistive sensor, O2 analyzer.
  • Actuators: High-speed voice-coil inspiratory valve, brushless blower turbine, proportional PEEP valve.
  • Real-Time Constraint: 1 ms closed-loop PID budget; 5 ms emergency overpressure relief valve clamp.

9. Hospital Syringe Infusion Pump — IEC 62304 Class C

Administers intravenous medications with nanoliter precision over extended therapy durations.

  • Silicon: STM32F407 (168 MHz Cortex-M4F) + TI MSP430FR5969 diverse safety supervisor.
  • Sensors: Optical rotary encoder on lead screw, force load cell (occlusion), ultrasonic bubble detector.
  • Actuators: Bipolar microstepping motor (Trinamic TMC2209), emergency solenoid pinch clamp.
  • Real-Time Constraint: 4 ms motor shutdown and tube clamp trigger upon ultrasonic bubble detection.

10. Multi-Parameter Bedside Patient Monitor — IEC 62304 Class B/C

Continuously acquires and processes 12-lead ECG, pulse oximetry SpO2, and NIBP blood pressure.

  • Silicon: ADI ADAS1000 ECG AFE + STM32F767 + TI Sitara AM6254 (Embedded Linux host).
  • Sensors: Isolated defibrillator-proof ECG leads (5 kV), optical finger probe, NIBP cuff pressure transducer.
  • Actuators: NIBP inflation air pump and deflation valves, isolated clinical alarm speaker.
  • Real-Time Constraint: 20 ms QRS-complex detection to flag ventricular fibrillation and sound audible alarm.

Domain 3: Industrial Automation & Smart Grid

11. Modular Industrial PLC — IEC 61508 SIL 3

Ruggedized logic controller executing cyclic ladder logic routines in harsh industrial plants.

  • Silicon: TI Sitara AM6442 (Dual Cortex-A53 + 4× Cortex-R5F real-time fieldbus cores).
  • Sensors: Optoisolated 24V DC inputs (IEC 61131-2 Type 1/3), 4-20mA current loop ADCs, RTDs.
  • Actuators: 24V solid-state high-side protected switches (ST VN808), EtherCAT / PROFINET slaves.
  • Real-Time Constraint: 1.0 ms jitter-free cyclic scan time across 256 digital and analog I/O points.

12. Industrial Variable Frequency Drive (VFD) — IEC 61800-5-2 SIL 3

Regulates torque, velocity, and flux in 3-phase AC industrial motors with high energy efficiency.

  • Silicon: TI C2000 TMS320F28388D (Dual 200 MHz DSPs with TMU) + Cortex-M4 comms core.
  • Sensors: 3-phase current sensing via isolated delta-sigma modulators (AMC1306), DC bus voltage, resolver.
  • Actuators: 6× isolated gate drivers switching 1200V SiC MOSFETs/IGBTs with hardware dead-time.
  • Real-Time Constraint: 62.5 μs FOC current loop calculation budget (16 kHz Space-Vector PWM).

13. Smart Grid Electricity Meter (AMI) — ANSI C12.20 Class 0.2

Measures active/reactive energy with revenue-grade metrology, reporting over NB-IoT / RF mesh.

  • Silicon: Microchip SAM4Cx (Dual Cortex-M4: Metrology + App) or ADE9000 + STM32L4.
  • Sensors: Rogowski coils / Current Transformers (CT), precision voltage dividers, tamper Hall switches.
  • Actuators: 100A bistable latching disconnect relay, calibration pulse LED, cellular NB-IoT modem.
  • Real-Time Constraint: 8.0 kHz simultaneous voltage/current sampling for true RMS power factor calculation.

14. Substation Digital Protection Relay — IEC 61850 / IEC 60255

Monitors 3-phase high-voltage power lines and commands circuit breakers to trip on electrical faults.

  • Silicon: NXP QorIQ P2020 / Xilinx Zynq UltraScale+ with hardware IEEE 1588 PTP.
  • Sensors: 16-bit simultaneous ADCs sampling PT and CT secondaries, arc-flash fiber sensors.
  • Actuators: High-speed 10A 250VDC tripping output relays, redundant optical fiber transceivers.
  • Real-Time Constraint: 15 ms fault identification and trip pulse; <3 ms IEC 61850 GOOSE network dispatch.

15. Autonomous Mobile Robot (AMR) — ISO 3691-4 SIL 2

Hauls 1,000 kg warehouse pallets autonomously, avoiding humans and navigating dynamic aisles.

  • Silicon: NVIDIA Jetson Orin Nano (Perception & SLAM) + STM32G474 (Motor & Safety Real-Time).
  • Sensors: Dual 2D safety laser scanners (LiDAR), 3D depth cameras, wheel quadrature magnetic encoders.
  • Actuators: Dual 48V 30A brushless hub motors, fail-safe spring-applied electromagnetic holding brakes.
  • Real-Time Constraint: 20 ms emergency stop brake engagement upon safety LiDAR zone breach.

Domain 4: Aerospace, Energy & Connected IoT

16. Quadcopter Flight Controller & Autopilot — DO-178C DAL B

Stabilizes multi-rotor drone attitude in high winds and executes autonomous waypoint missions.

  • Silicon: STM32H753 (480 MHz Cortex-M7 with DP-FPU running PX4 on NuttX RTOS).
  • Sensors: Dual redundant vibration-isolated 6-DoF SPI IMUs (ICM-42688-P), barometer, magnetometer, RTK GPS.
  • Actuators: 4–8× DShot600 digital ESC communication channels with bidirectional RPM telemetry.
  • Real-Time Constraint: 125 μs total loop latency budget (8.0 kHz gyro sampling, EKF, and PID loop).

17. CubeSat On-Board Computer (OBC) — NASA Class D / ECSS

Manages attitude determination, power distribution, and telemetry for nanosatellites in Low Earth Orbit.

  • Silicon: Radiation-tolerant Microchip SAMV71Q21RT (300 MHz Cortex-M7 with ECC) + redundant FRAM.
  • Sensors: Sun sensors, 3-axis magnetometers, CMOS star tracker imaging sensor, thermistors.
  • Actuators: 3-axis reaction wheel brushless motors, magnetorquer electromagnetic torque coils.
  • Real-Time Constraint: Continuous Triple Modular Redundancy (TMR) memory scrubbing for single-event upsets.

18. Solar Grid-Tie Microinverter with MPPT — IEEE 1547 / UL 1741 SA

Extracts maximum photovoltaic power and converts DC into 240V AC with anti-islanding safety.

  • Silicon: TI C2000 TMS320F280049C (100 MHz real-time DSP with internal PGAs and comparators).
  • Sensors: PV input voltage/current sensors, AC grid zero-crossing comparator, grid PLL phase tracker.
  • Actuators: High-voltage GaN HEMT full-bridge inverter gate drivers (100 kHz), grid disconnect relay.
  • Real-Time Constraint: 100 ms anti-islanding shutdown upon utility grid loss to protect line workers.

19. Advanced Biometric Health Smartwatch — FDA 510(k) De Novo

Monitors continuous cardiovascular vitals, ECG atrial fibrillation, and sleep staging with 14-day battery life.

  • Silicon: Ambiq Apollo4 Blue Plus (Cortex-M4F @ 4 μA/MHz) + Nordic nRF5340 wireless core.
  • Sensors: Multi-wavelength optical PPG bio-sensor, titanium bezel ECG electrode, skin temp, 6-axis IMU.
  • Actuators: Linear Resonant Actuator (LRA) driven by TI DRV2605L, 1.4-inch round AMOLED MIPI display.
  • Real-Time Constraint: 99.2% of operating life spent in deep sleep at 15 μA, waking up only via DMA interrupts.

20. Commercial 350 kW EV DC Ultra-Fast Charger — IEC 61851-23 / ISO 15118

Delivers 500 Amperes at 800 Volts to recharge electric vehicles in 15 minutes with liquid-cooled cables.

  • Silicon: NXP i.MX 8M Nano (ISO 15118 Powerline Comms & OCPP 2.0.1) + STM32H723 power controller.
  • Sensors: 1,000V DC bus voltage transducers, 600A Hall current transducers, cable coolant PT1000s, insulation monitor.
  • Actuators: 500A rated DC contactor drivers, motorized plug locking pin, variable-speed coolant pumps.
  • Real-Time Constraint: 100 ms cable discharge to <60V upon insulation breakdown or pilot signal loss.

fields.title: Ref 5: Standards & Protocols
fields.content:
Engineering Reference 5

Standards, Protocols & Datasheets Compendium

Writing safety-critical Embedded C requires adhering to international regulatory frameworks and standard communication bus protocols. This compendium summarizes the governing functional safety standards, hardware communication physical layers, and semiconductor documentation.

5.1 International Functional Safety Standards

Standard Industry Domain Safety Integrity Classification Core Firmware Mandates
ISO 26262 Road Vehicles (Automotive) ASIL A, B, C, D (D = Highest) Strict MISRA-C compliance, 100% MC/DC test coverage, hardware lockstep, safe state transitions.
IEC 62304 Medical Device Software Class A (No injury), B (Non-serious), C (Death/Serious injury) Static memory allocation (no heap), strict requirement-to-test traceability, defensive architecture.
IEC 61508 Industrial Functional Safety SIL 1, SIL 2, SIL 3, SIL 4 Dual-channel redundancy (1oo2 / 2oo3), diagnostic coverage >99%, hardware watchdog timer supervision.
DO-178C Commercial & Military Aviation DAL A (Catastrophic) down to DAL E (No effect) Exhaustive requirements verification, zero dead code, object-code to source-code traceability for Level A.
IEEE 1547 / UL 1741 Solar & Grid Energy Inverters Category I, II, III (Grid ride-through) Anti-islanding disconnection in <100 ms, frequency and voltage disturbance trip curves.

5.2 Embedded Communication Bus Protocol Comparison

Bus Protocol Physical Layer & Wiring Maximum Throughput Maximum Reach Key Strengths & Primary Use Case
SPI (Serial Peripheral Interface) 4-Wire synchronous (SCK, MOSI, MISO, CS#) 10 MHz – 80+ MHz < 30 cm (On-board PCB) Ultra-fast full-duplex streaming with zero protocol overhead; perfect for IMUs and Flash memory.
I2C / I3C 2-Wire open-drain with pull-ups (SCL, SDA) 100 kHz (Std), 400 kHz (Fast), 12.5 MHz (I3C) < 50 cm (On-board PCB) Multi-device addressing on 2 shared pins; standard for temperature, barometers, and EEPROMs.
CAN 2.0B / CAN-FD Differential twisted-pair (CAN_H, CAN_L, 120Ω termination) 1.0 Mbps (CAN 2.0B), 5.0–8.0 Mbps (CAN-FD) 40 meters (at 1 Mbps) to 1,000 m (at 50 kbps) Hardware arbitration, differential noise rejection, CRC check; universal automotive standard.
Automotive Ethernet Single unshielded twisted-pair (100BASE-T1 / 1000BASE-T1) 100 Mbps – 1.0 Gbps 15 meters High-bandwidth point-to-point IP data for ADAS radar, cameras, and domain controllers.
RS-485 / Modbus Differential pair (A, B) with multi-drop transceivers 10 Mbps (short distance) or 115.2 kbps Up to 1,200 meters Immunity to industrial ground loops and electrical factory noise; standard for PLCs and smart meters.

fields.title: Visualize Execution: The Complete STM32 Firmware Journey
fields.content:
<style>
        :root {
            --bg-deep: #070b14;
            --bg-card: #0f172a;
            --bg-card-hover: #17223b;
            --bg-input: #1e293b;
            --border-color: #243552;
            --border-highlight: #38bdf8;
            --text-main: #f1f5f9;
            --text-muted: #94a3b8;
            --text-dim: #64748b;
            
            --blue: #38bdf8;
            --blue-glow: rgba(56, 189, 248, 0.25);
            --green: #10b981;
            --green-glow: rgba(16, 185, 129, 0.25);
            --amber: #f59e0b;
            --amber-glow: rgba(245, 158, 11, 0.25);
            --red: #ef4444;
            --red-glow: rgba(239, 68, 68, 0.25);
            --purple: #a855f7;
            --purple-glow: rgba(168, 85, 247, 0.25);
            --cyan: #06b6d4;

            --font-sans: system-ui, -apple-system, BlinkMacSystemFont, "Segoe UI", Roboto, "Helvetica Neue", Arial, sans-serif;
            --font-mono: "Fira Code", SFMono-Regular, Menlo, Monaco, Consolas, "Liberation Mono", monospace;
        }

        [data-theme="light"] {
            --bg-deep: #f8fafc;
            --bg-card: #ffffff;
            --bg-card-hover: #f1f5f9;
            --bg-input: #e2e8f0;
            --border-color: #cbd5e1;
            --border-highlight: #0284c7;
            --text-main: #0f172a;
            --text-muted: #475569;
            --text-dim: #64748b;
            --blue-glow: rgba(2, 132, 199, 0.15);
            --green-glow: rgba(16, 185, 129, 0.15);
            --amber-glow: rgba(217, 119, 6, 0.15);
            --red-glow: rgba(220, 38, 38, 0.15);
            --purple-glow: rgba(147, 51, 234, 0.15);
        }

        * {
            box-sizing: border-box;
            margin: 0;
            padding: 0;
        }

        body {
            background-color: var(--bg-deep);
            color: var(--text-main);
            font-family: var(--font-sans);
            line-height: 1.65;
            -webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;
            overflow-x: hidden;
        }

        a {
            color: var(--blue);
            text-decoration: none;
            transition: color 0.2s ease;
        }
        a:hover {
            text-decoration: underline;
        }

        /* Top Navigation Bar */
        .top-navbar {
            position: sticky;
            top: 0;
            z-index: 1000;
            background: rgba(15, 23, 42, 0.88);
            backdrop-filter: blur(12px);
            border-bottom: 1px solid var(--border-color);
            display: flex;
            align-items: center;
            justify-content: space-between;
            padding: 0.75rem 1.5rem;
        }
        [data-theme="light"] .top-navbar {
            background: rgba(255, 255, 255, 0.92);
        }

        .navbar-brand {
            display: flex;
            align-items: center;
            gap: 0.75rem;
            font-weight: 700;
            font-size: 1.1rem;
            color: var(--text-main);
        }
        .navbar-brand .mcu-chip {
            background: linear-gradient(135deg, #0284c7, #38bdf8);
            color: #fff;
            padding: 0.25rem 0.6rem;
            border-radius: 6px;
            font-family: var(--font-mono);
            font-size: 0.8rem;
            letter-spacing: 0.05em;
            box-shadow: 0 0 10px var(--blue-glow);
        }

        .nav-controls {
            display: flex;
            align-items: center;
            gap: 1rem;
        }

        .btn-toggle, .btn-action {
            background: var(--bg-card);
            border: 1px solid var(--border-color);
            color: var(--text-main);
            padding: 0.4rem 0.85rem;
            border-radius: 6px;
            cursor: pointer;
            font-size: 0.85rem;
            display: inline-flex;
            align-items: center;
            gap: 0.5rem;
            transition: all 0.2s ease;
        }
        .btn-toggle:hover, .btn-action:hover {
            border-color: var(--blue);
            box-shadow: 0 0 8px var(--blue-glow);
        }

        /* Course Back link */
        .back-to-course {
            font-size: 0.85rem;
            color: var(--text-muted);
            display: flex;
            align-items: center;
            gap: 0.35rem;
        }
        .back-to-course:hover {
            color: var(--blue);
        }

        /* Main Container Layout with Sticky Scenario Directory */
        .app-layout {
            display: grid;
            grid-template-columns: 280px 1fr;
            max-width: 1600px;
            margin: 0 auto;
            min-height: calc(100vh - 60px);
        }

        @media (max-width: 1024px) {
            .app-layout {
                grid-template-columns: 1fr;
            }
            .sidebar-nav {
                display: none;
            }
        }

        /* Sidebar Progress & Scenario Navigator */
        .sidebar-nav {
            position: sticky;
            top: 60px;
            height: calc(100vh - 60px);
            overflow-y: auto;
            background: var(--bg-card);
            border-right: 1px solid var(--border-color);
            padding: 1.25rem 1rem;
        }

        .sidebar-nav h3 {
            font-size: 0.75rem;
            text-transform: uppercase;
            letter-spacing: 0.08em;
            color: var(--text-dim);
            margin-bottom: 0.75rem;
        }

        .progress-bar-container {
            background: var(--bg-input);
            border-radius: 999px;
            height: 6px;
            width: 100%;
            margin-bottom: 1rem;
            overflow: hidden;
        }
        .progress-bar-fill {
            background: linear-gradient(90deg, var(--blue), var(--green));
            height: 100%;
            width: 5%;
            transition: width 0.3s ease;
        }

        .scenario-list {
            list-style: none;
            display: flex;
            flex-direction: column;
            gap: 0.25rem;
        }

        .scenario-item a {
            display: flex;
            align-items: center;
            gap: 0.5rem;
            padding: 0.5rem 0.75rem;
            border-radius: 6px;
            font-size: 0.82rem;
            color: var(--text-muted);
            text-decoration: none;
            transition: all 0.15s ease;
        }
        .scenario-item a:hover {
            background: var(--bg-card-hover);
            color: var(--blue);
        }
        .scenario-item.active a {
            background: var(--bg-card-hover);
            color: var(--blue);
            font-weight: 600;
            border-left: 3px solid var(--blue);
        }
        .scenario-item .badge {
            font-family: var(--font-mono);
            font-size: 0.7rem;
            opacity: 0.7;
            min-width: 1.5rem;
        }

        /* Main Content Container */
        .content-area {
            padding: 2.5rem 3.5rem;
            max-width: 1200px;
        }
        @media (max-width: 768px) {
            .content-area {
                padding: 1.5rem;
            }
        }

        /* Header Hero Banner */
        .hero-banner {
            background: radial-gradient(circle at top right, rgba(56, 189, 248, 0.15), transparent 70%),
                        linear-gradient(180deg, var(--bg-card) 0%, rgba(15, 23, 42, 0.4) 100%);
            border: 1px solid var(--border-color);
            border-radius: 14px;
            padding: 2.5rem;
            margin-bottom: 3rem;
            position: relative;
            overflow: hidden;
            box-shadow: 0 10px 25px rgba(0, 0, 0, 0.25);
        }
        .hero-tag {
            display: inline-flex;
            align-items: center;
            gap: 0.5rem;
            background: var(--blue-glow);
            border: 1px solid var(--blue);
            color: var(--blue);
            font-family: var(--font-mono);
            font-size: 0.75rem;
            font-weight: 600;
            text-transform: uppercase;
            letter-spacing: 0.05em;
            padding: 0.25rem 0.75rem;
            border-radius: 999px;
            margin-bottom: 1rem;
        }
        .hero-banner h1 {
            font-size: 2.4rem;
            line-height: 1.2;
            margin-bottom: 1rem;
            background: linear-gradient(135deg, #ffffff 30%, #94a3b8 100%);
            -webkit-background-clip: text;
            -webkit-text-fill-color: transparent;
        }
        [data-theme="light"] .hero-banner h1 {
            background: linear-gradient(135deg, #0f172a 30%, #334155 100%);
            -webkit-background-clip: text;
            -webkit-text-fill-color: transparent;
        }
        .hero-lead {
            font-size: 1.1rem;
            color: var(--text-muted);
            max-width: 900px;
            margin-bottom: 1.5rem;
        }
        .hero-badges {
            display: flex;
            flex-wrap: wrap;
            gap: 0.75rem;
        }
        .meta-pill {
            background: var(--bg-input);
            border: 1px solid var(--border-color);
            padding: 0.35rem 0.75rem;
            border-radius: 8px;
            font-size: 0.8rem;
            display: inline-flex;
            align-items: center;
            gap: 0.4rem;
            color: var(--text-muted);
        }
        .meta-pill strong {
            color: var(--text-main);
        }

        /* Scenario Card Architecture */
        .scenario-card {
            background: var(--bg-card);
            border: 1px solid var(--border-color);
            border-radius: 12px;
            padding: 2.25rem;
            margin-bottom: 3rem;
            scroll-margin-top: 80px;
            transition: border-color 0.2s ease, box-shadow 0.2s ease;
        }
        .scenario-card:hover {
            border-color: rgba(56, 189, 248, 0.4);
            box-shadow: 0 4px 20px rgba(0, 0, 0, 0.15);
        }

        .scenario-header {
            display: flex;
            align-items: flex-start;
            justify-content: space-between;
            gap: 1rem;
            margin-bottom: 1.25rem;
            border-bottom: 1px solid var(--border-color);
            padding-bottom: 1rem;
        }
        .scenario-num {
            background: var(--bg-input);
            border: 1px solid var(--border-color);
            color: var(--blue);
            font-family: var(--font-mono);
            font-weight: 700;
            font-size: 0.85rem;
            padding: 0.25rem 0.6rem;
            border-radius: 6px;
        }
        .scenario-title-area h2 {
            font-size: 1.55rem;
            color: var(--text-main);
            margin-bottom: 0.35rem;
        }
        .scenario-goal {
            font-size: 0.95rem;
            color: var(--blue);
            font-weight: 500;
        }

        /* 8-Element Scenario Sections */
        .grid-problem-observation {
            display: grid;
            grid-template-columns: 1fr 1fr;
            gap: 1.25rem;
            margin-bottom: 1.5rem;
        }
        @media (max-width: 768px) {
            .grid-problem-observation {
                grid-template-columns: 1fr;
            }
        }
        .box-sub {
            background: var(--bg-input);
            border: 1px solid var(--border-color);
            border-radius: 8px;
            padding: 1rem 1.25rem;
        }
        .box-sub h4 {
            font-size: 0.82rem;
            text-transform: uppercase;
            letter-spacing: 0.06em;
            margin-bottom: 0.4rem;
            display: flex;
            align-items: center;
            gap: 0.4rem;
        }
        .box-sub.problem h4 { color: var(--amber); }
        .box-sub.observation h4 { color: var(--cyan); }
        .box-sub.internal h4 { color: var(--purple); }

        .internal-box {
            background: rgba(168, 85, 247, 0.05);
            border-left: 3px solid var(--purple);
            padding: 1rem 1.25rem;
            border-radius: 0 8px 8px 0;
            margin-bottom: 1.5rem;
            font-size: 0.95rem;
        }
        .internal-box h4 {
            color: var(--purple);
            font-size: 0.85rem;
            text-transform: uppercase;
            letter-spacing: 0.05em;
            margin-bottom: 0.4rem;
        }

        /* Visual Workbench & Interactive Stage Display */
        .visual-display-area {
            background: #090d16;
            border: 1px solid var(--border-color);
            border-radius: 10px;
            padding: 1.5rem;
            margin-bottom: 1.75rem;
            position: relative;
        }
        [data-theme="light"] .visual-display-area {
            background: #f1f5f9;
        }

        .visual-header {
            display: flex;
            justify-content: space-between;
            align-items: center;
            margin-bottom: 1rem;
            padding-bottom: 0.5rem;
            border-bottom: 1px solid rgba(255, 255, 255, 0.07);
        }
        .visual-title {
            font-size: 0.8rem;
            font-family: var(--font-mono);
            color: var(--text-dim);
            text-transform: uppercase;
            letter-spacing: 0.05em;
        }
        .visual-actions {
            display: flex;
            gap: 0.5rem;
        }

        /* Code Presentation */
        .code-container {
            background: #090e17;
            border: 1px solid var(--border-color);
            border-radius: 8px;
            margin-bottom: 1.5rem;
            overflow: hidden;
        }
        .code-toolbar {
            background: var(--bg-input);
            display: flex;
            align-items: center;
            justify-content: space-between;
            padding: 0.5rem 1rem;
            border-bottom: 1px solid var(--border-color);
        }
        .code-tabs {
            display: flex;
            gap: 0.5rem;
        }
        .code-tab-btn {
            background: transparent;
            border: none;
            color: var(--text-muted);
            font-size: 0.78rem;
            padding: 0.25rem 0.6rem;
            border-radius: 4px;
            cursor: pointer;
            font-family: var(--font-mono);
        }
        .code-tab-btn.active {
            background: var(--bg-card);
            color: var(--blue);
            font-weight: 600;
        }
        .btn-copy {
            background: transparent;
            border: 1px solid var(--border-color);
            color: var(--text-dim);
            padding: 0.2rem 0.5rem;
            border-radius: 4px;
            font-size: 0.75rem;
            cursor: pointer;
            transition: all 0.2s ease;
        }
        .btn-copy:hover {
            color: var(--text-main);
            border-color: var(--blue);
        }
        pre.code-block {
            padding: 1.25rem;
            overflow-x: auto;
            font-family: var(--font-mono);
            font-size: 0.86rem;
            line-height: 1.55;
            color: #e2e8f0;
        }
        [data-theme="light"] pre.code-block {
            color: #1e293b;
            background: #ffffff;
        }

        /* Check your understanding Quiz inside scenarios */
        .checkpoint-card {
            background: rgba(56, 189, 248, 0.04);
            border: 1px solid rgba(56, 189, 248, 0.25);
            border-radius: 8px;
            padding: 1.25rem;
            margin-bottom: 1.25rem;
        }
        .checkpoint-card h4 {
            color: var(--blue);
            font-size: 0.85rem;
            text-transform: uppercase;
            letter-spacing: 0.05em;

<!-- VIEW 2: WHEN WE LOAD THE PROGRAM -->
<div id="view-load" style="display:none;">
<div class="phase-flow-card" style="border-color:var(--amber);">
<div style="display:flex; justify-content:space-between; align-items:center; margin-bottom:1rem; border-bottom:1px solid rgba(245,158,11,0.25); padding-bottom:0.75rem;">
<h3 style="color:var(--amber); font-size:1.3rem; margin:0;">⚡ Exactly What Happens When We LOAD the Program (Flashing Phase)</h3>
<span class="meta-pill" style="border-color:var(--amber); color:var(--amber);">Target: Flash Array @ 0x08000000</span>
</div>
<p style="color:var(--text-muted); font-size:0.92rem; line-height:1.6;">
                            When you click <strong>"Run"</strong> or <strong>"Flash"</strong> in your toolchain (or execute <code>STM32_Programmer_CLI</code>), the computer does not execute your C code. Instead, the binary is converted into electrical programming pulses to write non-volatile memory bits:
                        </p>
<div class="flow-step-list">
<div class="flow-step-item load-highlight">
<div class="flow-step-num" style="background:var(--amber); color:#000;">01</div>
<div>
<strong style="color:var(--amber);">Host PC Sends Firmware Packets over USB</strong>
<div style="color:var(--text-muted); font-size:0.82rem; margin-top:0.2rem;">
                                        The PC flashing utility reads <code>firmware.bin</code> or extracts loadable sections from <code>firmware.elf</code>, packaging 64-byte USB packets to the on-board ST-LINK MCU.
                                    </div>
</div>
</div>
<div class="flow-step-item load-highlight">
<div class="flow-step-num" style="background:var(--amber); color:#000;">02</div>
<div>
<strong style="color:var(--amber);">ST-LINK Halts the Cortex-M4 CPU Core via SWD</strong>
<div style="color:var(--text-muted); font-size:0.82rem; margin-top:0.2rem;">
                                        ST-LINK asserts the <strong>NRST</strong> pin or writes to the Debug Halting Control and Status Register (DHCSR) over the 2-wire Serial Wire Debug lines (<strong>SWDIO</strong> and <strong>SWCLK</strong>). The CPU freezes immediately.
                                    </div>
</div>
</div>
<div class="flow-step-item load-highlight">
<div class="flow-step-num" style="background:var(--amber); color:#000;">03</div>
<div>
<strong style="color:var(--amber);">Flash Memory Controller Unlocks Security Registers</strong>
<div style="color:var(--text-muted); font-size:0.82rem; margin-top:0.2rem;">
                                        To prevent accidental erasure from runaway code, the STM32 Flash control register (<code>FLASH_CR</code>) is locked by default. ST-LINK writes unlock keys <code>KEY1 = 0x45670123</code> and <code>KEY2 = 0xCDEF89AB</code> into <code>FLASH_KEYR</code>.
                                    </div>
</div>
</div>
<div class="flow-step-item load-highlight">
<div class="flow-step-num" style="background:var(--amber); color:#000;">04</div>
<div>
<strong style="color:var(--amber);">Internal Charge Pump Erases Target Flash Sectors</strong>
<div style="color:var(--text-muted); font-size:0.82rem; margin-top:0.2rem;">
                                        Flash memory cannot overwrite a <code>0</code> with a <code>1</code>; it must first be erased to all <code>0xFF</code> bytes. An internal charge pump steps up voltage to ~12V to tunnel electrons out of the floating gates of sectors 0 through 3.
                                    </div>
</div>
</div>
<div class="flow-step-item load-highlight">
<div class="flow-step-num" style="background:var(--amber); color:#000;">05</div>
<div>
<strong style="color:var(--amber);">32-Bit Words Burned Row-by-Row into Flash starting at 0x08000000</strong>
<div style="color:var(--text-muted); font-size:0.82rem; margin-top:0.2rem;">
                                        Machine instructions are clocked into the Flash Programming Data Register 32 bits at a time. The first two 32-bit words written are the <strong>Initial Stack Pointer (_estack)</strong> and the <strong>Reset_Handler Address</strong>!
                                    </div>
</div>
</div>
<div class="flow-step-item load-highlight">
<div class="flow-step-num" style="background:var(--amber); color:#000;">06</div>
<div>
<strong style="color:var(--amber);">Verification Checksum Read-Back</strong>
<div style="color:var(--text-muted); font-size:0.82rem; margin-top:0.2rem;">
                                        ST-LINK reads back all programmed flash memory locations and computes a CRC-32 hash to guarantee that zero bit-flip errors occurred during burning.
                                    </div>
</div>
</div>
<div class="flow-step-item load-highlight">
<div class="flow-step-num" style="background:var(--amber); color:#000;">07</div>
<div>
<strong style="color:var(--amber);">Hardware Reset Pulse Releases MCU to Run</strong>
<div style="color:var(--text-muted); font-size:0.82rem; margin-top:0.2rem;">
                                        The programmer pulls NRST LOW for 20ms and then releases it HIGH, handing control over to the ARM Cortex-M silicon core. The COM LED stops blinking red and turns solid green.
                                    </div>
</div>
</div>
</div>
</div>
</div>
<!-- VIEW 3: WHEN WE RUN THE PROGRAM -->
<div id="view-run" style="display:none;">
<div class="phase-flow-card" style="border-color:var(--green);">
<div style="display:flex; justify-content:space-between; align-items:center; margin-bottom:1rem; border-bottom:1px solid rgba(16,185,129,0.25); padding-bottom:0.75rem;">
<h3 style="color:var(--green); font-size:1.3rem; margin:0;">🚀 Exactly What Happens When We RUN the Program (Execution Phase)</h3>
<span class="meta-pill" style="border-color:var(--green); color:var(--green);">Target: CPU Core • SRAM • Peripherals</span>
</div>
<p style="color:var(--text-muted); font-size:0.92rem; line-height:1.6;">
                            Once reset is released, the physical semiconductor takes over autonomously at 84 million cycles per second. Notice how execution flows from hardware vector registers into memory initialization, and finally into GPIO, PIR, and UART peripherals:
                        </p>
<div class="flow-step-list">
<div class="flow-step-item run-highlight">
<div class="flow-step-num" style="background:var(--green); color:#000;">01</div>
<div>
<strong style="color:var(--green);">Power Stabilizes & Hardware Loads Vector Table Words</strong>
<div style="color:var(--text-muted); font-size:0.82rem; margin-top:0.2rem;">
                                        Internal Power-On Reset (POR) comparator detects VDD > 1.7V. CPU reads address <code>0x08000000</code> and loads it into <strong>MSP (R13)</strong>. Then reads <code>0x08000004</code> and loads it into <strong>PC (R15)</strong>.
                                    </div>
</div>
</div>
<div class="flow-step-item run-highlight">
<div class="flow-step-num" style="background:var(--green); color:#000;">02</div>
<div>
<strong style="color:var(--green);">Reset_Handler Copies .data from Flash to RAM & Zeros .bss</strong>
<div style="color:var(--text-muted); font-size:0.82rem; margin-top:0.2rem;">
                                        Before your C code starts, a tight assembly loop copies initial variable values from Flash (LMA) into volatile SRAM (VMA at <code>0x20000000</code>), and fills the <code>.bss</code> section with zeros.
                                    </div>
</div>
</div>
<div class="flow-step-item run-highlight">
<div class="flow-step-num" style="background:var(--green); color:#000;">03</div>
<div>
<strong style="color:var(--green);">SystemInit() Synthesizes 84 MHz System Clock (PLL)</strong>
<div style="color:var(--text-muted); font-size:0.82rem; margin-top:0.2rem;">
                                        Switches the CPU clock from the uncalibrated 16 MHz internal RC oscillator (HSI) to the high-accuracy 8 MHz quartz crystal (HSE). The Phase-Locked Loop (PLL) multiplies this to 84 MHz HCLK and sets Flash wait states to 2.
                                    </div>
</div>
</div>
<div class="flow-step-item run-highlight">
<div class="flow-step-num" style="background:var(--green); color:#000;">04</div>
<div>
<strong style="color:var(--green);">main() is Reached: HAL_Init() Configures SysTick (1 ms)</strong>
<div style="color:var(--text-muted); font-size:0.82rem; margin-top:0.2rem;">
                                        The application entry point begins! <code>HAL_Init()</code> sets NVIC interrupt priority grouping and configures the 24-bit SysTick hardware countdown timer to generate an interrupt every 1.0 millisecond for <code>HAL_Delay()</code>.
                                    </div>
</div>
</div>
<div class="flow-step-item run-highlight">
<div class="flow-step-num" style="background:var(--green); color:#000;">05</div>
<div>
<strong style="color:var(--green);">RCC Clock Gating Powers GPIOA, GPIOB, and USART2 Buses</strong>
<div style="color:var(--text-muted); font-size:0.82rem; margin-top:0.2rem;">
                                        The MCU enables bits in <code>RCC->AHB1ENR</code> and <code>RCC->APB1ENR</code>. Without this step, writing to GPIO or UART registers would cause a bus fault because peripheral clocks are gated off to conserve battery power!
                                    </div>
</div>
</div>
<div class="flow-step-item run-highlight">
<div class="flow-step-num" style="background:var(--green); color:#000;">06</div>
<div>
<strong style="color:var(--green);">GPIO Driver Sinks Current → Green LED LD2 Emits Light</strong>
<div style="color:var(--text-muted); font-size:0.82rem; margin-top:0.2rem;">
                                        Firmware writes to <code>GPIOA->BSRR</code> bit 5. The silicon P-MOSFET turns ON, driving physical pin PA5 to 3.3V. 8 milliamperes of current flow through the 510-ohm resistor into LED LD2, exciting photons!
                                    </div>
</div>
</div>
<div class="flow-step-item run-highlight">
<div class="flow-step-num" style="background:var(--green); color:#000;">07</div>
<div>
<strong style="color:var(--green);">PIR Motion Sensor Drives PB0 HIGH → Schmitt Trigger Latches</strong>
<div style="color:var(--text-muted); font-size:0.82rem; margin-top:0.2rem;">
                                        When someone walks in front of the pyroelectric lens, the PIR module drives pin PB0 to 3.3V. The internal Schmitt trigger cleans up noise and sets bit 0 of <code>GPIOB->IDR</code>, which firmware reads or detects via EXTI0.
                                    </div>
</div>
</div>
<div class="flow-step-item run-highlight">
<div class="flow-step-num" style="background:var(--green); color:#000;">08</div>
<div>
<strong style="color:var(--green);">USART2 Serializes ASCII Bytes onto PA2 TX Wire @ 115,200 Baud</strong>
<div style="color:var(--text-muted); font-size:0.82rem; margin-top:0.2rem;">
<code>HAL_UART_Transmit()</code> writes byte <code>'M'</code> into <code>USART2->DR</code>. The hardware shift register shifts out 1 Start bit, 8 data bits, and 1 Stop bit at 8.68 µs per bit, streaming text to the ST-LINK USB Virtual COM Port!
                                    </div>
</div>
</div>
</div>
</div>
</div>
</section>

<pre class="code-block"><code># Complete end-to-end command sequence for STM32F4:
arm-none-eabi-gcc -E main.c -o main.i                             # 1. Preprocess
arm-none-eabi-gcc -S -mcpu=cortex-m4 -mthumb main.i -o main.s     # 2. Compile to Assembly
arm-none-eabi-as -mcpu=cortex-m4 -mthumb main.s -o main.o        # 3. Assemble to Object

arm-none-eabi-objcopy -O binary firmware.elf firmware.bin         # 5. Extract raw binary</code></pre>

<pre class="code-block" id="c2-hal"><code>int main(void)
{
    HAL_Init();               // Reset peripherals, initialize Flash & SysTick
    SystemClock_Config();     // Configure clock tree (HCLK = 84 MHz)
    MX_GPIO_Init();           // Configure PA5 as push-pull output

    while (1)
    {
        HAL_GPIO_TogglePin(GPIOA, GPIO_PIN_5); // Invert pin state
        HAL_Delay(500);                        // Non-blocking SysTick wait (500 ms)
    }
}</code></pre>
<pre class="code-block" id="c2-reg" style="display:none;"><code>int main(void)
{
    // 1. Enable AHB1 clock for GPIOA port
    RCC->AHB1ENR |= (1 << 0);

    // 2. Set Pin 5 as General Purpose Output (MODER[11:10] = 01)
    GPIOA->MODER &= ~(3 << (5 * 2));
    GPIOA->MODER |=  (1 << (5 * 2));

    while (1)
    {
        // 3. Atomically toggle Pin 5 via Output Data Register
        GPIOA->ODR ^= (1 << 5);

        // Approximate busy-wait loop
        for (volatile int i = 0; i < 500000; i++);
    }
}</code></pre>
</div>
<details class="tech-depth">
<summary>🔬 Deep-Dive: What Really Happens Inside the GPIO Peripheral</summary>
<div class="tech-depth-content">
<p>1. The CPU writes a 32-bit word across the <strong>AHB1 bus matrix</strong> to physical memory address <code>0x40020014</code> (GPIOA_ODR).</p>
<p>2. The internal flip-flop latches the updated bit value on the next peripheral clock edge.</p>
<p>3. The latch drives the gate of two complementary MOSFETs (P-MOS on top connected to VDD, N-MOS on bottom connected to VSS).</p>
<p>4. In push-pull mode, turning on the P-MOS establishes a low-impedance (~25Ω) path to 3.3V, causing electrons to flow out of the pin pad.</p>
</div>
</details>
<div class="checkpoint-card" style="margin-top:1.5rem;">
<h4>🧪 Check Your Understanding</h4>
<p class="checkpoint-question">What happens if you omit the call to enable the GPIO port clock in the RCC (Reset and Clock Control) register?</p>
<div class="checkpoint-options">
<div class="checkpoint-option" onclick="checkCheckpoint(this, false)">A. The LED blinks at half its normal speed</div>
<div class="checkpoint-option" onclick="checkCheckpoint(this, true)">B. Writes to GPIO registers are ignored or trigger a bus fault because peripheral logic is unpowered</div>
<div class="checkpoint-option" onclick="checkCheckpoint(this, false)">C. The compiler reports an unresolved symbol error</div>
<div class="checkpoint-option" onclick="checkCheckpoint(this, false)">D. The pin automatically defaults to an analog input mode</div>
</div>
<div class="checkpoint-feedback">Correct! Microcontrollers use clock-gating to conserve energy. Without activating the AHB1 clock to GPIOA, the entire register block remains dormant.</div>
</div>
<div class="grid-mistake-takeaway">
<div class="box-mistake">
<strong>Common Mistake</strong>
                        Using active-high assumptions for all boards. Some boards wire LEDs between VDD and the pin (active-low), meaning writing 0 turns the LED ON!
                    </div>
<div class="box-takeaway">
<strong>Practical Takeaway</strong>
                        Always consult the board schematic to check pin assignments (e.g., Nucleo-F401RE uses PA5, Nucleo-F103RB uses PA5, Discovery uses PD12-PD15).
                    </div>
</div>

<article class="scenario-card" id="scenario-4">
<div class="scenario-header">
<div class="scenario-title-area">
<h2>Compilation and Assembly</h2>
<div class="scenario-goal">Goal: Witness C statements translate into Cortex-M Thumb machine instructions.</div>
</div>
<span class="scenario-num">Scenario 04</span>
</div>
<div class="grid-problem-observation">
<div class="box-sub problem">
<h4>⚠️ Real-World Problem</h4>
<p>Engineers assume a single line of C code executes in one clock cycle, leading to failed timing constraints in high-speed bit-banging.</p>
</div>
<div class="box-sub observation">
<h4>👀 What Student Observes</h4>
<p>One C line like <code>GPIOA->ODR ^= (1 << 5);</code> turns into four distinct assembly instructions: LDR, LDR, EOR, and STR.</p>
</div>
</div>
<div class="internal-box">
<h4>⚙️ What is Happening Internally</h4>
<p>The compiler translates the Abstract Syntax Tree into ARM Thumb-2 instructions. Because Cortex-M is a <strong>Load/Store RISC architecture</strong>, the ALU cannot directly manipulate bits in physical peripheral registers. The processor must load the address into a general-purpose register, read the value over the bus, modify the bit in an internal register, and store the result back to memory.</p>
</div>

                                Invert bit 5 of the GPIOA Output Data Register located at <code>0x40020014</code>.

</div>

</div>
<div class="checkpoint-card">
<h4>🧪 Check Your Understanding</h4>
<p class="checkpoint-question">Why does a Cortex-M processor require both an LDR (Load) and an STR (Store) instruction to toggle an I/O bit in ODR?</p>
<div class="checkpoint-options">
<div class="checkpoint-option" onclick="checkCheckpoint(this, true)">A. ARM Cortex-M is a Load/Store architecture; arithmetic and bitwise logic only operate on internal CPU registers</div>
<div class="checkpoint-option" onclick="checkCheckpoint(this, false)">B. The memory bus cannot handle 32-bit operations</div>
<div class="checkpoint-option" onclick="checkCheckpoint(this, false)">C. The peripheral bus requires two clock cycles to wake up</div>
<div class="checkpoint-option" onclick="checkCheckpoint(this, false)">D. The compiler intentionally slows down execution to prevent bus saturation</div>
</div>
<div class="checkpoint-feedback">Correct! Unlike CISC architectures like x86 that have direct memory-modifying instructions, ARM requires loading data into CPU registers (R0-R12) before ALU manipulation.</div>
</div>
<div class="grid-mistake-takeaway">
<div class="box-mistake">
<strong>Common Mistake</strong>
                        Forgetting <code>-mthumb</code> when invoking GCC manually, causing the toolchain to emit 32-bit ARM instructions that Cortex-M microcontrollers cannot decode, triggering an immediate HardFault!
                    </div>
<div class="box-takeaway">
<strong>Practical Takeaway</strong>
                        For atomic pin changes that don't suffer from interrupt race conditions during read-modify-write, use the BSRR (Bit Set/Reset Register) instead of ODR!
                    </div>
</div>

<td style="padding:0.5rem;">*UND*</td>
<td style="padding:0.5rem;"><span style="background:rgba(245,158,11,0.2);color:var(--amber);padding:2px 6px;border-radius:4px;">UNRESOLVED</span></td>
<td style="padding:0.5rem; color:var(--blue);">stm32f4xx_hal_gpio.o</td>
</tr>

</div>
</div>
<div class="code-container">

<button class="btn-copy" onclick="copyCode(this)">Copy</button>
</div>
<pre class="code-block"><code># List symbols inside an object file:
arm-none-eabi-nm main.o

# Sample output:
# 00000000 T main                 <- 'T' means Defined in Text section
#          U HAL_Init             <- 'U' means Undefined Reference!
#          U HAL_GPIO_TogglePin   <- 'U' means Undefined Reference!
#          U SystemClock_Config   <- 'U' means Undefined Reference!</code></pre>
</div>
<div class="checkpoint-card">
<h4>🧪 Check Your Understanding</h4>
<p class="checkpoint-question">If you include <code>stm32f4xx_hal.h</code> in your code, why can you still get an "undefined reference to HAL_Init" linker error?</p>
<div class="checkpoint-options">
<div class="checkpoint-option" onclick="checkCheckpoint(this, false)">A. The header file was corrupted during download</div>
<div class="checkpoint-option" onclick="checkCheckpoint(this, true)">B. Header files only declare function prototypes for the compiler; the actual object file (stm32f4xx_hal.o) was not provided to the linker</div>
<div class="checkpoint-option" onclick="checkCheckpoint(this, false)">C. The microcontroller flash was already locked</div>
<div class="checkpoint-option" onclick="checkCheckpoint(this, false)">D. C requires function definitions to be in the same source file</div>
</div>
<div class="checkpoint-feedback">Correct! Headers provide declarations (promises) to satisfy the compiler. The linker requires the actual compiled definition in an object file or archive library (.a).</div>
</div>
<div class="grid-mistake-takeaway">
<div class="box-mistake">
<strong>Common Mistake</strong>
                        Believing that <code>#include "file.h"</code> automatically compiles and links <code>file.c</code>. Header files do not bring in object files!
                    </div>
<div class="box-takeaway">
<strong>Practical Takeaway</strong>
                        Whenever you see "undefined reference", check your Makefile or CMakeLists.txt to ensure the corresponding <code>.c</code> file is added to the compilation list.
                    </div>
</div>

<!-- SCENARIO 6 -->
<article class="scenario-card" id="scenario-6">
<div class="scenario-header">
<div class="scenario-title-area">
<h2>Linker and Linker Script</h2>
<div class="scenario-goal">Goal: Master physical address placement for Flash, RAM, .text, .data, and .bss.</div>
</div>
<span class="scenario-num">Scenario 06</span>
</div>
<div class="grid-problem-observation">
<div class="box-sub problem">
<h4>⚠️ Real-World Problem</h4>
<p>Firmware builds fine but crashes immediately on boot because code was placed into volatile RAM or RAM variables were mapped past physical memory bounds.</p>
</div>
<div class="box-sub observation">
<h4>👀 What Student Observes</h4>
<p>The linker script (<code>.ld</code>) assigns every byte an exact 32-bit physical address starting at <code>0x08000000</code> for Flash and <code>0x20000000</code> for SRAM.</p>
</div>
</div>
<div class="internal-box">
<h4>⚙️ What is Happening Internally</h4>
<p>The GNU Linker takes all <code>.o</code> files, resolves symbol addresses, and organizes them according to the rules in <code>stm32.ld</code>. It places <code>.isr_vector</code> at the flash origin, appends <code>.text</code> (code) and <code>.rodata</code> (constants), assigns <code>.data</code> a Load Memory Address (LMA) in Flash and Virtual Memory Address (VMA) in RAM, and allocates space for <code>.bss</code>, Stack, and Heap in RAM.</p>
</div>
<!-- Interactive Memory Map -->
<div class="visual-display-area">
<div class="visual-header">
<span class="visual-title">Interactive STM32 Memory Map (Flash vs SRAM Architecture)</span>
<div class="visual-actions">
<span style="font-family:var(--font-mono);font-size:0.75rem;color:var(--text-dim);">STM32F401RE: 512KB Flash, 96KB SRAM</span>
</div>
</div>
<div class="mem-layout">
<!-- Flash Memory Column -->
<div class="mem-block">
<h4>
<span>FLASH MEMORY (Non-Volatile)</span>
<span>0x08000000</span>
</h4>
<div class="mem-stack">
<div class="mem-segment seg-vector" title="Interrupt Vector Table (Addresses of handlers)">
<span>.isr_vector (Vector Table)</span>
<span>0x08000000</span>
</div>
<div class="mem-segment seg-text" title="Compiled executable machine code">
<span>.text (Program Instructions)</span>
<span>0x08000400</span>
</div>
<div class="mem-segment seg-rodata" title="Read-only string literals and const arrays">
<span>.rodata (Constants & Strings)</span>
<span>0x08008200</span>
</div>
<div class="mem-segment seg-data" title="Initial flash values of initialized global variables">
<span>.data (Initial Values in Flash - LMA)</span>
<span>0x08009100</span>
</div>
<div style="padding:1rem; text-align:center; color:var(--text-dim); font-size:0.75rem; border:1px dashed var(--border-color); border-radius:4px; margin-top:0.5rem;">
                                    Unused Flash Memory (~470 KB free)
                                </div>
</div>
</div>
<!-- SRAM Memory Column -->
<div class="mem-block">
<h4>
<span>SRAM MEMORY (Volatile)</span>
<span>0x20000000</span>
</h4>
<div class="mem-stack">
<div class="mem-segment seg-data" title="Copied from Flash to RAM during Reset_Handler">
<span>.data (Active RAM Execution - VMA)</span>
<span>0x20000000</span>
</div>
<div class="mem-segment seg-bss" title="Zero-initialized global variables">
<span>.bss (Zeroed out at startup)</span>
<span>0x20000180</span>
</div>
<div style="padding:0.75rem; text-align:center; color:var(--text-dim); font-size:0.75rem; border:1px dashed var(--border-color); border-radius:4px; margin:0.3rem 0;">
                                    Heap (malloc • grows downward ↓)
                                </div>
<div class="mem-segment seg-stack" title="Main Stack Pointer (MSP) grows downward from end of RAM">
<span>Stack (MSP Top • grows upward ↑)</span>
<span>0x20018000 (_estack)</span>
</div>
</div>
</div>
</div>
</div>
<div class="code-container">
<div class="code-toolbar">
<span style="font-family:var(--font-mono);font-size:0.8rem;color:var(--text-dim);">Annotated Linker Script Excerpt (stm32f4.ld)</span>
<button class="btn-copy" onclick="copyCode(this)">Copy</button>
</div>
<pre class="code-block"><code>MEMORY
{
  FLASH (rx)  : ORIGIN = 0x08000000, LENGTH = 512K
  RAM   (xrw) : ORIGIN = 0x20000000, LENGTH = 96K
}

SECTIONS
{
  .isr_vector : { KEEP(*(.isr_vector)) } > FLASH       /* Vector table at base */
  .text       : { *(.text*) *(.rodata*) } > FLASH       /* Code and constants */
  .data : 
  {
    _sdata = .;
    *(.data*)
    _edata = .;
  } > RAM AT > FLASH                                   /* VMA in RAM, LMA in Flash */
  
  .bss :
  {
    _sbss = .;
    *(.bss*)
    _ebss = .;
  } > RAM                                             /* Uninitialized data in RAM */
}</code></pre>
</div>
<div class="checkpoint-card">
<h4>🧪 Check Your Understanding</h4>
<p class="checkpoint-question">Why does the <code>.data</code> section have two addresses (an LMA in Flash and a VMA in RAM)?</p>
<div class="checkpoint-options">
<div class="checkpoint-option" onclick="checkCheckpoint(this, false)">A. It prevents hackers from accessing variable values</div>
<div class="checkpoint-option" onclick="checkCheckpoint(this, true)">B. RAM loses its contents when power is turned off; initial values must be stored in permanent Flash and copied into RAM at boot</div>
<div class="checkpoint-option" onclick="checkCheckpoint(this, false)">C. The ARM core requires duplicate copies for error parity check</div>
<div class="checkpoint-option" onclick="checkCheckpoint(this, false)">D. Flash memory cannot be read at runtime</div>
</div>
<div class="checkpoint-feedback">Correct! Global variables like <code>int count = 42;</code> must retain '42' after power loss (stored in Flash LMA), but need write access at runtime (executed from RAM VMA).</div>
</div>
<div class="grid-mistake-takeaway">
<div class="box-mistake">
<strong>Common Mistake</strong>
                        Assuming the Stack starts at <code>0x20000000</code>. On ARM Cortex-M, the stack is full-descending: it starts at the <em>top of RAM</em> (e.g., <code>0x20018000</code>) and grows downward!
                    </div>
<div class="box-takeaway">
<strong>Practical Takeaway</strong>
                        Examine the map file (<code>-Wl,-Map=firmware.map</code>) after every build to monitor flash and RAM utilization.
                    </div>
</div>
</article>
<!-- SCENARIO 7 -->
<article class="scenario-card" id="scenario-7">
<div class="scenario-header">
<div class="scenario-title-area">
<h2>Understanding the ELF File</h2>
<div class="scenario-goal">Goal: Inspect the primary development binary package with readelf, size, and nm.</div>
</div>
<span class="scenario-num">Scenario 07</span>
</div>
<div class="grid-problem-observation">
<div class="box-sub problem">
<h4>⚠️ Real-World Problem</h4>
<p>A student sees their <code>firmware.elf</code> is 850 KB and panics, thinking it will not fit on their 512 KB microcontroller flash!</p>
</div>
<div class="box-sub observation">
<h4>👀 What Student Observes</h4>
<p>While the ELF file is 850 KB on their PC, the <code>arm-none-eabi-size</code> tool reveals that only 18 KB of actual flash is consumed.</p>
</div>
</div>
<div class="internal-box">
<h4>⚙️ What is Happening Internally</h4>
<p>An ELF (Executable and Linkable Format) file contains much more than executable code. It bundles ELF headers, section tables, DWARF debug line numbers, source file strings, and variable name symbols. This debug metadata is used solely by the host debugger (GDB) on the PC and is never flashed onto the target microcontroller.</p>

<pre class="code-block"><code># Run GNU size to inspect real microcontroller memory consumption:

# Output:
#    text    data     bss     dec     hex filename

# Calculation:
# Total Flash Consumed = text + data = 17840 + 420 = 18,260 Bytes (~17.8 KB)
# Total RAM Consumed   = data + bss  = 420 + 2144   = 2,564 Bytes (~2.5 KB)</code></pre>
</div>
<div class="checkpoint-card">
<h4>🧪 Check Your Understanding</h4>
<p class="checkpoint-question">Why is the <code>firmware.elf</code> file much larger on your hard drive than the actual microcontroller flash capacity?</p>
<div class="checkpoint-options">
<div class="checkpoint-option" onclick="checkCheckpoint(this, false)">A. The compiler generates bloated uncompressed instructions</div>
<div class="checkpoint-option" onclick="checkCheckpoint(this, true)">B. The ELF contains DWARF debug tables, function names, and line number mappings intended solely for the PC debugger</div>
<div class="checkpoint-option" onclick="checkCheckpoint(this, false)">C. Microcontroller flash uses hardware compression to shrink the file</div>
<div class="checkpoint-option" onclick="checkCheckpoint(this, false)">D. The ELF includes copies of the entire operating system kernel</div>
</div>
<div class="checkpoint-feedback">Correct! Debug symbols (line numbers, variable names, call graphs) take up the vast majority of an ELF file, but are stripped during flash extraction.</div>
</div>
<div class="grid-mistake-takeaway">
<div class="box-mistake">
<strong>Common Mistake</strong>
                        Looking at the file size in Windows Explorer or Mac Finder and thinking the microcontroller flash is exhausted. Always use <code>arm-none-eabi-size</code>!
                    </div>
<div class="box-takeaway">
<strong>Practical Takeaway</strong>
                        Never delete your <code>.elf</code> file after building—it is the only artifact that allows GDB to map hardware memory back to your C source lines!
                    </div>
</div>
</article>
<!-- SCENARIO 8 -->
<article class="scenario-card" id="scenario-8">
<div class="scenario-header">
<div class="scenario-title-area">
<h2>Converting ELF to BIN and HEX</h2>
<div class="scenario-goal">Goal: Understand objcopy, Intel HEX record structures, and addressless raw BIN files.</div>
</div>
<span class="scenario-num">Scenario 08</span>
</div>
<div class="grid-problem-observation">
<div class="box-sub problem">
<h4>⚠️ Real-World Problem</h4>
<p>An engineer flashes a raw <code>.bin</code> file without specifying a target memory address, causing the chip to hang because bytes were written to address 0x0 instead of 0x08000000.</p>
</div>
<div class="box-sub observation">
<h4>👀 What Student Observes</h4>
<p><code>firmware.hex</code> is an ASCII text file with checksums and addresses, while <code>firmware.bin</code> is a stream of pure bytes with zero headers.</p>
</div>
</div>
<div class="internal-box">
<h4>⚙️ What is Happening Internally</h4>
<p><code>arm-none-eabi-objcopy</code> strips away the ELF envelope. For Intel HEX, it formats bytes into ASCII records specifying destination memory offsets and longitudinal checksums. For raw BIN, it extracts sequential machine code bytes exactly as they will sit in flash, requiring the programmer to provide the start address (<code>0x08000000</code>) externally.</p>
</div>

<h4>🧪 Check Your Understanding</h4>
<p class="checkpoint-question">Why must you explicitly pass <code>0x08000000</code> when flashing a <code>firmware.bin</code> file with STM32CubeProgrammer?</p>
<div class="checkpoint-options">
<div class="checkpoint-option" onclick="checkCheckpoint(this, true)">A. A .bin file contains raw machine bytes only, with zero headers or destination address information</div>
<div class="checkpoint-option" onclick="checkCheckpoint(this, false)">B. The programmer needs to verify the license key of the chip</div>
<div class="checkpoint-option" onclick="checkCheckpoint(this, false)">C. 0x08000000 is the baud rate of the ST-LINK interface</div>
<div class="checkpoint-option" onclick="checkCheckpoint(this, false)">D. To distinguish between Cortex-M3 and Cortex-M4 architectures</div>
</div>
<div class="checkpoint-feedback">Correct! A BIN file starts at byte 0 and ends at byte N. It does not know where in the 4GB address space it belongs without an explicit base parameter.</div>
</div>
<div class="grid-mistake-takeaway">
<div class="box-mistake">
<strong>Common Mistake</strong>
                        Flashing an application binary meant for a bootloader (e.g. at <code>0x08008000</code>) to the default address <code>0x08000000</code>, wiping out the bootloader!
                    </div>
<div class="box-takeaway">
<strong>Practical Takeaway</strong>
                        Use Intel HEX for factory programming rigs because each record explicitly dictates its destination address.
                    </div>
</div>
</article>

<article class="scenario-card" id="scenario-9">
<div class="scenario-header">
<div class="scenario-title-area">
<h2>Programming the STM32 Flash</h2>
<div class="scenario-goal">Goal: Master the physical ST-LINK SWD hardware chain, erase, write, and verify.</div>
</div>
<span class="scenario-num">Scenario 09</span>
</div>
<div class="grid-problem-observation">
<div class="box-sub problem">
<h4>⚠️ Real-World Problem</h4>
<p>Programming fails with: <code>Error: No STM32 target found!</code> and the student does not know how to diagnose the hardware debug interface.</p>
</div>
<div class="box-sub observation">
<h4>👀 What Student Observes</h4>
<p>ST-LINK LED blinks red/green, the on-chip flash controller unlocks, erases sectors, writes data blocks, verifies CRC, and pulses the NRST pin.</p>
</div>
</div>
<div class="internal-box">
<h4>⚙️ What is Happening Internally</h4>
<p>The host PC communicates with the on-board ST-LINK MCU via USB. The ST-LINK talks to the STM32's internal <strong>Debug Access Port (DAP)</strong> using ARM Serial Wire Debug (SWD), which requires just two physical lines: <strong>SWDIO</strong> (bi-directional data) and <strong>SWCLK</strong> (clock), plus GND. The flash controller unlocks using security keys <code>KEY1=0x45670123</code> and <code>KEY2=0xCDEF89AB</code>, erases selected high-voltage flash sectors, and programs bytes using high internal charge-pump voltages.</p>
</div>

<pre class="code-block"><code># Full command to erase, program, verify, and run:
STM32_Programmer_CLI \
  -c port=SWD mode=UR reset=HWrst \
  -d firmware.elf \
  -v \
  -rst

# Execution sequence performed by tool:
# 1. Connect under reset (-c port=SWD mode=UR)
# 2. Unlock FLASH_CR register
# 3. Mass-erase or sector-erase target pages
# 4. Program flash rows via 32-bit word writes
# 5. Verify byte checksums (-v)
# 6. Release hardware reset line (-rst) to start CPU execution</code></pre>
</div>

<p class="checkpoint-question">How many physical signal wires are strictly required for ARM Serial Wire Debug (SWD) communication?</p>
<div class="checkpoint-options">
<div class="checkpoint-option" onclick="checkCheckpoint(this, true)">A. 2 signal wires (SWDIO and SWCLK), plus a common ground (GND)</div>
<div class="checkpoint-option" onclick="checkCheckpoint(this, false)">B. 4 wires (MISO, MOSI, SCK, CS)</div>
<div class="checkpoint-option" onclick="checkCheckpoint(this, false)">C. 8 parallel data lines</div>
<div class="checkpoint-option" onclick="checkCheckpoint(this, false)">D. 1 single wire containing power and data</div>
</div>
<div class="checkpoint-feedback">Correct! SWD replaces legacy 5-pin JTAG with just SWDIO (bidirectional data) and SWCLK (clock), saving valuable pins for GPIOs.</div>
</div>

<div class="box-mistake">
<strong>Common Mistake</strong>
                        Disabling the SWD pins in firmware (reassigning PA13/PA14 as GPIOs). Once booted, the ST-LINK can no longer connect without pulling NRST low during connection ("Connect Under Reset")!

<strong>Practical Takeaway</strong>

<article class="scenario-card" id="scenario-10">
<div class="scenario-header">
<div class="scenario-title-area">
<h2>What Happens When Power is Switched On?</h2>
<div class="scenario-goal">Goal: Master the Cortex-M hardware reset sequence, MSP loading, and Reset_Handler.</div>
</div>
<span class="scenario-num">Scenario 10</span>
</div>
<div class="grid-problem-observation">
<div class="box-sub problem">
<h4>⚠️ Real-World Problem</h4>
<p>Students believe <code>main()</code> is the very first function executed by the microcontroller when power is applied.</p>
</div>
<div class="box-sub observation">
<h4>👀 What Student Observes</h4>
<p>Upon power-up, hundreds of machine instructions execute to initialize memory and clocks before the CPU ever reaches the first line of <code>main()</code>.</p>
</div>
</div>
<div class="internal-box">
<h4>⚙️ What is Happening Internally</h4>
<p>The ARM Cortex-M hardware follows a fixed architectural startup model:
                    1. When VDD rises above the Power-On Reset (POR) threshold (~1.7V), reset is released.
                    2. The hardware automatically reads 32-bit word 0 from address <code>0x08000000</code> and loads it into the <strong>Main Stack Pointer (MSP)</strong>.
                    3. The hardware reads 32-bit word 1 from address <code>0x08000004</code> and loads it into the <strong>Program Counter (PC)</strong>.
                    4. The CPU begins executing instructions at the address pointed to by PC, which is the <code>Reset_Handler</code> assembly function!</p>
</div>

<pre class="code-block"><code>/* Vector Table definition placed at address 0x08000000 */
.section .isr_vector,"a",%progbits
.type g_pfnVectors, %object
g_pfnVectors:
  .word _estack               /* Word 0 (0x08000000): Top of Stack -> loaded into MSP */
  .word Reset_Handler         /* Word 1 (0x08000004): Entry point   -> loaded into PC */
  .word NMI_Handler           /* Word 2 (0x08000008): Non-Maskable Interrupt */
  .word HardFault_Handler     /* Word 3 (0x0800000C): Critical Crash Handler */

/* The actual Reset Handler */
.section .text.Reset_Handler
.weak Reset_Handler
Reset_Handler:
  ldr   sp, =_estack          /* Redundantly enforce stack pointer */
  bl    SystemInit            /* Setup clock tree & enable FPU */
  bl    copy_data_and_zero_bss/* Prepare memory */
  bl    main                  /* Finally enter C application code! */
  b     .                     /* Trap in infinite loop if main() returns */</code></pre>

<p class="checkpoint-question">What is located at physical memory address <code>0x08000000</code> on an STM32 microcontroller?</p>
<div class="checkpoint-options">

<div class="checkpoint-option" onclick="checkCheckpoint(this, true)">B. The initial value of the Main Stack Pointer (_estack)</div>
<div class="checkpoint-option" onclick="checkCheckpoint(this, false)">C. The ASCII string "STM32"</div>
<div class="checkpoint-option" onclick="checkCheckpoint(this, false)">D. The configuration registers of the PLL clock</div>
</div>
<div class="checkpoint-feedback">Correct! The Cortex-M architecture requires the very first 32-bit word in vector space to be the initial stack pointer address.</div>
</div>
<div class="grid-mistake-takeaway">
<div class="box-mistake">
<strong>Common Mistake</strong>
                        Allowing <code>main()</code> to return! If <code>main()</code> finishes, execution falls off into random memory, causing a HardFault unless caught by a startup loop.
                    </div>
<div class="box-takeaway">
<strong>Practical Takeaway</strong>
                        All Cortex-M microcontroller families (M0, M3, M4, M7, M33) share this exact same two-word hardware startup sequence.
                    </div>
</div>

<pre class="code-block"><code>/* Symbols provided by the linker script (.ld): */
extern uint32_t _sidata; /* Start of .data values in Flash */
extern uint32_t _sdata;  /* Start of .data in RAM */
extern uint32_t _edata;  /* End of .data in RAM */
extern uint32_t _sbss;   /* Start of .bss in RAM */
extern uint32_t _ebss;   /* End of .bss in RAM */

void copy_data_and_zero_bss(void)
{
    // 1. Copy initialized data from Flash to RAM
    uint32_t *src = &_sidata;
    uint32_t *dst = &_sdata;
    while (dst < &_edata) {
        *dst++ = *src++;
    }

    // 2. Zero-out the uninitialized BSS section in RAM
    dst = &_sbss;
    while (dst < &_ebss) {
        *dst++ = 0;
    }
}</code></pre>

<div class="checkpoint-option" onclick="checkCheckpoint(this, false)">B. Over the SWD debugger cable from the host computer</div>
<div class="checkpoint-option" onclick="checkCheckpoint(this, false)">C. From the microcontroller's internal ROM bootloader</div>
<div class="checkpoint-option" onclick="checkCheckpoint(this, false)">D. The compiler hardcodes them into CPU register R0</div>
</div>
<div class="checkpoint-feedback">Correct! The linker burns the initial values into Flash right after the code segment, and the startup code copies them into RAM at boot time.</div>
</div>

<div class="box-mistake">

<div class="box-takeaway">
<strong>Practical Takeaway</strong>
                        Only static and global variables are automatically zeroed by the BSS startup loop. Always explicitly initialize local stack variables!

</div>

<article class="scenario-card" id="scenario-12">
<div class="scenario-header">
<div class="scenario-title-area">
<h2>Program Execution and the Fetch-Decode-Execute Cycle</h2>
<div class="scenario-goal">Goal: Understand the CPU engine: Program Counter, Flash bus fetch, decoding, and ALU execution.</div>
</div>
<span class="scenario-num">Scenario 12</span>
</div>
<div class="grid-problem-observation">
<div class="box-sub problem">
<h4>⚠️ Real-World Problem</h4>
<p>Students imagine the microcontroller executes whole C statements simultaneously, failing to understand how branching and pipeline stalls affect real-time control.</p>
</div>
<div class="box-sub observation">
<h4>👀 What Student Observes</h4>
<p>The Program Counter (PC) register increments monotonically (<code>0x08000210</code>, <code>0x08000214</code>), fetching 16/32-bit opcodes on every clock cycle, until a branch jumps back to repeat the loop.</p>
</div>
</div>
<div class="internal-box">
<h4>⚙️ What is Happening Internally</h4>
<p>The CPU is a finite state machine running the 3-stage pipeline:
                    1. <strong>Fetch:</strong> CPU places PC value on the I-Code bus, reading a 16-bit or 32-bit Thumb instruction from Flash memory.
                    2. <strong>Decode:</strong> The instruction decoder breaks down register operands, immediate values, and operation codes.
                    3. <strong>Execute:</strong> The ALU performs addition, bitwise manipulation, or memory bus transactions, and updates the PC (typically PC += 2 or PC += 4).</p>
</div>

<article class="scenario-card" id="scenario-15">
<div class="scenario-header">
<div class="scenario-title-area">
<h2>Polling versus Interrupt (EXTI)</h2>
<div class="scenario-goal">Goal: Contrast CPU busy-waiting against asynchronous event-driven hardware interrupts.</div>
</div>
<span class="scenario-num">Scenario 15</span>
</div>
<div class="grid-problem-observation">
<div class="box-sub problem">
<h4>⚠️ Real-World Problem</h4>
<p>A fast 5-millisecond sensor pulse is missed because the CPU was blocked inside a 500ms <code>HAL_Delay()</code> loop.</p>
</div>
<div class="box-sub observation">
<h4>👀 What Student Observes</h4>
<p>With interrupts enabled, the PIR sensor instantly invokes the callback function even when the CPU is running other tasks.</p>
</div>
</div>
<div class="internal-box">
<h4>⚙️ What is Happening Internally</h4>
<p>In Polling, the CPU constantly burns power asking "has the pin changed?". With Interrupts, the pin is connected to the <strong>External Interrupt Controller (EXTI)</strong> edge-detector hardware. When a rising edge occurs, EXTI asserts an interrupt line to the <strong>Nested Vectored Interrupt Controller (NVIC)</strong>. The NVIC automatically pushes registers R0-R3, R12, LR, PC, and xPSR onto the Stack (hardware stacking), updates PC to the ISR address, and begins running the handler in under 12 clock cycles!</p>
</div>
<!-- Side-by-Side Architectural Comparison -->
<div class="visual-display-area">
<div class="visual-header">
<span class="visual-title">Architectural Flow: Polling vs. EXTI Interrupt</span>
</div>
<div style="display:grid; grid-template-columns:1fr 1fr; gap:1.25rem;">
<div class="box-sub">
<h4 style="color:var(--amber);">Method A: Polling (Busy-Waiting)</h4>
<div style="font-family:var(--font-mono);font-size:0.78rem;line-height:1.7;color:var(--text-muted);">
                                1. Loop starts<br/>
                                2. Read IDR register<br/>
                                3. If no motion → Wait 100ms<br/>
                                4. Repeat forever...<br/>
<span style="color:var(--red);">Drawback: High latency, 100% CPU waste, misses fast pulses</span>
</div>
</div>
<div class="box-sub">
<h4 style="color:var(--green);">Method B: EXTI Interrupt (Event-Driven)</h4>
<div style="font-family:var(--font-mono);font-size:0.78rem;line-height:1.7;color:var(--text-muted);">
                                1. CPU sleeps or computes other tasks<br/>
                                2. PIR edge hits hardware EXTI0 line<br/>
                                3. NVIC pre-empts CPU in 12 cycles<br/>
                                4. HAL_GPIO_EXTI_Callback() fires<br/>
<span style="color:var(--green);">Advantage: Zero CPU overhead, sub-microsecond response</span>
</div>
</div>
</div>
</div>
<div class="code-container">
<div class="code-toolbar">
<span style="font-family:var(--font-mono);font-size:0.8rem;color:var(--text-dim);">STM32 EXTI ISR Callback Routine</span>
<button class="btn-copy" onclick="copyCode(this)">Copy</button>
</div>
<pre class="code-block"><code>volatile uint8_t g_motion_detected = 0;

// Hardware ISR callback called by EXTI0_IRQHandler:
void HAL_GPIO_EXTI_Callback(uint16_t GPIO_Pin)
{
    if (GPIO_Pin == PIR_PIN)
    {
        // Keep ISR ultra-short! Set a flag and exit:
        g_motion_detected = 1;
    }
}

int main(void)
{
    // ... init HAL, GPIO, NVIC ...
    while (1)
    {
        if (g_motion_detected)
        {
            g_motion_detected = 0; // Clear flag
            handle_motion_event(); // Do heavy work in main loop!
        }
        __WFI(); // Sleep CPU until next interrupt (low power)
    }
}</code></pre>
</div>
<div class="checkpoint-card">
<h4>🧪 Check Your Understanding</h4>
<p class="checkpoint-question">Why must global variables shared between an Interrupt Service Routine (ISR) and the main loop be declared with the <code>volatile</code> keyword?</p>
<div class="checkpoint-options">
<div class="checkpoint-option" onclick="checkCheckpoint(this, true)">A. To prevent compiler optimization from caching the variable in a CPU register instead of re-reading memory</div>
<div class="checkpoint-option" onclick="checkCheckpoint(this, false)">B. To allocate the variable into non-volatile Flash memory</div>
<div class="checkpoint-option" onclick="checkCheckpoint(this, false)">C. To make the variable readable over UART</div>
<div class="checkpoint-option" onclick="checkCheckpoint(this, false)">D. To automatically prevent stack overflow</div>
</div>
<div class="checkpoint-feedback">Correct! Without <code>volatile</code>, the compiler optimizes <code>while(!g_motion_detected)</code> into an infinite register loop, unaware that an ISR can modify it asynchronously.</div>
</div>
<div class="grid-mistake-takeaway">
<div class="box-mistake">
<strong>Common Mistake</strong>
                        Calling <code>HAL_Delay()</code> inside an interrupt callback! Because <code>HAL_Delay()</code> depends on SysTick interrupts, calling it inside an ISR with equal or higher priority causes a permanent system lockup.
                    </div>
<div class="box-takeaway">
<strong>Practical Takeaway</strong>
                        Keep ISRs lean: set a volatile flag, clear the pending interrupt bit, and defer heavy processing, printing, or delays to the main loop!
                    </div>
</div>
</article>

<div class="internal-box">
<h4>⚙️ What is Happening Internally</h4>
<p>UART is an asynchronous protocol (no shared clock wire). Both sides must agree on the bit duration (1 / 115200 = 8.68 µs per bit). When <code>HAL_UART_Transmit()</code> writes byte <code>'M'</code> (ASCII 0x4D = <code>0b01001101</code>) into the Data Register (DR), the hardware serial shift register transmits:
                    1. <strong>Start Bit:</strong> Drives line from idle HIGH to LOW for 1 bit-time.
                    2. <strong>8 Data Bits:</strong> Transmitted LSB-first (1, 0, 1, 1, 0, 0, 1, 0).
                    3. <strong>Stop Bit:</strong> Returns line to idle HIGH for 1 bit-time.</p>
</div>
